To start this review off I'll be talking about it two different ways, first to people who have played the older game and second to the people who have never played WQ at all.
TO THE PEOPLE THAT PLAYED THE OLDER, FREE WOLF QUEST:
It's pretty much exactly just like the original form of the game, there is the single player and the multiplayer; multiplayer gives you the option to join someone else's game or start your own. You can choose from 2 different play style modes: Pack Life, and Raising Pups. Pack life is what it sounds like you're in a map with other players and you basically just hang out/RP or go hunt stuff but Raising Pups allows the server owner to give birth and multiple players can choose a den site and raise the pups together. But just like the single player mode the multiplayer pups game doesn't last very long at all and once you complete bringing the puppies to the "star on the map" the game is over. Only thing new is a new map and customization.
TO THE PEOPLE THAT HAVE NEVER PLAYED:
Look above, you play as a wolf in various settings like forests in Yellowstone to abandoned towns. You can join up with other packs on multiplayer and "live the life as a wolf" but in reality you're going to be doing the same mundane tasks over and over again. Sadly in multiplayer you can only have "phrase chat" which basically only allows you to talk in the chat by clicking on pre-set words the game gives you. If you want to be able to talk openly you'll have to go into a private match, customization is a nice addition to this game you can choose pelt styles, your color, ears styles, radio collars, and even scars, your howl type, and even a limpy leg which will allow you to stand out in the pack. In my personal opinion WQ tends to get pretty boring after 30 mins. to an hour of  playing as there really isn't anything to do...Hopefully now that the game is being treated as such we'll get more content that will help with this.
All in all Wolf Quest is pretty fun, I've been playing for years and I'm really happy to see that it's finally being treated like an offical game, and that it will hopefully keep growing to be a wolf survival game that everyone's been wanting. The price for this game isn't bads at all and I'd honestly say it's pretty worth it if you have friends to play with!

This game in terms of tone and story is a lot like a slightly cutesy Metroid/Dark Souls hybrid. So if that's enough to sell you, you have nothing to worry about, pick it up.
Now for the gameplay that'll decide it for the rest of us. Momodora is a 2d platformer rpg-light. You don't strictly level up, but you do buy items and get more powerful as you go. It's mostly your simple side scrolling metroid-vania style game. You have a melee attack with a 3 hit combo, and a long range you can charge up. Then as you get more items that upgrade your abilities, you can progress to other areas. Again, fairly standard.
What's also bog standard is that inevitable moment where you're not sure where to go anymore and end up going all over the map multiple times. Perhaps this is intentional, as it made enemy attack patterns get easier to predict. But either way that moment isn't fun. This problem has plagued metroidvania games for years, and the only solution made has been to tell you where to go outright. Which naturally feels like being treated like an idiot. Which also detracts from the experience. Momodora doesn't go this route of holding your hand. So unless you're prepared for this moment, it's gonna break the fun you're having.
It's hard to really explain much else. It's a fairly simple game that doesn't break much ground. You can already see the animation and art quality on display. And the music is easily found online. If you only want these two aspects, you've practically already got them now.
I do however, recommend playing through the game to get it all in one package. You aren't exactly missing out by not doing so. But it is still a good game in its own right. Just a slightly forgetable one when you get down to mechanics.

Thief is the lastest game in a franchise that started back in 1998 with Thief: The Dark Project, Thief II: The Metal Age in 2000 and Thief: Deadly Shadows in 2004. Ten years later we now have the lastest game simply named Thief. I can already say I don't like it when titles get so confusing and can make it difficult for consumers to know which one is the first, second and so on. The game industry isn't alone in this sin and often happens in the movie industry, and is something which always makes me shake my head in annoyance.
In any case Thief hasn't forgotten its heritage from the past, and has retrained many of the core mechanics, which I will now get into. The setting is set in a fantasy world which looks like the victorian age with ekstra gadgets, or simply called steampunk. As you probably already guessed Thief is a game about sneaking around and stealing various items without getting caught, or get caught and escape if you can. You have the ability to knock enemies unconcious or kill them with your sword or bow. Speaking of the bow you have many differernt arrows such as water arrows for extinguishing torches, arrows which kill or to create distractions. As the master thief Garret you have the ability to hide really well in shadows as guards roam about. How well you are hidden is indicated by a meter. Fighting with a sword if you get caught is  challenging, and you can easily be killed which certainly only further indicates this is a game intended for people loving stealth games.
You play in a big city which acts like an open world with various zones. You have the ability to break into homes, collect items which give you gold or simply look nice in your own special collection where you reside when you're not doing any dirty deeds.
The story never really caught my attention. Perhaps because I haven't been that much into the franchise, but it never made me care much for it. Instead the side quests had my attention more. Although the gameplay is rather simple it is for the most part fun and challenging due to the many approaches you can have to every mission. Something which personally reminded me somewhat of what makes the Hitman franchise popular.
The graphics are great with plenty of steam, smoke, shadows and lights to make the world come alive. In the end the game becomes rather repetitive, but I still recommend it to people who either like the franchise or stealth games as it fulfills the basics.

"Hey," said one developer one day, "let's make a game with random potion effects."
"Okay," said his friend.
"Hey," said the first developer, "let's make their effects remain known for the run the player is in (I.E. all red potions will have effects identical to the first one) and randomize that each run."
"Okay," said his friend.
"Hey," said the first developer, "let's make a disproportionately large number of negative effects, so drinking a potion is almost always a negative."
"Oka- wait, what?"
"Yeah," said the first developer, "and let's make some of those effects REALLY punishing, like losing 30 health (you start with 100, and have almost no way to heal) or taking 10% more damage for the rest of the run!"
"No, that sounds awful-" began his friend to respond.
"Also, let's make a large number of maximum health boosting items but very few actual HEALING items or buffs, and let's make most of those items ALSO boost maximum health, AND make them all incredibly rare so that players can beat 7+ levels while seeing maybe ONE of them!" said the first developer, eyes gleaming in blissful ignorance.
Before his friend could respond, he continued: "Let's also make the player able to encounter the same boss twice in one run."
"Wouldn't that be boring?" Asked his friend.
"Pah," scoffed the developer, waving his hand dismissively. "Besides, making a construct (list, array, whatever) with the bosses the player has defeated and checking before spawning a boss is way too much effort."
"That would take about two minutes at worst-"
...
This is that game. I have numerous other gripes with it (for example: when minimizing it on windows 7, it's not on the taskbar, so you have to alt+tab to it or task manager it back up), but I feel it is sufficient to summerize my experience with the following:
I've beaten 3+ bosses in one run numerous times. The number of times I've seen a healing buff is... Two.
I've crushed my way without taking any damage through numerous stages... The number of healing items I've seen from non-bosses? Six.
"Well that's just variance!" I hear you say, "Surely you cannot give a negative review over that, when the game handles well, runs well, and is solid in other areas?"
"It's how I feel after having played the game," I reply, "If I have a miserable time playing, then I will leave a negative review. It's nothing to get worked up about."

And I may have been on the Twofold perk (fire two arrows instead of one, which is useless for melee), but I used my melee weapon for basically the entirety of the run anyway. Because +5HP\kill is completely silly given the scarcity of healing items.
I am thus changing my view on the game to: "This game's only challenge is in finding a Crimson Sword. 4/10"

It's impressive in how many ways they miss the mark of what makes for an enjoyable tower defense game. There's little introduction or explanation to gameplay concepts. For example, the 4th level introduces its first weather effect, except it doesn't really tell you when this is happening, or what its effect is. You have to go out of your way to find such simple things.
You know what other amazing feature it possesses? Enemies drop a cube of additional resources upon death, which you are required to hover your mouse over to collect. Maps become several screens large even from the first level, so if you create a few killzones, you have to constantly cycle between them to scavenge your rewards. It's kind of ludicrous in a terrible way, honestly.
I would best describe Defense Technica as a half-hearted mash-up of Defense Grid (in look, feel, and mechanisms [you quickly acquire what is essentially the orbital laser, towers pop out of the ground in little boxes, etc]) and Kingdom Rush (towers are limited, but gain upgrade paths). Maybe somewhere in there is a kernal of a good idea, but it's not easily accessable, and it's hugely unpolished.
Sadly, this is a purchase I regret.

I actually played this game a while back, but saw it up and decided to throw some support to the developers of the game by reviewing it.  This game is very unique.  It does an amazing job of establishing an oppressive, depressing atmosphere that your characters are trying to survive in.  The game also hits you in the feels at times.  Example:
*********   SPOILER  *********
My first playthrough, I'm exploring the destroyed school and am very nervous because I don't realize that it's actually a pretty safe area.  My character is armed with only a kitchen knife that I managed to scrape together out of materials back at the pad.  My characters are all hungry, and I need to find either food or some valuables that I can barter.  I find my way into a room that has no one in it, and a sign marked "steal".  I click on it, and I find some alcohol, tobacco, and a diamond!  So I take it.  Then a man comes running up to me, angry, and punches me.  So I stab him to death.  Another man runs in and says "What are you doing!?"  So I stab him to death.  Walking out of the room, all of the homeless people in the hallway are sobbing, and I realize that I just stole the only possessions of a homeless man, then stabbed him and his friend to death.  I felt really bad.
Pros: Game is fun to play in multiple play throughs with different sets of characters.  The atmosphere is top notch, and attention to detail (like guitar playing skill of different characters) is pretty awesome.  Exploring can really feel tense and scary, and AI has pretty realistic reactions (i.e. complete criminals will shoot you on site, while homeowners will warn you to go away before opening fire).
Cons: Does get repetitive after a while.  The first time exploring maps is interesting and fun, but once you've played them all, there's not much "exploration" fun anymore.
All in all, great game I'd recommend to anyone.  I paid $10 for it a while back on some sail, got 40+ hours out of it (which is more than I can say for many $50 games) and think it's definitely worth your time, if for no other reason how very unique and atmospheric it is.  And love that sketchbook art style!

Although Rack N Ruin doesn’t quite manage to distinguish itself from other games in its genre, it’s a good effort. If looking at the trailer you think you might like it, you’re probably right, just be aware that it’s more a top down shooter with some Zelda-level puzzles than an exploration game.
For the most part the game is very linear, I suspect most people will clear it in between six to eight hours on their first play through. Big arrows on the map tell you where to go, and there are typically only a handful of small side areas to venture into while you’re moving around. Poking around in the various caves and side paths mostly only yields oddball items that pile up in your inventory (I still have no idea what some of them even do), various healing items and souls (currency). There are also some more significant finds like spells and ability upgrades, though they felt a bit sparse to me and don’t really change the game. Notably lacking from RnR compared to the likes of say, Legend of Zelda, are any items/abilities that grant special movement, save for a couple consumable items that grant a speed boost.
Mechanically the only major complaint I have about the game is that it treats the triggers on Xbox controllers as an axis, which it technically is, but this makes it so that when you’re locked on (Holding LT) and try to change primary weapons (RT) the effect is that RT and LT cancel out, you stop locking on briefly and no weapon change happens. Rebinding is supported thankfully, but this seems like a glaring oversight. It’s worth noting that the lock-on and spam fireball style of combat might be too simple for some players to enjoy, and certainly Rack N Ruin rests somewhere on the low end of the challenge spectrum for better or worse. Aside from a soft lock forcing me to redo a dungeon I didn’t experience any real frustration. I did switch from hard to normal mode part way through though, but as far as I can tell that mainly changes the amount of health enemies have. I could very well be wrong there (I didn’t test it much), but it felt better.
The story and characters of the game are...very lackluster. If you’re thinking of buying the game for the writing, I don’t understand you. The theme of being a demon (or whatever) out for the destruction of generic fantasy world is mostly wasted. You’re essentially a Saturday morning cartoon villain trying to start a line of hot topic shirts, and you never feel like the exploder of worlds the story claims you are. Anyway it’s not hard to skip that if you aren’t interested, but it is there, slightly taking away from the game.
I doubt I’d go out of my way to recommend Rack N Ruin to a friend over other games, but I did enjoy it and it is at least competent at what it does.

I'll preface this review by saying that it's highly unlikely that anybody is checking out Depression Quest in total ignorance of the massive storm of internet drama surrounding it, and I'm no exception. Thus, my view of this piece of "interactive (non)fiction" isn't the product of going in completely blind.
I don't have any problems with visual novels, "story games," and "walking simulators" on principle, since they can be great experiences if executed well (insert plug for The Stanley Parable here). However, Depression Quest has some major issues that ultimately cause it to fall flat. The writing is poor on a technical level: it's difficult to get immersed in a text-heavy experience when you have to wrestle with typos, ambiguous pronoun references, and unnecessary alliteration. In addition, instead of being written in a way that evokes certain emotions in the reader, Depression Quest explicitly tells you how you feel every step of the way. This caused me to approach the experience in a disconnected, analytical manner. Finally, perhaps due to my disconnect with the "player character," it was far too simple to determine the proper series of choices to guide the character toward a solution to their depression (protip: don't lay in bed all week).
In conclusion, although I personally can't speak to whether or not Depression Quest is an accurate representation of chronic depression, I couldn't force myself to care about the events in the story due to awkward, weak execution. But hey, if you don't believe me, it's free and only takes about half an hour to go through once, so it's not too hard to form your own opinion.

However, I stuck with it, and began to understand that it's basically a Choose Your Own Adventure novel about depression.  By the end of the "game", (which you can "win" by getting the protagonist out of depression) I was actually fairly impressed, it's very unique and clever.  I work in mental health, and found the game to be a very accurate portrayal of what it's like to suffer from major depressive disorder and social anxiety.  I actually feel like I understand my clients better now.  I can rat off diagnositc criteria from the DSM, but I rarely read a detailed account of what it's like to live depression.  I would encourage anyone interested in learning more about depression to go through this "experience", which is really not a video game in the tradition sense.

It is very, very, very hard to make those decisions, and you will try your damnedest to counter them. I appreciate very much that the game tries so hard to show the internal struggles that jeapardize this kind of life.
Depression Quest is a stunning experience. As an individual currently in therapy, I am very grateful for this reinforcement that if I keep working at it, my story will also have a good ending.

I felt the need to write about this game since when I looked earlier I had close to 150 hours on it. I've been playing this since it's release and have been keeping up with the updates. Over time the game went over drastic changes both via patches and DLC but still stays the same game. In short I most certainly recommend this game but warn people that it will test their patience.
This is a rouge like sci-fi game where when you die you have to start over. While some of the recent updates lets you start at a specific level, for the most part the feature is not as relavent as it was when it was introduced. You start at floor 1 and work your way down to floor 40.  The floors get progressivly larger and filled with more dangerous enemies. All gear is randomly generated through the floors so there is no guarantee of anything. You need food to survive? Tough luck, I've had characters that starved before. Game gives you ton of ammo but no weapons? Yeah that will happen too. A lot of times your overall progress depends on luck while your small term progress (going from room to room, encounter to encounter) depends on your knowledge of the game and your cautious nature.
Crafting is present in the game and it's rather important. Some of the best items are found via crafting. You can craft by either putting random stuff in appropriate medium, follow a recipe you found in the game or elsewhere. My suggestion is to bookmark the wiki page with recipes. it will make your life significantly easier and with less frustration than usual. But beware that even if you do have the proper ingrediants the craft can fail and you lose all your ingrediants upon fail...Yeah
The game started with three classes: Marine, Scout and Engineer, each more or less the same but with different starting attributes. Now with two DLCs, where there is inclusion of several non human classes and entirerly new psi magic system the game expanded to a better complexity.
Game is fully turn based so you can take your time, leave the game in the background etc. So why to play this game? Well success in this game feels legitimate. It's an extremely harsh environment where with a great deal of skill, knowledge and luck you can prevail. If that strikes your fancy this game should give you a great deal of entertainment, but betware that there is plenty of trial and error and just bad luck to happen. I had an enemy destroy my pocket tesseract(larger inventory), this threw my armor out of my inventory, which made the next attack kill me, all during the enemy's turn. Stuff like that will happen. If you have the nerve to look past it and start over you will certainly find a great deal of fun here.

I first began using Steam during the 2015 summer sale. I found a bunch of games for dirt-cheap prices that looked great. One of those games was The Cat Lady. I got it for less than $3 on a whim. The name attracted me, and after seeing it had a lot of positive reviews, I figured it was worth a try. Normally I don't play horror games, as I prefer watching other people play them due to getting scared too easily.
I am not sure what caused me to look past the horror label for this one, but I am so glad that I did. What I got for those measly three dollars was one of the best games I have ever played. For fifteen hours, I was utterly hooked by the tragic story and amazing characters. I suffer from depression, though not to the extent of the protagonist (I have never seriously considered suicide, for instance.) To say it is portrayed well is an understatement. If you suffer from depression, or knows somebody who does, my guess is that you will be stunned at how accurately it is shown here. That played a big role in why I was totally absorbed. However, there are many more positives to be spoken of, as shown below.
I still can't believe how much The Cat Lady affected me. It is a tragic and beautiful tale that is conveyed brilliantly through the characterization, dialogue, and gameplay. I have so much respect for it that I made up for my sin of not buying it at full price by getting the remake of Downfall the moment it came out on Steam, rather than waiting for it to go on a big sale (which I do for most games.) I think I heard that physical copies exist of The Cat Lady, and if so, I will go buy it just to say I have it. That is how much I love it.
10/10. This is a very rare score for me to give. No game is perfect, but The Cat Lady comes so close to it. Its positives vastly outweigh its negatives, and its story and characters are among the best I have ever had the privilege of experiencing. If you believe you can handle the mature tone and the many serious topics it brings up, I urge you to play it. The payoff is completely worth it.

The Cat Lady is a revival of old-school point-and-click adventure games with plenty of puzzles, using items, and talking to different people. However, some main differences: 1- there are no arbitrary puzzles. All the solutions seem to make sense, so you don't wrack your brain trying to just randomly combine any item to hopefully advance the story. And that leads us to our second main difference: the story.
The Cat Lady is a horror game that is all about creepy atmosphere, pop-up scares, and a very depressing tone of the life of a failed suicide victim, Susan Ashworth. She has been blessed (or cursed) with the inability to die, so she goes through a story of personal loathing, and getting through the pointlessness of life in general.
This title can be thought of like a mini-series about themes not often explored in media. It is thoughtful, thought-provoking, and ultimately satisfying to experience.

WolfQuest, along with Shelter 2, is one of the few animal simulation games that I really enjoyed and thought was extremely realistic along with what happens in nature. It was nice graphics for the time it was made (which I think is good in general), the soundtrack is great, the controls work really well, and it was interesting gameplay.
The starts off saying you're a two-year-old Gray Wolf in Yellowstone, that's looking for a mate and den to live in. You hunt about 8 Elk to get 800 exp. and then you go off to wolf territory to get yourself this wolf of your dreams..er, the wolf you created dreams.
After you get your mate (which can take either a short time or a rather long time, one time it took me around 15 minutes because I didn't exactly understand what to do at first, haha), you can either stay on the mountain and explore and hunt more, or you can go to the creek where you will raise your cubs and start a family.
Now, after you get to the creek, you look for a den. After you find the den you desire, you do a few more things to confirm the territory, and then the four puppies are born! If you have enough exp., you can name 'em. Naming the little things is pretty fun after a while, if I say so myself.
After the pups are born and named/left un-named, you begin to take care of them! You have to keep them heathly, well-fed, and..well...alive, for the most part.
Afterwards, you have to bring your puppies on a long and potentially dangerous journey. you have to keep atleast one cub alive until you reach your destination, and then, guess what? Congrats, you've finished the game!
Anyways, sorry if that was a little too long. WolfQuest in my opinion is a 9.5 out of 10, and would be a 10/10 if it had told me I needed an account to get achievments..I spent hours getting all of 'em only to realize my steam account had not picked up on any I'd gotten and I had to completely restart everything. It was kinda annoying.

Actually having to use your senses makes it interesting as does cutting off an elk from the group to get it, raising a family, and things like hunting bears requiring a pack of your own make it more realistic. However, the biggest negative for me were the controls. Using the keyboard feels okay though a few things are pretty unresponsive no matter how you set up things. That said, totally worth it if you like these type of games (or like me and just really like the canine family) then pick it up on sale. The asking price at the monent isn't really worth it.

All Civilization games boil down to a simple fact: Good Concept, ♥♥♥♥♥♥ execution.
CivBE is no exception, and with the amount of bugs in this game, and no incoming bug fixes for this game from the devs, its no wonder why this game is dead in the modding department.
Known Bugs that have killed my games:
1) Having to load mods twice in order to get keep the game from disabling the in-game UI.

--It's true, and this game is even less mod-friendly than it's predecessors, so much so that the only way to make new maps is to import old maps from other civ games,
2) The game, no matter its map size, can only handle (at max) 12 players, CivBE:RT is vanilla capped at 10 civs.
--This goes back to being mod unfriendly, the Codex mods that add new civs to the game disables map packs that the base game RT uses, which effectively neuters your ability to have good replayability due to the fact that you can't add new maps or new civs without having the game lock up over anti-mod security (Oh, did you not think that wasn't in the game?)
3) When using mods the game will lock up domination diplomacies, this prevents you from ending the turn and your only remaining action is to start a new game after you're already 300 turns into this current game. This is a result of the anti-mod security kicking in.
If you don't mind playing a vanilla game, then go ahead and buy this game, but if you want a dynamic grand strategy experience: look elsewhere.

Dungeons of Dredmor is something you get when you take an appropriately brutal Rouge-like game and mix it with not only the offbeat comedy of an RPG a la Earthbound but with geeky shout-outs strewn into a pile on the murky floor. It'll take you roughly 20 hours to finish the game since you'll need a LOT of experience in order to take on the final boss whom is mixed amongst his followers on the final floor of the dungeon (so you can either find him right away or be forced to search every room, in either case it doesn't end well). You'll need to grind to survive, especially on later floors. Thankfully there's an option for those who don't live on level grinding like myself so I can recommend this game to just about anyone who likes a good RPG. In other words, expect to die a lot but not enough to make the game unfun.
If I were to sum up Dungeons of Dredmor to an emotion, it would be that of finding a Monster Zoo in this game: complete surprise followed by fearing for your life.

After finishing the first floor of the mysterious Dungeon of Dredmor, I was hooked.

Oh, and the game is completely unforgiving, and will insult you time and time again with witty remarks from the enemies and smart, well-written descriptions of everything in-game.

TO THOSE THINKING ABOUT PLAYING THIEF WITH AN OLDER CPU!
If youre thinking about running this game on an older-gen quad-core or worse, you might want to give that a second thought. The minimum recommended settings are no joke-Thief seems to be very cpu-intensive.
Im currently running an Intel Q8300 2.5ghz (older-gen quad core) and Asus GTX750ti 2gb, and 6gb ram. I can run just about any current game with playable framerates on high or very high settings.
In Thief ive benchmarked ingame using graphics settings from Low to Very High (with Vsync and SSAA turned off) and the result is the same: average is between 12-14fps, and max is 30ish fps. My cpu is running right around 90-99% on all cores (Thief appears to be well optimized for multicore cpus) but my graphics settings dont affect the framerates at all.-what most would call being cpu-bound.
Im going to recommend the game because ive played through some of it on ps3 and enjoyed it (although i have issues with the story/characters/sound implemention) and update this review to be more thorough once i can upgrade my pc and do a full playthrough.
(Also, if textures are set to 'very high' my VRAM is almost capped out, it hit 1996mb or so out of my 2 gigs. just a heads up for those with a low VRAM card, although i assume the game will reduce the quality of textures on the fly if so.)
(note: I found the first chapter to be barely playable, averaging around 20-25fps, with a lot of mouse/movement lag.)

I love how all these "not recommended" reviews have 20-30-40 hours of playtime on them - you know why? The game is fun to play - SHOCKER. It's what thief was always about, atmosphere, immersion, the thrill of... thieving. Excellent setting, good polish. I expected a little more out of hte character work after seeing what this studio can do w/ Deus Ex 3, but frankly, Thief isn't Mass Effect - it's THIEF, and man is it fun to STEAL things and creep around. The game looks great, Garrett's sense of presence is almost second to none in any other FPS, and it's more appealing than Assassin's creed because it looks and feels like an old Looking Glass game (with a modern day engine under it).
The soundtrack was a bit unobtrusive but I suppose in reality that's fitting, it's Thief after all. I do wish it were a little more open-ended, but honestly, it's just FUN. It's not innovative or groundbreaking, it's not Game of the Year, but it is fun to play, memorable, and it's very accessible/easy to play.
Eidos Montreal makes good stuff; they really have a good style about them. I fear they may have lost a bit of substance in the pursuit of style, but frankly, comparing Thief to Dishonored (because everyone does) is a little apples to oranges - Dishonored is extremely out in left field with whimsical supernatural stuff and cartoony styling - Thief is very dark and more grippingly tense, where Dishonored's tension is impossible to take very seriously because it's so cartoony.
Thief is a nice painting; it's not for everyone. It's definitely a piece of fine art though.

I actually played this game a while back, but saw it up and decided to throw some support to the developers of the game by reviewing it.  This game is very unique.  It does an amazing job of establishing an oppressive, depressing atmosphere that your characters are trying to survive in.  The game also hits you in the feels at times.  Example:
*********   SPOILER  *********
My first playthrough, I'm exploring the destroyed school and am very nervous because I don't realize that it's actually a pretty safe area.  My character is armed with only a kitchen knife that I managed to scrape together out of materials back at the pad.  My characters are all hungry, and I need to find either food or some valuables that I can barter.  I find my way into a room that has no one in it, and a sign marked "steal".  I click on it, and I find some alcohol, tobacco, and a diamond!  So I take it.  Then a man comes running up to me, angry, and punches me.  So I stab him to death.  Another man runs in and says "What are you doing!?"  So I stab him to death.  Walking out of the room, all of the homeless people in the hallway are sobbing, and I realize that I just stole the only possessions of a homeless man, then stabbed him and his friend to death.  I felt really bad.
Pros: Game is fun to play in multiple play throughs with different sets of characters.  The atmosphere is top notch, and attention to detail (like guitar playing skill of different characters) is pretty awesome.  Exploring can really feel tense and scary, and AI has pretty realistic reactions (i.e. complete criminals will shoot you on site, while homeowners will warn you to go away before opening fire).
Cons: Does get repetitive after a while.  The first time exploring maps is interesting and fun, but once you've played them all, there's not much "exploration" fun anymore.
All in all, great game I'd recommend to anyone.  I paid $10 for it a while back on some sail, got 40+ hours out of it (which is more than I can say for many $50 games) and think it's definitely worth your time, if for no other reason how very unique and atmospheric it is.  And love that sketchbook art style!

As someone who has been diagnosed with clinical depression at the age of 17 (now 22), as well as living with a diagnosed manic depressive older brother and formerly suicidal sister, I felt like this game, Depression Quest, could help me gain stability in parts of my life where I lack.
As it turns out, it is nothing short of insulting. Depression Quest takes the impossible  weight and drain of simply feeling /bad/, and reduces it to a rather whiney, irritating and self-absorbed narrative. It /then/ takes the raging emotional battles and incredible fears cloud rational thought and displays them as so many single-line responses. I KNOW WHAT TO DO. I KNOW A SEEING THERAPIST IS THE CORRECT CHOICE. I KNOW LYING BACK IN BED IS THE WRONG CHOICE. It's not about what you should do, it's about how in the heck to conquor all that negativity and emotional drag to get anywhere. It's about how to consciously break those cycles of self-hating thoughts and stop those feelings before they happen. Bear in mind these are only my objections to the depiction of depression as a disorder.
Depression Quest as a game? I have literally read popup books that were more interactive, and I use the term correctly. The 1996 classic Wishbone and the Amazing Odyssey was 100 times the game this one could ever hope to be, and it had a neato dog. I tried to think of games that came close to being as frustrating to play, aside from personally offensive, and I counted to None! None games! Ah ah aaaahhh!

PROS:

•	Floating in the air while walking over mountains.
•	Items can be duplicated by replacing one item for another inside chests (aka) Berries can become an entire set of   Leather armor per EACH berry.

One of the most "finished" ubisoft titles of 2014, Far Cry 4 continues the franchise in the himalayan mountains in the war-torn region known as Kyrat where Ajay Ghale returns to his parents home to spread his mothers ashes. Upon arriving he is stopped by the incredibly flamboyant Pagan Min and his army. Ajay soon has a heshen bad removed from his head to be in Pagan Pins fortress, kindly offered a serving of Crab Rangoon, but Ajay's guest isn't so lucky and is taken away. Shortly after you're asked to stay put, but being held by somebody who you're not sure if your♥♥♥♥♥♥is safe it might be the best time to be smuggled out by the locals.
Fun characters, impressive visuals, some very cool weapons once you finish the game, it seems like all positives in this exceptionally fun game. Sadly the game becomes repetetive and boring after about the 75% campaign completion mark. This was one of my gripes for Far Cry 3, but because the world was so well done with some much to do you don't ever notice it in Far Cry 4, until the home stretch is in sight. I will however mention the music in the final mission was fantastic.
It uses the same engine as Far Cry 3, you may not tell the difference until you play it. With this said it is very different and more refined than Far Cry 3, however I would be unforgiving if Ubisoft were to do the same with Far Cry 5. There's a 'Blood Dragon' spinoff in the works for Far Cry 4 which I'm looking forward to and some DLC which I plan on getting.
Far Cry 4 holds an interesting story in an interesting location, but there's much more pointlessness to the story because in any ending the story doesn't change and you can just kill everybody who drives the story after it's complete. I confess, I would have loved to be able to visit the mountains and prison again on demand, but it seems this will only happen via DLC and paying more money. So in a vast open world experience in a modified version of Far Cry 3's engine we reep the same results regardless of our choices and being limited to your location even once you finish the game. Open world only implies you can go where you want when you want, with risk of being killed by the locals or wildlife. Unfortunately Ubisoft have locked you to the confines of areas you've unlocked and anything past that you'll see "you're leaving the mission zone", "this is a dangerous area, turn back" ect and because of these small problems as well as altitude limitations the gameplay feels as though Ubisoft have cheaped out on the expansiveness of this game. You shouldn't be surprised though, every Ubisoft title comes with these problems.
Other problems include compatibility and optimization when using higher graphical settings and presets. Again there's another ongoing problem with Ubisoft and SLI, but let's not go there again. It's extremely demanding for what it is due to bad optimization, as if Ubisoft don't really care for us PC gamers, but again this is nothing new. Once you've found the best configuration for your machine, you'll be on your way. I do believe this game is a great benchmarking tool, I've recieved up to 70% GPU usage on both graphics cards once the driver was modified for SLI and identified a shortage of power delivery to be fixed this week.

This game is... a peculiar case. The graphics are good enough for what they're supposed to do and the gameplay is easy enough to understand even without playing the tutorial. For this reason I recommend getting the Gold Edition from the get go as it ups the number of available classes to ten. It also adds the gameplay element of psionics, which is the magic-version of this game.
What however is probably the biggest critique I have for this game is the absurd ability of the RNG to absolutely shaft you. I had a perfectly good run once with plenty of ammo and weapons, but no food drops whatsoever, which doomed my run to end with starvation, which was actually pretty sad to watch given how it's not instant, but procedual death as your character becomes weaker until suffering the so called Stat-death or simply being overwhelmed by enemies because of the ton of debuffs that gets heaped onto you.
Nonetheless, if you're into Roguelikes and you want one settled in a Sci-Fi setting then I can wholeheartedly recommend this game.

This game is about depression, suicide, sociopathy and death.  Therefore, it is not for everyone.  However, if you're in the mood for a scary yet contemplative choice-based story that sensitively and deftly deals with one or more of the above issues, then by all means, have at!
There is one caveat: you MUSt be able to put up with clunky adventure game mechanics and some painfully bad voice-acting.  I was able to, but if those are absolute deal-breakers for you, give this one a pass.

The bloody mess of Susan Ashworth's world is crafted from depression. The Cat Lady deals with ideas about life in a direct fashion, and refuses to beat around the bush when it questions what it means to be alive. As I followed along with the story, which is told through an animated, interactive film, the sometimes messy dialogue [and voice acting] seemed to fade away. The writing is simply stunning. Though there are moments that I felt I had seen coming, there are far more scenarios where I couldn't have possibly thought of what happened. Remigiusz Michalski snuck some very subtle humour in the way certain characters act, and when it worked, it really worked.
Praise aside, the game is not without its flaws. The controls feel clunky at times, as you browse the game's interface (and that's all you do in this game, aside from walk and listen). On top of that, the art style, though gorgeous, sometimes popped so that a bike would look like a wall, for an instance. And, as previously mentioned, the voice acting suffers from certain characters being ridiculously overreacted.
That being said, the game is $10 ($8 on sale). I more than got my moneys worth for the story told here, and would gladly play it again to make different choices when the times came.

Overall Conclusion first for reader's benefit:
This game is for story seekers into dark and twisted themes who don't mind a slow pace.
It took me a bit to get past the low-res graphics, but I found that the creepy, gestural animations more than made up for that.  Along with the well-timed soundtrack, the whole package came together to make for a haunting experience.
I would recommend The Cat Lady for anyone who is into dark, story-driven games.  The narrative was compelling enough to get me through the slow parts and left me wanting more after the high points.  The voice acting, though oddly inconsistent in quality, works really well with the atmosphere.  The whole game kinda feels a bit hobbled together in a way that actually adds to the twisted nature of the story.  There are a few clever puzzles sprinkled throughout, but they are not an integral part of the game and in some cases slow the pace to a frustrating degree.
Scares were scared, cringes were cringed, and laughs were laughed.  I had a good time with this one.

WolfQuest is a wildlife simulation game developed by the Minnesota Zoo and Eduweb. The game's main purpose is to help players understand wolves and the roles they play in nature by playing a gray wolf themselves. You to learn about wolf ecology by living the life of a wild wolf in Yellowstone National Park and is a family-friendly, fun game for people of all ages.

This is a great game once you get used to all the stuff that isn't as great. I mean you don't have to buy this game for the story and it isn't like the previous thief's in any way. The flat characters and map are the biggest flaws of this game but the stealth gameplay makes it a really enjoyable experience.

The old Thief games were the story of a thief just trying to survive in a dog-eat-dog world. Garret, in those games, was snarky and arrogant, yet realistic in his expectations and aspirations, and surrounded by characters that made sense.
Thief 2014, on the other hand, loses all of the above, choosing instead to uplift Garret into something much more, connected to a seemingly dead spirit of a woman and adding all sorts of mumbo-jumbo that has no place in the old games. The story, therefore, feels fragmented, annoying and unnecessary.
But heck, what if we don't care for the story, but just want some good stealthy gameplay, sneaking around and so on?
Sad to say, but that's not here either. In order for a game to have a workable stealth -system, it needs to have reliable and credible enemies to sneak around and avoid. It was within my first 30 minutes with Thief 2014 that I saw a guard get stuck on a slight incline, his feet shuffling and jerking endlessly while his torso and head would not move. He was standing in the only passage through the early area, so my options were to either knock him out (which is discouraged by the theme of the game) or reload a save. Similiar AI glitches happened on numerous occasions during my 6 or 7 hours with the game, after which I got sick and quit.
Audio, too, fails to impress in any way. Voice actors are sub-par (oh, and several times faces will not animate while characters speak, for some reason) and the music has, so far, been forgettable.
As a final note: this game required me to do quite a bit of work before I could play. I suffered from a glitch in which the game would change the texture quality on the fly, between high and low, every 5 seconds or so. This required me to exit the game and start the separate configuration utility and disable automatic texture quality (this setting is not available in-game). Additionally the game has HORRIBLE mouse acceleration issues, with the camera lurching around beyond control, always feeling a bit slow and lazy. This issue required me to do some googling and disable the mouse acceleration in a config -file in the game's installation folder. Again, no in-game setting allowed me to adjust or change this in any way.
All said, I doubt I'll ever finish Thief 2014, and I don't recommend it to anyone. For a VERY similiar game with much more enjoyable gameplay, try Dishonored instead.

This game made me question who I am as a person. Aside from Spec Ops: The Line, I can't think of many games that had the power to do that.
This game is essentially the polar opposite of the traditional FPS power fantasy. It forces you into the perspectives of bystanders, civilians just trying to survive in a combat zone. If the characters under your control die, there is no "respawn." They DIE, because you, the player, screwed up.
Is this game fun? No, but that's ok, because it's not trying to be. War is hell, after all. BUT, it is engaging as hell. You find yourself wanting to progress through it just to see what scenarios the game puts you in next. If you're desperate, are you willing to steal things, kill innocent  people, for cans of food, a bag of sugar, a drop of water?
In essence, so long as you go into this game looking not for fun, but an experience that makes you question things (most of all, yourself as a person), you will come out of it satisfied.

Rack N Ruin is a quite and surprisingly good game that has some problems which prevents this game from being one of better this year I’ve played and probably one of my favourites this year. Gameplay is fun, because you will kill a lot of different monsters, people and bosses with your fire (your first skill) as you progress on your quest to conquer the world.

A non-biased quick look @ the game:
A very competent top-down RPG style arcade adventure with a great art style. Rack N Ruin is a fusion of a top-down action adventure game and a classic arcade shooter. Take control of Rack, a maniacal demon wizard with a gleeful appetite for destruction, and embark on a grand adventure across a world filled with magic and wonder. Then transform the once enchanting world into a hellish nightmare. As the world falls deeper into darkness, Rack's power will grow, and the champions of good will rise to face him.
Engage the legions of good in fast hectic combat that gives Rack N Ruin a special action oriented twist unique to the genre. Explore a vast open world filled with treachery and secrets at every turn. Then dive into delicately crafted dungeons, each with distinctive themes and foes to conquer. The entire world of Rack N Ruin is lovingly hand-crafted, and uniquely laid out. Every bit of the game is hand-painted in detailed high definition.
Story: Sitting atop his throne, the dark lord Ruin rules over much of the known universe. His demon lords march outward into the cosmos subjugating planets for Ruin's ever growing demonic empire. One such creature is Rack, a small, sharp tongued, and diminutive demon lord. Rack's talent for destruction and conquest is unmatched amongst Ruin's legions. However, Rack has one issue that infuriates his dark master. He doesn't subjugate, or enslave any world he is sent to conquer. He just blows the planet up, and moves on. Planets turned into asteroid belts make poor slaves, so Ruin is giving Rack one last chance to conquer a world without jump starting the apocalypse, or be cast into the eternal abyss. Will Rack obey his master? Absolutely not!
Features: Burn through hordes of foes with 4 core elemental weapons.
Unleash death with an array of 24 spells, items, and contraptions.
Interactive items that allow the player to create unique item interactions and combos based on the elemental weapon type.
Weave through complex bullet patterns while smiting titanic bosses and over 30 unique enemies.
Explore an enchanted benevolent world, and then transform it into a nightmarish image of its former self.
Ransack castles, pillage dungeons, escape prisons, navigate gloomy caves, and awaken ancient evils.
Meet a charming cast of townsfolk, and collect their souls.
Upgrade your weapons by selling the souls of innocents to an ancient wizard.
Unravel devious puzzles, and scour the land for over 100 secrets.
Play on Windows, Mac, and Linux completely DRM free like the Gods and Demons meant PC gaming to be.
Customize your destruction with fully remappable controls for Keyboards, Mice, and Gamepads.
And, of course, destroy the world. - Highly Recommended!

While the game has some attributes that warrant interest, the game is ultimately hampered by a clunky UI that feels like a bad console port. Between the requirement to start over from the beginning of a level if you make a small mistake (aiming for a perfect game), the lack of ease with which towers are placed and upgraded, the absence of a game save feature (it autosaves, but you can't restart from a save, you have to always restart from the beginning so I'm not sure what value "autosave" has except to save your progress between levels.) and much else... Ultimately this game comes across as the scrawney adopted younger sibling to Defense Grid-- you feel absolutely no loyalty to it, and it as it cannot surpass it's older sibling you wonder (no matter how bad a person you think this might make you) if you might be able to return it from whence it came.

Big pile of meh. It tries too hard to copy Defense Grid, but without the story, or interesting AI voice, and without a decent difficulty too. Boy does Defense Technica's difficulty spike like crazy, with Defense Grid, there was checkpoints and you could hit backspace to go back to the last checkpoint in case you made tower placements mistakes, it was also a bit more forgiving in terms of tower effectiveness versus vertain enemies. With Technica? You're restarting the map, and you will be doing that, often.
Treat this more like a Roguelike Tower Defense, because it's highly unlikely you'll finish a level on the first attempt, it's about experimenting with different placements and towers and upgrades until you get a combination that works. You NEED the best tower for each kind of enemy, because other turrets will barely scratch them.
Personally I don't have the patience to do the same level a dozen times just to defeat it for the first time. A hard mode or custom game mode maybe, but not my first playthrough.

For people wanting a 'game' as such this will not entertain you. The object of this 'game' is not entertainment but to communicate intimately a specific condition and inform sufferers and non-sufferers alike of the progression and range of impacts Depression has on a person's life.
Controversy around the author aside - myself being someone suffering from depression - I found this game shockingly accurate to the point of slightly haunting.
This interactive narrative illustrates in such graphic detail the emotions, progression and choices available to someone suffering this debilitating condition.
The internet inhabitants of non-sufferers and broader society through just simply not having the 'minds eye' to comprehend what this FEELS like and as a result may call depressed people wimps, weak or someone that needs to harden (the F) up. Depression Quest is unique as it seeks to bridge that gap through an intimate experience and inform everyone that 'plays' this 'game'.
Depending on the wisdom of your 'life choices' in this game - you either find life getting easier and more options available to control your situation or you find that things get progressively worse.
The interesting thing about this that it is almost NOT a simulation. Though I am one person I found the emotions, situations, relationships and choices available so intimately real that much of the 'middle game' brought me to tears.
In real life I'm actually moving the mid to late game on the positive arc so this has been a shockingly confronting but largely inspirational experience and as a result booked a consult with a psychologist today.
Though basic in its design it made for an amazing experience - thoroughly well thought out.
I highly recommend this to everyone however the warning at the start is appreciated. Anyone feeling suicidal should NOT play this and seek help first. For those on uneven ground - this WILL bring things to the surface so be warned if you are not strong enough to face your demons. For everyone else - enjoy the glimpse.

It also helps show what it's like for someone who is depressed.

I have severe chronic depression/anxiety.  Suicidal, attempts, diagnosed and everything.
Upon opening Depression Quest, I began crying almost immediately, and throughout the rest of it.  There's a certain quality to this game -- not quite catharsis (for me), but something immense at reading the constant turmoil and fragility and self-hatred and desperate need to eradicate existence put into words.  Maybe it's the acknowledgement or even validation of all of this.
It means so much to read a simulated experience that essentially captures my life and to know that the makers share/understand my depression -- particularly with how depression robs me of the choice to take care of myself or feed myself or clean, much less step out the door for classes.
My depression outright creates an inability to function, and to see that laid out in the inaccessible options only meaningfully illustrates how frustration with myself builds, pinpointing part of the origin of the mantra of "crazy ♥♥♥♥ing ♥♥♥♥♥ ♥♥♥♥ up" I can't stop thinking, because my depression underlies and characterizes and saturates everything about and within me.
Depression Quest understands how even though I do have resources and wonderful people in my life, I can't miraculously stop being depressed and how that makes me hate myself more for always ♥♥♥♥ing failing them.
What's more, playing this makes me want to tell the character they matter and they are worth taking care of themselves -- things I can't tell myself, because that's how it is -- it's easier to offer care and affirmation than to do so for myself when all I can believe is that I'm not worth care.
As for the gameplay, I've seen and played many games/visual novels like this, including here on Steam, and thoroughly appreciated them.  Frankly, the criticism of it is ableist, misogynistic ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, garnered particularly due to the visibility of this release.
Depression Quest is well-written, understanding, and important.  Zoe Quinn has made something beautiful and even healing.

Sword of the Stars!
There are some things in gaming that will just never, ever get old, going deeper and deeper into a dungeon while looting everything there possibly is to loot being one of them.  You can't miss with this basic premise, but you can certainly sweeten the pot.  Making the loot drool worthy is a complicated exercise in tug-of-war: too strong, and you'll never find improvments, not enough and you have your players getting bored.  SotS deftly walks this tightrope with a deep crafting system and the depth of the game itself.
Let me explain what I mean by that a little more:  The game is pretty difficult (if you're playing correctly :^)) but there are A LOT of cool things to find that can be a big help.  Whether it's a electronic chip that boosts your computer skill to max level, or a sick, sick piece of armor, every cool find is made cooler by the hope of getting deeper into your run they represent.
You start the game having to choose a difficulty (at least hard for the most fun) and a class.  The differences in the classes are refreshingly pronounced and greatly influence how the game plays out.  The Commando has a big advantage with starting equipment and stats, but doesn't grow as fast as the Scout (whom will get one or two shotted on the first few floors of the Pit).
Combat is fluid and lovely. The game is actually turn based so standing still gives you time to size up situations and make a decision.  Everything takes place on a grid.  The game has a magic ability to shoot at the square you want even when you misclick.  Seriously, it's uncanny.
As with most roguelikes, your goal is to get as far as you can.  I think you can actually beat this game but it's harder than a mother ♥♥♥♥er.  Replay value is built in with the roguelike genre, but The Pit particularly so since the game changes even more than normal from run to run and class to class.

Sword of the Stars: The Pit offers countless hours of exciting and challenging gameplay! It has everything you want in a roguelike RPG: randomised levels, tense exploration, survival, character progression, crafting, traps, foraging, a cool sci-fi environment, and hundreds of enemies, items, recipes, and weapons!
The Pit throws your chosen character into a deadly underground alien facility in search of a cure for a deadly plague wreaking havoc across your world. I spotted Sword of the Stars: The Pit listed as a flash sale on Steam for 75% off of the normal price of $9.99 for a low down price of $2.49. Curse you Valve and your ridiculous summer sales! You managed to suck quite a few bucks out of my debit card on games I may or may not ever get around to and Sword of the Stars seemed to be one of them. Intrigued on trying a top down turn based RPG rogue game this time I decided to try out The Pit and see what is up.
The plot of The Pit, as simple as it is, is pretty straightforward. The Zombie Apocalypse or something close to it is occurring on some remote planet and some magical mcguffin that could end it all might be in some place referred to as unoriginality as… The Pit. So you start up a game as a Marine, Engineer, or Scout (actually a pilot, but we called her the scout class anyway!). Ready. Set. Procedurally generated dungeon crawl!
And off I went with a Marine, hacking and shooting my way through a seemingly unending supply of rodents and bats. Then a few robots, a couple aliens, all the while watching my health and food bars slowly drain away. And then refill them up with heal kits or rations I brought along then watch them drain away again. Then fill up health from leveling up then watch it drain away again. And then finally, I died. It wasn’t some great last stand or some frightful fleeing for my life, just eventually ran out of health and died. Ho Hum.
And then I went again with an engineer. There’s lots of… things scattered randomly around in the rooms and they can be opened with different skills. The engineer is the best at this but he is horribly outgunned and unless you get lucky with one of these loot drops eventually he’s going to die soon to. And then I tried the scout expecting a more sneaky fast person who can run past everything. Nope. The scout is just like the Marine except she’s better at using crappier weapons. *sigh* Speaking of weapons the promo page on Steam boats of “Over 50 weapons and armors with a variety of special effects including flamethrowers, rocket launchers, plasma cannons and powered Brawler armor!” but all I found in my play-throughs were a dinky sword, a piece of ‘stealth’ armor, and a rifle. Meh. I’m sure there’s better stuff way deep down but I never made it and started getting bored quickly.
And I started to try to figure exactly why this game is so hum drum boring. At first glance there appears to be some very some good ideas. A complex and important skill system. Lots of loot, a variety of different looking enemies, a randomly generated experience each time you go. But each level looks depressingly bland, the enemies all act boringly stupid, and I was yet to find any awesome loot to scratch at that progressing itch. Outside of having slightly higher chance of succeeding at unlocking things and getting a free heal, leveling up feels downright pointless. I didn’t feel exceptionally stronger at level 5 as I did at level 1. Worse is I felt an incessant need to scour each level and attempt to open every box, fix every console, and unlock every door in hopes of collecting every precious drop of exp I could get my hands on. All in a false hope it would make me strong enough to press on but instead it just wasted my time. There even appears to be a complicated intricate crafting system but I could only scratch the surface of it while trying in vain to get deeper into THE PIT.
After seeing a rogue-like game done so well, The Pit feels uninspired. Each time you go into a level you pretty much stand in one spot fighting enemies, waiting for them all to rush at you one at a time. Walk around the level clearing up what’s left and then go deeper. If you are unlucky you’ll run into a high level mob earlier than you should and get crippled. Or worse, you’ll run into a trap and want to rage quit. I wouldn’t exactly call the game unforgivingly difficult, more of just cheaply difficult. Open up a door and stand face to face with a giant machine gun toting mech that fills you with bullets, or worse, the only way to progress is to pass through a door trap. Unlike floor traps which you have a chance of detecting and deactivating, I found no way to deactivate door traps. The most sadistic of all destroys a random item from your inventory. And if it decides to destroy one of your weapons or your ammo, well you might as well just quit now and start anew.
In stills the graphics look decent for the sprite style often common of indie games but in action it feels incredibly blocky. It feels exactly like what it is, token pieces moving around a large square grid system. And for turn based combat it is an incredibly uninspired repetition of: point, click, kill. Target an enemy, shoot ‘em with a gun or hack at them with a melee weapon. Or after you’ve gotten really deep and your melee weapon was destroyed and you’re out of ammo, hit them with your fists until they kill you. I especially hate the limitations placed on combat with only 2 moves and performing a combat action ends your turn. The game could have really taken a page from other turn based RPGs with a more intricate action point system that actually felt like I was doing more than just standing in one place and clicking. There also are no stances, cover to hide behind, you cannot move after attacking, jump, sprint, anything. The light scout has no real speed bonus nor does the heavy marine have any speed penalty. Its just simple and dull and really needs a lot of work.
In the end, even though the game cost me less than what I’d spend for lunch, I wouldn’t recommend it. There is a lot of potential here for a nice intricate game but the combat system is just so bloody boring and uninspired.
Final Score:
Graphics: 4/10
Game Play: 2/10
Music / Ambiance: 3/10
Story: 4/10
Value: 8/10
Overall: 4.2/10

(In the interests of full disclosure, this review is based on the Gold Edition - which should be considered the best option available).
It's nethack, but not your father or your mother's nethack. This is tried and tested "Get in from the frozen exterior of a planet into a secret underground base that extends downwards further than any greedy dwarf dared dig." model, but brought up to date with a solid lick of paint, high resolution graphics, and a clear and consistent approach to enemies, objects and overall design.
The story, what there is, is much the norm for such roguelikes, it's merely the pretext for getting you to the front of the dungeon, the reality is that this is a true roguelike, you go as far as you can, aiming to reach the bottom of the pit, or die messily along the way. You only have one life, no do-overs. Unlike a lot of "modern" nethacks, this one goes back to roll style checks for skill tests, and gives an extensive list of possible talents to sculpt and model your character. The Gold edition additionally features several extra classes, giving you a respectable pool of choices, both human and nonhuman in nature (playing as an alien ranger is -awesome- ).
Scattered throughout each randomly generated floor is a variety of traps, both tile and door based, locked chests and rooms, and various devices that may help or hinder your ability to progress. Ranging from defunct cookers that need repairing to prepare a simple blandwich (Don't ask what's in one, really, you don't want to know..), to advanced and somewhat dotty security computers that may just as readily electrocute you as deactivate the several heavily armed and armoured droids patrolling the area.
The game operates functionally as a turn based game, with each discrete action you take allowing the AI the opportunity to respond (hint - if the game pauses briefly between moves, there's something nearby, and it's almost certainly unfriendly). You take an action, the AI takes an action, repeat until either you or whatever the AI sent your way has collapsed in a pool of it's own fluids.
When dealing with multiple foes, target selection becomes important, you can if you feel confident let the computer handle targetting and it does a sensible enough job, but on occasion you'll want to step in yourself to ensure that the scariest thing dies first. Combat employs a wide variety of melee and projectile weapons, and in keeping with the future sci-fi aesthetic, these can be pretty fantastical, including laser, plasma and other interesting effects.
With the addition of extra characters, Mind Games and all the extra ways to die, The Pit has become highly complex, very well supported, and a deep and involving creature, there's now many ways to die, many ways to survive, and many accomodations for various playstyles. This is -not- however, baby's first nethack. You will want to start with say, Dungeons of Dredmor, because this one will kill you in good order if you're not at least familiar with the concept of being pragmatic and cautious and making efficient use of your time. Hunger can ruin your life far easier than you might expect.
In such games, death can come in many ways, here is no exception. Simply being impaled is for novices, try being irradiated, choked by a mimic pretending to be a med station, diseased by an out of control experiment, or being melted in acid. It is important to note that in these games - Death is an opportunity to learn, not a signal of failure. Go in expecting to die a lot, and the ultimate victory will be that much sweeter.
This game is not for the faint of heart, but it is well worth the effort, and for an intermediate roguelike player, someone who's cut their teeth on more forgiving entries to the genre (Dungeons of Dredmor is a great place to start), this is the logical progression. Welcome to The Pit. Enjoy your stay.

This game is for story seekers into dark and twisted themes who don't mind a slow pace.
It took me a bit to get past the low-res graphics, but I found that the creepy, gestural animations more than made up for that.  Along with the well-timed soundtrack, the whole package came together to make for a haunting experience.
I would recommend The Cat Lady for anyone who is into dark, story-driven games.  The narrative was compelling enough to get me through the slow parts and left me wanting more after the high points.  The voice acting, though oddly inconsistent in quality, works really well with the atmosphere.  The whole game kinda feels a bit hobbled together in a way that actually adds to the twisted nature of the story.  There are a few clever puzzles sprinkled throughout, but they are not an integral part of the game and in some cases slow the pace to a frustrating degree.
Scares were scared, cringes were cringed, and laughs were laughed.  I had a good time with this one.

CONS

As someone who's never played Thief I was interested in trying out the newest game in the series. To put it simply, Thief 4 is a fun game with some big issues.
Story - You are Garrett, Master Thief. During the tutorial your friend goes missing and you must rescue her while robbing the city blind. Overall the story's pretty generic so there's not much to talk about. It serves its purpose although the characters are quite bland and unmemorable (the only ones I liked are your fence Basso, and Garrett himself).
Gameplay - The gameplay is a mix of stealth, action and stealing. You'll be sent on various missions and have to use your skills to complete them. I liked these missions. There were various ways to get through them, the environments are diverse and Garrett has a lot of tools are his disposal. Arrows in particular are a big focus and can be used to light fires, distract guards and so much more. You can buy these with gold you earn from stealing loot (which includes both regular items and special collectibles) and there's loot EVERYWHERE. It really feels like you're a Master Thief who's robbing the city of everything it owns.
Unfortunately being a thief has its dangers and if you get seen then you're pretty much screwed. Garrett can only take a few hits and dying will send you back to your last save (although you CAN sneak behind guards and knock them out first). This brings me to another negative which is the hub city itself. Things are put VERY far apart and often have several loading screens in the way, which turns city exploration into a huge drag as you have to find the particular gate/window that gets you to the next area. Overall the missions are fun but city exploration is sluggish and can slow down the experience.
Graphics - Here we go... Thief 4 looks great and there's LOTS of graphical options too. However it's horribly optimized and ran poorly on my computer. I did research and it's a common issue so keep that in mind if you get the game.
Music - Nothing much to say here. Pretty generic but serves its purpose.
Difficulty & Replayability - I played through Thief on Normal and found it pretty easy, that being said there's a great amount of customization with the difficulty and you can tailor the experience to your personal tastes. This increases the replayability but I don't see myself playing through this game again. There are a lot of collectibles if you'd like to though.
Final Verdict - Thief 4 is a fun game with some big issues. If you can get past the poor optimization, generic story and sluggish exploration then you'll find an enjoyable game. I would recommened it, but only when it goes on sale.

On the surface, This War of Mine is a survival strategy/simulation game. You rebuild and improve an abandoned house in the daytime, and at night you scavenge for supplies. The mechanics are simple – certain supplies are required for certain improvements. You need wood to build a bed, weapon parts to build a saw, water and meat to cook, and bait to set traps. At night, you sneak around different areas in varying states of destruction – a field hospital set up in the ruins of an old one, a flophouse for the lowest vagrants, the home of an old husband and wife just trying to hold on – sneaking around, avoiding conflict, and grabbing as many supplies as you can carry. The controls are simple. It’s quite literally point and click.
The gameplay, however, is almost unimportant, except that it forces you to make choices, hard, brutal choices. Food is always scarce, and when I played through the game, my characters were always starving. I saw them complaining every day about their empty stomachs. I could either let my characters starve, or rob an old couple blind. I took everything from them as they watched, helpless, begging for me to leave them something. It put a knot in the pit of my stomach. When I picked the game up again, my characters were horrified at what they had done.
The most chilling moment was when I had a character kill a man. It was the first time I encountered another person, and I didn’t know how they would react. I didn’t want to lose, didn’t want my character to die. So before the vagrant I ran into could do anything, I beat him to death with a shovel. In the next room, there were even more vagrants who all simply ignored me. When I returned home, the character who killed the vagrant was depressed. She was wracked with guilt.
This is the success of This War of Mine. It puts you into the mind of the starving, the dispossessed and the desperate. It shows you that survival is not easy, that the truest victims of war are not fallen soldiers but the innocents left behind. This War of Mine isn’t just a reaction to the endless stream of war-glorifying shooters, it is a response to all war and anti-war art that focuses on combatants as the sole recipients of horror. Wilfred Owen, Kurt Vonnegut, Tim O’Brien, all hallowed names in the annals of war literature and criticism. Yet they all focused on the burdens borne by the soldiers and overlooked, as many do, the civilians stuck in the boot-churned mud. This War of Mine challenges literature’s view on war and in doing so become literature itself. It is so rare that games become art, but the sickening feeling in my stomach every time I see one virtual character mourn another tells me that this one is, in fact, a work of art. e

I'm recommending this game despite not intending to finish it, because I think it's a good game - I just don't personally like it enough to get through it.
The game has puzzles, and essentially is one big puzzle as you figure out how to get around the map and unlock new areas. The problem for me is, I just don't seem to have the kind of brain that can figure these things out. My progress in the game, after about 5 hours, has been stunted by my total inability to figure out one of the puzzles without looking up a guide or asking for help on the forums. For some players, that's a great challenge and they'll enjoy it and the subsequent "♥♥♥♥ yeah" moment as they finally get the solution. I just simply don't have the patience for it, it's a personal failing and not the game's fault.
My main criticisms that I think the game DOES fail on however, are the map and enemy respawns/persistence. The in game map is not terribly useful, and doesn't show exactly where you are, only which area you are in, and there is no mini-map which means you might get lost fairly often. Enemy respawns can make getting around a bit tedious as going through areas a dozen times (lots of backtracking in the game) means you will have to clear out the same enemies over and over, you can dodge past them easily enough but it's a nuisance. There also seems to be a lack of persistance with the things you do, puzzles will unsolve themselves as you progress, making you do them again if you backtrack, saves don't seem to save you where you are, rather at a nearby "checkpoint", and loading can also see puzzles reset. It makes it feel like what you're doing is pretty futile.
My favourite thing about the game is the interactions you have with the other characters in the world, the writing is funny and snappy, and there's even a bit of lore thrown into the mix. Combat is also reasonably satisfying, although I recommend playing on hard as it's not super challenging. I only managed to fight the first boss, but it required tactics and good use of the items to beat.
Despite my criticisms, the game is a fun top down shooter with lovely artwork and witty writing, I just wish I had the patience to bash my head against the puzzles and finish it, but I don't. If you fancy a Zelda-like puzzle game with some almost bullethell-esque combat then give this a try.

This game tries to imitate Defense Grid (which is the best tower defense I've ever played), but contains a lot of failures :
- There are no checkpoints ... and some levels last 30 minutes, it's horrible!
- There is no pause either. (you can't freeze time and put some turrets)
- You can speed up the time (x2), but if you do that the turrets will be less effective!
- There is no minimap and you can't zoom-out to see the whole map.
- You can't change the targeting priority of your turrets.
- The interface is failed ! It was designed to play with a controller, which is cool for people playing on consoles, but isn't effective with a mouse and a keyboard.
- The first half of the campaign is boring : no difficulty, no mazing, no original turrets. Fortunately, in the second half, you gain acces to more interesting turrets, you can start mazing and levels become challenging.
- There is no other game modes, just the campaign.
The level transformation idea is interesting, though it isn't used a lot. The graphics are good and I like the mecha-style of the turrets.
The game isn't entirely bad, but it contains a lot of frustrating things. Buy it only on big sale, prefer Defense Grid or Defenders Quest.

Disclosure: I owe this game a great personal debt for the role it played in helping me to turn someone I love onto a healthier path.
Depression Quest is a well-written, extremely honest, deeply affecting piece of interactive fiction, in which a single, ingenious mechanical twist (that your current depression rating will lock out the most healthy and constructive options that would otherwise be available to you, reinforcing the downward spiral) goes incredible lengths to embed the player into the mindset of a person suffering from this paralyzing illness.
P r e t t y      D a m n        B a d

Lets get the negatives out of the way
