okay, this game. it looks good and I wanted to like it, but its flaws make it unplayable.
so - launched the game, it gave me two options: play Evil Hazard, or maybe you'd like to play Evil Hazard. that second one is fullscreen although you'd never know it, but beware of picking it because this game seeemingly has no exit function other than x-ing it out. escape doesn't work; it makes a "ping" noise but does nothing; Q does nothing, no button I pressed worked. so there's no way to get out of it in fullscreen beyond task manager; maybe I'm wrong and it's hidden somewhere, but why would you do that? give me a readily visible means to close out of it; that's just basic. we'll come back to another basic in a minute.
upon launch, either fullscreen or windowed, the game presents a pixel-art logo (I like pixel art so this is not a negative for me) that sparkles and gleams v e r y s l o w l y and it seems like an odd choice but whatever. then the game invites you to "PRESS TO START." uhhh, okay? press what? I know you don't mean any buttons on my controller because there's no support for that, so I make a good guess, hit enter, and am rewarded with success: new game, load game, or options. there actually are no options; two separate volume controls and a window size control. don't think about rebinding keys because it isn't happening for you. oh, and if you hit escape from the second menu, it pings helpfully and superimposes the "PRESS TO START" command over it. awesome.
anyway, start the game. it has some control instruction which is handled very straightforwardly by flatly scrawling it across the screen with a "hit h to toggle" command, so at least there's no mystery here; hit space to jump, and... s a i l across the screen like Luigi from Mario 2 just stepping out of a moonlander. mein gott, is the control and movement intended to be this mushy or is the game just that painfully laggy? my machine runs Skyrim on ultra-high quality with no problem; it handles Risk of Rain on Monsoon dfficulty three or four loops in, no problem... if this is bogging me down it's the game, not the computer, and that's assuming that isn't just ... how this game plays. the store page video didn't really shed any light on it either. the combat seems like it could be good but the opioid languor with which it proceeds makes it impossible to tell. oh yeah, and that other basic I mentioned above? there's no pause. inventory doesn't pause; it just obscures a still-active screen with the inventory (a decision other games than this have made, granted, and which I fail to understand in any context outside of online play). map doesn't pause either; it doesn't provide a map - oh no, it takes you TO an overworld map, the existence of which was not hinted at beforehand and which ends your progress in the level it dumps you in at the start. and escape... well, escape just pings stupidly and achieves nothing.
so in summary I cannot recommend this game without some serious fixing; it seems like a kernel of a good idea executed very frustratingly.

SOTS: The Pit is a modern take on "Rogue" or "DND" where you explore a randomly generated dungeon hoping to grab the treasure at the end, but this time, with a bit of a sci-fi twist. Wide variety of weapons, locks, armor, and plenty of recipes for crafting makes for a different game as you play through. Unfortunately, hunger, disease, poison, and other nasty effects await you as well (but there are counter-agents you can find or synthesize, if you find the right places and ingredients). Graphics are low-tech but that's part of the "oldskool" charm. No two game will be like, with 3 separate starting types. (Optional DLC adds 10 more levels and 2 more starting types). If you like this sort of dungeon crawl, give it a try!

A laptop-friendly strategic roguelike. This game is pretty complicated despite looking so simple and is insanely frustrating the deeper into the levels you get. The variety of foes you face keeps you constantly judging your current tactics and there are a multitude of risks and little things you can do to min/max your character. Given recent updates, there are even more characters and options on how you want to clear your way down the depths of this hellish dungeon.
I'd say it's a pretty good game, but I find it hard to agitate myself into getting back to it. It's not exactly a game like Binding of Isaac you can pick up for ten minutes and do a whole run (or most of a whole run), be satisfied and put it down for something else. You have to sink a lot of time into each run to really get it anywhere, but at least it lets you save your progress, unlike other roguelikes.

Although I wasn't expecting to see Dinosis Survival's environments be quite so large and impressive, I also wasn't expecting to see my character miraculously clip into and out of solid objects often, including boulders (seen here:
) gas cans, pallets, and other various inconsequential objects scattered throughout the environment.
That and some other goofy glitches aside, this game does two things very well for me that make me enjoy it when approaching it in search of an affordable, immersive "dinosaur game"
It captures the mass / size of the (at times, scary/imposing) dinosaurs, and has a "living" feeling jungle area around it, whether it be through the ambient noise of bugs, a pterodactyl flying by in the distance, or  shadows being cast from the surrounding foiliage.
The level variety you encounter is a lot more diverse (and large) than I thought it would be in the game itself, including a variety of waterfalls, rivers, open grassy areas, cliffsides, and outposts. Unfortunately, you eventually run into "invisible walls" preventing you from navigating further up a cliff, for instance. After having wandered that far along the edges of the game area, I tried to return down the same cliffside, fell about 3 feet, and somehow died. The dinosaurs are placed sporadically (thankfully) throughout the levels. They seem to match their habitat and their scarcity / absence from the game world makes for tense, "too quiet" scary moments when navigating the jungle before seeing a large one nearby.
How much you fight the dinosaurs inbetween the areas is more or less up to the player as the game tries to incorporate a stealth system with only marginal success. You can sneak around the dinosaurs if you want (which I did through a field of raptors and alligators...) but even if you try to pull a "stealth kill" (stealth hit?) with the crossbow on enemies while undetected it didnt seem to do anything other than♥♥♥♥♥♥it off and get it to swarm me. If you engage in combat it's a bit clumsy and unrewarding, consisting of just holding down the fire button and watching the enemy hopefully slump over before you run out of bullets. You have no dodge / evade so if they get close you're screwed. Ammo seems scarce.
The save system seems to throw a lot of people off in the forums, you hit F to set a campfire/checkpoint at that location. You don't get to save in different spots (or fast travel or anything like that, all on foot, no map...) it's just this one recurring campfire location to respawn from during your playthrough. Not having a map I'm surprised I haven't gotten more lost on the game, despite its large outdoor environments. The hunger / survival system seems much ado about nothing but maybe I'm in for a rude awakening. As far as exploring the terrain with much gusto all you'll really do is find an occasional keycard to open a door to progress to the next area, or a new weapon on the ground.
The player model (and some dinosaur models, including a creepy grinning stegosaurus..) could use some work. The player model does some WONKY♥♥♥♥♥♥sometimes, including his 1000 yard stare as he crouches, before somehow slipping his left arm under his knee... it looks super awkward and is hard to describe without seeing it in person but stay crouched long enough and that will inevitably happen. Maybe he's a contortionist. It's another of several graphical glitches in the game that break the immersion.
This game has its share of graphical glitches, including the clipping previously mentioned, and the player character model's arm goofily tucked under his leg while crouched, and another that breaks nearly all immersion toward the game, which is occassionally the dinosaurs will just get stuck mid-walk in a hillside and stand there unmoving in one location while doing their walk animation. It looks pretty shoddy in an otherwise graphically-immersive game. There is no first person view which is kind of a bummer, as is a lack of ANY controller support. The mouse and keyboard controls are logical (spacebar to jump , shift to run , WASD control,etc...) but not having controller support of any kind sucks.
Looking past its budgetary limitations, for its low price, large, varied jungle environment, and immersive (if not at times graphically comical due to glitches or low-res / simple models...) depiction of a jungle with dinosaurs, Dinosis Survival pretty much delievered to me exactly what I expected of it and I'm glad I bought it.

I hardly ever write reviews, but here's my two-cents.
While the game has an okay graphical style, the gameplay is just so old school. The stealth in this game is far from perfect. It seems like this game wasn't thoroughly tested, or was just neglected to make proper changes. It seems more like an Alpha phase for the game.
Stealth:
So when you're walking around concealed in the shadows, hostiles cannot see you at all unless you're close and in their peripheral vision. What's dumb is sometimes I will knock out a hostile NPC from the shadows and every guard around him will immediately turn into super hostile mode and come straight for me. Three seconds before that I was invisible to everyone. This mechanic is broken as far as I'm concerned.
What should happen is if the guards around the guard I'm knocking out somehow notice what's happening, they should not instantly go into super hostile mode and come straight for me for the kill. They should just investigate. It's more connected to what you see in movies. No I don't want exact realism in every single game I play because that wouldn't be fun, but I do want new mechanics. This is 2014, not 2005.
The Bow:
While the bow you have is a great tool, I think the way it works is also broken as far as I'm concerned. Number one, it makes a lot of noise when you're pulling on it. You would think a master thief would have a near-silent bow. If there was a realistic noise mechanic (which sometimes there's an overly dramatic one which I'll get to next) then every guard in the area would be investigating the area because I decided to shoot a rope arrow.
The rope arrow mechanic is also something super dumb. You cannot shoot the rope arrow just anywhere to climb. No, you have to shoot it at specific spots just like in Tomb Raider for it to do anything. This is such an old mechanic, it's stupid.
I could go on about the bow and how it is poorly implmented but it's not worth any more of my time.
Last but not least, the noise mechanic:
While playing the game you will often encounter things in the environment that will cause nearby guards to investigate your position. There's also birds and dogs in cages that will somehow always see you when you swoop (swoop is a near silent movement, by the way), which will also alert the nearby guards of something in your position (you) and cause them to investigate.
Other things you'll encounter are randomly broken glass in the environment that you have to walk slow on or everything around you (even birds and dogs) will be alerted and will investigate your position. Even if you swoop (shadowstep) it will make noise on the glass and will alert nearby hostiles. This mechanic is broken.
The swoop is not a running mechanic, it's more like a shadow-step mechanic yet it makes noise? This is broken as far as I'm concerned and overlooked by the developers and publishing company.
I could go on, but this game is not worth your time or money.

Well, before I start, I would just like to announce, I REALLY wish this game was good, because it had so much potential, but it failed in every way it could succeed greatly.
The game in general is not very well optimized for PC. I play it on high with my GTX 770 graphics card and my i5 quad core processor. Yeah I get good framerates but I feel like it should require a lot less. I remember having trouble running this on medium with my previous 1GB card, and it looks good but, should not be as performance hungry as it is.
The controlling of the character when playing has a very "blocky" feel, I would say. It feels like the game does everything for you, and there's animations for everything you do that just seems to drag out; opening doors, pickpocketing, locking picking, doing knockouts, and I feel a lot of it doesn't play very good, or atleast on keyboard and mouse.
The enemy AI are pretty horrible, and make not much sense. If you're standing and walking around in a shadow, even though you'd be harder to see, you could still be obviously visible, but god forbid if you do one little subtle thing like stand on a shard of glass or leave a door open that wasn't open before, they'll notice that of course! Takedowns could've also been promising, but if you try to take someone down and the enemy is less that 40 feet away from you, then they'll hear you, try to fight you, and you'll die, becaaaaaaaaaaaaaauseeee... combat is also terrible! You have the option to strike, and the option to dodge, Both are quite useless, and you'll only really win a fight one on one, but that won't happen of course because everyone will be alerted!
The features and your equipment could also be promising, but so could everything else in this game. You can have things like arrows you fire that can pull you up on to beams and get you on rooftops, which would've been a nice feature if they gave you more of them to get onto, and if you could actually find the trader that sells all the useful equipment. There is also some other things like water arrows that put out fires, which is alright but, doesn't fix everything else that's wrong with the game.
I find the story very lame, dull, drab, and other words describing generally painfully plain and boring. I'm on chapter 5 currently, and I've found there are 8 chapters, and these chapters are going by rather quickly. I would've thought with less content would mean more quality in that which it has, but apparently not.
Overall I find the game to be a bad rip off of Dishonored some how. It feels a lot like Dishonored in certain ways yet this game is executed so badly I hate to say the words "it's like Dishonored", which is definitely in my top 5 games I've ever played. Of course this game has features of it's own too, and I think I would've liked them, but like I keep saying, this game is just, a huge waste of potential which makes me actually angry that it had to go to waste. I suppose the best one word to describe this game with is; disappointment.

So I got this game from somebody on the PCMR subreddit. The controls are a bit wonky and it looks like something you'd find on a mobile appstore. It's a great time waster though, and at least it's not just 1 ship shooting the same thing over and over again.

For the record, before you read this look at my playtime and decide for yourself how many grains of salt this review is worth. It could be completely irrelevant to you. Anyways, I just want to start off saying you should buy this game. For 99 cents, it's got a fair amount of content. And it's a simply good game. The gameplay is fair, with the enemies actually having a good ramping difficulty curve. The ships are fun to unlock, albeit the way you unlock them is a bit strange. You see, you collect coins to unlock them, but the coins are a random drop from enemies, so it's sort of non-linear. The pixelated graphics look nice, and the particles... are excellent. The music is fine, but I like some more than others (Looking at you, ship #4). Overall, this is a simply fun game to play and is definitely worth it.
However, with that being said, no game is perfect. And there is 1 complaint I feel I should express. The power-ups make no sense from my view. Their icon is a simple colored circle with a letter in it, so good luck guessing what it is. However, once you use it it's pretty simple to figure out what that letter stands for. R = Rapid Fire, L = Lazer, H = Helper(?). So the symbols aren't a huge issue, but their balance is a bit off. For example, remember the Helper power-up I just mentioned? It is very overpowered. It's an AI-controlled projectile that auto-tracks the enemies around you and kills them. It can only hit once, but one time I just dodged enemies while it ground everything into a mushy pulp, racking up ~2000 points in score. That score did not feel rewarding, it did most of the work. And then there's the Magnet power-up, which I avoid like the plague. It constantly sucks ammo, and because of the ammo cooldown timer you cannot fire right when you press the button to fire, making it difficult to time your shots. And it's magnet powers aren't that impressive, as you're constantly moving away from the ammo.
TL;DR: Buy the game if you can, it's amazing, avoid the purple M.

I love this game.  Absolutely love it.   It's just a simple Roguelike, and clearly made by a very small, amateur team, but made with a lot of love.   The artwork feels like it was entirely done by "that guy in high school that was pretty good at drawing", and it's incredibly endearing.  The comedy is subtle yet very funny, the gameplay is an actual challenge (in that frustrating Roguelike way), and there's a genuine feeling of reward as you get more powerful and find better items.
I think my only complaint is that the crafting system is way too elaborate and extensive to be so useless.   You can become a master crafter, brewer, tinkerer, etc. and fill your precious inventory space with plenty of materials to make weapons that aren't *quite* as good as the ones you could just buy in a shop if you sold all those materials.

A whimsical rogue-like with loads of self-aware humor.  The game description mentions the skill path of Necronomiconomics, the economy of the undead - but fails to mention Flesh-smithing (Other men work with wood, stone, or metal.  We call them squeamish), Emo-mancy (with the Sigil of Whatever, which overwhelms your foes with apathy), and other tongue-in-cheek (or perhaps tongue-on-floor?) touches that make it well worth the five-dollar price point.
Although, I have to say, as an avid drinker - this game drives me to sobriety.  Drunk decisions tend to get me killed.

The comparison to Dark Souls is almost impossible to make, but it really is such a good take on the formula in 2D. The controls are super tight, the fights are fun as heck, and all the art/music/atmosphere has that signature Momodora Charm. I didn't think it was possible ot make a game that I liked more than Momo 2, but this one far and away takes the cake.

Momodora: Reverie Under the Moonlight was a game I was expecting mediocrity from, but was pleasantly surprised after the second boss. I played through the game on the "hard" difficulty, and while there were some attacks from enemies that killed me in one hit, I actually never felt frustrated with the game. I have also not played any of the other Momodora games, but I am considering them after playing this.
I'm not a particular fan of pixel art, nor do I drool over games that use pixel art. The pixel art to me is good, and I have no complaints with it. What I do like about the visuals is the use of contrast between the areas of the game, specifically the first area.
Coupled with the visuals is the music, which combined makes some good atmosphere for a 2D pixel game. I will also go so far as to say that the music even stands on its own. If you sometimes listen to music from games outside of playing them, I would recommend the soundtrack. The sound effects are retro in nature. I don't have much to say about the sounds. Nothing sticks out to me, though they make good use of the sounds as a que for some enemies to attack.
The game's combat consists of a melee attack (which you can perform in the air), a bow for ranged attacks (which you can charge), using a consumable items that either casts an attack spell or buffs you, and a dodge with I would say some very generous I-frames (invincibility frames).
The game goes off of a checkpoint system similar to Dark Souls with bonfires, but there is no autosave in the game and you save at these checkpoints (shrines). Health is restored and status effects are removed when you rest at them (save). Any consumable items you purchase or find in the game that have limited uses are also replenished when you rest at shrines. It's very streamlined and the game wants the player to keep moving.
I've seen some complain that the game is too short. While I can agree with this, I don't really see it as a negative. A first blind playthrough of the game I think would take someone maybe 4 hours to get through, but to collect everything in the game would require another play through
.
I found the game to be very enjoyable, and for a 2D pixel game it has some good atmosphere. It is short, but I don't see this as a negative. If anything it should push anyone to want to replay it and collect everything.
: 8/10

This game is my personal favorite in the entire Civilization franchise. No, not in recent memory, the entire bunch of games from the first one up to and including Civ V and VI, as well as Alpha Centauri -the other space colonization one.
Why? Simple. For all its faults -and it does have faults, like the tendency of the current writer(s) at Firaxis to produce long, long text walls of rambling nonsense that occasionally refer to bits of real-life science in the same way a person who doesn't actually know a celebrity will drop their name as though it still somehow aggrandizes them to do so... while at the same time utterly failing to get the reader interested. I.e. "This artifact we found appears to exist in a state which produces an effect resulting in an increase to our energy output." That is not writing, it is hot air in text form.
...For all its faults, including also a terrible diplomatic system involving trading in nebulous, largely worthless 'favors', completely replaced in the Rising Tide expansion with a remarkably less awful system involving a 'diplomatic influence' resource and a couple of ratings representing how much the other leaders respect and/or fear you (with the respect part based, admittedly, on randomly chosen personality factors and their associated likes and dislikes, which often come out as arbitrary as 'are you plundering trade routes, and if so, do they happen to like that for some reason?')...
...For all its faults, it has the most brilliant, open-ended tech tree -or rather, technology web, as it is now aptly known- in a Civ game to date, taking what was once a linear progression of "research fertilizer so you can then research dynamite and get artillery" and transfiguring it into "research whatever you like, or whatever leads to the things you like, based on any of a myriad possible faction concepts you may imagine, whether or not related to the faction you are technically playing as". Yes, there are limitations, but they are considerably less noticeable than in the 'main' series.
Furthermore, where basic Civ gives you the choice between 'get lucky with the starting position', 'restart if the starting position is bad' or the ever-delightful 'spend the whole game struggling to make up for your bad starting position, nevermind the fact you might also be playing at one of the higher difficulties'... Beyond Earth gives you powerful tools early on to make the most of almost any kind of terrain. Again, the expansion gives us more of the good stuff; aquatic cities, for one, so even if you start on a tiny island, it won't mean you're doomed to a tiny population until you research boating and find a better continent -unlike certain main series games I might mention. Oh, and you start with the ability to build boats, as well as the ability to produce farming and mining machinery and such, which is pretty nice.
Let's move on to the worlds: In basic Civ, you have one kind of world. It might be mostly grassland, or mostly plains and desert, mostly ocean, or a lot of hills, mountains, forests, but any way you slice it, it's going to look a lot like Earth. That's not a bad thing, necessarily, but it gets old.
Now, in Beyond Earth, you have
types of planet (five if you have Rising Tide as well).
Lush - Green and verdant, but otherwise rather unlike Earth. Quite alien vegetation.
Fungal - Blue-gray, covered in various fungal vegetation. Kooky and original.
Desert - Admittedly pretty boring, looks more or less like Dune or some other desert planet. Can be nice for a change, now and then, and there's this one Steam workshop mod that makes it reddish and sort of Mars-y!
Volcanic (RT) - Blackish-gray, desolate, harsh-style landscape. A young planet, perhaps; great for a meditative or dark feel.
Frozen (RT) - Glittering landscapes of ice, tundra, crystalline forests. Breathtaking beauty that might make you want to try a campaign without building (many) mines or farms. Or maybe that's just me.
"Yeah, okay", I hear you saying (or possibly not). "So it looks good. It has some variety. But it probably doesn't have a lot of interesting and partially customizable unit types!"
"Yes, it does!", I reply.
"Well, they probably suck", I hear you retort.
"Some of them do, but nearly all of them have upgrades that eventually place them on par with most other units", I counter.
"The AI probably cheats", I hear you grumble. "And I bet it keeps using that ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ healing 'promotion' every time one of its units earns enough experience."
"It does, but you can still kick the frick out of it at the top difficulty once you've gotten good enough at the game, and/or with a bit of luck and patience, depending on the circumstances", I conclude, and with that, our hypothetical discussion ends to the sounds of thunderous applause from an audience of millions, all seated in a great frontier stadium carved from ice by zillions of nanobots. Or something.
Moving right along, there is a great deal of fun to be had with this game. It can be played single player, with or without some interesting mods people have created for it in the Steam workshop, or in co-op multiplayer with some good friends, or competitive multiplayer with random internet people if you're a bit mental (or just like that sort of thing, I suppose).
My primary gripe with it as it appears on Steam right now, is the price tag. This game came out three years ago. We do not charge 60 euro (or dollars, I suppose) for the proper version (The Beyond Earth Collection, which includes Rising Tide, without which I do not recommend playing this game) of a game that is already several years old. Not unless we are entitled sweary-swear swearing muck mongers who have our heads so far up our own posteriors that were there only a glow-in-the-dark sticker on our foreheads, we could give ourselves an unassisted colonoscopy.
You could try buying it on Amazon or someplace, instead. You know, one of those places where the prices are regulated based on demand instead of wishful thinking. Or better yet, wait for a Steam sale, if Firaxis and/or their publishers can get it through their entitled skulls that people sometimes like to buy things at reasonable, affordable prices. 70-80% off should do it.

First a little background
I have played maplestory since early 2006 and I've kept playing since then. I have 6 level 200+ characters amd will continue to make more. I am an MMORPG fanatic and I really enjoy 2D side-scolling games. I recently got Maplestory on steam to avoid using the horrendus Nexon client.
Review
This game has a lot of grinding. A lot of grinding. Much like WoW, in Maplestory you constantly grind and are trying to level up your character to get better gear, a new job advancment, etc. That is one of the aspects I love the most about this game. In a game such as WoW you get new abilities every 4-5 levels depending on what level you are, in Maplestory you get things called job advancments. Basically, you have a certain moveset with certain abilities, you can upgrade these abilites until you reach a certain level, and then you get a new set of abilities. This is one of my favorite aspects of Maplestory and it really makes it unique. The player base in Maplestory is also awesome, everyone on here is extremely nice and it can be really fun to just talk to other players rather than grind. There are many other things for you to do besides grind of course; You can do "dungeons" where you are sent to a certain area for 10-15 levels and do quests for the NPCs there and have a lot of fun learning the lore, you can also fight massive bosses with other players. There are so many fun things to do in Maplestory which is why I have played the game for so long and will continue to do so.

+ side. The game itself is very good, no doubt. Spent lot of tyme playing it, and will do more.
- side. The sensitive disappointment is a very weak deck building interface.
* It is totally useless in finding synergic card combinations.
* Its filter by mana cost could be much more useful if designed better. If you have {W} (white mana) and {U} (blue mana) in your lands, and you want to filter the cards by mana cost so that to show only cards that can be paid by either of colors you have in your deck - then sorry, there is no way. What the game mana filters allows you to do, is for example to show cards which contain {W} or {U} and besides {W} or {U} any additional color. Why on earth would someone need to filter this way?
One could go to
to do fine card searching, but it is not that easy to narrow search down to only cards present in Magic Duels game.
The solution for that problem to me was to write my own Deck building application. It
* uses data from
* uses card images from
* uses waifu2x neural network algorithm to make the cards look acceptably good in higher resolution (the images in gatherer are really small).
* grabs available cards count from Magic Duels by making screenshots of the game and doing OCR (optical character recognition) to extract card names and their counts in my cards collection
* presents the cards in a handy UI which allows one to find card by their properties quick and effectively
* replicates the Magic Duels mana cost diagram for a built deck
* Allows saving and loading the decks to/from file.
As you could imagine doing all that was a lot of work, but without it, I would abandon playing Magic Duels a couple of months ago as the amount of available cars in the game is now over 1000. The game HAS to have decent search functionality for this amount. And really the Wizards of the Coast developers should really have taken care of that instead of me, not to mention that doing it for them would be much easier than to me as they have access to all the required data and do not need to use hacks like extracting text from screenshots and so on.

The comparison to Dark Souls is almost impossible to make, but it really is such a good take on the formula in 2D. The controls are super tight, the fights are fun as heck, and all the art/music/atmosphere has that signature Momodora Charm. I didn't think it was possible ot make a game that I liked more than Momo 2, but this one far and away takes the cake.

If you like Metroidvania games not just in level design, but also with obtaining new items and upgrades later into the game, then this is a game for you.
Momodora: Reverie Under the Moonlight was a game I was expecting mediocrity from, but was pleasantly surprised after the second boss. I played through the game on the "hard" difficulty, and while there were some attacks from enemies that killed me in one hit, I actually never felt frustrated with the game. I have also not played any of the other Momodora games, but I am considering them after playing this.
I'm not a particular fan of pixel art, nor do I drool over games that use pixel art. The pixel art to me is good, and I have no complaints with it. What I do like about the visuals is the use of contrast between the areas of the game, specifically the first area.
Coupled with the visuals is the music, which combined makes some good atmosphere for a 2D pixel game. I will also go so far as to say that the music even stands on its own. If you sometimes listen to music from games outside of playing them, I would recommend the soundtrack. The sound effects are retro in nature. I don't have much to say about the sounds. Nothing sticks out to me, though they make good use of the sounds as a que for some enemies to attack.
The game's combat consists of a melee attack (which you can perform in the air), a bow for ranged attacks (which you can charge), using a consumable items that either casts an attack spell or buffs you, and a dodge with I would say some very generous I-frames (invincibility frames).
The game goes off of a checkpoint system similar to Dark Souls with bonfires, but there is no autosave in the game and you save at these checkpoints (shrines). Health is restored and status effects are removed when you rest at them (save). Any consumable items you purchase or find in the game that have limited uses are also replenished when you rest at shrines. It's very streamlined and the game wants the player to keep moving.
I've seen some complain that the game is too short. While I can agree with this, I don't really see it as a negative. A first blind playthrough of the game I think would take someone maybe 4 hours to get through, but to collect everything in the game would require another play through
.
I found the game to be very enjoyable, and for a 2D pixel game it has some good atmosphere. It is short, but I don't see this as a negative. If anything it should push anyone to want to replay it and collect everything.

A huge step up in quality and design from Momodora III (and I loved this game), Momodora RUtM leaves the stage progression behind and offers one single map you can explore in the order you chose (post-SotN Castlevania comes to mind). The game looks beautiful and the spritework is incredibly cute and pleasant to look at.
The music, while on the more ambiant side does a great job at conveying various mood through your journey.
The combat feels great, even though the roll is a bit tricky to master since the invincibility frames are scarce. Bossfights are tough but not too hard and I've never felt the game was being cheap or injust to me.
The plot is minimalist and is told in a way that invites comparison to Dark Souls or Bloodborne.
It's way longer than Momodora III (which took me like 5 hours to 100%) but you will most likely finish it in about 10h or less, it does have some good replay value though, especially if you intend to 100% it, which is tough but far from impossible.
Overall great atmosphere, great bossfights, lovely 2D art and a nice difficulty curve.
If you are interested in a dungeon crawler with lots of pop culture referances and humor take a peak at Dungeons of Dredmor.

A game as dark and desperate as its subject material. Until you learn how to play it.
The atmosphere, the art, the music. It's a beautiful package. The first couple plays through this game really did have an impact emotionally and psychologically. The characters are so real it's easy to become attached to them, it's hard to see them make the tough choices. The gameplay is tight, the UI is clear and useful. The other people you run across can be simultaneously familiar and yet coldly distant. Doing the dirty work that must be done to survive is exciting and immersive. You know you're being awful, and don't want to be caught doing it.
Once the effect wears off, and you begin to approach the game from a strictly technical perspective, it becomes quite easy to stay alive. It also becomes fairly simple to plunder every structure you come across and leave none standing to tell the tale. The various story customizations and additional characters and locations to incorporate make the game strongly replayable, but you won't unlearn the important lessons of your earlier attempts.

I got this game a wile back (wintersale i guess) and kinda ignored the fact i really have it. So i played the "usual" games i play normaly. So a wile back, i was looking into my games which are existing somewhere in my big "library void" and found this game again and gave it a try.
From the very first moment, i know, this game let people change their mind (or at least let them think twice about stuff) and that this game is not everyones "cup of tea"...
Its hard to explain the game but i try it. As i said, this game is not really for everyone since it could make people very fast "depressive" since its dark and "hopeless" from the very first moment.
The game begins with a quote which tell us
This "quote" alone already tells us how the game works at most. You play not even a handful civilians which have their own backgroundstory, "abilitys" and "rating" of the war. Some of them might already start hurt, sick or like. You have a big house where the people "tries" to find cover from the war which is running outside.
Said that let you maybe guess that you are not a "warfighter" here - you only try to survive the war.
You begin with very little stuff you can find at the house you start so that you actually can build stuff you might need the most, like a bed or strove coz you only have a workbench at the startpoint. You also can work at your home and "people" at the day time coz this time is the "quite time" where you need to repair your home, eat food, get sleep, build stuff, smoke, drink coffee (yea, the last 2 ones are even part of the game...), trade and much more.
Thats just one side of the game and, in my opinion, the more easier one. The hard one is the Nighttime alias the "plunder" time.
At the night time, the game let you choose to go outside on a plunder tour or stay at home and cover or sleep. Since in the very beginning, you have nearly nothing and you need stuff, you are more or less forced to go plunder old homes, stores, warehouses and like. This tours are easy at the beginning but as longer the game is as harder it gets the stuff you might need right now. next to this are some people of yours only good in plunder tours with a big bagback wile others might are slow or faster but only can hold a hand full of items.
Wile the day and night time, you also have really to fight with inner moments and moral decisions. Like you have someone who needs sleep but is the best one to go on plunder tours, someone is hurt but is the best one to defend your home, youre nearly out of food but you also need something to burn to keep the place warm and and and. So this means youre forced to leave something behind. At the day time, you might let someone not sleep so he can build XY stuff and give someone else the medicine he actually could also need. At the night time, You might go plunder for some junk and wood to keep the place warm insteed of food wile maybe someone is starving. Its mostly hard to go only for "one opinion" since the stuff you might have (or need) is only that much to keep the house and player running for maybe the next 2 days...
At the night time on the plunder tours (mostly in the later game) you also might cross your ways with bandits or even the army or sharpshooters which will harm you for sure and might kill you. Since your people are  not armed (at the beginning) or even not "build for war", you should avoid such confrontation of any kind or youre losing your people very quickly. Next to this is the "fight system" more or less sometimes pur luck. You maybe have a knife and the "enemy" a gun and you go close combat but maybe your guy hasnt slept well or he is already hurt or sick. that all makes it harder for the one you sended to plunder to fight actually, next to this if you might fight innocent people your people can lose moral or even get desperately or depressive, which let them work slower or forget about things they might should do, like guard the home.
This War of Mine is really a great made game which let people really fight sometimes with their innerself. You have really moral decisions to choose and think about the consequences which might happen.
which enjoy survival games or games like Organ Trail, which is also in the same style at least but not for people which maybe cant stand the pressure of moral decisions.

On balance this really isn't a great game.  It DOES hook you in and you find that you have devoted some hours to what is really just boring monotony and after you've invsted tons of hours you are liable to suddenly find your characters quickly all die with little you can do about it.
The graphics are basic, essentially you generally control 3+ cartoon like sprites and there is nothing else moving on screen, yet the game hogs CPU resources like you were playing Halo !  Just crazy.
The major thing I didn't like about the game is that it appears to deliberately make life difficult for you.  Doesn't matter what decisions you make, the game will find a way to level you out.  It's like games like Oblivion where, when you finnaly get a God like sword and look forward to carving through swathes of monsters, you find the game has levelled up all the monsters so it's no different.  Very unrewarding.
So here, if you have lots of timber and components and need cogs to make something, when you go out and scavenge you'll find tons more timber and components and sweet FA cogs.
If your party has bandages but no meds, sure enough the characters will become sick leaving you stranded.  If you have meds but no bandages then sure enough, the house will be raided overnight and characters will be wounded and without bandages quickly deteriorate.
The moral aspects of the game are a horrible element imo.  Just stupid.   If the scavenger does anything remotely "bad" the whole party gets depressed.  I mean you're surviving a war so stealing for example is highly likely to happen, but if you do it, expect the game to brutally punish you by dropping moral of the party.  Characters go from Sad, to Depressed to Broken pretty quickly and trying to recover that position once the juggernaut has started rolling is very difficult.  If you don't have books or armchairs or coffee, smokes etc then it's a quick decline.  The most stupid aspect is Broken status.  Your character won't do anything at all.  Will just stand or sit there and is useless from that point on, may as well be dead.
In the final analysis it feels like you are just following the pre-programmed route for the game, you don't really have choices, though it creates the illusion that you do.  You have to play the way the game wants you to or it stuffs you.
There are the basics of a good idea here, but as implemented it's just a time waster that deliberately skews the numbers against you to prolongue the play time.  You win if the game wants you to win.
When you do finally win after all the hours and effort expended in monotnous repetitive actions, what do you get?  A black screen with 2 words in white . . .  "You Survived".
Too much of the mechanics (resource management) doesn't make sense.  You have the ability to build rat traps (with the appropriate resources) but once you've built 2, the GAME doesn't let you build more !  No reason why the characters couldn't or shouldn't, they have the resources, but no, the game just says no, 2 is it, I'm removing the option after that point.
So, as I said, the game doesn't let you get ahead.  You don't really have choices.  You DO have to build a stove, a heater, a water distiller, beds etc.  No choice, you build them or die.  You can't inventively do anything, you can't out-think the game, you can't therefore experiment how you might survive in such a war.   You are merely playing numbers.  X timbers + Y components = item.  Item + something else = another item.  etc etc.   Always on the back foot, always fighting a game that won't let you get ahead.  It presents options for stealing and killing people, but if you do, the game punishes you.  Ultimately just silly.
It is in the end a glorified time waster that doesn't reward at any stage.

This... is not much of a game. I will point that out straight away. I find it inappropriate to call it one.
But being all about words and discreet visuals, it's all about putting you in the state of mind of someone who is depressed.
So it's all about words and reading. But the writing isn't too great and there's minor typos (such as "Camero", missing punctuation, etc.). And the language is rather plain. Yet, most depressed people would hardly be poetic, so it fits.
Audio-visually, Depression Quest presents itself simply, static filters and little environmental sound effects set to a constant piano loop (albeit one too short). The points are delivered.
There is no gameplay. It is simply a mildly branching story. And it's short. You can finish a readthrough in less than half an hour. (Then again, I'm a relatively fast reader.)
So how realistic is it? You'll likely find other reviews suggesting it is not. But, it is.
People do not understand "depression". For most people, the "blues" just come and go. They don't constantly eat away at you. Depression Quest depicts someone suffering from this "unnatural" state of mind, a medical condition that has only become officially recognized in the last half a century.
The character's situation is given little backstory. Though, one might find the situation "promising" and good, that it's actually such good circumstances that there's no reason to be unhappy. Yet, the seemingly most successful and happy stars have killed themselves, and depression is an ailment that can strike anybody without reason. Just like a genetic defect.
Perhaps it's not a fully accurate representation. It probably isn't.
Perhaps you, a non-sufferer, feel it's absolutely ridiculous; that the character you play has a totally obnoxious way of thinking. Perhaps you
a sufferer, undergoing treatment or otherwise and you find that the story does not match your experience.
Depression is a highly individualized ailment. If it were to be described as a criminal, it would be one who modifies their strategy to the individual target, striking them oh so differently.
Just go ahead and read the Discussions on the Community Hub, or even anywhere else. The realism of the story has been debated there and so forth.
But how do I recommend this? In short, I can't really recommend it. It's something that won't be enjoyable. But, if you intend to experience Depression Quest, enjoyment should not be your objective. You should want to "play" Depression Quest to experience one viewpoint (of many possible) of a medical ailment.

This is a tentative recommendation. Beyond Earth is good, but...
The Good: It pick up where Civ V left off, improving the tech tree (now a web), making diplomacy and espionage more useful, and adding some much need unit variety. It's also very pretty.
The Bad: The UI. The UI in Civ V was decent, but not in Beyond Earth. It's bad, especially in the Tech Web.
The Ugly: The AI. The AI is dumber than a bag of hammers. The AI has always been the Achilles' Heel of the Civ franchise, but Beyond Earth's is particularly horrendous. Example: on multiple occasions, an enemy with whom I was at war continued to complement me on my achievements, raising their rating of me. The AI also doesn't seem to gauge military strength very well. Again, on multiple occasions, I had weaker factions declare war on me out of the blue. Borders also don't seem to matter to the AI, as far-flung AI will declare war, despite being 30+ tiles away.
Bottom line: If you liked Civ V, you'll like Beyond Earth. It feel like an expansion for Civ V, but it is still fun. Some genuine improvements were made and some steps were taken backwards, but mostly it improves on what Civ V was already doing well.

Flower Shop: Winter in Fairbrook is the sequel to its predecessor, Flower Shop: Summer in Fairbrook, obviously. However, instead of playing as a guy attempting to romance one of four dateable females, this time around, the player takes on the role of a female attempting to romance one of four dateable guys. As the summary of the story is already outlined in the game description, I won't repeat that here. Instead, I'll give my perspective of this game, especially comparing it to its predecessor.
Now, I found Winter in Fairbrook to be enjoyable and it definitely has longer replayability overall, as indicated by my gaming time when comparing the times of both games. I tend to play games to their full completion, making sure to get all the possible endings, achievements, etc. It has a lighter storyline generally than Summer in Fairbrook. (For those who have played Summer in Fairbrook, we're all aware that near the ending, a tragic event happens.) I did enjoy the extra scenes at the end, especially the snowball fights. The gameplay is basically the same as before. Instead of growing crops, though, the player is growing flowers. Of course, each guy has a kiss scene as well as normal and special endings, which was the same for each girl in Summer in Fairbrook.
There was something that I noticed in regards to differences. In Summer in Fairbrook, if the player earned over a certain amount of money, he/she got the special ending in which Steve (the MC) would stay on the farm. However, in Winter in Fairbrook, if the player earned over a certain amount of money, he/she would get a special ending in which Natalie (the MC) would get to be with the guy of his/her choice. However, Natalie wouldn't go back to work in the flower shop. That only happens if the player gets the normal ending. That seemed a little odd to me.
I did feel that there were some weak points in Winter in Fairbrook. There were the typos and grammar errors but honestly, I expected them to appear. However, there were certain scenes in which Natalie's expression didn't correspond to what was displayed in the text which felt a little unusual. Also, I felt that it was harder to like Natalie's character. In the beginning, she comes off as a spoiled brat who works at the flower shop only because her parents force her to get a job over winter break. Although the endings with each guy show that Natalie changes into someone hardworking, I felt that the story didn't really show that change well. There were times, like halfway through the game, where I felt that Natalie still came off as a spoiled brat. In that sense, I thought that Summer in Fairbrook did a better job of effectively portraying the change in Steve's character.
Overall, though, the game was fun to play and there's lots of replayability value. Also, I liked how the gallery was set up again so that the player can replay certain endings and scenes. I would recommend this game to anyone who's a fan of Flower Shop: Summer in Fairbrook and who likes stat building games. ^^

The singleplayer game is boring. Just intensely, unrelentingly boring. The levels are too large, the enemy swarms are too large, too common, and entirely cliched. Most dungeon crawlers make up for this by having the endless combat reward you with loot or skills until they've trained you to salivate every time you hear the mouse clicking of combat but the character advancement, which is done entirely through buying from vendors using coins you find laying around in barrels and crates, is too slow and too unrelated to the endless swarms of enemies you have to fight through for it to pass on any glamor to the fighting. Even when you do finally purchase a skill it's probably going to be weak and a pain to use, rather than any kind of awe-inspiring new ability you can't wait to try out. It's a samey, repetitive slog that fails to reward you in any way or give you any reason to keep going.
There might be an entertaining game here in multiplayer given the possible interactions between different classes, but, in my experience, joining a public multiplayer game will usually get you instantly kicked and if you host a public multiplayer game you'll maybe get one or two people who play for about 5 minutes each before losing connection.
It might be worthwhile to try out Hammerwatch if you know people who want to play as a group beforehand, assuming the tendency to lose connection isn't as big a problem as it seemed to be for me. If you don't have a pre-existing group, you're better off with just about any other dungeon crawler. Any of them is bound to have better mechanics for solo play and I would bet most of them will have communities large enough for you to find a group if you don't have one to begin with.
The pixel art is very nice looking, I have to give it that.

Someone made an exceptionally ugly and un-fun action RPG. How original. I understand I'm in the minority if you look at the Steam ratings. I just don't agree with them.
Hammerwatch is a fairly basic, straightforward action RPG. It's a dungeon crawl that compensates for the few enemy types with an overabundance of them. It's the same game that I've played and seen dozens of times. There are no new mechanics to speak of here. It's spam the attack button and clear out enemies. Rinse and Repeat. Careful positioning of your character and taking care to min/max your build is what's needed.
Here's the problem. That sounds like every other action RPG game in the last 20 years. In this case the devs decided that since they didn't have any graphical skills, they should just create ugly pixel blobs for everything and try to pass it off as "retro". I saw better looking games on my Atari 2600. I'm not kidding either. I'm all for a unique and interesting art style. It doesn't have to have modern graphics. But I find these muddled and frankly dull. With the same kind of gameplay I've experienced a dozen times before, I'm not finding any joy in Mudville.
Why would I want to play this over any dozens of other games that do the same thing, look better and play better? Maybe there's some cool novel mechanic or awesome story later on (though by all indications there isn't), but if there is I can't be bothered trying to find it given the derivative gameplay and horrendous graphics. I get the sense when I play this I should just go play a similar game that does it better and looks better.
I hate to hammer on the graphics so much but when they're this off-putting, it's a massive issue. The meal may taste OK but if it looks like a plate of dog doo your dinner guests won't want to eat it. That's how Hammerwatch makes me feel. Then when I play it and get the feeling that I've done all this before there's no incentive to go on.
Again, I recognize that I'm in the minority here but I'm not giving bonus points for ugly, derivative games just because they're indie.

Hammerwatch came out just a few years ago via steam's greenlight and is extremely good. It offers you exactly what you would expect from hack and slash genre plus a few extra things. I am yet to find more enjoyable game where all you do is run around and kill stuff. The secret areas are a different thing though.
I believe this is my first game of its genre and I must say I enjoyed it a lot. There are 6 classes to choose from. All give you different abilities and game strategies. There are no skill trees, instead you can purchase your skills and stats from the shopkeepers during the game. There are different possible combos for every class. You will have to look for hidden doors, which is not always easy. Sometimes you have to go around 1 level a few times to actually see everything and find out if something moved due to your actions. Game keeps you in pace. Closer to the end the pace of killing enemies and you dying becomes a bit faster. I must say that the game is actually not frustrating at all. You enjoy every gold coin you find to spend on yourself.
The sound is very not friendly to new users. You have to install a program yourself, which is actually located in the files, but it does not tell you where and why. Without sound this game would actually suck. But, once you get it going it's just amazing. It makes the gameplay so much better and gives you a feel of really old game. I found a bug, when you get to special are the sound from previous area plays together with the new area's sound. Otherwise, the music is very pleasant and I have not grown tired of it at all.
Graphically the game looks like it was made for SEGA during 90's, but it's still a modern game. You can actually adjust the post effects so that you game looks not even 90's but 80's. You can get a rounded yellowish screen, how about that for a change on your nice flat screen huh? Everything you see is perfectly understandable and there are no visuals artifacts because the graphics are so simple. In all, graphical solution adds up to the feel you get while playing Hammerwatch.
Controlls in general are a fine, but can be a bit wonky for some classes like range for example. Shooting and walking can be a bit of nuisance sometimes. There's only like 8 buttons to push, so you should be fine with any character to be honest.
Replayabilty is under question. I guess once you finish the game with every class there's not much to do unless you gather friends to play online.
In the end the game is so good for the offered price. I would even say that buying the game at a full price is not going to disappoint you.

Caveblazers is possibly the best platformer game I've ever played.  The controls seem incredibly natural and the way the player's character moves and jumps seems completely intuative.
Players must traverse a series of caves, picking up weapons, magic items, potions and gold.  The player may also find 'Blessings' which increase characters stats, or enable special abilities, such as the incredibly useful 'double' jump.
I would say the difficulty level of the game seems just about perfect (although possibly erring on the difficult side), allowing player progression, while remaining challenging.   Each run will increase progression towards the unlocking of an item or a character 'perk' which is selectable at the start, giving the player the choice to orient their character 'build' towards a specific direction. (ie melee/ranged/magical etc)...
I really love the atmosphere created in the game, with the main NPC character ocassionally pointing out apparent futility in entering the randomly generated caves.
Players are able to participate in a Daily Run, to compete for position on the online leaderboards.
I play using an Xbox controller for PC, which is fully supported, and works really well.
I really loved games like Jet Set Willy, Ghosts 'n Goblins and Manic Miner when I was younger, and the RPG element in Caveblazers really gives the platformer/shooter/explorer concept a lot of depth.

+ side. The game itself is very good, no doubt. Spent lot of tyme playing it, and will do more.
- side. The sensitive disappointment is a very weak deck building interface.
* It is totally useless in finding synergic card combinations.
* Its filter by mana cost could be much more useful if designed better. If you have {W} (white mana) and {U} (blue mana) in your lands, and you want to filter the cards by mana cost so that to show only cards that can be paid by either of colors you have in your deck - then sorry, there is no way. What the game mana filters allows you to do, is for example to show cards which contain {W} or {U} and besides {W} or {U} any additional color. Why on earth would someone need to filter this way?
One could go to
to do fine card searching, but it is not that easy to narrow search down to only cards present in Magic Duels game.
The solution for that problem to me was to write my own Deck building application. It
* uses data from
* uses card images from
* uses waifu2x neural network algorithm to make the cards look acceptably good in higher resolution (the images in gatherer are really small).
* grabs available cards count from Magic Duels by making screenshots of the game and doing OCR (optical character recognition) to extract card names and their counts in my cards collection
* presents the cards in a handy UI which allows one to find card by their properties quick and effectively
* replicates the Magic Duels mana cost diagram for a built deck
* Allows saving and loading the decks to/from file.
As you could imagine doing all that was a lot of work, but without it, I would abandon playing Magic Duels a couple of months ago as the amount of available cars in the game is now over 1000. The game HAS to have decent search functionality for this amount. And really the Wizards of the Coast developers should really have taken care of that instead of me, not to mention that doing it for them would be much easier than to me as they have access to all the required data and do not need to use hacks like extracting text from screenshots and so on.

I had some negative criticism about this game at first, and although some of the problems I have with it still stand, The dev Nickervision has been extremely cool about taking my critique seriously and adding things to the game based on my suggestions. That's something I've never ever experienced before, so props to him.
As for the game its a pretty simple score attack asteroids clone with some interesting powerups, a little variation in enemies, a few different ships, and some pretty jammin music.
The game is fun to play as a casual arcade game, and for $1 you can't beat the value, so I'd recommend it. However there are a few areas where I think this game falls short / could be improved.
-Overall the game feels very slow. I’m sure some users like this / are used to this and so I do not necessarily think it has to be changed for the main game mode, but I personally like fast paced games, and I would like a "Hard Mode" or "Super Speed" mode where everything is faster, your ship, the enemies and how fast the enemies appear on screen. Also I think the biggest difficulty is how cramped the screen gets when it fills up with enemies, for this new mode it would be cool to see the screen expanded so you had more movement space.
-There is not too much diversity in what you are shooting at, I have not gotten too far so there may be more enemies later, but the game is hard enough that you will spend most of your time shooting at circles and the occasional ship before dying and starting over. Since I'm going to be spending most of my time in the first part of the game it should be engaging.
-The powerups still feel a little lacking to me, some suggestions I have for new ones are: lightning, plasma beam, multiple guided missiles, sin wave ray? My favorite powerups are the lightsaber and the one that shoots energy bombs, because they feel unique, the rest are just slight variations on the starting gun.
-With powerups I would also like to see some kind of tier or upgrade system. players want to be able to upgrade their weapons and hopefully be overpowered, this could be implemented in another mode perhaps where along with ammo dead enemies also drop another type of pickup that upgrades your current weapon if you pick up enough. Also I think primary and secondary upgrades should be separate, you should be able to have the shield or magnet with another weapon.
-The coin system feels lacking, I would rather pick up 20 coins per run and need 500 to get the next ship than maybe pick up 1 coin and only need 10. If i play a round and get no coins, it feels unsatisfying, also different tiers of coins would be fun, red, blue green, and different values for each
-The main upgrade system could also be reworked, buying new ships is nice, and I know you cant have too much change due to the leaderboards, but as a player I would like to be able to permanently upgrade my ship or have some external options to use my coins and feel like I have a sense of progression.
In closing: More enemy variation, crazier powerups, more upgrades, and a sense of progression would all be additions that would make what is already a good game into something with more replayability and addictiveness.

: "this game is going to be great! I can't wait!"
: "I won this game in a giveaway... can I give it back?"
: "okay, I'll just give it some time."
You will experience many feelings throughout your own playthrough of
. Whether good or bad,  this game does have potential. While what is has to offer has been presented in a very clunky and buggy format, in the back of our mind, we ultimately have to remember that this is an "EAG" (and requires a little more TLC than most).
Your mission is to survive during an unforgivable era, where the plague is apparant and danger peeks from every corner. Various classes offer their own unique benefits; your goal is straightforward though: survive. In order to, you must either scavenge camps that are littered throughout the map, hunt for wild game, mercilessly murder guards and bandits, and gather food (ranging from wild berries, carrots, cabbage, etc.) In a nut shell, your typical survival game.
So, what does
have to offer beyond this description? Well, let's get down to business:
I'm not going to sugarcoat it: the interface is terrible. There are windows all over and, overall, it's just an unorganised mess that got under my skin within minutes. Hopefully this will be addressed and improved with future patches.
Unless you own an actual gaming computer, you will not be enjoying the beautiful graphics that
has to offer. This is, in my opinion, one of the biggest pluses of the game. Unfortunately, due to my non-gaming setup, I am unable to experience thie game in its full glory. If you are blessed enough to have an amazing rig though, pay attention to the detail in the environment. How the grass ripples through the land. How the fog settles through the dark environment that you call "home". All in all, they truly did an amazing job...
... But then you have what I like to affectionately call "the derps". What are "the derps"? Well... the boar that zooms away from you after you attempt to kill it. The militia men who develop deep cuts on their back yet remain stationary (but then suddenly zoom away from you). This includes the deer as well: anything that moves, it will zoom away. I'm going to take a guess and say that the developer's are really into
.
The audio is another big plus: it offers an accurate depiction of the sound of a boar, gathering berries and stuffing it into your knapsack, trees rustling, and, not that I have any experience in this (I swear!) the 'whoosing' sound of a weapon flying at, and into, someone, etc.
While I am still not a big fan of the controls, it has improved slightly since the latest update/patch. CAPS LOCK is no longer the "menu" button, and "E", which is the "pick up" key (kind of important), actually works now (and in unison with the left mouse, too). Other controls could be made a lot easier. Keep up with the improvements.
+ Gameplay is a little more optimised and smoother than before.
+ The audio has a lot to offer and is of good quality
+ Overall, the graphics are amazing. More on this in the "Con" section.
+ Better use of some keys - you no longer have to hit "Caps Lock" in order to open menu.
+ Servers have definitely improved a lot since I first wrote this review. Before, you couldn't evenenter one, but now you can. It does take awhile to load, but that may be due to issues on my end.
+ Developer's are very active on their forums. They are willing to address the many issues of the game and have been working to better improve the game play experience. While there still remains many problems, hopefully they are all worked out and the developer's can offer the vision that they truly hoped to present.
- Deer can float.
- Why can't I be a woman?
- Please... PvP needs to be fixed.
- The music is great. Even when you don't want to listen to it, it's great. Please, let me turn it off.
- Clunky design of the interface can make for a very irritating game experience. As of 29 April, the inventory is still a mess.
- The combat system that
has adopted is more appropriate for a late 1990s game. It is unacceptable for its release year and expect it to improve vastly over time.
- Walking into the mountain side is not a treat: you will glitch. I've taken a screenshot if you want to see what I mean. Also, your body will randomly disappear into the mountain side as well - screenshot proof as well.
- Game crashes are not as frequent as people claim them to be. They are apparant, however, yet really only occur once every 30 minutes or so.
- Combat is still extremely glitchy. Last time, aiming at an NPC was next to impossible because you had to be extremely close range. Now aim is still off AND you can see through your own body, thus making it next to impossible to view your assailant. This is not a 1990s game - please fix this.
- The "zoom" glitch is still apparant - I tried to kill a deer and it went different directions quite rapidly. There is no way to approach this deer without startling it, or I'm just doing something wrong. Could there be a "stealth mode" option? Or just fix the zoom's.
- In regards to the combat, NPCs should be rebalanced. As it stands, the peasant class stands no chance versus bandits or guards. Also, if I draw a weapon, everyone shouldn't be rushing me at the same time. I wanted to kill a deer but I guess it was protected by the king: I died to 4 guards instantly - where did they even come from?! They should stop being so sensitive.
For now, I
recommend this game if you are
. As with all EAG's, you are the guinea pig, therefore you will find your experience to be subpar at best. I will be giving this game a tentative "yes" recommendation, however, due to the fact that I find myself coming back - regardless of past experience. I really do have high hopes for this title and will update this review the more I play the game.
Since my last review, the game has still not been updated. When a game has a 19,99$ price tag, I expect patches and updates to be frequent - especially when it's in Early Access. The developers, while friendly and willing to work with the community, have thus far failed to live up to expectations with their updates (which, I repeat, are infrequent).
I decided to give the game another go, and I really do find myself enjoying it a lot more now that I've familiarised myself. I'll reiterate this again: get this game if you're into EAG's. If you, however, would rather have a finished product, avoid this game like the plague (no pun intended).

Before you read my review, know that I only got 75% through before ragequitting.
This game is interesting and has many aspects that make it interesting, but ultimately, not worth the playthrough.
First of all, I really enjoyed the visual aspects, how well it "played" (controls, etc.), and the overall aesthetics (visuals, sounds, environments, etc.). I thought the story and characters were interesting and piqued my interest initially. Furthermore, the city and it's elements caught my attention while I played. It's important to note that the motion capture or animation (not sure which) used in this game did a great job in capturing how people move and I think is very realistic.
That all being said, the game left a tremendous amount to be desired. Initially and as I progressed, the story failed to engage me. So his lady-friend is dead, why do I care? He doesn't answer to anyone as he is a thief and nothing more: why is he so selfish? Why are there thieves and no other real criminals? So much of this seems 2-dimensional, so to speak.
The gameplay also made me upset. While this "master thief" is very good at stealing and can slink through the shadows with his cool gadgets, climbing abilities, and impressive stealth, why does the combat aspect of this game fail so miserably? He can swipe cups, jewels, letter openers (I'm going off the top of my head) but the sword on the ground in front of you isn't available despite the guard that is clearly about to kill you? There is no easy way to defend yourself?
The controls occasionally fail to impress as well. Even remapping key bindings does only so much, especially as it seems like your only option is to run away.
Furthermore his "powers" and upgrades take a lot to unlock and still only make so much of the game more playable and barely so at that.
Honestly I think anything out of the Assassin's Creed or Splinter Cell lineup would be better than this. I've thought about reinstalling it but on second thought, I have better things to do.

A game as dark and desperate as its subject material. Until you learn how to play it.
The atmosphere, the art, the music. It's a beautiful package. The first couple plays through this game really did have an impact emotionally and psychologically. The characters are so real it's easy to become attached to them, it's hard to see them make the tough choices. The gameplay is tight, the UI is clear and useful. The other people you run across can be simultaneously familiar and yet coldly distant. Doing the dirty work that must be done to survive is exciting and immersive. You know you're being awful, and don't want to be caught doing it.
Once the effect wears off, and you begin to approach the game from a strictly technical perspective, it becomes quite easy to stay alive. It also becomes fairly simple to plunder every structure you come across and leave none standing to tell the tale. The various story customizations and additional characters and locations to incorporate make the game strongly replayable, but you won't unlearn the important lessons of your earlier attempts.

I got this game a wile back (wintersale i guess) and kinda ignored the fact i really have it. So i played the "usual" games i play normaly. So a wile back, i was looking into my games which are existing somewhere in my big "library void" and found this game again and gave it a try.
From the very first moment, i know, this game let people change their mind (or at least let them think twice about stuff) and that this game is not everyones "cup of tea"...
Its hard to explain the game but i try it. As i said, this game is not really for everyone since it could make people very fast "depressive" since its dark and "hopeless" from the very first moment.
The game begins with a quote which tell us
This "quote" alone already tells us how the game works at most. You play not even a handful civilians which have their own backgroundstory, "abilitys" and "rating" of the war. Some of them might already start hurt, sick or like. You have a big house where the people "tries" to find cover from the war which is running outside.
Said that let you maybe guess that you are not a "warfighter" here - you only try to survive the war.
You begin with very little stuff you can find at the house you start so that you actually can build stuff you might need the most, like a bed or strove coz you only have a workbench at the startpoint. You also can work at your home and "people" at the day time coz this time is the "quite time" where you need to repair your home, eat food, get sleep, build stuff, smoke, drink coffee (yea, the last 2 ones are even part of the game...), trade and much more.
Thats just one side of the game and, in my opinion, the more easier one. The hard one is the Nighttime alias the "plunder" time.
At the night time, the game let you choose to go outside on a plunder tour or stay at home and cover or sleep. Since in the very beginning, you have nearly nothing and you need stuff, you are more or less forced to go plunder old homes, stores, warehouses and like. This tours are easy at the beginning but as longer the game is as harder it gets the stuff you might need right now. next to this are some people of yours only good in plunder tours with a big bagback wile others might are slow or faster but only can hold a hand full of items.
Wile the day and night time, you also have really to fight with inner moments and moral decisions. Like you have someone who needs sleep but is the best one to go on plunder tours, someone is hurt but is the best one to defend your home, youre nearly out of food but you also need something to burn to keep the place warm and and and. So this means youre forced to leave something behind. At the day time, you might let someone not sleep so he can build XY stuff and give someone else the medicine he actually could also need. At the night time, You might go plunder for some junk and wood to keep the place warm insteed of food wile maybe someone is starving. Its mostly hard to go only for "one opinion" since the stuff you might have (or need) is only that much to keep the house and player running for maybe the next 2 days...
At the night time on the plunder tours (mostly in the later game) you also might cross your ways with bandits or even the army or sharpshooters which will harm you for sure and might kill you. Since your people are  not armed (at the beginning) or even not "build for war", you should avoid such confrontation of any kind or youre losing your people very quickly. Next to this is the "fight system" more or less sometimes pur luck. You maybe have a knife and the "enemy" a gun and you go close combat but maybe your guy hasnt slept well or he is already hurt or sick. that all makes it harder for the one you sended to plunder to fight actually, next to this if you might fight innocent people your people can lose moral or even get desperately or depressive, which let them work slower or forget about things they might should do, like guard the home.
This War of Mine is really a great made game which let people really fight sometimes with their innerself. You have really moral decisions to choose and think about the consequences which might happen.
which enjoy survival games or games like Organ Trail, which is also in the same style at least but not for people which maybe cant stand the pressure of moral decisions.
