As the game begins, we find our depressed, bitter, and cynical protagonist Susan Ashworth on the floor of her flat. Susan has just downed 34 sleeping pills in an attempt to end her life and she passes from the world but is plucked from the brink of death by a supernatural being who tasks her with finding and killing 5 individuals who thrive on the pain and suffering of others. Susan finds out that she has a crucial advantage over these "parasites," as the narrative calls them: she cannot die. In fact, throughout the game Susan will be maimed and killed in brutal ways but shortly comes back to life, unscathed. You might think that this takes away from the game's tension, but it only adds to the atmosphere. Susan's life is a living hell, partially of her own creation, and she has no escape from it.
The game deals with some pretty heavy issues such as depression, suicide, substance abuse, and many other typical "adult fears." Although it has several moments that are borderline or full-blown jump scares, most of the horror comes from what the game puts right in front of you, plain to see. The game runs at a low resolution and the character animations are somewhat jerky, but part of me believes that this was an aesthetic choice and the game works beautifully even with said limitations. The narrative is excellent, if short (I finished in 7.5 hours) and even manages to be somewhat uplifting when all is said and done. I'd recommend it to any fans of classic adventure games or fans of horror in general. It's one of those low-profile gems that is a rarity in modern gaming. It will stick with you LONG after you stop playing.

Predynastic Egypt is a resource management and optimization game in which you overcome trials and ordeals and establish Egypt as unified kingdom.
From humble beginnings with simple decisions to make to managing a large amount of workers while planning several turns ahead, Predynastic Egypt offers a pleasant if a bit simple of an experience. There aren't a lot of different mechanics involved, but they do not need to be. With a simple foundation and easily controlled, intuitive basic gameplay you'll be able to manage your tribe and deal with what Egypt has to offer. Multiple difficulty options allow you to customize the game to your liking while everything is explained in enough detail that you will not have to worry about not knowing what is going on, though it still doesn't give you more information than you really need.
One concern is replayability. As it is the same map every time, with the same ordeals every time at the same turns it becomes predictable and later playthroughs will feel repetitive. At the highest difficulties, it's all about solving everything perfectly, with perfect timing on everything and good luck on the random events. If you enjoy achievement hunting, you will get plenty of replayability out of it, but otherwise there isn't much reason to play it a second time.
As for the trials and ordeals, they are challenging when you first go through them, but fair. With a bit of planning and forward thinking you can win the game on your first try. Playthroughs after the first will make it a lot easier and unless you actively avoid doing them it is difficult to really fail at any of them.
A relaxed atmosphere and simple base mechanic means this is mostly a casual game, pleasant to play and worth the time to get it, Predynastic Egypt does what it tells you it does, does it very well, and overall delivers a good experience at a good price.

Bit Blaster isn't the best game out there, but it's fun enough that I got about an additional hour of enjoyment out of it for the purposes of this re-reveiw (see below for old reveiw).
While many of my old criticisms still stand, the recent update done by the developer Nickervision added enough new content that I found it more worthwhile to play (now on my newly unlocked fourth ship which I quickly came to prefer over the previous three).
Much of the combat is as I described before, but I'd like to reiterate how the powerups are the best part of this game. They often change the way the game is played in ways both large and small. with some, the best strategy is to be calm and fire conservatively like with the blue explosive power up, while with others, the best strategy is to spray and pray, like with the richocheting pink power up. I quickly found ones that I prefered. My favorite was always the purple one that acted like a short range shot gun.
Of course, minor critisisms became more pronounced the longer I played. It's often very easy to take multiple hits in quick succession for ships with shields due to the lack of invinsibility frames. The scoreboard is pretty meaningless and hard to get to considering this is a game where the only goal is to get a high score.
In fact, after a while, the game gets pretty samey. Since the score is such an after thought, the only reason to play the game is for the game's own sake. Once every round of bit blasting feels like the last one, it starts to get boring. After the first few ship unlocks, it takes too long to get the next ship for that to be a proper motivation to keep playing.
Still, for all it's faults, I had a decent ammount of fun with it. For the price of a dollar, I think it's worth a try, especially if it's on sale.
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Ship combat is not Bit Blaster's strength. Bullets only eject from the front of the ship, and the ship can only go forward with an incredibly large turning radius. It's clunky. That's not to say that you can't get good at it, it's just not fun to get good at.
What is Bit Blaster XL's strength then? well, it has some kick♥♥♥♥♥music. That alone kept me going for longer than I would normally have.
I think the real strength of Bit Blaster is its power up system. Each power up is completely unique and has the potential to be completely game changing. Sure, there are the mundane ones that just make you fire faster or also shoot from your butt, but there are also the ones that make large balls the same size as your ship bounce off the walls of the screen, filling the entire thing with your bullets, or the ones that make explosives that blow up everything in front of your ship, or the one that gives you a short range laser that makes you have to get up in the business of anythin you want to kill.
They're pretty sweet, I'll admit.
Still, it's not enough to carry the game for me. The terrible controls really hinder the game, and the space ships that I unlocked before quitting were pretty lack luster. Maybe someone else will find it more fun than I did.

So, my thoughts on this one? It's a very pretty game. Faux-Nepal is appropriately exotic for the setting. All the gameplay mechanics from Far Cry 3 have been smoothed including the UI. The main antagonist(Pagan Min) is easily the most interesting person in the game, and happily is around until the end - I liked having not one but multiple times to either execute him or spare him, but of course I shot down his helo without an eye blink cause he's a ridiculous mass murdering psycho, but I appreciated having the option not to. Same with Sabal and Amita, although to be fair there should have been an achievement for tracking them down after the end credits and then killing whichever one you sided with in-game, because frankly they both needed to die to, and here again I appreciate the trouble Ubi Montreal went to to set up a final cutscene for each of them after the end credits where you could see either of them at their worst and then gun them down. I just think it should have been an achievement.
Also, the mountainous terrain felt authentic, which means that walking anywhere meant having to CLIMB, and climb, and climb, and climb, and climb, and climb, .....and basically I wouldn't have bothered with half the side quests in the game without the addition of the helicopter to the available vehicles. Also the radio towers weren't supposed to be annoying in this game, but they that's a big fat lie.  Luckily, you can use the helo to fly to the top of most of them.  The helo plus the thumper also a great time.
In Far Cry 3 the bow and arrow was my favorite weapon. In this game it was made redundant very quickly by the inclusion of the signature weapons silenced M14clone(better range, better firepower, just as quiet). Alternatively, the signature weapon version of the MG42(nicknamed Buzzaw) was just the most fun I've had with an FPS in ages. It was just so satisfying mowing anything down, flunkies, heavies, rhinos - basically it turns the most annoying baddies into gnats to swat.  Fans of the anime film Jin Roh should get a kick.
Fuun stuff to do:  Shoot down a helicopter with a mortar.  Wingsuit into fortresses and procede to take down everyone without being detected(total badassery).  Do all the nanimal control quests with the Buzzaw, and madman giggle the whole time:)
Some ideas for DLC - 1) eagle shoot , ie set up an anti-aircraft gun in the game where the player can shoot down eagles with a flak cannon. Also a mini-game where the quest is to eradicate them from the map wouldn't hurt either.
2) Do the same for wolves, rhinos, tigers, dholes, leopards and any other animal that started chewing on my leg while I was trying to set up a quiet headshot during a mission objective.
So 4 out of 5 ultimately. The game is more polished than it's predecessor, even though I have to be honest the story isn't quite on the level of Far Cry 3.  Just not as engaging.
P.S. No seriously, I want an achievement for gunningdown Sabal or Amita after the end credits roll. And an Eagle shoot, I HATE those f*&^ing things.

What is it?
This War of Mine is a third-person survival game, based loosely on the events of the Siege of Sarajevo, during the Bosnian Civil War.
The game has you control a series of unique civilian characters with the sole purpose of outlasting the war. The odds are pitted against you, as the weather, aggressive bandits and a scarcity of resources all conspire to kill you.
What works?
This game is incredibly successful in translating the atmosphere of a warzone. The gameplay elements help to drive home both the depressing nature of war and the central theme of the game; the battle to survive in a world of scarce resources.
Two elements in particular are worth focusing on…
Weather:
The weather system is brutal, and once the Eastern European winter swarms in, the ceaseless fight to stay warm and healthy begins. Temperatures quickly drop below freezing and your characters’ only hope is to focus all their energy on staying warm. Should you fail to keep your shelter warm, your characters will get sick, and this sets into motion a whole range of trade-off decisions trying to heal your sick.
Medication is not easy to come by and far too expensive to buy through trade. This then leaves you with two options. First, set out at night into the dangerous inner city, littered with trigger happy snipers and hope like hell that you scavenge some medication from the rubble of fallen houses. Second, divert all your resources you were using in keeping your healthy survivors warm, to set up a herbal factory and produce the medication yourself. This is incredibly time-consuming though and your quest in healing one member of your shelter may result in the death of all the others anyway.
Bandits:
As the battle to survive intensifies, bandits emerge and aggressively invade your shelter in the hope of stealing your precious resources. These resources must then be spent in shoring up your shelter with a series of makeshift fortifications to keep future bandits out. Fail to do this and you will return home with your supply store looted. You can always put somebody on guard, but leave him without a weapon to defend himself, and he will suffer an injury, leaving you with another mission of trying to keep one member of your team from dying while simultaneously not jeopardizing the lives of the rest.
In both these situations each choice becomes an exercise in compromise; a tradeoff. Do you try save the sick/injured and potentially jeopardize the chances of survival of all other members, or do you allow the one member to die and risk sending the remaining characters into severe bouts of survivor’s guilt and depression?
A quick word on aesthetics:
I found the music to be monotonous and bland, but although it is not spectacular, it rather ironically helps reinforce the atmosphere of the game, the feeling of a bleak, endless war.
There is obviously no multi-million budget for the game, and as such, no next-gen physics were used to deliver the game’s graphics.
This didn’t result in poor visuals though. Instead the game is delivered through a sereis of beautiful pencil sketches which helps reinforce the theme of resourcefulness; taking what you have available and making something worthwhile out of it.
Where it fell short:
This game does drag on at times and there is no way of speeding it up. An option to speed up gameplay or even to pause and strategize without the game screen blurring would be great! The option to minimize the game to your desktop without having to completely exit the game also seems like an intuitive feature missing.
In Sum:
The successful creation of a warzone atmosphere, the attention to resourcefulness and strategy, right down to the extreme difficulty of the gameplay, combine to make this game one of the most successful l’ve ever played, at achieving its core, thematic goals.
I would highly recommend this game at 8 out of 10.

Very short review this time, if I went for a longform review, it'd get heated and more biased than I personally wish to keep it.
Pros:
- Cool mechanics of either controlling the battlefield as an RTS commander in building buildings, researching a VERY tiny array of technologies and upgrades, and using strategy to outmaneuver the enemy commander, or by using tactics as an FPS soldier where your reflexes, aim and reaction skills are more important.
- Nicely implemented point capture system where soldiers must capture points on the map to generate resources the Commander uses for literally everything.
- Maps are very varied, and have a usually large area to play in, having plenty of side paths to flank the enemy with in a few maps.
- Each class has a sub-class archetype, and you can unlock little boosts as you level up your account or classes which can further make your class more versatile, such as a shield at a high account level which ignores a shot but refreshes slowly, and more damage or ammo.
Cons.
- AI seems utterly barebones. Every single map usually has one or two ways one or two AI can get stuck on the environment. AI commonly get stuck in corners on their way to something, with no scripts to avoid getting stuck walking and then jumping into a corner. AI commonly get stuck inside buildings, and they then get literally stuck IN buildings while they're constructing.
AI sometimes don't even fire at enemies, while the other team's AI is fast to start shooting at all enemy targets.
AI almost never attacks buildings, if they do, 9/10 times they hit a building, they're shooting at an enemy soldier.
- No way to instruct AI to be a specific arrangement of classes/subclasses in a player-empty multiplayer server.
- AI Commanders aren't a thing, making singleplayer matches, or player-empty multiplayer games only you are in... pathetically easy to play as a commander.
- The most I've seen in a single multiplayer server in the last couple of weeks, is only aronud 4-6 players. Out of around 10 servers, only one ever has players, not including two "players" whom are only just bots in spectate mode (I can only imagine).
All problems with AI mean nothing in a full multiplayer game, however I'm certain that won't happen anymore.
- AKA: Not enough people playing the game period.
- Building placement is often arbitrary in every map. Sometimes you can't put buildings down in some open places, while you can put buildings inside of some level geometry, like walls, railings, and even poles.
- Buildings like to teleport or randomly spawn on some servers or maps, placing inside other buildings, and sometimes even in walls of the level.
OTher than those things, the game is fairly decent. It literally just needs more players to play more often.
Note: I do realize that it is Summer, but my points still stand either way. Those who play video games, will play them still. The fact that they work, or go to school, doesn't really influence it all that much, not really IMO.
As it stands, the game is sort of dead. There are atleast 4 daily players, but still. This is a game designed for full 32 player games, and I've never seen that happen in this game in the entire time I've played it.
I still recommend this game however, as... if more people own the game and play it consistently, then honestly the game is a total and complete blast.

1. Listen to customer feedback in any noticeable way shape or form.  Seriously guys, get on it.
2.
release a product that has the bugs FIXED.  That said, if they started listening to player feedback they could probably find bugs faster and get them fixed, but that's slightly beside the point.  Every patch comes with a LONG list of bugs they found but either didn't bother to fix or couldn't get to it?
Seriously Stainless, get it together and fix what could be an amazing game.  People would be far more willing to drop money on your game if it worked fully and didn't have ridiculous bugs that should have been fixed long ago still hanging around.  I know I would be perfectly willing to drop $25 on this game if the bugs were actually fixed. Anyway, sorry for the wall of text for readers, but long story short: if you were looking for a perfect M:tG experience on the computer with fancy graphics and a comfortable UI...you aren't going to get that, but you are going to get an interesting experience of its own that, while it has a lot of problems, is very much its own game. I believe it's safe to say that The Cat Lady is the "Silent Hill" of adventure games. The story ain't overly long but very creepy and very well told. It's a trip into the deepest and darkest corners of the soul of Susan, the main character in this game. She's suffering from depression and decides to commit suicide. What happens next is a soul trip of surreal horrors where she faces and challenges the darkness that tortured her soul for years of her life.
The game has got quite a few shocking and disturbing moments and with its elements of depression, suicide, murder, perversion and violence it's clearly not a story for children. And the visuals add to this. The graphics style is quite unique and hardly ever used in games. Have a look at the screenshots and videos. Long parts of the game are quite monochrome, others play with colors some, which greatly adds to the atmosphere. The quality of graphics is not top
notch. The whole execution of the game is not, but hey, it's an indie adventure and what really counts here is the
art of story telling. I think lovers of classic adventure games can easily forgive the low native resolution of the graphics, the sometimes toenail-curling voice acting and the lack of mouse controls (you play entirely with keyboard only) as the game rewards you with a truely creepy story in a truely creepy setting. Fans of psycho horror stories should definitely give it a try.

"Have you ever felt like a game was made just for you? Like it was pandering to your own sensibilities and sense of humor?"
Yeah...
The Cat Lady is a 2D sidescrolling adventure title that features dark, macabre settings and situations. If you're sensitive about suicide or think mental illness is merely matter of willpower, you might not enjoy or understand this game.
If you want to know enough about the story, I'll talk about it here, but it'll be blacked out for those who wish to skip this part of the review.
The voice acting usually hits the mark and I feel like a lot of the characters are actually having a conversation instead of reading lines. There's a few actors who felt phoned in (two, in fact), but they're so minor it didn't really bother me.
The puzzles aren't really difficult, but sometimes finding the right item or information to progress can be frustrating. Exhausting all of the game mechanics will help you out though, as you can grab, use and examine objects, and the adventure game pro in you should always do all these things. Sometimes though you will have to just mess around with fussy positioning of your character.
There is a problem with some of the layering taking up massive amount of resources while in the highest "resolution". The resolution is probably actually 800x600, but there is some texture options that the setup offers that allow you to make the game look as it was intended with crisp background. The character models suffer a little and look a bit pixelly, but I didn't think that detracted too much from this title being that it didn't require mechanics that revolved around precision.
There are multiple endings, but I just played through it once and the ending was really emotionally satisfying.
All in all, I'd say that I really, really enjoyed my time with The Cat Lady and I think people who have similar dark tastes as I do would as well.

Lots of people say Civ BE is a game that dissapointed them. I am not one of those people. Don't get me wrong, BE isn't as good as Civ IV or V, but it isn't bad either. This is a futuristic game, not a historical one. Firaxis had to either make a plot or simply put people on another planet, and nowadays, a game without a plot is almost a forfeit. (Unless you are a indie dev, I loved Downwell.) People had to realize we were going to get fictional characters, because seeing Oda Nobunaga fighting Pachacuti of the Inca isn't going to be as interesting in the 30th century as it would in the Middle Ages. Overall, Firaxis needed to please it's hungry Civ fanboys, who didn't like Civ V as much as Civ IV, (I don't believe Brave New World was out yet) and neither DLC nor Civ VI was a good gamble. Playing it safe be making a game using the engine of another one is genius. Thats how Donkey Kong, Legend of Zelda, and SMB2 were born. The game is fun, and the unique gameplay makes for a great experience for fans of Civ and XCOM.

Beyond Earth is truly a very under-rated game. The biggest two reasons why there are so many negative reviews are:
1. some customers they are Sci-Fi fans. What they were expecting before purchasing were spaceships, laser guns and high-intelligence aliens. There are so many sci-fi products on the market, and most of them are focusing on combat, unlike Beyond Earth.
These customers didn't expected that in this game they will have to spend hundreds of turns to FINALLY see what they really want to see at the beginning.
2. some customers they had a deep experience with Civ 4 or Civ 5, they are real "history fans". They love to see those countries, cultures, leaders and weapons they know appear in game. However, this game Beyond Earth, I have to say, will certainly disappoint them.
3. some customers, when they are playing the Civ games, instead of enjoy the sence of human-history, they perfer the concept of the "Anthropology". They dont need to be Anthropology major, but they really love to spend some time every day to silghtly learn and experience the human society development process, in a causual way like gaming. For these customers, i would say they might like Beyond Earth, they might not like it.
But, regarding the quality of the game development, nice UI with Sci-Fi taste, nice features, highly detailed terrain, plants and alien-animals are great imagines! And most importantly, the BGM, they are, although not as cultural as Civ 5, but BGM in this game they are matching the space theme, and they sounds EPIC!
To some extent, this generation of Civ, Beyond Earth, is an art-work! Worth collecting! Even if it fails to fully re-cap the Anthropology concept.

*April 16 UPDATE*
Just the fact that the developer continued to reach out for 1 customers personal opinion gives me hope that the future of gaming isn't entirely doomed.  More devs should follow suit.
The addition of two game modes supporting both auto fire and non-auto fire is such a simple thing, but it makes a huge difference by giving the player the option.  I found the selective firing method provided a gaming experience that made me feel much more in control of the game rather than before where it was just a monotonous exercise in moving around.  You can time your shots and WAIT for enemies to position based on the type of special powerups you have now.  Originally the simple premise of the game was part of its charm, but also highlighted some flaws.  Putting the timing of movement and firing back in the player's control adds that little strategy that was missing before.
For the price, now I would definitely recommend this game.
*Original Review below (Negative)*
I like the concept of the game, but after about 45 minutes, you'll have all the achievements (except the higher score ones) and nothing else to do.  Even something as simple as some score multipliers would keep the game fresh a little longer.  With that said, the thing that needs the most work is the auto-shooting.
I'm not entirely opposed to the auto-shooting mechanic.  I mean, it's the developers game so it's his/her choice, but one thing that is unsatisfactory about it is the fact that as soon as you press "start" to begin a game, there about 5-6 enemies that slowly spawn over about 30 seconds, but your ship is forced to shoot off in the distance for what boils down to probably a 10% accuracy rate simply because there is nothing to shoot.
Now, no one cares about accuracy, it's not even a stat to track in this game, but I bring it up because of the simple fact that there is no DEFAULT unlimited ammo so when you run out of ammo (because you're forced to shoot into the void remember?), you simply STOP SHOOTING.  That's it.  The game is a SHOOTER!
What should happen is one of two things:
1.  If you have a special weapon and run out of that type of ammo, your ship should default to regular unlimited bullets.
2.  If you don't have a special weapon, you should never run out of the default bullets.  (Think Contra for the NES).
I'll change my review if the default bullet issue is addressed.  It's just not fun.  Even for $0.99.

Overall a nice indie title worth more than its price! You might have more fun with this than some overpriced AAA titles.

This game is a perfect example of the potential of video games. The media often portrays gamers as killers and claims that the Call of Duties and such make us unempathetic. This War of Mine is a huge middle finger to those people.
I bought this game during the Steam Sale with very little knowlege about it other than it was a shelter game. It has two stages, Day and Night. During the day you are in your shelter, building things, prepping, answering the door etc. At night one of you goes out to scavenge for food and risks being murdered or having to murder. It sounds so simple but damn, this game will rip your soul out and stamp on it.
The game isn't preachy or anything. It is your own empathy that punishes you for the things you do. The game gets into your head to the point you are really invested in these characters. It takes a long time to progress so you get really invested in the survival of these characters and caught in a difficult situation.
You must scavenge, you need to look after your family, but at what cost? You have the options to kill and steal, but doing so will mean intense guilt tripping.Your characters aren't killers, they're firefighters, students, normal people caught in a terrible situation. The masterful A.I. in this game means each character is not a generic badguy but a real person. Maybe you kill a woman who was going to alert the gunman in the house, only to find the gunman doesn't shoot you, he breaks down crying and ignores you as you loot his house. And as you loot you find a note and realized you just killed the light of his life and that your actions will probably cause this man to take his own life.
Perhaps you get cornered and your only choice is to fight your way out, you limp back to your house and discover that your actions have caused an elderly couple to be left defenceless to raiders. Maybe this game convinces you not to steal and murder and so you let you characters get sick and die because you don't want to hurt anyone... That's the sort of game this is. We wont see the mainstream media talk about a game like this, because it brings out the best in us, in the worst of situations.

While the game is fine and good, it's exactly what you expect from Magic: The Gathering. Problem is on the back-end: the game does crash unexpectedly (rarely) and the video options aren't great. Not that I was expecting marvellous visuals from a card game. Just feels like the same engine they've been using since Magic 201X, with all the bugs that came with it.

If you're looking for a F2P alternative to paper or Magic Online, you may want to look elsewhere.  The game is designed specifically to never give you the full MTG experience.  The only formats available for multiplayer are a very limited Modern Constructed and Two-Headed Giant.  No options for Limited, no Commander/EDH.  While the game has every set from Origins onward, it does not contain every card from those sets.  It only has enough cards to give you a basic idea of how those sets' mechanics work, as well as a general idea of their flavor.
This is not a game designed for experienced, hardcore MTG players.  This is a game for people who're interested in trying out MTG before spending money and for returning players who're looking to re-learn how the game is played.  In this regard, I can't recommend it enough.  The tutorials and deck building guides are great learning points, and the Story mode lets you familiarize yourself with some of the characters who make frequent appearances throughout the different sets.
The only real complaint I have is that as more sets come out, it becomes harder and harder for new players to be competitive, as they have to rely on the complete RNG from booster packs to get cards for their decks.  Hopefully they'll introduce an option to get individual cards from a set at some point.

Beautiful visuals and perfectly elegant sound combine with tight, responsive controls and an intriguing dark premise in Momodora: Reverie Under the Moonlight.
At first, I was daunted by the difficulty, even at the easiest difficulty. However, I soon remembered my old adventuring skills from games I grew up playing. Despite the welcoming art style, the game is not easy in any sense of the term, but it is fair, and that's something a lot of games now don't have. You'll notice, when you play Momodora, that a mindfulness to level design is present here. It's subtle -- which is part of why it's so excellent -- but the developer clearly put a *huge* amount of care into making sure everything was fair.
Speaking of which, the developer is also quick to respond to any question or request for help from the community, and clearly cares about players' enjoyment of the game. That really rated highly with me, especially when the game itself is already so well-made.
The story is a little minimalistic, and that might be discouraging for some. It's also not a particularly happy story, but it is satisfying in many ways. The dark elements and horror really make the aesthetic work perfectly and, for me, that was part of the strong appeal of the setting's immersion.
Some of the enemies might seem a little cheap sometimes, but really it's more that they're just challenging and later environments can be very tricky. Every enemy has a strategy, just like every boss has a pattern; an exciting added challenge is that if you beat a boss without taking damage, they will drop a special, usually very powerful, item. It adds genuine replay value, which is much appreciated.
Overall, Momodora satisfies and keeps its appeal strong even after completing it. There's great incentive for returning to it, and the developer is so active in the community that there's no possibility you will ever feel abandoned, or that the game isn't a priority to its developer. I'm highly impressed by both game and developer and, as long as you're up for a challenge, I unreservedly recommend Momodora: Reverie Under the Moonlight.

Writing a review about this game, although I haven’t played it for a while now, may sound strange to you, but I can’t let it drown in the abyss that is called Steam. It deals with problems like depression, loneliness, social and moral decay of society, problems that became stronger in Modern times. "Time is Money", isn’t that one of those sentences everybody hears or even says every day? If I ask you, whether or not you can tell me what the name of your neighbor is, how many of you could answer that question? And not to mention that sweet anonymity the internet has to offer, literally forcing millions of people to present their point of view to others, even if they haven’t been asked for.
So what is this all about? Meet Susan Ashworth, middle-aged, cynical, depressive, cat-loving and about to commit suicide. Spending her last breaths with her beloved Tomcat, Teacup, Susan finds herself in another world, not knowing if this is life, death or even something worse. A woman, calling herself “Queen of the maggots”, is waiting there, offering Susan something that will bring her in touch with five different strangers. And it seems like they don’t want to hold a tea party at all.
I won’t
spoil more information about the plot right here because it might alter your whole experience while playing, so let`s have a look at the game’s execution instead. The Cat Lady aims to be a psychological horror adventure, that is divided into different chapters and presented with side scrolling 2D-graphics. Although people seem to look strange, undefined and even ugly sometimes I can’t imagine a better setting for this game, especially in combination with the well drawn and often animated backgrounds. Items will get highlighted if they can be used, clicked or interacted with, some can be stored in a small inventory. Puzzles aren’t very hard at all, the plot is all that matters. Most of the time you have to find Object A, combine it with Object B or interact with Object C, but still there are some really special interactions while playing the game that I will never forget, may they be offensive or simply unique. You will also encounter many dialogues that may have a huge impact on your game or even ending so be aware of what to choose in the conversation trees.
This game is rated 18 and that for some reasons. Violence, murder, suicide, anger, rage,♥♥♥♥♥♥and psychological terror are only the tip of the iceberg of what this game has to offer. Since these themes only refer to human behaviour that has been like this for ages, there is nothing to feel offended about. It is illustrated gruesomely, but never without an aspect of art, like there is even a reference to a certain book of Stephen King that I don’t want to spoil here. Besides that, people who aren’t at least 18 yet may lack some experience in life. Understanding or feeling what this game wants to show can be hard for those who have never felt what living a life can imply sometimes.
Before I start to summarize the points I mentioned above, I want to bring up the amazing soundtrack. It manages to walk the line between honeymoon daylife and the feeling one might get, right before getting engulfed into the abyss of depression and psychotic horror.
I know I wrote a lot above but words cannot describe what playing and finishing this game made me feel. This is easily one my most beloved stories a game could offer, including all its violence and hate. You don`t have to suffer any mental problems to understand how Susan could get into all this but you might need some morbid interest and a big package of black humour to help her through it. I call it an indie masterpiece with great artwork, sound and plot.

This is a great little game! It's like a cross between Sid Meiers Civilisations, and the old city-builder games of Sierra, specifically Pharaoh from 1999. If you enjoy either of these you will likely enjoy this one!
The game is not large or long, as depending on your playspeed and how many playthroughs you do, it will take you between 10-25 hours to complete. And yes this game has some replayabiliy as you are not likely to 'beat' the game on your first try!
You play through the foundation of ancient Egypt. As you follow the path to unification the story explains where, how & why, through text, the history of the period. There are no actual building of the Pyramids, as those where built much later during the dynastic-periods.
The challenge of the game is to figure how to beat it, and this may take multiple playthroughs to do. If this is enjoyable or not is completely up to you, but as a Civilisation & City-builder veteran I really liked it. Also unlike those games, 'where you at one point in the middle of the game feel like you have already won and you just keep pressing that end turn button untill you see the victory screen', this game is actually challenging all the way through untill the end! It's designed with a specific playstyle in mind, not leaving much freedom to do things in multiple different ways. Whereas Civ V has 5 different ways of winning the game, Predynastic Egypt only have 1, and there is only one route to it.
You start off with a single 'worker' or 'citizen' to gather food and scout the fog-of-war with, untill you can gather enough food for your second. You assign these to workers to different tiles for different yields Civ-style. (+food, +production or +culture for ex). The game asks you to grow to three population to complete the first chapter. Later you unlock the ability to build buildings, spend culture for Discoveries and authority for Worship. Discoveries is the research off new stuff, and Worship gives you powerful but temporary buffs (like +1 food per farm for 3 turns).
The goal of the game is to grow your city, encounter local tribes and rival tribal-cities on the map of Egypt, and eventually unifying them into a single kingdom! These tribes you can also raid or trade with; before conquering or integrateing, to add to your proto-kingdom.
Different stages of the game has you complete different obectives to advance to the next stage, often accompanied with timed missions which you can succeed with a Bronze, Silver or Gold rating. These missions can be to build a temple-building for your god, or to defend against an invasion. The ever increasing challenge of these contributes to a much more difficult and interresting end-game. You are told in advance what type or resources you will need for the mission ahead in general, but no details.
Random events also happens that can help you a lot or harm you a lot. These will be frustrating for some players, those who despises randomness.
The occurrence of these can be turned down in the difficult menu, but not removed completely.
The Artsyle of the worker-cards, eventpictures, enviroments, backgrounds (On both Local-map and Egypt-map), are all great! The Iconc art of ancient Egypt is imitated well with lots of details.
Soundesign is also good as background music sets the tone and the ambient sound changes as you scroll over the map hovering over water, fields and cities.
Voice action is completely absent, but would be nice to have since there is a lot of description text...
The U.I design is as almost a copy of Civ V, with some elements like for ex. the dual-map from Pharaoh. This is a good thing!
I only encountered one bug. I was using a worship to give my farms +1 food for 3 turns, but an event popped up changing the worship to a % base insted. This caused all my farms to bugout, giving 0 food and becoming unworkable. This caused me to have -150 food and my population to die in starvation! Nothing I could to change it.
I managed to reload an earlier auto-save, and by doing things differently & in an inferior way I could avoid the bug. I reported to the bug to Clarus Victoria and will update this review if they fix the bug.

Lets try and keep this short. Do I like it? Yes. Do I recommend it to you? Depends on if you like Min-Maxing and replaying untill you 'figure out' the best way of doing things. Also you must have a stomach to handle RNG-events that can ♥♥♥♥ you up if timed badly.
Do you feel the need to have multiple separate, and very different, paths towards reaching the same goal? Personally I don't think this game needs that. You are here to solve a challenge by Min-Maxing and replaying, even if the path is somewhat linear. It's not necessary for every game to have the ability to be played in more then one way, and that is perfectly fine by me.
The management of Civilisations (albeit without the multiple ways of 'winning the game') and the atmosphere & nostalgia of Pharaoh 1999 + the others in that series is what made this fun for me!
You also got to look at the value-for-money. For this low price you get enjoyment for about 10-25 hours, tyring to find the solution for the pussle at hand. Is this good value for you? This cost me 6.99 on a discount, but I would still recommend it at full-price!

This is a fun game. But three things break it:
1. The extremely tight turn limit to achieve victory even on the easiest difficulty
2. The lack of gameplay flexibility to explore alternative strategies because of 1, leading to scripted gameplay where you must follow a fixed path to victory or lose
3. Random negative events that happen anytime, aggravating 1. and 2.
I don't think this game was properly tested on all difficulties. It recommends new players try the easiest difficulty, yet lacks the flexibility for the slightest margin of error even at that difficulty. Even those who manage to complete it on the hardest difficulty can only explain a single way to beat the game. They are unable to explain how to exploit different strategies to achieve victory even though the game gives the impression of such "flexibility" through a diverse tech tree and wide selection of building improvements. This is because the very short turn limit to achieve victory, coupled with arbitrary (by this I mean untested on all difficulties) victory requirements, negates such a notion.
Many available techs and building improvements could not be researched/built in my attempt to meet the victory requirements because of the short turn limit. For example, the tech point requirement for every subsequent tech scales up as part of the progression mechanic and the second last tech just before the victory tech costs 5000 tech points. This is fine in itself except that the victory tech itself costs 45000 tech points, which is a sudden ninefold jump in tech requirements and appears extremely arbitrary just to make the game "challenging" without proper testing on all difficulties as mentioned. Note that I proritized spending tech points only on techs that allow me to reach this victory tech in as short a path as possible to avoid wasting points on unnecessary techs. I also put a high priority to allocating workers on tiles that give huge tech point bonuses each turn and frequently played options that gave tech bonuses. Yet the game ended when I only had around half the required tech points needed for victory.
In other words, you have to play by the script or lose due to the lack of margin for error even on the easiest difficulty as explained earlier. Do not get me wrong. I like challenging games. But if the challenges do not scale according to the difficulty and are not tested for this, and scripted gameplay is forced on the player to win, there's really nothing to look forward to in the game in terms of replayability. This game is just worth a few hours of entertainment and no more than that.

You also can't save during these cut scenes, nor can you pause (unless you're running the game in a window, in which case it will pause if you click away to another application). Sometimes you'll go 10 or 15 minutes before the game goes back into interactive mode, allowing you to save.

Brief version.
- Upsides: Awesome atmosphere, good narrative style, nicely written sidemission, somewhat satisfying main plot.
- Downsides in a word: Gameplay. It isn't too bad, but it's so clearly flawed that it sometimes ruins the upsides.
- Evaluation: 6/10.
Longer version:
I played Thief's games a long time ago, and this pseudo-reboot/follow-up/whatever-it-is isn't anything close to the originals. Honestly, just the drop from 90+ metacritic score to 70 says something about a very wide gap, and that gap is real (and even bigger than 20 points out of 100).
So why the hell do I recommend this game? Because it's still a decent game, and it provides for good entertainment. It is a 6/10 game coming from a 9/10 and 10/10 series, so if you played the previous Thief's titles be warned: you'll be disappointed, mainly by gameplay mechanics. I'll start with the bad to end with the ok.
What is wrong about gameplay?
- Sounds: you can hear YOUR footsteps even when you stay still and turn around (wtf!) but you can't hear a GUARD's footsteps if he's around a corner more than 2/3 meters away. Bad. Plus, into the houses you just hear very loud random footsteps/conversations from the other floors of the building (which you can't access). This this could be very cool if played right, but it becomes annoying since it's too frequent, and the people in the city seems like a bunch of sleep-walkers.
- Random dialogues: while missions and main plot dialogues are satisfying to my taste, you keep overhearing like 6-7 exchanges over and over again while you roam the city, all from the same voices. Are those guys following you? Also, there is a chance that you overhear something useful, pointing you at thieving objectives like sub-sub-plots: cool... except it happened only 2 times in the whole game... meh...
- Stealth is often awkward, mainly for two reasons: sight and sound (again). Sight - you are hidden in the shadows or you are not. In the first event, guards may also walk close to you - too close - they then look your way and they... don't detect you. What? Not very realistic, not in a *realistic* stealth game. In the second event they may see you just right and from afar: it's ok, but isn't there any middle-ground? - Sound - surfaces almost do not matter unless it's glass: you crouch if you want to move silently or you stand to move faster, except on carpets where you can move faster and still be silent: that was so cool when pace of movent and sound were so important, in previous Thief's installments, but now they introduced the swoop: if you want to move fast then just stay crouched and *swoop* around. Noise/speed trade-off doesn't exist anymore.
- Swoop: sounds cool to me, and it really makes you feel a shadowy thief with great skill, but it's just too much prone to abuse. You want to go around faster? Swoop. You want to reach the back of a guard without alerting him when you WOULD alert him if you walked? Swoop. It's so abusable that it seems like a cheat rather than the cool tool it is supposed to be.
- Footprints: they made you leave footprints in a 2002 game (if I remember the year right), now in 2014 you randomly walk into oil, pools of blood and such and do not leave any trail, not even for a few steps. Are you kidding me? That was very disappointing.
AI is ok. Despite the many critics to that, I find the AI consistent enough, if you purge its behaviour from the effects of what's above. Only thing is: you are in a house with only 3 guards, you knock out the patrolling one: good. Wouldn't the other two notice he's missing, after a while? If so the game *realism* would have been so improved... but whatever.
Let's get to the upsides!
- Voice acting: some hardcore fans make themselves disgusted by the voice acting because it's different from how it was before. Why? Get over it, dudes, this one is good and well done.
- Story: it's not a story of overwhelmingly epic proportions, but it's very good and entertainig. Moreover it's very well-balanced between thieving, discovering things (you won't understand half of what's happening unless you search for the documents and read them), supernatural activity, crowd madness when they revolt... a good story, well written too.
- Atmosphere: awesome and very well designed, could only be better with less random-dialogues (see above) and more dialogues giving some insights on the city life. But grafically it's very good.
- Overall feeling: if you are able to get over the downsides, Thief leaves a lasting feeling of... playing a dark gothic, almost satisfying stealth game, and that's why I recommend it.
- Interface design: people complains a lot about it, and I wonder why. Focus makes the game like 100 times easier? Map indicators disturbs you and prevent you from feeling the exploration/orientation stuff you want? Frigging DISABLE it. I played with everything disabled and I like it, but there are many players too used to mmorpg (lost without map indicators) and some players who play to have a good time without having to pay too much attention (they are welcome to use focus). Who care? Let people play the game the way they want. Customizable difficulty/helpers are a BIG upside to this game IMO.
Last thing worth mentioning, not related to the game but to its development. Many of the flaws above were highlighted during early beta stages by fans screaming in anguish. Why didn't the developers listen to the often good advise? Did they WANT to make a mediocre game? That I cannot understand but it isn't a reason to hate the game, rather to despise the developers' hybris.

This game wasn't really built to entertain or inspire, so everyone giving it downvotes because it's not entertaining or inspiring misses the point.
Depression Quest sets out with a very clear goal - to open a window into the mind of someone living with depression - and it does precisely that. It's not a pretty, or exciting window in any way, but then neither is depression.
I only *barely* recommend it though, in that you can spend 30 mins on it, and maybe read one or two things that resonate with your own situation - that, plus I think it's a good thing that alternative viewpoints and experiences like this game get airtime on platforms like Steam. The remainder of my critique is the game itself:
* It doesn't go fullscreen without the background breaking
* There's an example option left from the SDK in the options menu - that's just sloppy workmanship
* The game doesn't explain much about itself
* The music is repetitive (15-second loop or something)
* Some of the fonts are barely legible, a big requirement for a text-based game
Mainly though, almost no creative effort was put into this game. I can accept that the story within it may be deeply personal and was a big challenge to write, but as a game, it's not a good one. No art to speak of, no real thought to user experience, and a tedious journey through the content. Hyperbole and a Half's Adventures in Depression did a much better job of illustrating (with actual pictures) what it was like living with depression, and the walls of text were made navigable.
So, 4/10, if anything, though I would suggest trying it (with an open mind) at least once.

As someone who has suffered from depression before, I can tell you up front that this is no way a good way to portray depression. The guy in the story seems to have his♥♥♥♥♥♥sorted out. Girlfriend, job, house, family and so on. The way you progress through the game is just to keep on picking certain options until you finish.
I always picked the options that were right, going to see a therapist, tablets and so on. This is not how it works. The ending I got seems to think that he just brushes it off as if it was nothing. Depressed people can not just say, "Well, tablets are good. I'm fine now." I don't think the creator of this game really knew what depression really is because it's nothing like the game.
A nit-picky thing is the title. Depression Quest is a stupid name. It sounds like you're on a quest for depression.
However, where the game flops in it's main purpose. It flourshies, sort of, in it's writing. It's very detailed and the multiple choice answers are there and will make you think. Do I want to go to a party even if I don't want to go? Or do I stay in and play with my cat?
But these all seems pointless when the main part of the game, the depression, is so quickly glanced over and easily dealt with. It's as if the game thinks depression is like stubbing your toe, you get a bit hurt, shout a little in anger, then continue your day as normal.
I can't reccomend this game when it's one purpose fails.

As a fan of the Civilization series since the first one, I bought this without even thinking about it, even though I had little time to play it until may 2017, 2 years later.
But I must say this one for me does not hold up to the quality I expect from civilization games at all, and I am not just refering to a couple of design flaws, the game is notorious for getting bugs and have the game crash between turns or during loading a savegame, making me unable to finish my game at all.
I guess if you aimed simply for the shortest path to victory, with no more than a handfull of city's, do not load savegames and play in one single playtrough this is playable, but even that is no guarantee for no facing game crashes. And any game that just does not work properly, even if it has some merit I will have to advise against buying.
Overall this game just lacks the "just one more turn" that for me enbody's civilization, and trades it in for "aim for the shortest path to victory" the hardest opponent you will fight is the constant crashes, and bad game design.
If you love Civilization, I'd advise against buying this one.
Now as for the game features itself
The Bad :

-your diplomatic options to end a war are severely limited : you cannot declare peace no matter how well you fight untill the enemy is willing to talk with you, meaning you'll have to wait many turns after already winning the war. You cannot vassalise your enemy's nor demand a minimum number of turns of peace of them, only a very small bit of their money and perhaps 1 or 2 city's that are much easier to conquer than to politically aquire.
-speaking of war, the AI is acting random, one moment your allied, helping them in war, agreeing on everything they want from you, the next they suddenly declare war for no obvious reason, you may have 9 relationship and 9 fear from them, they still do this.
-trade is non-existant, you cannot sell or buy technology, city's or even strategic goods with the other players.
-you cannot delite city's you build, only hope your enemy conquers them and burns them down.
-you cannot delite tile improvements ever, you can replace them with other improvements, but aside from remove road there is no way.
-if you pillage tile improvements it only damages them, not removes them.
-the ability of satelites to generation new resources only works on uninproved tiles (and you cannot turn improved tiles back into unimproved ones) and this ability gets available to late in game. Also it seems to be per satelite, meaning that in later game when your satelites last 360 turns, instead of 60, you just will have to wait 6 times longer to get those tile bonusses
-it is not possible to move a city from land to sea or reverse as was possible in this games predecessor alpha centauri
-water city's do not culturally expand, and can only take the tiles next to it, when moving, so they can only can grab coastal tiles, not inland ones.
-buying tiles is empire wide, making it insanely expensive to buy more than a handfull of tiles empire wide, further making water city's less usable/.
-it is not possible to culturally push borders or buy tiles your enemy controls
-you cannot change your unit upgrades after you selected one, so you are forced to stick with a bad chooice and/or delay upgrading a long time.
-there are tons on types of impassible and unbuildable tiles, making the concept of controlling the entire map, with hundreds of city's a chalenging puzzle to say the least and not a fun one.
-to few relics on even the largest of maps to unlock all wonders, buildings and ability's, it's always waiting wich one you'll get this time.
-while from a playable vieuwpoint you can control many city's if you not want to lose you still are limited to a maximum of 15, and more realistic 5-8 city's, as every city still increases the cost of reasearch and civilization bonusses and virtues a lot.
-this game even on the hardest difficulty is ridicously easy, oh the AI cheats and will beat you in any victory condition on hard difficulty, but it will build hardly any buildings or units, forcing you to an easy domination victory all day every day.
The Good :
-there are satelites in game that generate new bonus and strategic resources on tiles that not yet have any.
-you can build city's in the water that can move and hence can be relocated to a better position if so needed.
-you can grab a few extra tiles inside your borders by moving an floating city even if those tiles belong to your opponent.
-while you do unlock new units, you can unlock 3 tiers upgrades for regulair and 1 tier upgrade for special units. In every tier you have 1, 3 or even 6 multiple possible bonusses each unlocked by differentpre-requestments and those bonusses do stack alowing for a lot of unit customisation without overcomplicating things.
-it is again possible to own hundreds of city's and still have postibe health, the effects of "corruption" in this game called unhealth, have been tuned down to more reasonable levels.
-while this game still has the hated 1 unit per tile, at least in this game it is per type. I can have 1 military unit and 1 non military (trade unit, worker, settler) working/guarding the same tile, making this limit much more playable.
-lots of ruins to explore that yield relics that in turn can unlock special ability's, buildings or even wonders that cannot be obtained any other way.
-customisable civilization, a custom civ bonus that cannot be changed, though it can be upgraded, and you can pick 3 more, 1 from each group of 8 available bonusses those 3 you can change mid-game if you so please.
-no goverment type, but you get to pick from a wide range of virtues you unlock during the game that grand permanent bonusses, including extra bonusses for having enough of the same tier, or type on top of that alowing quite flexible playtrough.
Overall impression 2/10 : very buggy, and badly designed.

Let me start this off by saying that I have NOT played Far Cry 3 or any other Far Cry game. I hear a lot of people say that this game feels like DLC for Far Cry 3.
This game is amazing. I love the atmosphere and culture of Kyrat. I actually did some digging into Tibetan/Napallese history and culture beforehand, and as far as I can see the game is very accurate.
The core gameplay is very smooth and I was immersed in the game dispite some techincal issues (see below). You start out with a basic set of skills, you can shoot, you can stab, you can drive, you can fly, you can swim. There is a very cut and dry stealth system as well that isn't very extensive but it does the job.
There is a very unique crafting system in which you hunt for specific animals, skin them, and then craft item upgrades. Might I add that there is an extreme variety of wildlife, or at least it feels that way for me. So much so that they can start to annoy you. For example, you're trying to sneak up onto a group of enemies, when all of the sudden a freaking Eagle decides to swoop down and bite you! AN EAGLE!
Now for the graphics and performance!
Graphics: Pretty damn good. The hard textures like the water and rocks have much to be desired, but the grass and trees look amazing. Far Cry 4 has this "Fur" machanic that is supposed to make the fur look authentic, it looks pretty but sometimes the fur just doesn't look right. You'll see what I mean when you play the game. The lighting also is very pretty. I would recommend that you would keep the lighting on at least "High" because it contributes so much to the scenary.
Performance: It's not an Assassin's Creed Unity, but it still does suffer. A big issue, is when you fly or drive around the game the FPS drops suddenly to 30 and then back up to 70, at least for me. I'm running a GTX 970 on Ultra and even Medium I get dips to the 30's. Ubisoft has been releasing patches so we'll just have to see. Granted, this game is CPU intensive so keep that in mind.

On my second try, I survived 41 days...here's my story.
I began with three characters all working together, one whom is shy and can lurk quietly in the night, another who quit frankly is useless, but can cook well and another who was a hardened rebel soldier that went AWOL.
They began cleaning house is this old abandoned building, all working together to get rid of fallen rubble blocking ways to resource stocked rooms to see how long they had until they needed to worry.
Four days, they had about four days of resources until they needed to panic. I refused to let that happen. As the cook did more cleaning I had the soldier baracade some holes to remove the chances of them beeing looted, I had the shy girl listen to the radio, tuning into the four stations that could save their lives.
Night finally came by and they needed food, I decided the shy one was the most suited for the situation. I gave her a knife and pushed her into the supermarket. That night before she entered a soldier was about to♥♥♥♥♥♥a girl looking for food for her children.
I slit his throat, the girl fled.
Shaking she took the soldiers machine gun and ammo and continued to look for food. She came across barred halls and locked doors, but finally at the top of the building she found three cans of cat food.
One days meal, she fled.
The next day was the same, but as the girl came back from her successful night she was told people attempted to raid them! Nothing happened because they were just a scarred.
Were they though?
More nights go by and the girl is getting the hang of it, lockpicks and files at hand, and a knife hidden away for a stealth kill. She rummaged though areas she thought would be quiet, secret places no one expected to find anything, items with no possessors. But this eventually fatigued her and she needed her rest.
It was the soldiers turn to rumble, with the gun in hands he wasnt afriad to take what would help them survive. Night after night taking from those who he thought would eventually take from them, he was ruthless.
Until the night he barged into the quiet house of an elderly couple.
He kicked the door down, weapon hot and ready to share lead. But his sights only met with old, wrinkled faces of two afraid and confused folk. One was wondering where her hunband went (the one right next to her) and the other was begging for him to not shoot.
He couldnt waste a night, it could cost someones life.
So he continued through the house, looking through cupboards and the fridge, The old bag kept following him "please dont take that! my wife is sick!". The solider kept his head down and went intot he basement, looking around through the scrap. "Please, whatever you do just dont hurt her. We dont have much food left...". The soldeir eventually left, earlier than usual with only the necessities.
Theyll be ok...right?
That night hit him hard, harder than the other nights, he wouldnt leave his bed and the lack of cigarettes didnt help his mood. The cook could only do so much with the food he brought home, and the girl kept by the radio, waiting for the trumpts to call them home.
It wasnt trumpets, but something just as good came up.
The radio man announced that tobacco is becoming scarce, that theres a large demand and the supply is going nowhere but down. This brought a smile to the girls face, as she took her stash of tobacco leaves out. She hasnt felt this good since before the war, which to her felt like a lifetime ago, but only 3 weeks have gone by since she met her friends.
Weeks later and nothing different had happened other than the new stove and beds theyve propped up. The girl heard that it was gonna get colder, also that the rebels have fallen back and gov't troops have moved in, some areas wont be accessible for some time. As the cook cleaned and the solder napped a soft, but obvious tap was heard on the door. The girl opened it, and to her suprise was a man. He was shot, claims a sniper got him btu he ran as fast as he could to get away. He requested to stay, the girl left him at the door and talked to her friends, they had two options. Let him go and fear him coming back to rob them, or letting him stay and the cost of living goes up.
They let him stay.
Days go by, as the radio man said it got colder, the origional trio was tired. It was the new guys turn to pitch in, after all, hes fast and can carry more than the rest. He did this for a while, going out into the night, grabbing what he can then running, bullets wizzing by as he fled.
He was lucky, more than one.
Weeks later, one day after he came back from gathering he opened up the door to blood, that night while everyone was sleeping someone came in and injured the soldier. He was severly wounded and going a little insane. With a lack of bandages all they could was talk him down until he fell asleep.
The soldier fled later that night, taking a gun with him.
With three survivors left, and none with experience in combat they felt a little scarred. They were already tired, depressed and beginning to run out of food, winter was there and burning materials was becoming scarce.
They became desperate.
The runner went out a few nights, specifically to an old church. On the other side were a few people who have kept to themselves but werent afraid to fend themselves from intruders. With no choice the runner went in and took a few cans.
Someone heard him.
He flew down the ladder, a gun in his hand and no warning shot on sight. The runner was hit but ran towards the gunner with a knife and killed him, at this point the others heard the gunshots and ran towards them.
There was no time to loot the corpse, bleeding out the runner paced himself to the exit as the other gunners followed close behind, taking a few more shots at him. Limping now the runner makes it home, barely, before the sun rises.
At what cost?
The runner limped back with the bandaged, to which he immedietly placed on himself when he made it to saftey. Raiders tried to barge into the house again but the girl and cook fended them off. As the runner slept the bleeding off the girl made repairs and the cook did...well...nothing. He could do anything, now he must.
That night he went out with a shotgun. His goal? Food, bandaged and whatever else he could find of value.
He didnt come back.
That night was quiet, but the runner bleed to death.
The girl was alone. With everyone gone there wasnt a need to share food anymore.
But she was alone.
She eventaully had to go out on her own to the last place the crew never went to, because the snipers did.
All she had left was a knife, he one means to survive.
She made it there that night, found a scavenger just like her...as she rummaged through the garbage she found herself behind him.
She slit his throat, he had pills she needed. To her left was a large opening and a gunshot every now and then, she saw someone screaming for help behind a statue.
She ran to him.
Waiting for the bullet to hit the column she hid behind, she ran behind a van and waited again, bang, she ran again, barely making it to the statue.
The man was bleeding.
He asked her to help, he raised his hand in trust.
She did the same as before, he had food on him.
She returned home through the sewer system she found, the fresh corpse was right over the man hole cover.
Once the adrenaline rush left her had she then realized what she had done. She hid in the house, not knowing what to do anymore.
She was raided, no food left.
She was starving, tired, mind rotted from the war.
She killed herself the 41st day, never getting the chance to see the war end the day after.

Level design looks awkward like in many roguelike games, but it is entirely pre-designed. There are some pretty horrendous "puzzle" systems, most of which consist of re-exploring empty areas looking for switches, breakable walls, and de-activated traps to find new routes. Think Metroid-vania but without movement itself being an enjoyable experience. In fact, movement is pretty bad all around. You walk slowly when unhindered and attacking cuts your speed even further.
Also, there's a lives system. Why? Lives were introduced in arcade games to keep people from hogging the machines. There's no reason for this to be here in an individually owned singleplayer game. There's no reason to keep players from continuing and retrying in a pre-designed area, It's understandable in roguelike adventures where there's always something new each time you play, but here all it does is add a cheap attribute of difficulty.
It's a beautiful hack 'n' slash pixel-art dungeon crawler.... Gauntlet without the constant grind of "yer face needs foodz badly!".

Oh boy. This game.
Okay, I have marked that I recommend it, but it has some minor flaws that ruin what could have been a truly great game.
It's SLOW. Slow slow slow slow slow. My god is it slow. After Chapter 2 it's forgivable, but before that it's ridiculous.  So much text, so much voice-acting (which, don't get me wrong, is well done and sounds good), you'll forget you're playing a game sometimes and think you're watching a movie. It's like come on, when do I get to start the ♥♥♥♥ing game?! This IS a game, right?! I was like an hour and a half into the game-ahem, movie, before I finally got to do some puzzle-solving.
The controls. Okay, there's only like two keys in addition to the movement keys anyway, but cut me a break, it's 2015, we should be able to remap keys to wherever we want, in any game. To not have this feature is silly.
I'm not sure how to delete save files, which is a problem, because even if you name a save file the same name as one that already exists, it won't ask you to replace the old one, it'll just create another with the same exact name. Figure that one out. Moreover, where the hell is autosave? I know you can save whenever you want to, but I lost the first hour of progress the first time I tried playing because the game crashed. I was expecting there to be an autosave feature, like almost every other game these days.
You can skip individual lines that people say by hitting spacebar (which took me a little while to figure out, usually it's the esc. key or something), but you still have to wait through the pauses in conversation, and if you're trying to do another playthrough to get that Golden Ending, 99.9% of the dialogue you've seen already.
When you do get to do a bit of actual gameplay, the game is fun and not too heavy on the logic and moon-physics typical of these sorts of games. Immortality notwithstanding, Susan is bound by the same rules as anyone else. It's a little easy, but not TOO easy.
Now, the story itself. The Cat Lady is about a woman who tries to kill herself. She is given a second chance at life, so to speak, by an old woman who identifies herself as the Queen of Maggots. She has to kill 5 "parasites", sick, depraved people whom you won't feel the least bit bad about offing after a bit of plot and character development. All the while Susan works through her own depression and flashbacks of her past life. You'll feel for her and genuinely want to see her through this to the end, and the first parasite you kill will make you feel empowered. This is where the game really shines: Susan and Mitzi are fleshed out, well developed characters, with believable motivations and fears. Anyone who has any experience with depression, their own or someone elses, will relate. A statement about pain, loss, death, the human condition.
The images and settings often take on a psychedelic, surreal twist, and nothing is ever as it seems. There are some scary and creepy bits, but it's not a horror game in the normal sense of the term. There aren't really any jumpscares and that clearly wasn't the intent anyway, the game uses scary imagery as a means to an end, not the end itself.
If you can get past the annoying, stupid game mechanics problems that make the game way more inaccessible than it needs to be, you'll find a game that will keep you thinking long after you've shut it off.

Even though I saw a LP of this game before playing, I still thoroughly enjoyed playing it myself.
The Cat Lady is a dark adventure game starring Susan Ashworth, a woman who committed suicide and is offered a second chance by a mysterious lady who calls herself the Queen of Maggots. She says that Susan must kill 5 people called the Parasites. What happens next...must be experienced for yourself.
Of course this goes without saying, there is minimal gamplay here. It's just puzzle solving/fetch quests. The appeal of the game is the story and characters. The gem of this game is, in my opinion, the platonic chemistry between the protagonist and Mitzi, a woman who becomes Susan's roomate. She has a dark charm to her, and her views on the world along with her sense of humor works wonderfully with the dialogue between her and Susan. They are similar, and yet different enough such that I can emotionally invest in them (it doesn't sound like Susan is talking to a mirror). The other benefit of this relationship is that gives Susan a 3d personality. She likes to close herself to the world, but isn't willing to completely give up on it. She knows that there are good people  in the world, and, after some caution, decides to open herself up to Mitzi, leading to the root of Susan's despair (while the plot goes off the deep end, I might add). Be prepared for the story that goes to some dark, crazy, creepy places. I enjoyed the violent, disturbing imagery and symbolism because it matches the tone and atmosphere of the story. It gives me something to think about, for it is somewhat abstract and cryptic. The aesthetics are rudimentary, black/white graphics with selective coloring, which again, compliments the tone and atmosphere.
What I believe could have been better is a more seamless transition with the animation. There are many spots where there's an awkward delay. For example, moving Susan to chair so she can sit and talk with Mitzi results in her being frozen in place for a few seconds before actually sitting down. A similar issue exists with the dialogue; there are awkward pauses throughout. In addition, this may be because of concerns with audio quality (the developer not wanting the voice actors/actresses blowing out the microphone), but the volume of the voice actors/actresses are inconsistent. What I mean is, the subtitles sometimes indicate yelling, but the actor/actress isn't really yelling. A very small thing, but I would like to be able to delete my save files and turn on/off subtitles during any point in the game.
The one big fault I found with the game was its tie-in with the creator's previous game, Downfall. I don't mind an easter egg or eggs referring to the game. What I do mind is my encounter with Joe Davis, which felt out-of-place with the story as a whole. It came off as tacked-on with no real connection to the game other than more violent, disturbing imagery.
All-in-all, this game, I believe, really nailed the characters, particularly the back-and-forth between Susan and Mitzi. It showed Susan as someone who is going through depression (not just the sadness and the morbid mindset, but the hope of trusting in people again). The story was enjoyably messed up, but never over-the-top violent, and had an emotional pay-off.

I have seen other reviews comparing Predynastic Egypt to Civilisation. Well apart from being turn-bases, the fact that you have to manage your workers and have to develop new tech, the game does its own thing. It also has elements of the old city builder series like Pharaoh. But its more about recreating Hierakonpolis as it was. That means you don't get that much agency over where the farms, temples etc gets to be placed. It's not a sandbox game like that of Pharaoh. You are more guided by historical accuracy when it comes to that. But since I am a big history nerd too I quite like it.
the core of the game is going through the trials of developing Hierakonpolis, first as a small tribal village and then gradually scouting out and developing the area around the city. Hereby making it a hub for farming, worship, craftsmen and the training of your army. Later a map for whole Egypt opens op.
On this map you explore even more and deal with other tribes; trading with them, persuading them to join you or crushing them with your army.
Most of you time are spent on managing your workers. moving them from farming to for instance worship when you need the favour of a god to overcoming a trial/mission more easily. The main goal is to unite the tribes of Egypt, creating a single pantheon and the society that the dynasties of the Pharaohs would rule.
the good things:
- interesting historical setting that is incredibly well researched.
- the small animations of your workers, that look like old paintings from Egyptian tombs coming to life is incredibly well made. It makes the game look a lot more lively. It's almost a metaphor for the core of the game: bringing Egypt's history to life
- Challenges that require you to think and balance food, culture, production and getting new tech. As well as taking over other tribes or focusing on internal deveopment of your capital city.
the features that could use improvement:
- Combat. Currently, it's mostly a numbers game. The ones with the strongest army in terms of numbers wins. There are small battle events that can happen like "the enemy attacks from an ambush!" which is just written in text, nothing the player can do influence about it. I understand that combat is not the main feature of the game but it would be cool with more agency to the player in combat. Being able to choose tactics (like feint, hit-and-run, all-out attack etc) would be an improvement.
- Worker management; being able to at the click of a button to prioritise workers to different resources.  it can be a bit much having to manage every work individually.
Overall a great little indie game with great potential for a sequel - and it's cheap in price too!

I can forgive the absence of the hammers and the pagans, but only just.  What I can't forgive was a plotline that was forgettable enough that I couldn't be bothered to go back and play through the story levels again.  My thoughts may change in time.  If the story levels had been better designed AS levels I'm sure I would have thought differently.
In the end it was enjoyable and worth playing, and if they bother adding some good DLC it could even be great.  Given the layoffs at Eidos Montreal, I don't think that's likely though.  I finished it thinking "I should go back and play Dishonored again".  Not the resounding endorsement I had hoped to give.
