Its fun, and if you like rogue-likes, then sure, go buy it. Worth your money.
If you hate difficult games, however, I wouldn't go for this. The difficulty is absolutely unforgiving. There's an insane learning curve, too. The difference in skill needed to survive the first 2 levels versus the skill needed to beat the first boss is... just insane. Then it's 2 more levels, another boss, and the difficulty spikes are immense. It's also 100% randomly generated, meaning often times you'll find yourself in a totally ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t situation with little to no way to get out alive, or without suffering massive losses.
I get the game is supposed to be hard, I do. And if you're a masochist, you'll love it. But if you want a game to just casually play and enjoy, honestly? This isn't it. It's cute appearance is a sneaky cover for it's brutal difficulty and unforgiving enemies. It's like 2D dark souls. You do very little damage to enemies and enemies take a good 1/10 out of your health bar with each hit - Even more in later levels. That wouldn't even be too bad if healing existed (It does, but it might as well not, since it's so scarce and potentless).
My last gripe is that there's not much that will help you if you're not good at it at the very start. Dying after making "progress" (God knows how the game determines progress, it doesn't tell you) will unlock either cosmetics (Which are nice, but still useless), or new "classes", which are more like little tweaks to your character you can choose before your next run. But don't be fooled. None of them are straight upgrades. Practically every alteration that's good will come with something bad - Like the ranger perk, which will up your ranged damage but make you attack with a pillow instead of a sword. Or the cleric perk, which lets you heal yourself every 2 millenia for an amount that would make a bandage laugh, all while lowering your max health from 100 to 60 and reducing healing from all sources.
I don't mean to bash the game so hard. I just want you to know that this isn't an easy game. By any means. I've been forcing myself to play it for over a year now, normally only after a new update, and I still haven't gotten past the 2nd boss. I think the fun is supposed to come from mastering the combat and health management, and becoming skilled enough to get to the end, but it's hard to want to learn when the game kills you at every possible oppurtunity, often times before you've actually "learned" anything.
Oh yeah, and no multiplayer. Last time I heard, they weren't even planning on adding it.
Final Rating:
9/10 if you like physically and emotionally abusing yourself, or like Dark Souls (same thing, right?)
7.5/10 if you liked Spelunky or Risk of Rain (although it's more brutal than both combined)
3/10 if you just like rogue-likes. I haven't played a rogue-like that's ever been this unforgiving. And you WILL get sick of the level 1 music, very fast. The graphics are charming at first and will stay charming if you like old-fashioned graphics, and there's variety... But once you've seen and done it all, it becomes tedious.
Still gonna recommend it though. To me, it feels like a drug that's amazing, but wears off very fast, leaving you craving something stronger. Too bad it can't really give you much more.

Rupeck Games have taken the formula that made Derek Yu’s Spelunky one of the most beloved indie games of the past decade and tweaked it to provide gamers their own take on the rogue-like action adventure game. It’s a big ask for any studio let alone one that has never released a game onto Steam before. However, what they have to offer thus far in their early access release has left a positive impression not only on me but all but two of the Steam reviews as of writing.
Most important of all the game is already technically sound. The game play is smooth and thoroughly enjoyable. Nothing feels unfair. The graphics are simplistic but it is easy on the eye and allows you to focus at what is most important while the soundtrack has been carefully chosen to provide for deeper immersion. I quite enjoyed that a point of differentiation is that there are plenty of other cave diggers in these levels with you. It is up to you to discover whether they are friendly, apprehensive or literally out to kill you. Can you work with those that aren’t going to kill you or will you attempt to slaughter them to ensure that everything within the level is yours for the taking? Be mindful, however, that they hit hard and can be every bit as dangerous as the slimes, bats and other enemy minions out there. The developer has done a marvelous job at creating their artificial intelligence to the point where many times they feel every bit as much another human controlled player as artificially controlled. In this respect Rupeck Games label the game a pseudo-multiplayer game. The game takes on rogue-like aspects in that the game features permanent death as well as procedural level generation.
The inventory system is one of my favorite aspects of the game. You’ll find plenty of things out there that can aide in your journey. There are quite a few potions that are named after colors, for example, jade potion.  You likely wont ever be told what they actually do and their effects can have a negative consequence (e.g. causing slowness). Using a bad one at the wrong time can aide in your death so be careful!
The only real downside to the game is that it does not have an end point at this point in development. That is to come. So for those of you who like to have a game that has a certain point of closure you will not yet find that here.  Some may argue that the graphics are a little too simplistic but as I said I found them to be acceptable and others may argue that the game is not original enough but and again I would suggest that they need to look deeper into the game.
At a price tag of $4.99 I would suggest that the game is well worth the investment especially considering the potential of a price increase down the track.

Nuclear Dawn is a fun little FPS that reminds me immediately of games like Timesplitters, TF2, Dirty Bomb, Insurgency, and ESPECIALLY Unreal Tournament. It's a class-based shooter with various abilities available as you level up your character. There are initially four different classes, and each team has a Commander (with various upgrades including armor, ammo, etc). Each class has three drastically different loadout sets with various weapons in each one. This is where the TF2 influence shines clear through.
I mentioned Unreal Tournament, as well. Unreal Tournament is one of the most well-respected shooters released, and when I compare this game to it, I feel the need to explain myself. The pacing of both games is identical, with a mad dash to objectives resulting in very short life spans with quick spawn times. This allows you to filter in and out of combat with ease, allowing for you to change classes or weapons as needed during combat.
Really fun game in segments, but if it has a weakness, it would be in map structure. Nothing really sticks out in any of the maps, and they mostly seem to be several small rooms loosely connected to eachother, for the most part. Granted, this can be said of most multiplayer FPS games. Regardless, I don't think it's enough of a weakness to merit a poor review, so I'll say wait for a sale, or grab it right now in the Humble Bundle (Feb 25th, 2016)!

Thief (4) is a steampunk stealth game in first person view.
Singleplayer only.
Graphics:     9/10
I really enjoyed the graphics. The textures are well made and the particle effects are fitting and nice to look at.
The colors are really well chosen for a night scenario. The lighting and the shadows are very consistent. Although you will see very similar designed rooms and streets it'll never become boring. The equipment is very detailed.
Sound:     8/10
Dripping water, chatting people behind windows, crowing crows, and creaking floorboards. The game has the corrrect sound setting. Locating the enemy by his steps is easy. In comparison to its prequels the sounds improved a lot. But like in the other games of the franchise there is nearly no ambience music at all.
Level design:     9/10
I had everything I wanted in this game: A creepy hospital, a dark city with climbable roofs, sewers, airvents, a home, a big bank with a big safe :D and ancient ruins. This is a big plus of the game. The access to the all cityparts will become available mission for mission which gives you a variety in your actions. By designing realistic climbpaths you will notice quickly where you can get to and which ways are blocked. There are many ways to avoid danger and secret paths will lead to secret loot.
Gameplay/Handling/Equipment:     10/10
There is nothing to complain about the controls. You can switch your equipment in notime and you can move like a ninja through the shadows. The gameplay (knocking out enemies, avoiding traps, getting loot) has been consequently improved and I never saw any bugs. The equipment is upgradable and so are your skills. The upgrades are not that important (to be implemented into the game) but I like them. The bow is your weapon. The arrows are your tools. Rope arrows, water arrows and other useful inventions will help you to steal your enemies' underwear.
AI:     6/10
The AI is ok. Nothing special nowadays. The guards will search for you if you are too loud or stay in the light for too long. Sometimes they have a problem with the altitude, don't react properly and don't work as a team. Since there are no really interesting enemies in this game I give 6/10.
Story:     5/10
The story is not that interesting. The only thing you will count as important are the effects of the rebellion in the city. The whole cultist thing really isn't interesting at all. I think they could have made this part better. Sometimes the rebellion gave me a strange feeling I had in Splinter Cell 3: I'm a super stealthy agent in a real war. Doesn't really fit if you ask me.
But I like the characters and most of the sidequests. So I give 5/10

The Yawgh is a fun experience, somewhat similar to a game called Reigns. It's simple enough to play. Choose a location, face an event, make a choice, accept the results, and move on to the next location. These choices change your character, and the town. I've played through the game six times now. I've saved the town and suffered personal tragedy, and watched the town struggle, as I thrived.
There are a lot of outcomes in this game, and although they're generally predictable, they can also be surprising. The outcomes can be heroic, humorous or tragic. Although I think I've "won" this game, I'm going to play a few more times just to see how other choices play out.
On that note, this isn't the kind of game that you're going to play for over a hundred hours, but that's okay. It's less than the price of a movie ticket, can be enjoyed with friends, and will last you at least a couple of hours if you're willing to explore it.

This game was pretty buggy when it first came out. I dropped it and only recently picked it up again. Here are my thoughts. I'll start off with a TLDR and then explain in detail afterwards.
Overall thoughts: Get this game if you like Magic, you won't regret it.
Pros:
It's Magic for free.
Interface is well done and easy to pick up.
Multiplayer matchmaking is quick and games are fluid and fun.
Boosters award cards intelligently, and will not give you more cards than the legal allowed amount.
Cons:
The game still suffers random crashes.
No Draft modes/limited multiplayer modes.
In detail now.
Pros:
It's Magic for free. Unlike previous DotP games, the sets that are relased in this game are closely tied to the actual sets that are released in paper. You don't have to pay money for it and everything in game can be earned through the in-game currency. This by itself should merit a download if you enjoy the card game.
Interface is well done and easy to pick up. The game is chok full of step-by-step interactive tutorials as well as exclusive story mode campaigns for every expansion release. Unlike magic online, every action in game is very clearly explained to you and the very basics of the game is narrated to you as well. Anyone new to the game can learn everything there is to know without trouble.
Multiplayer matchmaking is quick and games are fluid and fun. Enough said.
Boosters award cards intelligently, and will not give you more cards than the legal allowed amount. So once you pick up four copies of a card, you won't get any more copies of that card. and once you complete the full set, that set will not longer be available for purchase. Thus, every booster will always increase your collection in a useful manner.
Cons:
The game still suffers random crashes, and if this happens, you will lose your progress, which is particularly relevant for daily quests. If you were close to finishing a daily, all of the progress made in that game will be gone. Thankfully, this hasn't happened that much for me, but it has happened. I think developers are actively working to minimize such occurances.
No Draft modes/limited multiplayer modes. This is a very minor nitpick to be honest. There are 3rd party apps you can use to simulate drafts and with a small group of players you can emulate this off game and construct the drafted deck in-game to play. This applies to most other 1v1 alternative game modes. This however requires you to own the full collection of cards so you can actually construct the deck you drafted. That said, this is actually easier to do than most games due to the way boosters handle duplicates.

Magic Duels has been surprisingly addicting. For one thing, it uses only recent card sets from the game, which now includes Origins, Battle for Zendikar, Oath of the Gatewatch, Shadows over Innistrad, and Eldrich Moon with Kaladesh on the way. I've to date, put over 160.6 hours into this game and can say finally say I'd recommend it. You start out by playing through the first story campaign of Origins, Gideon's campaign. The game teaches you how to play, which is frustrating to me as a person who's been playing non-online actual cards MTG for a year now, but is important for people who don't know what they're doing. The next most frustrating part is not having any good cards at the beginning. Use the deck builder, not the deck wizard(the deck wizard "assists" you while building a deck, but all it really does is say, "you don't want that really good card you have, take this 'meh' card instead!". Build yourself a mono-white deck full of enchantments and tiny flying creatures with a few instants and sorceries to supprt it. You will find it works well enough to beat easy AIs. Grind it out with the AIs or hop on the back of a hopefully good teammate in two headed giant. Grind away at the campaign modes, the Origins campaigns are the hardest and gave me the most trouble, in my opinion, but they will get you at least a couple packs plus extra starter box cards once you finish each season(Innistrad, Zendikar, Gatewatch, and Eldrich). Buy packs from the most recent season first because the community and daily challenges are usually dependent on them and you want to get as many coins as possible. Anyways, the game is challenging, but offers a good, free option opposed to the Duels of the Planeswalkers. The game is comprehensive enough that it satisfies me as a seasoned player, yet basic enough that it serves as a good introduction to Magic for casual or beginner players.

I know it's more of an interactive novel than a game, so I won't really mention any of the gameplay other than the fact that it sometimes is clunky and that can detract heavily from the game. It's not very well optimized. Other than that, the game does what it is supposed to do very well, which is give you a solid mindset from the point of veiw of a depressed 40-something woman. The main character and her writing are very well done, and the rest of the story reflects that. The only problem with the spectacular writing for story and the main character is that it really points out the flaws and lackluster writing/voice acting in every other character. It really seems like all the characters are secondary thoughts, plot devices to only move the story further. Other than that, it's just a slow moving bummer. The story, like I said, does what it sets out to do very well, which is to show a clear and accurate look at depression. The story moves slow enough that it feels like time is meaningless because you will always have to deal with the troubles in the game. I opted to kill myself (by stopping playing the game) early, so I honestly can't say whether I know if the ending is better than the story and pacing. I can appreciate art, but theater of pain can only hold me for so long, and this game tried to hold me for longer than it was worth.

As with PCMA, you get to take control of a fledgling civilization from the pre-historic times to the crucial times in world history. This game is akin to Civilization, but unlike Civ, you don't get tied in micromanagement - instead they use the Toynbee model of historical development: you get a new historical challenge from time to time (form a tribe, hold out against the followers of another agressive Egyptian deity, find a route to the Middle East to build a pyramid, etc.) and overcoming those challenges is essentially winning.
Yeah, you get to do some resource management and construction planning, but the big picture and overall historical landscape is far more important and weighing your decisions is likely to take more of your time than implementing them - no driving throngs of stack of units around the map, no conquering gazillions of enemy cities or building up tonnes of units to defend your many cities. Everything's more laid back, schematic and easy to manage, grand strategy style.
The overall look and feel is similar to that of PCMA, but I'd say it looks like that only on the surface - the whole gameplay (religion, minor tribes, combat) are very different and I'd say improved. What both games have in common is the pre-determined historical flow of events and the depth of detail - they call it "story-rich" nowadays - you really feel that you are making history here, from the first farm to the first Mastaba. While some local tribes and starting conditions are randomized, the game itself is not random - you WILL follow the path of the Egyptian civilization. Or die trying.
All in all, I love these two games because they manage to be educational without actually being boring as hell, like most of these types do, not to mention that they require attention to detail, thinking and planning. Easy to learn the basics, they are quite difficult to beat - so replayability is very high.
From my prospective, this developer has some serious potential. This game is fresh, it's not like anything else I've seen recently. Highly recommended.

In a post-Shovel Knight era, it's hard to look at the "Indie" label without a scrupulous eye for game design that doesn’t merely leverage on nostalgia nor old-school aesthetics. Momodora: Reverie Under the Moonlight is the 4th installment of a series of games developed by Guilherme Martins “rdein” that demonstrates how far a developer could go just from learning and improving upon a solid foundation and refining its execution, regardless of looks. At first glance, it might seem like another action exploration platformer in the same vein as Guacamelee, Super Metroid and post-Symphony of the Night Castlevania titles (often referred to as metroidvania). In fact, it shares more in common with the classic style Castlevania than, as others might claim, Dark Souls. Despite all semblances, Reverie manages to feel fresh and engaging; it doesn’t feel like just a mishmash of the aforementioned games. It manages to carve its own identity using the series own roots as a basis.
The Momodora games started out as action adventure games that bear more similarities to Daisuke “pixel” Amaya’s indie hit game Cave Story. The first game, in particular, shared similar super-deformed aesthetics as its source inspiration with the main character taking up the width and height of one in-game block. The game had a more linear focus with regards to its level design. Numerous weapon pickups were available, but the most apparent was the magic leaf that Isadora, the protagonist, wields as her primary melee attack as she desperately finds a way to revive her mother from mortality. This becomes one of the defining traits of the series continuing with the second game, Momodora II: Once again playing a female protagonist wielding a maple leaf, this time a girl named Momo, you’re out to hunt for the Undead Queen. Progression has been expanded upon to that of a standard metroidvania with ability based upgrades along with a more open world design. The presentation itself has taken an upgrade, and players would save and restore health in the now series-familiar prayer bells. By the 3rd game, players could choose to play either as Momo or Isadora, with boss battles becoming a prominent highlight, doubling in number from the previous installment. Momodora III opts for a more solid palette of colors accompanied with a cleaner design, showcasing more nuanced sprite animation than its predecessors. This is helped by the variety of environments with its distinct set of vibrant palettes.
All of these aspects coalesce resulting in this latest entry. Momodora: Reverie Under the Moonlight has the open-world design of Momodora II, the equipable item ability from Momodora III, and a protagonist who was merely hinted in lore from the previous games. You play as Kaho, a priestess hailing from the village of Lum, seeking a way to stop a curse from spreading to her homeland by traversing the Kingdom of Karst. Like its predecessors, themes of death and the sending off of spirits once again crop up. Not only does it feel darker in tone, but Reverie leverages on its evolved presentation, with the primary cast and non-playable characters represented in a less abbreviated stature than in the former games, putting more focus on positioning, dodging, and chaining attacks, with environmental and enemy placement feeling more dense, focused, and compact. Every screen prepares the player to be on their toes for an encounter, as seldom are there just rooms which merely serve as vistas for items and NPCs: While previous games in the series are no stranger to emphasizing enemy placement, Reverie does pull new tricks up its sleeve with regards to diversity and how they control the space within the screen, as often times one might feel pinned down in an inopportune spot, yet never does it feel unfair. Unlike preceding games, Kaho can now roll to get behind enemies to hit them from behind and pass otherwise undodgeable attacks unscathed. Combat is also more nuanced and meaty; there is a sense of weight to each stroke of the leaf Kaho unleashes and even the arrows she fires has a nice sense of swiftness, and all of this is mesmerizingly animated by the wonderful sprite work with a wide breath of expressiveness. Controlling the game not only look great, but feels right.
Reverie features a handful of entertaining and challenging boss battles. New to the series are obtaining items from bosses upon defeating them without getting hit (A similar reward mechanism is also present in Mega Man Zero 2). While these items are not prerequisite to obtaining the true ending of the game, many who feel the urge to get 100% completion (or are just obsessive compulsive like me) might find this feat particularly daunting, especially for first-time playthroughs. Luckily, a New Game + mode unlocks upon completion of the game and retains all your collectibles and most of your upgrades including your completed map, allowing to set oneself properly for the encounter ahead.
In terms of scope and design, Reverie’s open-world has a nicely knit network of areas that, while large, never feels overwhelming; backtracking is alleviated by some smart design choices, and retraversing sections to get from one screen to the next never felt like a chore. The map itself not only houses a handful of secrets, but places them in areas which make backtracking feel rewarding (This is not an easy feat to pull off, as many developers would sometimes keep upgrades and ability items as a sole reason to backtrack, not in-spite of). To help with matters, much like in Momodora III, prayer bells would eventually let you warp back to previously explored areas. Exploring 100% of the world is not that difficult a task, but the game itself is by no means too short.
Which brings us to Reverie’s overall length: After traversing 7 unique areas, the game never overstays its welcome and ends right before things begin feeling rote. Even despite repeated playthroughs, there are so many approaches one could take thanks to its non-linear progression: After the first boss, it is possible to beat consecutive bosses in any order which you see fit. The abilities you gain from each defeated boss can be subsequently used to your advantage in any other boss fight, creating a form of Mega Man style effect of boss progression. It is also possible to beat the game without defeating a single common enemy (known in-game as a Pacifist run), or try for the Insane difficulty that leaves you to perish in one hit; These are more bragging rights rewards than anything, but the fact that the game can be played and completed in either fashion shows how much thought went into its design.
If one is interested in wanting to see how far a single designer could take their idea by learning from each iteration, the Momodora series would be considered a textbook example of how to refine a franchise: Taking inspirations from various games, learning to experiment and keep what works, trim what doesn’t, while holding steadfast to the core principles, which in this case, is a maple leaf.

Published and developed by Rupeck Games, Caveblazers is a fast paced roguelike game with randomly generated levels, a vast amount of enemies, items and weapons that you can find whilst you play through each run of this game.
The first point to take from Caveblazers is that this game is categorized as a roguelike game. This game is suppose to be difficult and cruel to you throughout the time that you play it. That doesn’t mean, however, that this game isn’t fun. With the increasing difficulty of the game, it is very satisfying to complete just one level through your run, which is what a difficult game should have all together to make the player keep coming back to it. Although I did find that sometimes the game would be way too difficult and it discouraged me to play the game anymore.
With this game being categorized as a roguelike genre of gaming, it does offer the main mechanics that a game of this genre should have. With randomly generated levels, a dungeon crawler feel to it, the difficulty curve that should go at a steady pace and permadeath. Caveblazers does most of this fairly well, with each level being randomly generated it really does add replay value to this game making you come back to play more.
With the starting weapons that you acquire before entering the level, there are several types of attacks. Within the short tutorial that you are given before you enter the first level you are given a sword and bow in order to fight the enemies that are in the levels. The sword has a few functions that you can use, you have your normal slashing from left to right and then you have a upward and downward strike which is rather helpful when you are attacking enemies from above or below. The bow takes more accuracy and precious timing in order to get right, you are going to need to use the bow in order to hit enemies from a distance as just using your sword isn’t always going to work. I found that the key bindings for the bow and arrow a little weird for a weapon that requires accuracy and precious timing. You will need to use the arrow keys in order to aim your bow, therefore being restricted to only eight directions (Up, up left, left, left down etc.). I would of liked the option to be able to use the mouse to be able to aim the bow as this is a much more precious and better to use than the restricted arrow keys.
This game does seem to have a small amount of RPG elements that are implemented into the game, like artifacts that you can collect to increase your character’s stats and be able to progress through the game a little easier. You may encounter these artifacts throughout your runs that will increase your character’s stats, though these will be randomly chosen for you. Some of these artifacts include Knights bleeding, Blessing of Endurance, Volatile blessing and many more that will up your stats of the character that you play as throughout of of the runs.
Throughout your run you will find many items inside of chests and crates that you will have to smash open in order to obtain. These items will become vastly useful as you play through the game and get to the challenging levels. These items could range from upgrades of your weapons, consumables that you can use to heal up, and buff up your character for for the good or bad. Another item you will find a lot is money in chests and crates that you can spend on statues that will help your character.
The enemies AI is rather well played out, and the variety amount of enemies is rather nice. Some of the enemies will attack each other if they come across each one other with the possibility of them killing each other, making it easier for you. While some enemies have the same sort of mechanics as you do, being able to wall jump and hold the same starting weapons you own, there are other types of enemies such as bats, slimes and bandits that will attack you as well.
The soundtrack for this game is superb, it really sets the game up to be a fast paced sort of game that will require accuracy. Upon entering the caves, the music is very well suited to the atmosphere. This combined with the sound effects of each of the attacks and moves that you do are really nice, but I feel like they can sharpen up a bit on them.
With the new enemies that you will come across as you progress through each area there will be new enemies that you will encounter. The graphics of this game are rather nice, as you get through each area you will realize that the areas will change and will look different from the previous one. It does seem that the graphics aren’t as polished as some of them could be. The areas do give off that atmosphere that you are enclosed in a cave and that you are going in deeper into each of the areas.
+ Variety of weapons
+ Nicely designed graphics
+ Varied enemies and nice AI
+ Nice music and sound effects
+ Full controller support
- Bow hasn’t got the option to use mouse to aim
- Game can be a bit too difficult at times
- Sound effects could be worked on a bit
In conclusion, Caveblazers is a very fun but difficult roguelike game that requires accuracy and precious timing in order to be able to proceed through each of the levels.There is a nice variety of enemies, items and weapons that you can acquire throughout your runs. Although the bow needs the ability to be more accurate and the game’s sound effects need to be a bit more crisp, the game is very fun and addicting to play.

Logically you would think "Hey I can turn around and swing." but in this 'game' pushing the other direction will ALWAYS move you into the mob instead, to which any swing you make will go BEHIND the mob and miss all together. Apparently thats a thing...unlike Risk of Rain where you can actually face another direction without being forced to move.
The lowest level teir mobs do the most damage. One blob that jumps into you or a bat that flys at you, the very first mobs encountered in this game, can mannage to do upwards of 50 damage, or half of your health without any reason other than this game has no "invincibility" or "delay" when the enemy is detected as hitting you. They also can mannage to get between your melee swings if you can imagine how that happens, more often then not, which leaves you having to use bow only through the majority of the game.
The "Bow" is the right analog stick. Jump is the "A" button and Melee is the "X" button. Do you see the problem here? If being forced into using ranged attack because melee is complete feces, you are forced to have to constantly manuever between bow and jump and having a half second delay between each. At the pace this game is set, this makes no sense. It woudl have been fine to have Y as bow, and stop you from moving while shooting. That would have at least allowed you to jump and fire downward without delay or difficulty.
The Melee is a joke. Most things just go through your melee unless you are fortunate enough to find a rune with explosive melee attacks on it. Even then, you leave it up to compelete chance to actually function, since the explosions are  RANDOM.

If I thrust DOWN with melee attack (Aka Zelda 2) USUALLY I go in a straight line directly down even from the mid arc of my jump. This is unreliable. I'm a huge fan of the Spelunky+Roguelike formula; Vagante and Catacomb Kids are among my favourite games ever, and if you enjoy any of these, you'll feel right at home on Caveblazers.
Caveblazers catapults the basic gameplay from Spelunky into a much more chaotic (in a good way!) pacing.
The gameplay flows beautifully: platforming is fluid and fast, combat is dynamic with its inclusion of both melee and ranged capabilities from the get go and tactical thinking is constantly put at test, especially when evading and trying to get the upper hand on AI opponents.
But not only in the basics it really shines. Caveblazers is also pretty detailed when it comes to possibilities (like shooting downwards into wallgrab into walljump into second downward shot), it also features a character progression system without the use of experience points and levels, basing itself entirely into finding special runes which grant you added perks such as double jumps or randomly shooting lighting bolts. While this does break the traditional 'build your character as you desire' sort of philosophy in favor of a more random and unexpected gameplay progression, it helps settle variety and testing your skills in all possible ways feels refreshing.
As of the second patch (which came just a few days after release) the development in Early Access shows promise. Developers are actively looking for suggestions and actually implementing them in an efficient way.

This game was great. Scratch that, IS great. It is a retro hack and slash rpg that reminds you of N64 Zelda and the first Final Fantasy. Hammerwatch is a game of strategy. A game of skill. This isn't some crazy bullethell rogue-like where you run in, guns-a-blazin'. There is no luck involved in this game. If you die, it is entirely your fault. Hammerwatch is a top-down, RPG style game with an adorable 16-bit art style. The gameplay is top-notch, with tight controls and a variety of areas and enemies. It's reminescent of older games from the 90s such as the first Final Fantasies and other RPGs.
Hammerwatch consists of four areas: The Prison, The Armory, The Archives, and The Chambers. Each area consists of 2-3 floors of enemies, each having a unique attack pattern and movement. Each area has a unique art style and several secrets to find. You most certainly won't find everything in your first playthrough; I know I haven't. Each level has vendors that are appropriately leveled for that area, and different vendors sell you different powerups and upgrades, which is your way of leveling up.
The gameplay is on the spot, with tight controls, a solid feel, and even strafing. Everything that you have in your arsenal will be used in this, such as strafing, which is ever so useful for dodging shots. Every character is unique, from the Paladin with his powerful sword and insanely useful shield, to the stealthy Warlock, who has a menacing poison dagger by his side. Each class has a basic attack, a spell, and then two spells to unlock from upgrading. Rarely will you have a spell you don't use.
The level editor is also user-friendly and amazingly well-made. I'm working on a level myself, and I can say this from experience. It's easy to use and fun to mess with.
However, Hammerwatch does have a couple shortcomings. For example, a campaign that was randomly generated each playthrough would increase the replayability of this game greatly. The Ranger early game is also immensely powerful, with piercing arrows that can cross the entire play field.
Looking over these flaws, Hammerwatch is an amazing game I would recommend to all my friends. Seriously, give this game a shot.
Hammerwatch gets a 10/10.

Bit Blaster XL is a retro style game that is simple, fun, and very challenging. It is similar to several differnent classic arcade games that I have played, and I am a sucker for retro games. I have been really enjoying the game, and have even been catching myself trying again and again just trying to better my high score and place higher on the leaderboards.
Controls are simple. Your little ship moves automatically, with you being able to control its turning, as well as having control over a boost that depletes and recharges over time. Your ship fires automatically as well, and there are many different power-ups that spawn on the screen that you can pick up that will change your weapon. You weapon uses ammo which can be reloaded by shooting enemies and picking up their little green balls. All is simple, even death. There are no lives and if you get shot without your sheilds, you're done for!
The game also has a little currency system where enemies may occasionally drop gold coins, which you can use to purchase new ships!
In my opinion, This game is super well made, and as of the 1.1 version, all of the bugs below have been FIXED from what I have been able to witness. The developer gets an A+ for responding to reviews and fixing these bugs in a timely manner. Kudos to you Dev. :)
+ (FIXED) While using a controller, a "ghost" of myself would spawn with me and remain motionless while i fly around. If the ghost took damage, it would end the game for me.
+ (FIXED) The "H" power-up (Homing projectile) could be picked up but not fire a single homing shot. Only the basic weapon would remain active.
+ (FIXED) Enemy's red projectiles would sometimes do much more damage then they should, taking down multiple layers of your sheild instead of just one layer. I could be wrong in which some projectiles are meant to deal more damage, but I haven't seen any consistencies in damage output by certain enemies. (Bug perhaps? Would be nice to get some feedback from the devs on this.)
Main thing I would like to see in a future update would be more products in the shop. There is a total of only seven ships in the game, and when you buy them, there is nothing left to buy and gold then becomes obsolete, unless you want to collect lots of gold, like me! I would love to see additions to the shop to spend my gold on. (i.e. More ships, power-ups to unlock, ship appearences, rocket trails, enemy appearences, etc.)
This game has huge potential to become something even better than it already is. The Developer is super positive and proactive on fixing bugs, and I cannot wait to see what else could be in store for the future. I definitely would recommend this game to anyone who loves simple, casual, challenging indie games. This game is certainly worth the 99 cents!

The Starting Party: Anton, Pavle, Zlata, and Cyeta.
The four arrive in an abandoned house, setting up shelter until the war ends.
Things are looking good the first five days...
...and then Pavle is shot dead on Day 6 when attempting to defend a woman from being assaulted by a military soldier.
Everyone is sad.
Supplies are scarce.
Zlata, in despetartion, kills an elderly couple for resources.
Everyone gets sadder.
In order to redeem herself, Zlata helps a man get medication to his ailing father. She also helps some neighbors dig out trapped citizens from under a collapsed building.
Things are looking up, until Anton, who is an elderly man, develops a severe illness.
Then while on a scavenging trip, Zlata is gunned down by some thugs.
Cyeta goes to investigate, discovering that these thugs have prisoners locked up. She frees one. Cyeta comes by the corpse of Zlata. While mourning her friend, Cyeta takes a bullet to the head when another thug sneaks up on her.
Only Anton is left.
With poor health and no food, Anton decides he has nothing left to lose and sets out on a mission to avenge his fallen friends. He heads to the hotel where the thugs are based in. Armed only with a knife, Anton knows he probably won't make it back.
Anton stealthily sneaks into the building and quietly takes out two guards. He grabs a gun from one of them as well as some ammo. He guns down the rest of the thugs. They didn't even know what hit them.
For the next week, Anton survives by hinself by taking food and medication from the now empty hotel. However, Anton is still saddened over the loss of his friends.
Things then take a turn for the worse. Returning from scavenging one night, Anton dicovers that his supplies had been raided.
He has nothing now.
And then the cold of winter arrives.
Anton freezes to death. Alone.
------------------------------------
This game is very interesting and really made me feel like a POS for killing the elderly couple. It provides a challenge and a less talked about perspective on the horrors of war. Although there are some things that don't make sense, for example, after killing all the thugs and taking their supplies, Anton feels bad because he is worried how "those poor people" will survive without their supplies. And even though it is a horrid thing to kill any person, his sentiments really don't make sense since Anton literally killed all those thugs, so leaving taking the supplies would not affect the survival of them since they are all already dead. Despite that this game is a very beautiful and depressing.
Overall would reccomend.

I've been quite disappointed with this game, not through any comparison to the original Thief, but simply due to the quality of the game itself. The story itself is poorly written and at times makes no sense, almost as if whole chunks of it have just been left out. I also just didn't *care* about any of the characters or what happened next. Loading times sometimes occur when you wouldn't expect, like going through a window to a room within a level which already incurred a loading time to enter. Audio is poorly implemented with a lot of delays versus what is happening, and especially versus the subtitles on screen.
I did find myself enjoying some of the puzzles, but for each decent puzzle there are a couple of other muddly ones.
One saving grace perhaps is the look and feel of the environments you explore; this aspect of the game has had plenty of thought put into it and has lots of great detail to discover, but its not enough to make up for the above points and I didn't enjoy the core gameplay enough to really explore.
I kept giving the game a chance to improve which took me to about 8 hours, and since then I have decided to at least try and play it through to completion, but in general I wouldn't recommend the game to others.

5. There were a number of bugs that were fixed, although the game is still unperfect. Would love it if WotC dedicated more resources to Magic Duels

The Cat Lady is definitely the kind of game that comes to mind for me when people talk about video games as art. The story of Susan Ashworth is fantastically written, and had me enthralled even with it's lengthy (but completely necessary) dialogues, and was the first game in quite a while that made me feel as though I had been given a story from start to finish, with no plot holes or frustrating questions at the end. In fact, it was so well written that I actually got the same feeling as if I had just read a really good book, and after playing Skyrim for the last couple of weeks, I was very glad for it.
I really enjoyed the art work of the game, but the sound was occasionally a little below par, with the character voices either being mixed too high or low, or being distored for no reason. Having said that, I really enjoyed the ambient sounds and soundtrack, with the opening credits being particularly awesome.
Overall, a great game for anyone who loves well written scripts over strenuous gameplay. Very highly recommended.

Pre-Civilization Egypt focuses on recreating a historical reenactment of early Egypt from the years 6000-4000 BCE. The game has a pleasant and distinct art style, reminiscent of table top games. The rules are easy enough to pick up withing fifteen minutes and each playthrough will probably take around 4 hours depending on difficulty and how familiar you are with the game's mechanics.
The focus of the game is a historical timeline of Egypt but you manage the turn to turn efforts of growing the empire such as gathering food, building armies, worshiping gods, and trading with neighboring tribes. You'll have to improve your cities bu building land improvements and researching techs acquired through culture generation.
The game can be quite brutal at anything but the lowest difficulty leading to the dev describing it as the Dark Souls of the Turn Based genre of games.
In my opinion the price is reasonable and the gameplay solid, you'll probably get at least two playthroughs of this game completed before you loose interest.

I'm a huge fan of the Spelunky+Roguelike formula; Vagante and Catacomb Kids are among my favourite games ever, and if you enjoy any of these, you'll feel right at home on Caveblazers.
Caveblazers catapults the basic gameplay from Spelunky into a much more chaotic (in a good way!) pacing.
The gameplay flows beautifully: platforming is fluid and fast, combat is dynamic with its inclusion of both melee and ranged capabilities from the get go and tactical thinking is constantly put at test, especially when evading and trying to get the upper hand on AI opponents.
But not only in the basics it really shines. Caveblazers is also pretty detailed when it comes to possibilities (like shooting downwards into wallgrab into walljump into second downward shot), it also features a character progression system without the use of experience points and levels, basing itself entirely into finding special runes which grant you added perks such as double jumps or randomly shooting lighting bolts. While this does break the traditional 'build your character as you desire' sort of philosophy in favor of a more random and unexpected gameplay progression, it helps settle variety and testing your skills in all possible ways feels refreshing.
As of the second patch (which came just a few days after release) the development in Early Access shows promise. Developers are actively looking for suggestions and actually implementing them in an efficient way.

Before purchasing 'The Yawhg', I had thought it to be a light-hearted, "choose your own story", game. Yet, what I got instead was infinitely more intriguing.The game itself offers four differentiating characters that the player can control, and in doing so will ultimately decide their own life stories. It's left up to them to improve the skills of the characters, and to make wise decisions; some of which even prove to be a bit of a catch 22.
Something that I personally found to be fantastic, about The Yawhg, was that it's intended to be played from just one device. So, I can easily access play by myself, or with my friends. Whether they be online, or right next to me; which is truly brilliant. And whether or not the "antagonist" was defeated depended upon ALL of the players. Team work is imperative for the succession of this game.
Something else that stood out to me was the violent undertones, and low-key foreshadowing of impending doom, as The Yawhg [a so-called "storm"] approached its arrival to the town; in which the protagonists live. I'm probably running out of characters here, so I'll try to make this explanation quick. After The Yawhg has said to pass, the players are asked to select one of many professions, in an effort to re-construct the town, and whether or not they do it well depends entirely on how high their corresponding skill is. The Yawhg is just like a giant puzzle. All of the events that take place link to the game's ending, and it can be either good or bad.
Will you survive The Yawhg? And even if you do, will you be happy forevermore? Take a chance, and find out.

I was sitting on the fence about reviewing this game until an update came out yesterday that fixed almost everything I didn't like about it. Now I wholeheartedly recommend it.

3. Weapons and blessings make each run feel delightfully different from each other (Almost Isaac levels of different)
4. When you do cool maneuvers to get out of risky situations, you feel awesome. The game controls really well.
5. Most enemies are at just the right threat level.
6. Getting high scores is really satisfying.
Cons:
1. The typical potion system with colored potions having unknown effects is present in this game. Like other roguelikes with this system, potions are identified after being used once, but you can only use those potions on yourself, which, as usual, makes the whole system not worth trying out due to riskiness. It either needs a system where you can throw potions at enemies to identify their effect, or potions need to have mostly positive effects. Isaac's pills would be a good place to look. All pills are either positive or neutral except for 1 pill that deals 1 damage to you.
2. You can't tell how a pseudo-multiplayer enemy feels about you until they shoot the first arrow at you. Since they are by far the scariest potential enemy in the game, they NEED to have different colored shirts or something based on their "personality." You cant really exploit them as an interesting game mechanic if you have to hide from every single one you see to not take damage.

Initially, when I first heard of this game, I just figured, "hey, this looks kinda neat but I'm not paying $10 for it becuase I'm a lousy cheap♥♥♥♥♥" It looked like a cool concept to me and if it looks like a cool concept to you, then you're perhaps in for something of a treat.
Now, when I first played it on my own, I wasn't particularly entertained. I mean, yes, the different story paths were somewhat interesting and the various different endings were kinda cool but I wasn't really absorbed into it. It was just something I used to make a good 45 minutes pass by one day when I was feeling bored. Then, while with some friends the other night, I decided to pull it out because we all needed a game to play and this just so happened to be multiplayer and seemed like a nice change of pace from the usual stuff we always tend to play (e.g. Genital Jousting, Jackbox Party Pack, etc.) What I didn't expect was for us to keep playing over and over again for several more hours, as we found ourselves unusually entertained by this strange little game.
This is because where The Yawhg shines is in its multiplayer gameplay. As you each play through the runs as your individual character, you become attached to the story and are actually quite affected by the events that happen to you. Trying not to spoil any of the specific events as that would take away from your game experience overall, I will say that each event is quite interesting when it first happens. You feel fear, shock, and surprise as you're faced with various choices, unsure of their meaning or where they lead but finding yourself satisfied by the game's clever use of various fantasy cliches to create a coherent story for your character. But it's in this that the game's largest flaw lies. See, there's only a limited number of events that occur, and, though the game is likely designed to be played in sets of multiple consecutive runs, after a few playthroughs you start to see events repeat and they lose the impact that they originally had on the player. No longer does the story really have any sort of impact, and instead you begin picking choices just to try to get a different ending and experimenting, skipping through the game's incredibly creative dialogue and just rushing through each run. It's still enjoyable in a way, but it's a much less interesting experience as the game goes on and on which I was disappointed by to some extent.
The gameplay itself is quite simple. The game is more or less a choose-your-own-adventure book, and thus you play it by simply making choices on where to go, what to do, and how to react to the random event that always occurs. The gameplay is there to simply give the player choice, immersing them in the story that the game crafts and presents, and in that regard it succeeds. I truly don't think this game is for everyone, and if you're the type of person who's driven by a "win-lose" sort of mindset then this game might not necessarily appeal to you in terms of how it plays, because the enjoyment is not through feeling as though you "won" the game. It's through that feeling of autonomy and choice, the decision it grants that makes the player feel unique and able. It does, essentially, what it's supposed to do. The characters will recieved stat boosts that affect their decisions throughout the course of each run, and once you learn what different actions give you then there is some thinking that may go into character building in whatnot, but it's really not sophisticated enough to become the main draw of the game.
Graphically the game is quite appealing. The art is drawn cute but not excessively so, and the visuals are primarily presented in a still-painting format that simply serves to accompany the text as opposed to distracting from it, which I thought was a good design decision. The art style is haunting in a way, matching the somber yet somehow mildly humorous nature of this game. Truly, The Yawhg is not a particularly happy game, and it may give you chills if you're not ready for some of what it presents, and the art style adds greatly to this. Musically, the game has a very relaxing, quiet soundtrack, but I was bothered by the fact that often times it consisted of little 6-second loops playing over and over again as the players went through their days. It accompanies the game well enough but the fact that I could hear it looping was quite bothersome. However, there is a full track that plays at the end and beginning of every run that is so intensely haunting and emotional that my friends and I all found ourselves quite affected by it playing.
Essentially, the Yawhg is not a game that you'll find yourself playing very often if you do decide to buy it, which is something that you probably should keep in mind when making your purchase. Rather, it's a game that you'll pull out from time to time when you have enough time to forget many of the random events and are able to experience them fully again. Also, it's WAY better with friends. Trust me.

Writing this review I've only finished the standard campaign and haven't had time to get into the recently released expansion yet. I probably will though, I happen to like this game quite a bit. Hammerwatch is sort of a mix between a top-down shooter and an rpg if you feel a need to label games. The aesthetics are nostalgia inducing and the soundtrack is something of a modernized version of what you could hear back in the day while playing your nintendo, adding further to the feeling of nostalgia. I like it, it all ties together nicely and at times I got that same feeling I had back in the day when video games felt fresh and exciting to me.
You shoot spells or hack your way through four acts that has three levels each, and a boss at the end. The levels are well designed and have lots of secrets in them to explore. The hacking and slashing can get repetetive at times though and feels somewhat stuttery. Most of the time you have to pull a pack of monsters and back off to kill it and then rince and repeat time after time. The combat mechanics doesn't allow you to move and aim in different directions at the same time in a good way (using both sticks), so positioning and using the map to your advantage is important. This is also what i mean by stuttery feel, there's a lot of starting and stopping going on. If you take it for what it is though the movement and animations are very responsive and well functioning as a whole.
As you move forward you find shopkeepers that allow you to upgrade your spells,armor,healthpool etc in exchange for coins that you collect. Collecting the coins can also feel a bit tedious at times as you have to blow up thousands of barrels and other sorts of containers to get to them. Overall the rpg aspect of the game is shallow to say the least. And i wouldn't label the game with that tag.
You also need to find a bunch of planks while travelling through the castle. The usage of these planks was somewhat obscured to me from the get go and as a result I ended up missing a couple during the first levels. This is not a good idea, don't miss them damn planks is all I have to say about that.
In the end I enjoyed my playthrough, I could lean back in my chair and just hammer away at the controlpad not having to use my brain for precision or puzzles to much, it still had something to do though and I never felt bored. Worn out at times perhaps but not bored.

The Cat Lady is about depression. Full stop.
As a metaphor, it’s fairly effective. A world out to eat you up, an implacable day-by-day pain, a life full of untrustworthy strangers who’ll hurt you if you get close, so you maintain an edgy distance, hostile or fearful. I don’t personally think the crazy-surreal-violent plot is meant to be taken literally, but I suppose it doesn’t much matter if you do take it literal. The theme is the same. This is a long-form treatment of the disease, and at least one of the better video game ones. If the Cat Lady can be a little uneven (and that’s actually arguably a strength), it conveys mood descriptively, and allows for moments of triumph, hope, and humor.
Don’t expect anything polished. Do expect some goofiness, a general low-budgetality, typos, dreamy unexplained nonsense. But I found Cat Lady to be more effective than its occasionally clumsy components promised, and not as cruel as I feared. It’s not like Actual Sunlight, a game about depression where the “winner” of the game is preordained.
In fact, it reminded me a bit of Infinite Jest, another messy, uneven treatment, and one that’s messy and uneven perhaps precisely because if you’ve been there, if you’re in there, the way out isn’t clear and isn’t clean and isn’t sure. Sometimes it’s going to be dark for a while, because the lights just won’t work, no matter how desperately you try to turn them on. But you close your eyes, you take a deep breath, and you keep doing in the dark, because you have to. You feel out new patterns, because you have to.

To start with: I've never played the card game (although everyone played it, when I was young), but I guess it's an extremely good adaptation. It is a good strategy game that makes you to adapt permanently or perish. It’s great for casual players, who want to play a strategy game for thirty minutes or so and then return to work (or their wife).
There is a story/campaign mode which is alright - not great. It consists of usually five games for each season. You play it with pre-constructed decks, which is a pity. If you want a good story mode to play with your own decks you have to play the 2015 edition.
The main fun with origins is building your very own decks, trying them out against quite competent ai or multiplayer, optimizing, getting new cards and try out something new. Now, if you really want to have a good deck from the start and be always competitive this will be quite expensive or involve a lot of grinding. It is pay to win - but that is the very essence of a trading card game isn't it?
But if you don’t really care about a high multiplayer-ranking you can have a lot of fun with the game without spending a cent. If you want more cards without spending real money don’t miss the quests.
If you really want specific cards in your deck, this will be hard, because you can’t buy or trade them for other cards. On the other hand, you can consider it to be a challenge to build a good deck with the cards you have and not the ones you want. After all, the fun of strategy games is the intellectual challenge.
The game-mechanics have some faults and you really lose a lot of games due to poorly (I mean really poorly) shuffled decks – but it’s a card game, so I guess luck has to be a factor.
Crashes happen, but don’t really break the game.
All in all I really enjoy it. Thumbs up!

I knew, however, of a place that had lots of medicine.  Another band of survivors.  I had traded with them before.  But I was low on all my supplies now save for water and some firewood.  I took these to trade when I sent my friend on a  mission.  But I also had him take a shotgun and ammo.
I went to trade. They wouldn't give me any medicine for the food and water.  And they only would give me one bottle of pill for the shotgun.  Not even close to enough. I knew my character would die. But worse, my wife would die.
I wouldn't let her die.
My friend's character took the gun and killed the survivors. All of them. He grabbed all the medicine and food he could and came back.
Because of the medicine, my wife recovered.  My character recovered.  But my friend's character...he never did.
A week later, he just left. No words. Nothing.  He had been fighting depression ever since the killing.  We tried to reassure him. But it stayed with him.  And we never saw him again.
Two days later the war ended.  My wife's character and mine escaped back to their lives.  And part of me likes to think my friend's character did too.
None of this happened, truly. It was nothing but pixels on a screen in a video game.  But that play through hit me harder than any other game I have ever played.  Every choice you maker, from helping a sick mother down the street to killing for supplies stays with you. And part of the reason I haven’t played the game since is because I don't want to ride that emotional roller coaster again.
So if you play, and I VERY much think you should play, do yourself a favor and don't put your loved ones or friends in  it. It's amazing how it becomes deeply personal when you do.

Alright, so a lot of fans of the Thief series seem to dislike this reboot. Speaking as a fan of the Thief series, having played all of them through to their ends... I thoroughly enjoyed this game, and frankly, don't really see what the problem is that others have with it. Everyone's entitled to their opinions, though.
I will say that this reboot is considerably more action oriented than the previous games. You can actually fight and kill your way through the game, if you really want to...though I wouldn't personally recommend it, as you'll eat through a lot of your resources that way. I appreciate that they opened up the option, though, whereas in the previous games you could almost completely forget about trying to fight.
I love the fact that The City is pretty open for you to explore at will, between chapters, to loot and steal to your heart's content... although it does seem that it's better to wait until certain points in the game to "visit" some places in order to acquire more loot and collectibles.
There's usually a decent number of alternate paths you can take throughout the game that should enable you to play in a style that suits you: Predator (knockout/kill threats), Oppotunist (use the environment to your advantage), or Ghost (breeze through without being detected and arousing as little suspicion as possible). Granted, certain playstyles will net you more loot depending on which part of the game you're currently playing.
The Focus ability is a neat feature that was implemented and can be a big help if you find yourself unsure what to do, or where to go next. I also greatly appreciated that they put in people you can buy supplies and gear from here and there, and the ability to upgrade both equipment and skills.
The only real problem/issue I had with the game was the fact that once in a while threats would get stuck in their pathing, but it was nothing that a reload couldn't fix, didn't have to quit out of the game or anything. The plot was also pretty predictable, but so were the other games (to me, anyway) and I still felt that it was all delivered well. The graphics and whatnot can be a bit hard on your computer, though... might want to try and make sure you've got some fairly beefy hardware to handle it.
Overall, I think Thief received a pretty good makeover to bring the game up to current times while still keeping the basic soul of the series.

Thief (2014) is a "reboot" of the Thief franchise...& maybe could be considered a true-blue sequel to Thief: Deadly Shadows (Thief: DS). Thief (2014) feels like a sequel to Thief: DS, since this game takes place (again) in a somewhat open-world called The City for "The Master Thief" Garrett (the player) to explore + b/c this feels much more modern than the previous game. Also, some references also seem like a continuation to Thief: DS. Just like Thief: DS, there are main missions + side missions for him to take on, as well - which are often excellent, with numerous stealthy ways + directions to choose, in a mission (especially main ones). Also, Garrett can also just explore The City to enter people's houses + shops to rob them!
Garrett meets up with an old friend named Erin, for whom he was a mentor to. She has been greedy, trying to find a certain object, which could make her ultra-powerful + ultra-rich. Erin disappears after an incident + Garrett awakens quite a while later. A disease called The Gloom is spreading + an over-powerful figure has taken The City by storm, imposing his will on this now poverty-stricked + disease-ridden City. This part sounds very similar to another [excellent] stealth game Dishonored (in which that game took a lot of cues from the older Thief games). There is also a resistance building-up against this person, as well - which again, sounds right out of Dishonored's book. Garrett begins taking jobs again to make money + to gain information on Erin's where-abouts.
There's an interesting dynamic that goes on b/t Garrett + Erin, which I wish was further explored here. Garrett usually knocks people out, steals stuff & moves along. Of course, the player can also play deadly, if they actually feel like it & choose to do so (or not). Meanwhile, Erin's turned into the complete opposite of Garrett - willing to kill to get what she wants, without hesitation. Early on, this stuff is excellent. I do wish this was emphasized + explored a bit more, though.
I do wish certain story elements + characters were explored quite a bit further here + a bit more fleshed-out; & that certain events went a different direction - instead of sometimes taking the predictable or under-developered route. This stuff is seems to be one of the few weaknesses I've seen to find with this game.
Eidos Montreal has tried like hell to make this game appeal to both the hardcore, old-school Thief fans + for the modern gamer. Besides your typical difficulty levels that games usually allow the gamer to select, players can impose a Custom Difficulty Mode. Here, the gamer can decide what features they can turn off. A lot of these features that can be disabled (or left enabled) - they are the features modernizing the game. These can range from Disabling One-Hit Takedowns, Game Fails When You Are Seen, Disable Focus Mode, Disabling Shimmering Objects & numerous other things. Personally, on my first run-through - I played on Thief difficulty mode. More games should take this excellent approach of allowing such a deep customization of your difficulty + settings - which flat-out embarrasses most games that basically only have a few difficulty modes.
Like Hitman: Absolution, there is a new X-Ray mode (which is similar to the Batman: Arkham games) called Focus Mode. Garrett can basically see through walls + see enemies. It goes further than that, also. Garrett can even slow-down time, be faster in this mode, do lethal blows & even see important objects be highlighted even more so than normal. A lot of this depends also on your difficulty settings + what skills you upgrade. Depending on what you turn on + off, the game scores the difficulty setting. You're scored in-game, also.
The more Garrett does in the game-world, the more money he can make so he can buy Equipment from merchants & even can purchase Focus Points from a certain someone. Also, Focus Points can even be found in the game-world. This is how Garrett upgrades his skills. Skills can range from making Garrett faster; see more hidden objects in the game-world (& on the map); make him lockpick faster; be more deadly in Focus Mode; his attacks do more damage; upgrade the amount of equipment he can carry; & numerous other things.
Garrett no longer carries a sword - for his main weapon. Garrett only has his blackjack, which by default can make the game played quite a bit more stealthy (as long as you don't level-up down a more action-orientated approach). Getting into fights (especially early on) is not really the best idea, until you've followed Garrett's skills down a certain path. Garrett has his usual assortment of arrows for his bow: regular arrows to hit enemies with; rope arrows so he can climb ropes + reach certain areas; fire arrows to burn objects + enemies; water arrows to put out fires; explosive arrows - to name a few arrows. Also, Garrett has a claw + can climb certain walls w/ it. While a great majority of the game is in 1st-person perspective for the camera + you're seeing through his eyes, when Garrett is platforming on pipes & rappelling down some objects (like Lara Croft would in the Tomb Raider games or Nilin in Remember Me), the game switches to a 3rd-person perspective.
Thief (2014) gets the feel of being "The Master Thief" better than any other game I've seen. Besides the big things the Thief games always got right, there's also now a lot of subtle + little things that are emphasized big-time here. A new cover system has been added, as well - in which Garrett can glance, lean + look around objects. Garrett can switch from cover-to-cover. A bit similar to Blink Mode from Dishonored, Garrett can perform a "Swoop" move that moves him very quickly & hard-to-see for a moment - but, its range is very limited. While here you can't move very far + in that supernatural way like Dishonored allowed with Blink Mode - Garrett's "Swoop" seems like a way to speed-up the gameplay here a bit, making it a bit faster + more action-orientated.
That's not everything on subtlties, either! When putting his hands around paintings, we see Garrett's hands close-up, moving around to try + find the switch to find hidden objects. The same goes for bookshelves, as well - when Garrett's looking for a book that actually might pull a switch to reveal a hidden area. We see Garrett react to objects he finds in the game-world, that might be worth a lot of money. We see (mostly) from the 1st-person perspective, with Garrett opening drawers to cabinets, dressers & other things - moving quick + fast like a Thief would. Garrett has a home-base, in which he stores all of the important things + trophies that he's found, stolen + taken. Not only that - you can look at your stats in-game + even store equipment there, also.
Nixxes has done a good job with making the PC version look technically excellent - which seems like the norm for them, after seeing many of their recent ports for Square Enix + Eidos (Hitman: Absolution, Tomb Raider 2013, Sleeping Dogs, etc). Though, performance was all erratic on DX11 w/ most things on Normal on my PC (i7 950; 1 GB of GF GTX 560 Ti; 8 GB RAM; Win 7 64-bit) on its own - ranging from 40 frames to 60 frames per sec at any moment. Locking it down to a 40 frames maximum with EVGA Precision X certainly solved this issue.
If you really liked Thief: DS w/ the direction that game took with gameplay + modernizing the series (when it did), then I'm pretty much preaching to the choir here - play Thief 2014; it does this even more so than Thief: DS. If you weren't happy w/ the direction Thief: DS took [especially when compared to the previous 2 Thief games (Thief: The Dark Project / Gold + Thief II: The Metal Age)] - it's still possible the game might be for the old-school Thief fan b/c of its new Custom Difficulty Mode. After 31 hours w/ my 1st playthrough - Thief (2014) was really good, even despite its few flaws that just rob it from reaching greatness.
Grade = B+.

I won't try to write some hugely comprehensive review nor will I write in a fashion where I try to convince you to play it or not -- I'm just a gamer, assumably just like you...I'm not paid for writing reviews and though I don't mean this in a vein of sounding bitter, but I don't really care if you play the game or not.
First things first --- my simple "flow chart" of decision for this game -> Have you ever played Far Cry 3? If no -> Do you like open ended game play? Do you like games with "missions" and character skill trees/progression?  Required: Do you like first person shooters? If you like at least one of the "optional" questions and you answer yes to the required try this game...but look for it on a sale.  (Note: If you don't like shooters....um....stop reading this and just move on. Its a first person shooter).
If you played FC3 and you liked it -> No brainer...it would make virtually no logical sense if you enjoyed FC3 but don't like FC4. Conversely if you played FC3 and hated it -- you'll probably hate FC4.
Moving on.....as you might have figured out I enjoyed FC3 and I really like open ended games. I don't like heavy scripting in my game worlds...I want to feel like I'm in control of what I do. FC4 delivers on that.
The game looks beautiful, FC3 looked really good as well...I actually think FC4 looks a bit better. Granted I'm running my resolution / graphic settings on high/ultra (forget what the game calls the highest settings)....the water, the mountains, the grass, the trees, etc. all look photorealistic. Even the animals look realistic. The grass, flowers, leaves in the trees, all move in sync with the wind for added realism.
The point to the "pretty" and detailed graphics ----> immersion factor.
Good variety of weapons ....actually a lot more weapons than other shooter games I've played.
Tons of things to do in the game BESIDES just banging out the main campaign story. I have over 30 hours in the game but I'm not even 20% complete on the campaign. How is this possible? Well -- side quests and exploring my friends....there's tons of side quests in this game, in my opinion -- they are all fun. Granted, like any game, over time it gets repetitive but to a degree I think no game can answer that because its human nature and not the fault of a game to say "really THAT mission again?".... The best a game can do is offer enough variety that the amount of repetitive content is kept  to a minimum. I think FC4 does a decent job of that.
My favorite things in the game?
I like playing stealth and trying to use  minimum resources (including ammo) to accomplish my objective. To me that makes the game much more fun to actually care about not getting killed or seen. To this end I really have fun liberating bell towers and outposts. Then there are fortresses -- think of outposts on steriods. The game even suggests you do NOT try to take them on solo (you can play co-op  or call in npc "guns for hire") ...well I tried to take one on solo...yeah i got owned. Man it was fun though...and that's what i like about this game so much, even where I get owned (make no mistake I have died a lot in the game already testing my tactics and limits of what i can do solo) I'm *usually* having fun.
So what don't I like or wish was different?
Well despite I like how "alive" the game world feels with wildlife roaming free...it does get aggravating when you are stealthily approaching an outpost - ready to take that shot to disable the alarms and out of nowhere a friggin bear or tiger jumps you. Now the aggravation to me isn't that this happens at all -- its I feel it happens far too much and it makes no sense when you scan the entire area before you do your mission and you see nothing.....so what does a tiger just teleport on the high cliff edge to my back?
The other thing is the game has some annoying "balance of reality issues" as I call it.....some animals are unrealistically tough....and some guns are too weak. Great example of each -- honey badgers....I've shot them with literally six arrows or many bullets before they die...that's just stupid. Yet I've dropped a huge yak with two shots from the same gun. Granted head shots matter but still it feels weird to me. There's an M700 sniper rifle in the game....in real life this weapon is well respected from both military and SWAT teams at least all over the USA....in this game I feel its too weak...I'm sorry but two shots center mass and the bad guy doesn't die? Really...its a friggin M700 rifle.
But as I'm getting good at head shots...and head shots are (rightfully) one shot , one kill....the annoyance with the m700 is very slight.
One last thing that's cool about this game -- while the AI isn't brillant, its pretty good...sound matters in this game. So if you shoot an elephant gun (btw the sounds of this game are pretty awesome...but I have a good sound card and 5.1 surround on my system too)  within just 100 or 200 yards of baddies ...they will react "What the hell was that?!" and they will look for the source of the sound. At the same time if you use a silenced gun (or better your bow -- the bow is friggin awesome in this game btw) they won't react the same.
There's a LOT to love in this game...I know I'm going to replay the crap out of it and pour tons of hours into it. There's cool moves you can do to -- like equip a wing suit and swoop in on baddies like you are super man and then go right into a weapon take down--which looks pretty bad♥♥♥♥♥and its fun . :)  You can ride an elephant and plow over vehicles mean while you can have a side arm ready to blow people away AS your elephant is running them over. :)
Anyway....I wrote a LOT more than I intended to....can you tell I like this game a lot? :)
I bought the game on a sale so I didn't even pay $50 for it....very well worth it. I'm pleased.
