The Yawhg is a cute little CYOA game. It's about how 1 to 4 people spend their time around a fantasy setting town before a catastrophe. It has simple choice and consequence mechanics, base on where you spend your time, and binary choices as reactions to events. You have a pool of stats which increase every day, which effects outcomes. What's novel about it is that it has local multiplayer, which is rather unusual as far as Interactive Fiction goes. The graphics are hand drawn and rather expressive, and the music is relaxing and melancholy. In the end, you see the results of your characters' actions, and if you save the town or now and to what degree. It's on Humble Bundle as of 12/18 for 60% off at $4, which is a fine price for what this is. There's decent replay value, and it's good for short gaming sessions. This isn't the most mind blowing or reactive CYOA, but it's fun, and the multiplayer aspect makes it unique.

Cool art, nice music, overall a decent style but where's the game? Click through a bunch of dialogue boxes in order to increase your base stats ready for the return of the Yawhg and then... click through a couple more that tell you how you did. There's no real story here either. The game can be completed in five minutes and isn't worth returning to.

Recommended for:
LEGO Traveller's Tales fans.
People who have seen the movies.
Completionists.
Pros:
- Good, friendly humor in the spirit of the movies appropiate for young and old.
- Interesting story level design, albeit with repetition (if you've seen one sailboat)
- excellent animations. Your character Captain (!) Jack Sparrow sometimes fights dirty during a swordfight and smashes a bottle on your opponent's head or slips a banana under his feet.
Contras:
- Story cutscenes make nearly no sense if you haven't seen the movies.
- Hublevel not as big as in the later Tt games (Well, it's one of their older games, so no biggie).
- Unimaginative mini-boss fights.
- Acrobatic sequences and walking narrow paths over abysses and poisonous swamps get frustrating very fast due to lack of precision and static perspective (using XBOX-Controller). Seems to be the crux in all LEGO Tt games. Ditto gamebreaking glitches, when script sequences and/or NPC get stuck, so that you have to reload the level to proceed beyond.
All in all LEGO PotC is only mediocre as far as Traveller's Tales LEGO games concerned.

What makes a fantasy story?  It's a question that has plenty of answers, but as far as the general public consciousness and especially as far as video games, "fantasy" tends to gravitate towards certain common tropes.  There's magic, good monarchies, evil empires, often some sort of destiny, perhaps a generational cycle extending back centuries, some kind of god-figure (whether actual or just some Great Person), some kind of opposing devil-figure, sometimes the power of friendship, and an apocalyptic battle for the fate of whatever setting houses the story.  Being that
is among the vast crop of fantasy RPGs that use the same set of buzzwords, yet was drawn from a different mythological and cultural tradition, I found myself curious and decided to give it a go.
You play as Enzo Kori-Odan, crown prince of the isolated city of Zama, soon to be king of the same.  However, things happen, and the story begins in earnest with Enzo and his wife Erine exiled and yearning to regain the throne.  The thing that interested me most about the early going was the dialogue with the tutorial boss; it actually felt more like the final boss dialogue for another game, where resolve makes all the difference and honor wins the day.  Here?  Nope.  Enzo is derided as naive...and he is.  Painfully and thoroughly, he is, and the rest of the game becomes, rather than a quest to regain his throne, a pilgrimmage to learn more about himself and the world.  Instead of accumulating external resources or combat experience, Enzo's milestones of power lie in maturing his philosophy.  The plotline and especially the cosmology feel fresh and have versimilitude, especially compared to the glut of cheap copypasted revelations and Tolkien-cribbed myths in so many other RPGs.
Obviously, all this would be useless without something to contrast with, so various characters, enemies and allies alike, have their own philosophies and views for the world (side note, two of the strongest characters in this respect are queens of their respective peoples, and both incredibly upfront and proactive in their rule).  Usually this would all be tied up with some kind of great evil that provides an existential threat to fight, but here, the biggest problem is figuring out what Enzo and Erine actually want for Zama, themselves, and the world.  All in all, it's a surprisingly philosophical story, especially given how typical the actual game feels.
It might sound like I'm calling the game a masterpiece, but sadly, it is not.  Whether due to lack of experience, limitations of their in-house engine, or lack of budget, the game lacks polish in almost every aspect.  The powerful themes of the story often end up hampered by puerile humor that isn't even funny in that guilty pleasure way, at least not often.   Philosophical asides from Enzo and Erine are bordered with scenes of Erine being a clingy jealous nag and Enzo being A Man I Can't Help It (TM).  It doesn't help that the localization is not particularly adroit, albeit understandable.
Outside of the writing, the map design sometimes feels akin to the Zelda CDi games, where you have to jump around to find what parts of the background and foreground are meant to be platforms, or you find yourself stuck on some weird geometry or are arrested by an invisible wall.  The interface has different categories for showing skills and inventory and such, but it really needs a redesign to make it more intuitive, and I can easily imagine newcomers getting lost (mostly because I did).  That being said, the fact that the status menu, the chests, and the teleporters throughout the game are basically high-tech gourds is a nice touch.
Combat is supposed to be a highlight of the game, and it is very fast and fluid, but it has its own flaws.  Perhaps the saddest is the gameplay compared to the fight cutscenes, which are intricate, dramatic, and a real treat to watch.  The guy who choreographed those deserves a goddamn medal.  Meanwhile, the combat animations lack impact (they could have used Mariel Cartwright's GDC talk about animation), and often the big flashy effects hide what's actually happening.  As far as gameplay, it's also rather iffily balanced.  Firstly, it demands a lot of attention for what actually happens.  Aside from HP, there's an AP bar (for skills) and stamina (for blocking and dodging).  Stamina, however, isn't like Dark Souls where it mainly works to control battle tempo.  It actually stays depleted, requiring items to fully replenish at any real speed.  It really gets in the way of how fast and fluid the combat wants to be.  Also, while it can be a plus, oftentimes combat's very easy...at least until you blunder into the middle of a large group and get stunlocked.  Erine is usually available as a combo breaker, and items are there to give you a quick heal if need be, but combat in general lacks feedback.  Speaking of items, they add a lot of unnecessary complication to the control scheme.  This isn't to say that I want the items to vanish entirely; I have a soft spot for food in video games, and even the simple dishes described sound mouth-watering and interesting, and they do tie in to a neat mini-leveling thing where if Enzo or Erine eat enough, they can apply a small bonus to one of their meters.  Still, I just think having them be healing items you shovel into yourself by the dozen to replenish whatever meter needs them feels like makework that distracts from your Aurion skills and your teamwork with Erine.
That's a lot of text, so I'll sum it up here:
is basically a diamond in the rough.  There are plenty of flaws, serious enough that if you're here just for the gameplay, I wouldn't really bother.  That being said, I really want to see Kiro'o Games get the funding and experience for something that matches their clear passion and ambition.  Even as it is, the game is still worth picking up if you're looking for a story that delivers a fresh take on the cliches of the genre, and if they had the ability and chance to deliver a more polished title, I'd absolutely be on board.

First impressions of an Early Acess Game
I am going to level with you, I hate multiplayer online games. With the passion of a thousand burning suns. It seems like whenever I go online there is some 12 year old dropping racial epithets, uber-leveled trolls making life impossible for new guys, amoung other annoyances.
So when i first saw that one of Caveblazer's talking points is "faux online play" i was interested. After buying it and settling into a game session, I was slightly put off by the fact that it seems to be a copy/paste of spelunky. The intro is similar, the cave mechanic is similar, the only things that are different is the art style and allocation of items (starting and otherwise)
But then i played the game a bit more...
Caveblazers is undoubtedly inspired by spelunky, and as a guy who enjoyed that game immesely, it really kind of felt like slipping to a comfortable pair of shoes. The diferences begin there however, as the enemy types take much more effort to kill, primarily because you are going into the cave with a rusty sword and a fairly mediocre bow. Also: where spelunky has a "here is a generic set of tools, get used to them as they are the normal, with speciality items being the exception", caveblazers loves to throw all sorts of shennanigans at you. From unlabeled potions of various colors, all sorts of upgrades for your bow and sword (including but not limited to: explosive, flak arrows, poison arrows, ice arrows, fire sword, 0 damage sword, the list goes on) as well as blessings, passive yet amazingly useful bonuses and perks.
Another interesting point i mentioned earlier is the "faux multiplayer" aspect of it. You are not the only adventurer in the cave! Every level has at least one, somtimes up to 3 (as far as i have seen at this early access stage) AI of varying temperment. Some of them will aggro the enemies, clearing the way for you. Some will ignore you entirely, darting in and out of your screen for a moment. While others will instantly go on the offensive and attack you without provocation! In this regard, while it is frustrating to lose an awesome build/run because some AI decided to be a jerk, it does lend a darker feel to the game. Not unlike dayZ, where each time you see another adventurer pop into view, you give it distance and try to judge what its attempting to do, before making a decision about it. Another good part about the AI is that it is generally well programmed, pathfinding nicely and even giving you space when you find loot (it wont swoop in and steal all the prizes and blessings you just knocked out of a chest).
All in all this game has a lot of potential, and I look forward to watching it evolve over time! Its sale price right now was $4.49 and i would reccomend getting it if you are a fan of spelunky and other rougelike games

It's like Vagante and Spelunky had a baby together and then the baby grew up and developed its own identity separate from its parents.  As far as roguelite games go, the movement is very fluid and the combat very challenging.  Moving around is a lot of fun, and the combat feels very visceral in spite of the low-count pixel-art.  It's fast, frenetic and you will die a LOT.
You might be wonder what the hell "pseudo-multiplayer" is.  All it really is, is that other adventurers exist that are the same as your own character, complete with inventory items and potions and healing items and everything.  Everything you can do, they can do.  They're controlled by AI.  I'm not a fan of "pseudo-multiplayer" as a term, but that's neither here nor there.  These other adventurers can be friendly, they could care less about you, or they could just be absolute ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s and murder you.  You never know how they'll react when they find you, and it adds an interesting layer of tension.
As you progress you can collect items, upgrade your equipment, find terrible potions, find helpful potions, gain blessings (pretty much just beneficial passive effects), and murder your fellow adventurers.
The game is still early but it exhibits a LOT of potential.  For 5 bucks, I think there's a lot to love here and I can only see it getting better and better.

I can say, without a doubt, Caveblazers is shaping up to be the best roguelike platformer I have ever played. I can definitely see it being the comparative game for all others that will follow further into development and release.
I had issues getting a Playstation 4 controller to work with the game so I can only speak for keyboard controls, but even with this minor issue (and the only bug I could find overall) [EDIT: I have been told PS4 controller support will come in the future, not a bug] the controls are incredibly responsive and easy to figure out. You get so drawn into playing the game that each keystroke just feels like a natural extension of yourself. I never expected to be as immersed as I was in the game and this was a major factor towards that.
Graphically the game is sound. I am a huge fan of pixel graphics, but only when they are done properly. And boy, were they done properly here. The animation is deliberate and fluid. Every entity's walk cycle is gorgeous. The particle and lighting effects are beautiful. Personally speaking, I loved the arrow effects that would change with each blessing and bow that you encounter.
Gameplay wise Caveblazers is refreshing. I have never been the biggest fan of a roguelike game in the past, but can typically appreciate them for their merits. This was never the case in this game. I found the challenge to push as far as I could to be more rewarding than in other roguelikes I have enjoyed in the past (See: Dungeon Souls & Hero Siege). Another aspect I noticed keeping me coming back was the joy I got from actually exploring the stage and finding as much loot as I possibly could. Generally speaking, I am not a completionist of this sort, but Caveblazers has such a sense of exploration and discovery driving the gameplay that I simply couldn't help myself.
There is a lot to talk about and experience within Caveblazers, but as I stated before, this is a game about discovery and I'd rather you have a chance to see it for yourself. This is one early access title you do not want to miss out on supporting. Buy this game and buy it today.

I have a question for you, reader: do you enjoy Spelunky, the roguelite darling that captured the hearts and minds of, well, a lot of people? Then have I got good news for you! Claveblazers IS Spelunky... which is pretty much damning Caveblazers with praise. Yes, it's mechanically sound. Yes, it has some interesting little deviations from the Spelunky formula. Yes, there are a lot of interesting additions planned for the full launch.
It is, however,  unabashedly Spelunky Lite in nearly every meaningful way. There's imitation, and then there's Caveblazers.
You play as a tiny man/kid/dude armed with sword and bow, who's heard tell of a legend: find this cave, blaze within, profit. An ornery old man warns you against this, forgetting he's an NPC in a videogame and CAN'T TELL ME WHAT TO DO. He is disregarded, and your adventure begins in earnest.
For Spelunky people this is all familiar territory: you enter a randomly generated vertical dungeon and descend, smashing crates and chests for loot, items, mysterious potions, and treasure, while avoiding traps and killing cave denizens. Variety at the moment is wanting... there's only one trap I've encountered so far (standard spike trap), and you'll slay a lot of the same bats, slimes, and little dudes over and over again.
Treasure is used as a currency for various shrines that can give you all manner of boosts, and there are little blessings sprinkled randomly throughout each dungeon that can provide the same for free.
However, this is a PSEUDO-MUTIPLAYER title, meaning little dudes that look identical to you will spawn on occasion during your descent. I'm... not entirely sure if they're always hostile or not (apparently their behavior is randomized – friendly, enemy, fearful). First playthrough I'm pretty certain the little pseudo-player fella that spawned for me was friendly until I peppered him with too much arrow fire. But after that every single one that spawned hated my guts – fortunately they hate the standard enemies with nearly the same enthusiasm, and they can all kill each other well enough.
These pseudo-players can grab power-ups, items, treasure and weapons just like you so it's critical you stay ahead of them. They also employ a more human-like strategy to ruining (or assisting!) your day, so best kill them or get out of the level as quickly as possible.
It's a cute little game, and I enjoy it. The combat feels good – enemies move fast, and each fatal blow feels impactful. The sounds (music, combat, ambiance) are excellent, the dungeon layouts are interesting, the RNG-y bits are RNG-y... it's just a bit more hollow, and a bit less charming than Spelunky. Now it's Early Access which means they intend to add new weapons and enemies, bosses, a proper endgame, customization – all that good stuff.
I recommend Caveblazers in that it is a fun game that feels complete. Even if they don't finish every planned feature, it's an excellent little game that stands on its own currently. If you have any doubts or wish to see any feature properly implemented and not just hypothetical in hypothetical land, I recommend holding off and seeing how Caveblazers develops.

Caveblazers is a difficult, randomised platformer that resurrects that feeling of "just one more go" from when you first played Spelunky, adding a greater focus on combat and random items.
It feels like a patchwork of existing ideas, most obviously from Spelunky, but also from modern roguelites such as Risk of Rain and true roguelikes such as Nethack. It also throws in cool ideas of its own, such as the AI bots that pretend to be other players, competing for the same loot as you.
Like Spelunky, you start at the top and make your way down a random cave, fighting enemies and collecting treasures. But Caveblazers adds loads more special items to collect (and store in your RPG-style inventory). They're vital to keep your health up and upgrade your weapons so you can keep up with the game's increasing difficulty.
Gameplay review video:
Speaking of weapons, from the start you're armed with a sword and a bow. Don't expect to be immediately good with them - you'll need practice with both (this is not an easy game!). The sword has a short range and requires expert timing to avoid being damaged, even by the most basic enemies. The bow is slick and endlessly useful, but only fires in eight directions, despite using the right analogue stick to shoot. Both can get swapped out with better versions as you rummage through crates and chests.
Once you get a groove on, you'll notice the level styles change satisfyingly fast - the first four levels of Spelunky are all the same, whereas in Caveblazers you've already reached a temple by level 3. More area styles (and more items, enemies etc) are promised in future updates.
Other roguelike elements include differently coloured potions that you need to drink to establish which potion it is (with good or bad effects), the ability to spend money at Risk of Rain-style shrines, rings that bestow bonus effects (but you only have 2 ring slots), magic wands and other special effect items.
The "pseudo-multiplayer" idea is fun. Basically, the game spawns intelligent bots that look just like you, who go round collecting treasure and fighting enemies, just like you. Apparently they have different personalities, but usually they just try to murder you. They offer quite a fight - they can do anything you can, including healing and using special items - and are therefore best avoided. Also, it's a shame they don't drop any loot upon death.
The graphics are a touch disappointing - they're in the style of the original free version of Spelunky, which feels a bit tired in 2016. The screens aren't very exciting to look at, especially since so many of the elements (such as chests, spikes, bats and slimes) are over-familiar. Even just a little more set decoration would polish things up nicely.
Caveblazers has only just hit early access, so quibbles aside I'm eager to see how the game develops. It's already fun and slick for an alpha game, and crucially doesn't feel half-broken or massively incomplete.
In summary, Caveblazers feels like somebody thought "What if I take Spelunky, keep the stuff that it does well, ditch anything annoying and focus more on the actual fighting?". And it works. It's not original and should try harder to get out of Spelunky's shadow, but damn, it's hard to put down.
* Game version reviewed: alpha 0.1.1 (29 March 2016)
*

While the art style and simplistic animation may be offputting at first, what first appears to be a shallow low-budget game quickly snowballs into an intense, strange, harrowing experience. You will have to suspend your disbelief a number of times, and yet it seems stronger for it.
If you have ever experienced depression (particularly without a support network), or ever lapsed into isolation, this game will resonate powerfully with you. If you enjoy horror or supernatural themes, but are sick of jumpscares and want something with a more personal, emotional plot? You'll find this really refreshing. What the game lacks in animation, voice acting quality and budget, it makes up with personality, emotion and freshness. Even where the voice acting was rough-edged, it still managed to portray flavoured characters and add depth to a deliberately flat, gray world.
My review may not sound flattering, but I really can't find the words to explain this gem. If you ever have the chance to pick it up on a sale, I wouldn't hesitate. Horror enthusiasts may not want to wait that long.
I'm baffled why this game isn't more discussed or acknowledged.

This game does an excellent job of illustrating what depression feels like to those who suffer from this crippling disease. It also helps those who deal with depression see how seeking help in the forms of medication and therapy can bring relief.
This game saved my life 10/10.

GENERAL
I feel that DQ could not quite decide what it wanted to be on a practical level.
Functionally, the intro page describes it as "an amalgamation of the experiences of the developers and several people close to them" but also "as real a simulation of depression as possible"
Therein may be the fundamental flaw from which others grow.
Sadly, it is my opinion that in trying to serve different masters, it served none of them particularly.
NARRATIVE DESIGN
As an autobiographical narrative, the author ("I") is protagonist.  In a simulation, the audience ("you") is protagonist
During play, the strictures of the autobiographical ("experiences of the developers") narrative PROJECTED onto the audience (the narration is in the second person : "you" - you do this, you feel that).
Which, I find, doesn't give the audience suitable opportunity to emotionally "buy into" the persona of the protagonist.  This is exacerbated by the style which requires to not only identify with, but identify AS the protagonist.  The audience is simply being told what they think, do and feel  - which I found alienating (from a gameplay/audience perspective) ---  there was simply no opportunity to form a  personal "me" in the narrative's "you"
The intro page does acknowledge the fact that the design is, essentially, autobiographically based (on the developers and people close to them) which may be causing the narrative to suffer from clustering effects (those CLOSE to them)
giving a somewhat myopic perspective on the subject.  At times, for example, mental/emotional states are described that are possibly more akin to various anxiety disorders (social anxiety, panic-related, etc).
While it's not particularly unusual for depressive and anxiety disorders to coexist, it is not inherent in a depressive experience and so preaches not to the choir, but only to the tenors narrowing the accessibility
window and possibly diluting the depressive issue by unduly injecting such a limited perspective.
I feel the design would have better served if the developers would have
1) used a narrative style that did not attempt to subsume the identity of the audience, bu would allow the audience to come to terms the the protagonist
2) looked beyond their immediate sphere for other perspectives to more fully explore the issue and refine focus (to depressive issues)
3) [this may be an oversight on my part, I looked for, but did not see a ref] worked with accredited clinicians in the development of this
GAMEPLAY
This is, essentially, a text-based adventure game of the 'choose your own adventure' style.  While necessarily limited int terms of degrees of freedom granted to the audience, I find if they are done well they
can have value.  The caveat there is that with such limits, they must be well executed.
This is especially important as one of the stated goals is to work as "real a simulation...as possible"; an area of experience that CYOA isn't particularly amenable to.
The concept of option non-availability and eventual option collapse to express the depressive experience as a "trap" has merit.
The exclusion of a presented options without any exploration, however, is somewhat trite and pushes the story, very obviously, "into the chute" of the author's ultimate thesis, pulling the audience out of an
interactive (and/or sympathetic) experience
A more fully developed optional tree where, for example, "dead end" behaviors can be explored and demonstrated as non-viable (and perhaps THEN disallowed) would, I feel, make the material more audience experience centered.
Additionally, a more fully developed tree using a variety of types of depressive experiences could allow the audience to encounter a depressive experience that is more relatable to themselves.
The descriptive text, itself, I found to be overly verbose - or at least presented as monolithic slab after monolithic slab causing reader fatigue.  Discussion of various solutions (raw culling of text, reformatting, etc) is beyond the scope
of this review.
The intro page describes sound as an element of the play experience. I feel this is overstated : The sound is essentially a very short, static background music track and does not actually inform gameplay (change with status, provide environmental cues, etc)
While BG music may help set a tone, that can be said of any game or presentation using music and isn't inherent to the play.  It could even be argued that a more personalized music track relating to depressive experience may have greater impact.
CONCLUSION
I find DQ similar to many early personal expression efforts across a variety of media in that it serves, largely as catharsis for the author and can tend to serve the author more than the audience.
As a literary piece, it may have been better presented in a more traditional linear format such as a novella or series of essays
As a game (or other interactive experience) it feels like a beginning effort (a "hello world" application) and could have benefited from 'more time to bake'
As a piece of popular public commentary, it may be much like many recent sociopolitical documentary films - the gravity or popularity of the subject matter itself perhaps drove the piece into a state of prominence that is beyond its scope .

With Pre-Civilization Egypt, Clarus Victoria had an opportunity to take Pre-Civilization Marble Age forward. You generally expect a sequel to be at least as able as its predecessor, this is one step forward, two steps back. Instead of Warcraft I to Warcraft II to III, we see Hero of the Kingdom I become Hero of the Kingdom II - a stale rebake of a mediocre game.
It feels unfinished, should be early access. The text interrupts are poorly written and detract rather than enhance. Extremely narrow strategic choices, inferior to Pre-Civilization Marble Age.  You have no access to any information and no options to control anything. No infopedia and no explanation of how much of the mechanics break down. You have no idea where construction will take place, until its built, and surprise it will be on certain preset tiles. Rather than Marble Age blossoming into a more sophisticated, interesting and complete game this is more like being delivered a still partly frozen pizza.
Worst of all, its frustrating rather than fun.
I do not recommend this, even on sale

Two minor suggestions: the number of surprises in the game make it pretty hard to win on the first playthrough, even on the easiest difficulty; more foreshadowing or sense of pace would help. Also, Enter, space, or some other key as a shortcut for End Turn.

I've played the Pre-Civ series since the flash games. This game is still decently fun, but it strays a bit too much from the formula IMO, and ends up feeling like a normal boardgame too much. Because of how the tech tree is built, you actually can't stray from a breadth first approach very easily and end up doing a lot of the same build orders a lot unlike the previous games. Still a fun game but I'd recommend Marble Age over this if you had to choose.

Much like the prior Pre-Civilization games, this game is about doing "the right things, at the right times."  It's less of a game and more of a story that you must play over and over again, until you get it right.  Memorizing events and refining your play style until you do exactly what you need to do, in the correct order.
The game gives you very little breathing room; mistakes cost you the game, and a mistake can be as simple as choosing the wrong bonus.
A typical play through of a game is 1.5 to 2 hours, depending on how much you decide to read.  Your first play through, and likely several after, you will get crushed.  That's the point of these games - to get you to be as accurate as possible with your decisions and pass all the in-game trials.  It's a puzzle, afterall.
If I had any feedback: I'd love to see a Pre-Civilization game be much more forgiving.  All of the games in this series require you to be absolute in your decision making process.  Sometimes, I just want to have fun, rather than guess my way through a game a few times until I get it right.
Admittedly, I actually found Pre-Civilization Mable Age more fun than Egypt.  It felt longer and more forgiving; though the way in which Egypt is presented to you I like a heck of a lot more (It looks far less like a Flash or Mobile game, and more like an actual game).  The ending of Pre-Civilization Egypt will seriously sneak up on you during your first play through.  I was very taken back when the game was telling me I had only 17 turns left.  Felt short.
All in all, this is a game you'll play a few times and try to master, but unless you're extremely meticilious, you'll get frustrated and annoyed.  If you enjoyed any of the prior Pre-Civilization games, you'll enjoy Egypt: It's more of the same, presented better, yet shorter.

I really like the format of this game and I hope to see more like it. It has elements of a citybuilder and grand strategy, but is a bit more "linear" than your typical strategy game. This means that cities grow more organically and you get to focus on a scale of decisionmaking that makes sense for the scale of your empire. Early on, you are deciding which forest you want to forage in. End game, you are choosing what form of tribute you want from neighboring colonies so you can defeat your rival kingdom. This transition would be hard to pull off in a sandbox game.
I think this game is easily worth the full price. Hope to see some more games from this developer covering different eras of history (or fantasy/scifi)!

LEGO Pirates of the Carribean is another title in the LEGO series by Traveler's Tales. It tells the tale which spans accross the entire franchise (at the date writing this review) in a fun, cheeky and childish way which is friendly to everybody.
It features the same engine and core mechanics as many other LEGO titles in the series, but it is obviously a much earlier version. It lacks the story telling components introduced in later releases and it does depend on the user to know the story well before actually playing. It attempts to present itself in a way which does sufficiently tell the story, but without prior knowledge it still has unfinished links in this translation.
There are various bugs in this game which are both infuriating and game-breaking. Quite often you'll be able to jump into a spot with no way of escaping other than restarting the game, and some technical issues causing crashes. Limiting the framefrate to less than 60 seems to fix those problems though. On top of all the problems with this game, I really enjoyed the franchise specific animations and the swordplay mechanics, especially later in teh game.
Overall it's a great game which you can have a lot of fun with the franchise and LEGO. If you're able to iron out the frustrating parts, it's definitely worth the time and I would recommend it.

This is probably just best retro styled, addictive, and fast paced arcade shoot 'em up on steam, and its only $1. How can you go wrong. The game has great pixel graphics, you could run this on your mothers toaster. The gameplay is very simple, you could teach this game to a person whos never played a game in their life. You turn left and right, and you press a button to boost. Thats it. As you go objects fly past you and and green pickups that refill your ammo as you are constantly shooting. There are also powerup weapons that come along and change your shot type, this offers variety to the game and you arent stuck with the same straight line shot every run. The longer you stay alive shooting objects and ships the more harder it gets, spawn rates increase, harder enemies come along and the whole screen is basically flooded with stuff to dodge and manouver. When you die you can return to the ship selection where you can unlock new "bit blasters" with the yellow coins you collect in runs. Each ship has different stats but as you progress that ships become slightly better every time. Another thing i like about this game is when you die you can just hit one button and youre back in the game again, no uneccesary screens to go through, however it takes a while for the difficulty to ramp up back to where the game is actually fun. After you unlock all the ships the only thing to go for is to increase your high score which is ok but i think there still should be some more progression after unlocking everything. I know this is a 1 dollar game but i dont know what to do with all my coins. But yeh this game is pretty much the best $1 you will spend in along time and you can basically guarantee you will get you "dollars worth" out of the game.

So, I have been playing MTG on paper for 5 or 6 years now, I've also played all of the previous Duels of the Planeswalkers games, so I would say I have a decent opinion on this game.
Magic duels is a perfect game for beginners learning to play Magic the gathering. The UI is simple yet effective, the cards in the game are interesting yet simple, and pretty much a very pleasant game to enjoy.
(You can also be creative with your deckbuilding, like me and my friends made pseudo-highlander decks in Duels and it was hella fun!)
The game also updates it's content frequently, (better or for worse) and is totally FREE!
However, I would not recommend this for older MTG players, because of the lack of cards in the game, and the lack of depth in the game that many veterans of the game may find lacking.
In the previous DotP-games, there were decks that had really powerful cards, like future sight, primordial hydra and Kozilek, the butcher of truth.
Furthermore, the game lacks any sort of variety in terms of other gameplay modes, there's the single player campaign, single player mode and multiplayer mode, but that's basically it. The only mode that really chances fundementally the rules of the match is two-headed giant, but even that is flawed.
The other games in the series however had really unique modes like archenemy and planechase, that I really enjoyed.
So, to recap, this is not for the MTG veteran trying to find a free version of MTGO, but is rather a fun game to enjoy for new players, or for people who just enjoy playing a slightly kitchen table-y version of Magic.
Would Recommend.

I literally have no interest in the controversy surrounding this game and I'm no professional, and I can say that this was an interesting experience. Not good, not bad, interesting.
Objectively, it should not be a game. It's a work of (non)fiction that has the sole gameplay mechanic of clicking on stuff. I ignore the developer and focus on the game, and the problem is that this is not a game. This is an unique kind of party game that you don't find anywhere else. Rather than a party game where you have mindless fun and game, this is a game where you and your friends take on a role and roleplay together. As such, it is a really good roleplay game, where all of the actions have direct or/and indirect consequences and changes the outcome of the game. With every playthrough, every decision and consequences differs, and so every playthrough is unique in it's own way. The art-style is nice, the music (albeit repetitive) suits the mood, the gameplay is simple and engaging, and when played with friends, i have no doubt that it'll be a fun party game, possibly even better when drunk.
As a single player game however, it completely lacks any kind of weight. This is the reason why i cannot recommend this to anyone who does not have a friend to play couch co-op with, because that is the only way this game is meant to be played. 0.2 hours is all that it takes for me to finish one playthrough, and that's with me reading every single text. It's really short, really shallow as well, and does not leave a lasting impression. Like i mentioned before, this game is meant to be played with other people, who will contribute their own depths to the story. Playing it alone however, means that there's nothing much to do, except absentmindedly pick choices and read the consequences, alone.
I want to love this game, because this kind of game with choices, branching story, consequences that impacts the story, and character building, but there's not enough for me to love about this game
TL;DR if you have someone to go couch co-op with, i would recommend buying it. If you don't have, don't buy this.

Except for a few minor bugs (and a couple levels that seemed out of character compared to the rest of the game), I thought it was practically perfect for what it was trying to do. It didn't overstay its welcome, it threw up just enough horror and gore to keep you interested but let your imagination fill in the goriest blanks, and it managed to sustain a good pace, atmosphere, and tension over its short length.

You can see how truly great this game is when all the (very few) negative reviews are about whiny people that don't like platforming ~ exploration and / or difficult stuff. It's ok to dislike those things, but if you do, why bother playing - and most important, reviewing - a game that's all about this?
Well, that aside, let's talk about the product. Momodora is one of the greatest surprises I've ever had, first because of its price compared to the content you get (not anything too broad, but enough to keep you tuned for about 4~6 hours) and because of the quality of said content. The game is very pretty, visually and aurally combined, and you can feel the passion the devs put into their work at every single room of the map. The controls are simple but effective, and besides one or two design quirks that personally I would've changed (the interaction between the attack and roll animations, and the invincibility frames of the latter) there's nothing to complain about - you have melee and ranged attacks, dodge, double-jump and items with various active and passive effects to use. The level design makes good use of that variation, and from time to time you'll find yourself using everything at your disposal to keep progressing between all the nine areas from the map, each one with its own theme and boss. The difficulty level can be quite challenging too, but in a fair way, encouraging players to adapt to their enemies' pattern and play it safe until they can predict and master the outcomes. This is more evident during boss fights, where bosses that appears to be a menacing threat at first can be killed without damaging the player after understanding how and when they'll attack.
All in all Momodora is an incredible game, a very inexpensive experience that will entertain and please you without overstaying its welcome (the game knows how to end without wearing its novel value) but giving enought reasons (collectible items, new difficulties, achievements) to be played again if you wish to. For fans of the Metroidvania genre (the non-linear and exploration heavy 2D formula popularized by, you guessed it, Metroid and Castlevania) this game will be more than enough to enter that sweet spot of great recent representatives, alongside Salt and Sanctuary, Ori and The Blind Forest, and Axiom Verge. All the praise Momodora receives is well deserved, and if you like anything about the genre, give it a try. You will not be disappointed.

Aurion: Legacy of the Kori-Odan or Aurion: l'heritage des Koriodan surprised me as a game. So at first I thought it was going to be a simple, exiled royals gather forces to get their kingdom back storyline. But to my surprise, the game is highly philosophical, even the powers and the mixes of powers are based on traits and philosophical approaches to governance and leadership. The plots in each zone examine political approaches to different scenarios and how systems are not perfect. The magic of the world is explained perfectly and even the antagonists both major and minor allow you to understand their personal philosophies as it ties into their powers.
The biggest questions in the game deal with history, prejudice, politics and how to have oneself on the political stage, that and magical African anime powers. What surprised me and I found refreshing, is that you never ever get to fight the most powerful antagonists because they are just too strong, both physically and politically, there is no overthrowing the system, there is only, making sure you survive the system. Most anime and game tropes have you becoming strong enough in a short period to beat a foe that has decades ahead of you in training and put more work into it than you, not this game. And because of that, it feels like a more real world. I plan to replay to see if there was more that i missed and take my time.
One of my favourite aspects is the marriage and personal growth system in the game. Since the MCs are a married couple, their powers only get stronger as their relationship grows and improves. The husband and wife both undergo massive character development and work through rocky times together to prevent them from being one dimensional, they have different ideas, strengths and opinions and they don't always agree. They fall out, but they pull each other up. Its subtle but it shows that marriage, like the political systems and philosophies the game weaves into its world, is not perfect, but it is always something to be worked on. I thank the studio for making not only a purely African game, but a great one that made me think and actually want to replay an RPG.

I'll try to keep this as impartial as possible.  My game time was 16.5 hrs. I held off writing a review until i had beaten it so here we go:
Lets talk about the pros first:
1) Beautifully drawn art
- The 2D character sprites and environments are quite beautiful and diverse. Never did i felt it was underwhelming or constantly repeating. Every area was a breath of fresh air.
2) Characters
- Its really hard not to like the main charancters Enzo and Erine. Thier story and trials really jerked me to the core. They were properly fleshed out. Other supporting characters had thier own stories and they actually felt like real people with their own lives rather than placeholders
3) Gameplay(pro)
- Its a classic 2D brawl beat-em-up and once you master the controls you can pull of some crazy combos
4) Story
- I'd say better than average, there is one part later in the game where a certain 'past' is revealed and it is actually heartbreaking and tear inducing.
5) 60fps
- A few drops here and there but nothing major or gamebreaking
6) Mythology
- Honestly seeing so many games borrowing from Greek and Norse mythology has gotten boring. So it was a breath of fresh air when i saw this one has its roots in African mythos, a world and culture i am absolutely unfamilar with, so i had a blast myself in experiencing something new.
Cons:
1) Load Times
- Ranging from 5-20 seconds they are a pain. Honestly I got used to them but I suppose in games where you have to get into battles every minute or so , players can get irritated
2) Minor fps drops
- Especially when you are fighting a boss. I have noticed sometimes when a boss charges and unleashed a special attack there is a  huge fps drop for a second or two which blindsides you because you have no idea where that attack will come and you usually fall victim to it.
3) Translation
- Again nothing gamebreaking but sometimes you get lost in the conversation, and have to scratch your head over what they are talking about.
4) Control Scheme
- The buttons required to pull off moves or combos are really spread out and in pretty strange combinations. So many times have i unleased a support fireball rather than support healing. You really need to master it to progress.
5) Gameplay (con)
- The thing i absolutely hate is in each battle you are thrust with 8-10 enemies and unless you keep jumping around they can pretty much gang up on you. If they corner you  or surround you from both sides you're as good as dead.
Honourable mentions:
1)Erine
-Seldom I have seen in games a strong and powerful woman who is both a Queen and a wife. Her inclusion was very surprising to me since i thought early on she would just be a damsel in distress. But no, she fights with you, supports you, she is a constant pillar in the MC's life...... and damn is she hot! :P I just wish they had options for alternate costumes.
2) The royal couple
-I cant help but compare the two MCs to the FFXV couple. One king goes on a joyride with his boyband while the other travels the world in exile seeing how people live and ease thier burdens and how to solve political issues so he can better rule over his own people when he get back.
- One queen who is nothing more than eyecandy and a damsel in distress while the other who properly supports her husband, fights alongside him, makes decisions and takes the lead when he is feeling down.
Final Verdict: 8/10
Its definitely recommended. I really liked the game and hope the devs create a sequel or at least a spin off. With more options than we were given this time (extra costumes hue :3 )

I used to like this game a lot, after all it's Magic: The Gathering for free and with full deckbuilding capabilites. However, since the latest update, it's lost quite some appeal for me, since the daily quest rewards by now pressure players into PvP, which is something that I'm not overly comfortable with.
But that is only what tipped the scales for this game to fall out of my favour. It was never a really great game to start with and I would have admitted that much earlier on already, if Steam had not for some reason prevented my review from showing up previously (I don't know why): While mechanics-wise Magic: Duels relatively decently captures the MTG rules (with some deckbuilding exceptions that I won't go into detail on here), the game's UI is absolutely horrible. There is so much clicking needed to navigate menus, it's just annoying. Even worse are the animation settings which default to "show me every unneccessary animation there is", which really delays the game's flow - especially in multiplayer, when you've shut down most animations to increase the pace of the game to interactive levels, but you opponents haven't and you're forced to sit out them watching useless damage animations.
On the positive side, it is a free game after all and no player really needs to spend money on it to obtain everything there is to obtain. In-game currency can be obtained relatively easily through daily quests and duels against AI or (more lucratively) human opponents, and using these I was usually able to obtain on average one booster every day, which is decent advancement if you ask me.
Nevertheless, I won't recommend this game to everyone. It is definitely all right for fans of MTG who shy back from the more costly Magic: Online, but want to play a casual game of Magic once in a while nonetheless. And it may also be a nice way to learn the ropes of the TCG without spending money. But as a game in itself, Magic Duels is not really satisfactory over a long time, especially due to the clunky and misconstructed AI.
The matchmaking system is extremely unbalanced and its niegh impossible to progress unless you throw money at it. overall fun but frustrating.

I purchased this game on a fluke and it ended up my favorite game of all time. I've been playing Nuclear Dawn since the beginning. The game had a surge in popularity, the participation died off dramatically, and saw another surge in popularity again. This is bacause there is no actual game developer, and the Nuclear Dawn community has taken the task of fixing in-game glitches, improved balancing experienced and new players at map startup, created mods, and create gaming events that have brought all the core fans back to the fore.
Nuclear Dawn is a fast-paced Real Time Strategy (RTS) and a First Person Shooter (FPS) game combined in one. One person elects to be the "Commander", enters the team HQ and the view becomes an RTS, for all other players its an FPS. Other temmates are respinsible for capturing tertiary points that bring in income to the Commander to build supply stations, ammunition, turrets and new spawn points.
The main challenges for the Commander are: power management, strategic placement of forward structures, and resource management.
The main challenge for the other teammates are: capturing tertiary poins, maintining control of those tertiary points and defending the forward structures and power grid the commander builds up. This is accomplished by the teammates evenly dividing themselves into one of four soldier classes: Stealth, Assault, Exo, and Support. All classes have critical strengths and one achilles heel against one type of class. For example: Charge in with all heavy eight Exo gunners, three cloaked Stealth scouts can kill them all with one stab in the back. So a balanced team with all four classes is crucial for success.
On that last point is the game's greatest triumph and greatest failure. Your quality gaming experience depends on how well your team cooperates with the commander and with each other. If a commander has a disorganized team, the team refuses to take orders from the commander, or simply the entire team goes ranged scouts with sniper rifles (has happened to me several times)...the game is doomed for that team, and makes for an emotionally intense, grueling, and demoralizing 20-45 minutes of "turtle-ing" at the base accompanied with teammates pointing fingers of blame, general freaking out and some verbal abuse. But...if the team is quick to respond to the commander's requests, has an even distribution of class types, whether win or loose, it makes for the most memorable, magical, endorphin-rush-to-the-brain-gaming experiences you could experience. That is what keeps players returning to this game. That is also why fans of this game are so incredibly loyal.
That being said...the less desirable, grueling gaming experiences have driven off many players. When I used to play hardcore 4 hours a day there were anywhere from 10 to 15 servers active with 12-35 players on at any given time around the world. Today there are only two servers with 3-10 active players plus bots at on high traffic hours of the day. The only times there are high numbers are when ND parties are organized and that usually happens twice a month.
Requirements for pleasant gameplay:
1. GET A MICROPHONE!!!! - Nobody can play in a fast paced environment without team chat. Teammates or the Commander may request favors, give orders, ask for tactical support, or may need status updates...typing responses is out of the question. Typing is so laborious that all non-microphone players eventually stop typing all together, killing the tactial advantage of communication within the team.
2. COOPERATE WITH TEAMMATES AND THE COMMANDER - This is not a one person game. It's solely dependent on how well the team can act as a unit.
3. EVENLY DIVIDE THE CLASSES YOU PICK - Your about to respawn and there's no medic on your team? Man up, stop being a Scout with a sniper rifle missing all your head shots and support the heavy Exos.
4. LEARN HOW TO BE AN EFFECTIVE COMMANDER - This can only be learned with experience and my video tutorials at:

Note these tutorials are very old, but the core strategies remain effective. Do I recommend this game? Absolutely. Would you be playing this game often with other users? At the current rate of participation, unless you have a few friends that don't mind giving ND a shot with you, probably not.

This game looked cool and I had some high hopes for it, but it seems Firaxis didn't give a ♥♥♥♥ about this one. There's a lot that just simply angers me in this game.
To start there's not enough civilizations, and the civilizations only have a single recorded voice line. AI is just far too easy in this game and I'm not even that great in Civ,  this is probably due to being able to win over civilizations by military size or through making them happy by doing certain quests. Which brings me to my next points.
Quests, The Tech Tree and Diplomacy.
Quests aren't fleshed out enough, and most just feel rushed or last minute attempts to add something else to the game, some seem to be broken or don't make any sense. Although I do like the concept of quests in a Civ game. Moving on to the Tech Tree, this is probably what makes me annoyed the most, it looks very unorganised and just generally all over the place compared to Civ V / VI, I feel like this sort of tree as well could be very confusing for a new player compared to the design used in Civ V / Civ VI.
Now talking about Diplomacy, I didn't find it too bad it just felt like they tried something new except it didn't work out. You can use diplomatic points to increase your standing with other civilizations, or you can just choose to lower it and of course go to war. You can also use these points to make agreements with other civilizations but I don't know if it's actually worth doing so yet.
I think mainly I just hate the UI in this game along with the fact that it feels empty and not worked on enough. It's good if Firaxis were trying some things but if anything I would've said this is more of a mod/expansion of Civ V than a whole new game. Unfortunately the state of this game has made me lose respect and expectations of what Firaxis will do. So whether I buy Civ VI or not is a tricky one.

Edit: So after the patch the game seems better, at least now one has the option to play an actual easy difficulty and finish the game without too much complex god-like strategy skills and memorization for what lies ahead. Normally I hate easy difficulties and like a good challenge, but in this case it felt way too hard on the easy difficulty and for the wrong reasons, and there isn't a clear way to know you'r not doiing well until the end of that game so it can be frustrating at that point.
Anyway, I realize I was a bit too harsh on tha game before, I probably expected too much of a 9$ game. And above all, the developers response have been awesome, and I value this almost as much as a good game. I wish them well, it's a good first try (if it is) and maybe we'll get better games from them in the future.
A note to the developer tho: yes I am from Egypt and I love storytelling in games, but it needs to be a bit less subtle to grab my attention, needs to play a bigger part somehow..it didn't really connect with me in the game.
I'm changing this to a positive review, for 9 bucks and a few hours, I did have some good fun even if it didn't last forever, but I guess that's fair :)

I've played a couple of games so far, and I enjoy this. This is honestly a really great game with enough ideas to make it a pretty unique Civ game, especially with the DLC. I'm not sure what the reason for a lot of the hate is, I've really enjoyed this.
Only true problem I've come across is the diplomacy (which is pretty♥♥♥♥♥♥in every Civ game tbf). I like the concepts of Diplomatic Capital and the Fear / Respect system, but I think there's some issues with the way they do it. Firstly, when you make a peace agreement with another civ, everyone who is enemies with that civ will lose respect for you because you "trust" them. I understand them losing respect if you change your relationship for the better with these civs, but the fact that you have diplomatic consequences for NOT wanting to be at war is pretty stupid. That's all I came across that I really disliked. Really wish the Civ games would adopt a less transparent approach to diplomacy, but it's bearable I guess.
I really love the way the game looks, and I feel like the military units are a lot more interesting to battle with than they are in Civ 5 or 6. I like being able to build a lot of improvements on water as well as entire cities (ie. farms, mines, academies, etc.). I also really love the character design of the leaders (Arshia Kishk, Han Jae-Moon, Kavitha Thakur). I also really like the stories behind it, I think there's a lot more feeling behind this game than in the main Civ games because there's a real story. I think the Affinity system is really great especially.
Also it's a lot, lot better with mods, honestly. I feel like there are a few mods which really complete this experience for me, making it more enjoyable and Civ-like:
- Affinities as Yields
- Awesome Loadout and Sponsors
- Social Engineering
Conclusion: It's upsetting that a lot of the reviews are negative based on it "not being as good as Civ5" which I feel is an unfair comparison. It's a really good game--though buy it when it's on sale; $70 for the game and the DLC is too much. But if you can get it for cheap (like the last Humble Bundle) it's really worth it, I had a lot of fun with this, it's definitely worth playing if you loved Civ5 and want to try something a bit different.

Pre-Civilization Egypt is part simulation, part history lesson. It's highly atmospheric, and very addictive in that 'just one more turn' sort of way. Multiple levels of difficulty make for high replayability, too. Be warned: the game comes to a very abrupt end -- by design -- in about 3000 BC (something that I find quite refreshing -- some games these days can drag on far too long!).
I've played it through twice now, and lost both times (the second time by just one turn, curse it!). Each playthrough took me about ten hours, and as I'm sure I'll try it again, I consider this game excellent value for money.
It's a fun little game. I enjoyed it and would recommend it to others. It's easily worth the 8€ and I would in all likelihood buy a sequal.

A relaxing turn-by-turn strategy/puzzle game about resource management. Each play-through runs into the same major events, but there are minor events that mix it up a bit. Knowing the major events coming up is part of the gameplay, so it doesn't really feel unreplayable.
For some reason it reminds me about the 12 Tasks of Hercules series, though it plays nothing like those games. Probably because, at it's core, it is about resource management.
It's got an original slant, it's atmospheric, and I'd love to see more of these.
UPDATE: And now that I'm a bit further along in played hours, I find it kind've relaxing. A bit like playing solitaire: you know what the tasks are, but how you get there is the trick, and no one game is going to knock your socks off.

The game mechanincs is very similar to Sid Meier's Civilization, and is focused on the historical events that lead to the rise of the Egyptian unified empire. I recommend this game because I had fun playing it, and also because of it's historical accuracy. After playing Egypt Pre-civilization, the player will have an understanding of the events and factors responsible for the development of the ancient Egyptian civilization that would be otherwise difficult or boring to many people to obtain by just reading books and academic papers. I think Egypt Pre-civilization is an example of how video games are an excelent tool to teach knowledge of the real world.
This game is for you if:
* You like Sid Meier's Civilization
* You are interested in ancient Egypt or ancient history
This game is not for you if:
* You are looking for a game as good or better than Sid Meier's Civilization
* You're not interested in Egyptian history at all
Other factors that can drive away people from this game is that is very linear, following the sequence of events that lead to the unification of the Egyptian empire, and that it may be very difficult to win. But again, these drawbacks are otherwise contributing to achieve perhaps the mean goal of the game: teach ancient Egyptian history. On the other hand, I really liked the art design, it's beautiful and captures very well the character of Egyptian art.

This game offers a very rich historical gaming experience and oh boy does it deliver!
It's an educational linear turn-based historical simulation strategy that will lead you through the history of Ancient Egypt. Starting from 5000 B.C. you will guide the nomadic and humble Egyptian tribe through all the hardships to prosperity and power culminating in the Unification of Lower and Upper Egypt. Get ready to witness evolutionary breakthroughs that enabled early Egyptians to march into faraway lands, fight catastrophes, hardships and ultimately establish first Egyptian state. Will you be able to re-enact the events that unfolded historically or will you doom your fledgling chiefdom into forgotten annals of history? Get an intimate knowledge about events that took place before the Classic Egypt eras through this unique game.
This game really made me understand the evolution of the Egyptian civilization. It all makes so much sense now! It really made me understand the whole history of the area much more. This is such an interesting chapter of the human history and developers have done an amazing job at portraying first steps of the human civilizational evolution in Egypt!
I really like the ambient of the game, background music, voices, the way upgrades are applied on the map, the way your tribe evolves from meager beginnings to a powerful state, the paintings that are shown when a major event happens, etc. There is a lot of replayability in it too because there's always a new strategy you would like to try out to better the results and maybe delve into higher difficulties and see how your strategic wisdom (or it's lack) will bode for the people you guide.
The game is not too simple and not too hard, it does stuff very nicely. It is rather unique in what it does. At the release the game did end rather abruptly and the unification warning did not trigger soon enough to warn the player. Wasn't able to complete it because the game didn't provide me with enough information. This has been resolved in the patch now.

This game is the spiritual successor to BloodLine Champions (BLC for short), which is also free to play on steam. Before we get in to the nitty gritty of this review, I want to make it clear that I have played well over 700-800 hours on the original game, and 300+ hours of Battlerite at the time of writing this review.
I was around for Season 1 of both BLC and Battlerite (back then BLC was a standalone so my hours are not counted properly, and honestly I've lost count, profile is private anyways). I also was a Titan on BLC (~$80 or so purchase, mostly cosmetic, however does unlock all characters) simply to support the developers financially.
The game itself is a top down fast paced action arena brawler, featuring many different, unique characters. There are "archetypes" however healers can do plenty of damage, and some tanks can heal quite a bit, so you aren't really locked into a role in the way some other games do. The game has a very high skill ceiling, which some players may find immensely rewarding.
If you do try this game, I STRONGLY recommend that you both:
Play 2s only until you learn the game, and then swap to 3s, as it is the more balanced game mode.
AND
Play with friends, to avoid getting trolled by derankers.
Lets get on to the pros and the cons, compared to the old game:
Pros:
>Graphics are improved (technically. more about this below)
>New Engine (I think?)
>More players than BLC (for now)
Unfortunately, that is all of the pros.
Cons:
>The game overall, feels slower than BLC. If you have played BLC you will understand what I mean
>The game has a much more child friendly, cartoonish feel to it. The art, maps, music, all of it feel watered down when compared to the spirit of the original game (seriously go launch BLC and stare at the Blood Gate). BLC had a more serious, "tribal" feel that I sincerely miss
>The skins are mostly garbage, it seems like the artists used the paint bucket tool for half of the cosmetics, whereas in BLC they were unique and actually worth buying
>The servers feel a bit sluggish sometimes, and are prone to downtime
>No clans, global chat, etc. It was commonplace on BLC for friendly discussion to be going on almost at all times in global chat, or possibly coordinating casual matches for fun.
>The community is cancer. This game has a worse community than League of Legends, and this is not something I say lightly.
>The matchmaking is a joke. Smurfing is rampant, blatant throwers (derankers) in almost every 4th or 5th game you play at anything below Diamond rank. Frequently you will report a player on your team, and get him in the next match, on your team, for a 2nd game of punishment. The algorithms clearly either do not take in to account reports, or there aren't enough players on at some times, so you will be forced to play with the same people who made the game so unenjoyable. "ELO hell" is a very real thing. This needs to be addressed, or the game will die.
>The reports "system" needs work, badly. There is no notification if someone you reported has action taken against them, so what the current system amounts to, is speaking aloud, at your computer screen, the name of the offending player. Nobody but you will hear it, and that sums it up nicely. Even if action is taken against them, there is nothing to prevent them from making another account and offending even harder on the new one, as the game is free to play. Additionally, it is possible to get a chat mute, or possibly a ban from simply saying something back to toxic players.
The moderators view any incident of verbal abuse equally, regardless of how one sided it may be, or who "started it". This sounds good in theory, however humans aren't unfeeling automatons. When a player is having a bad day, and you will have a bad day after encountering the average players in matchmaking, after they spam N****R or one of the many other fun bad words they spam, YOU can get a mute or ban for simply telling them to shove it. They WILL report you as well as they know exactly how to play the system like a fiddle. "Should have just muted them" -Developer with "Social Difficulties"
Although the player count is higher, and queue times are shorter than they were back when the game costed money, the quality of the matches has severely degraded. To be fully honest, it feels like a quick cash grab, and nothing more. You are pressured to buy champions with real money as they take a very long time to purchase using farmed in game currency.
Note that it WAS this way back in BLC, but they COULD have taken a new direction with this new game, but greed got in the way. I cannot take a so called "competitive" game seriously that does not allow the player to play all characters, to learn how to counter them better. This is one of the main arguments against League of Legends, vs Dota 2 (though far from the only one).
You may think this is an ethical business model, and I can see arguments both ways, however Dota 2 has a completely free model, where ONLY cosmetic items cost money, and they are immensely successful financially. Yes, the player count is lower for this game, but if they fixed the problems I think it would have a huge community. Sadly, it seems this game is doomed to follow the same path as BLC did. Whoever is making decisions at $tunlock $tudios has learned nothing from the demise of BLC.
Overall, I simply cannot recommend this game, it just isn't fun. I tried my very hardest to give it a fair chance, but it's just not the same game that I once loved.
Rest in peace old friend, you will be missed.

I'm a big fan of the Lego Travller's Tales games and I've played them all, either on PC or console. LEGO® Pirates of the Caribbean: The Video Game takes some of my favorite movie content and applies it to the fun formula that is used in these types of games.
So is it worth it? Well yes, but if you're as big a fan of the POTC series as I am, you might find yourself a bit dissappointed. My biggest dissappointment with the game was the lack of Hans Zimmer's great score, which is an essential part of the success of the movies. You'll find many recognizable tracks such as "Jack Sparrow" and "The Kraken" but much of the score is missing and instead is replaced with mediocre music that doesn't compliment Zimmer's score. Why? Well I have two guesses:
1. The creators of the game did not believe the music would fit with the pace of the levels they designed. If this is true, I completely disagree with their decision.
2.  Because the game is using Disney intellectual property, obtaining the rights to the music was expensive for Travller's Tales. I find this the more probable case.
My other problem with the game is that it's buggy. I haven't experienced the crashes that other people have, but I have encountered annoying bugs. The most annoying takes place on the last level, where an event doesn't take place as it's supposed to and you're pretty much stuck. The only way to beat the level is to restart and go through the whole thing, hoping it doesn't bug out again. I've encountered this bug on both the PC and console versions.
So would I recommend the game? Well despite the minor bugs and the lack of Zimmer's score, I would say yes. It's a fun game that uses familiar lego mechanics and captures the spirit of the movies. If you're a fan of TT lego games or the POTC movies, you'll probably enjoy this game.

This game is kind of weird for most games. Do not think it is completely immersive. It is more of a fictional-example for a documentary in my opinion. It still hosts a very real theme, and that is that people who have had depression feel like they can't get help because of how others have become increasingly judgemental of others.

The difficult thing about reccomending a game like Depression Quest is that sharing it with someone implies that you think they'll get something positive out of it.  There is no surface level positivity in Depression Quest.  It is not "fun," it barely qualifies as a "game" by a lot of people's standards, and it can be upsetting if played in the wrong mindset.
It is, however, highly reccommended by me as someone who sufferes from Depression.
Explaining what Depression feels like vs being "depressed" is a battle people with Depression struggle with constantly.  it is not about feeling sad, it's about feeling a complete absense of anything at best and extreme self loathing at worst.  This game perfectly encapsulates how it feels to suffer from Depression, right down to the interface.  The inability to choose options based on how well managed your Depression is extremely on point.  If you don't have Depression, it can be frustrating that you don't have the option to speak your mind or seek professional help right away, but that is what Depression does to you.  It robs you of your ability to make decisions like that, and it prevents you from looking at yourself objectively and saying "I need help."  Some people never escape that.  This game does an amazing job of capturing that feeling and putting it into words.
Do not play this game if you are looking for an entertaining "game."  Play this game if you need help understanding someone in your life who has Depression, or if you yourself are suffering and need reassurance that you are not alone.  You are not alone!

This is as much a game as other non-AAA and non-mainstream games are. A close analog I can think of would probably be the Stanley Parable which, for all its 1st POV and GUI and mouse, pretty much is a "Choose-Your-Own-Adventure Book" but in 3D. DQ hearkens back to earlier-era text-based games. It's no surprise that the game's epigraph come from David Foster Wallace, who crafted in boredom and addiction and depression as much as Pynchon does paranoia, as the closest prose relation (as well as most probable genesis) is his short story "The Depressed Person".
My one criticism is actually a rather common one when it comes to western RPGs as well as love songs (not to mention Bella Swan in Twilight): by making the protagonist's circumstances and personality so general, you'e actually making them less universal. Providing specficity is what creates resonance, as specificity provides more opportunity for empathy. Largely, though, due to the nature of the game and the fact that you are making the choices, you're able to tailor the 2nd person POV so it can be more like a mirror and you can be the one whose actually making these decisions. I felt immersed in this than I ever did Fallout 3, and in a fraction of the time too.
Overall, an amazing game that everyone ought to play.

Content Warning: Mental Health, Misogyny, Suicide
In the wake of Robin Williams' Death, everybody who speaks English should download and play 'Depression Quest'.
It's a free, tiny 'game' on Steam's Downloadable Game service, although it's really a choose-your-own-adventure type of deal. That means you mostly read text, listen to audio, and make decisions on how to move the plot forward. Simple, but it's like looking in a mirror sometimes.
It is a harrowing interactive experience that will teach anyone who's depressed that they are not alone (and that they have an illness and deserve treatment). It will teach everyone who's not what depression can be like.
I am depressed. Most of the time I think of my general lack of purpose, productivity or motivation as something that makes me an awful person who wouldn't deserve good things, who shouldn't have good friends. On good days I can remember that those are symptoms of depression, and that they are lies.
I know this is stilted and ridiculous to say so on social media. I am actually telling you this because there's something else you should know.
DQ was also created (mostly) by Zoe Quinn, who is now the target of an online hate campaign that includes slander, misogynistic threats to her safety and hacking of her online accounts. I like to think that by playing Depression Quest, we are showing our support.
Again, it's free and only 100 MB download. If you have relatives or friends that are depressed, or you think you might be depressed, please take advantage of this opportunity.
An emotional rollercoaster that truly brings focus to the problem of depression. Somewhat short and to the point. A great experience. 9 out of 10.

Enemies drop ammo pickups to replenish your limited ammo (though you always have your basic gun, running out simply takes away your active weapon powerup) and coins which can be spent on new craft.
