Wow. This game, is just amazing. It's one of those games that takes you for a ride on the emotional rollercoaster. What is "The Cat Lady" exactly? When I first got this game, I wasn't really surprised, even the name was kinda plain for me, didn't really catch my attention. I was expecting some kind of survival horror 2-D game like The Lone Survivor, but I was wrong. It's more like....It feels like Clock Tower, for example.
The cat lady is like one of those old point and click games, minus the pointing and clicking, because you move around and interact with stuff using your keyboard. It's not quite a survival horror game like I thought, it's got it's scary parts, but I wouldn't go as far to call it like that. It feels more like a psychological kind of game. And man, it doesn't fail at that.
You are Susan Ashworth, a lonely, severely depressed woman who tried to commit suicide at the beggining of the game. As you progress, you'll find out why, and what made her feel like she did.
Now, let's talk about the points of this game.
+ The visuals. The graphics are gritty, almost comic like, they are pretty good, and most of the time, the atmosphere and the backgrounds are haunting, dark and scary, or just plain depresing with lots of gray and black. That's something I love!
+ The music is amazing. You get both instrumental songs, and songs with lyrics that are haunting and sorrowful. The whole soundtrack of this game is definitely worth it, you should give it a try even if you don't play the game.
+ The plot, characters, and character development. As I said before, it's one of those emotional rollercoaster kind of games, sometimes you can even feel the depression and loneliness of the main character, it makes you think about suicide, not as in killing yourself, it makes you think about suicide as in why it happens, what drives somebody to try to take his or her own life, and what makes somebody cling to life with a smile on their face. I don't wanna spoil anything, but I just wanna say that this was top notch.
+ Voice Acting. It's pretty damn good, or at least, so I think. It's quite soothing at times, emotional at others.
+ The endings. Powerful enough, even if they were mostly text based in the form of a last narration.
- To be fair, I encountered a few technical issues now and then. For example, (correct me if I'm wrong), you can't overwrite save files, so, I had saves like "Save 1, Save 2, Save 3", so on, and so on 'til 30 or so. Also, I encountered some kind of issue, I inspected something, snatched a knife, accidentally inspected it again, and it made my game crash. I didn't save, so I had to backtrack all the way to that point again. It isn't really disruptive, if you don't intentionally or accidentally inspect certain items twice.
- It seems like you cannot change the resolution. (Correct me if I'm wrong)
- This game suffers from some framerate issues, that are only worsened by the fog in some parts of the game. Most of the time, it's just mild FPS lag, nothing too bad. BUT, there comes a point where you are outside of your apartment with fog all around it. My god. The framerates dropped so bad, that something that would be like 1 minute long took me like 5 or so. Dead serious. Thank goodness, it only happened at that specific point of the game on chapter 3? If I'm correct?
All in all, this game is definitely worth it, it's not particularly challenging, other than basic problem solving skills most of the time, and the plot and plot twists are amazing. Try it for yourself, if you are into games like this, perhaps like clock tower, you won't be dissapointed.

Apocalyptic yet hopeful. The Yawhg rewards us with a short exciting story about a doomed city from the viewpoint of humble citizens. The story so simple, so unexpected and engaging though, replayability is a must.
If you appreciate short plays, unexpected outcomes, and playing with the hand of fate you will love The Yawhg (the game, not the Yawhg itself).

The Yawhg is quite an interesting game; in such a way that it isn't really a game persay. It's an interactive journey. The Yawhg is about the titular event that will happen after 6 weeks, and what it might be is unclear. It's an incredible storyteller, and I got back into it after seeing a kickstarted game named Monster Prom, which is like the cruder little sibling of The Yawhg.
Not to say it's bad, but I couldn't help but draw connections.
Each week in The Yawhg, each character (up to four characters, controlled by 1-4 people) goes to one location, and raises one of their 6 stats. Then, a random event will happen, and you choose one of two choices, usually requiring certain stats to be successful. This repeats for the 6 weeks, but it's far from dull. The consequent events are impacted by your previous choices, giving a sense of reality and impact to your choices.
I won't spoil what happens after The Yawhg, because it's more fun to find out yourself. The game's only $9.99, it's great with friends, and it's bitesized fun at 20-30 minutes per game. Just go buy it, you won't regret it.

"Momodora: Reverie Under the Moonlight" (previously titled "Momodora IV") is a side-scrolling action-adventure game with strong emphasis on combat. This was my first experience with the "Momodora" series so I didn't particularly care about the plot, but as far as I could tell it's pretty simple and not exactly something to be writting home about.
Visually, this game is incredible. With a light Victorian influence, it's presented in a pixel art style somewhat reminiscent to that of classic SNK Playmore's titles from the Neo Geo era such as "The King of Fighters" and "The Last Blade". Character sprites are pretty detailed, the animation is smooth and fluid, and the backdrops to the environments you'll be fighting your way through are beautiful and atmospheric.
In terms of gameplay, I'll start off by saying that "Momodora IV" is one of the games with best game feel that I've played in years. You'll take control of Koha, an adorable priestess armed with a bow and a maple leaf (for long- and close-ranged combat, respectively). Melee combat feels pretty good, and I'd particularly say it's one of the strongest points of the game. You get a fair amount of audiovisual and haptic feedback while fighting, so it feels pretty satisfying to smash enemies in the face with a maple leaf. Using the bow to engage enemies from afar is quite nice too; you can almost always rely on your bow to fight tough enemies while keeping a safe distance. You also have a roll command to avoid attacks, traps, and other kinds of hazards.
As far as Metroidvanias go, "Momodora IV" gives you plenty of freedom to roam and explore without having the player being seriously hindered by the lack of unlockable abilities. However, the game doesn't give you a lot of incentives for backtracking once you obtain said abilities, which for a Metroidvania is a bit of a shame. You can explore and revisit some areas in the game to obtain health upgrades, find item sellers, and collect ivory bugs that can be traded for "munny". Apart from that, there's not really much else you can do.
Something I didn't exactly expect from this game was its difficulty. This game is hard, and I had my head handed to me many times until I started to switch my approach to something more methodical. Usually in this type of game, you're not harshly punished for taking damage, and even when you do it's easy to come by health recovery methods. "Momodora IV", however, wants to make sure you think before you act: enemies cause a lot of damage (some of them will even kill you in one hit), you don't have a whole lot of health, and the amount of health recovery items at your disposal is pretty limited (think of it like the Estus flasks from "Dark Souls").
Occasionally, however, it feels like the game is hard for the wrong reasons. One thing that bugged me throughout the entire game was the fact that you can take damage from enemies if they touch you. I think that makes no sense, considering the game's strong focus on melee combat. That makes some boss battles incredibly annoying to deal with. And speaking of which, the bosses in this game are ridiculous and will make you want to pull your hair out not because they're tough or challenging, but because of how poorly designed they are. Their attack patterns are nonsense, the hitboxes are dumb, the one-hit kills pretty much mean trial-and-error, and most of the time they'll keep pushing you around since they can damage you merely by walking, forcing you to fight from a distance. Oh, and somehow the easiest boss
— something's wrong there!
Another thing that bothered me a lot is this game's strange obsession with projectiles getting thrown at you by off-screen enemies. Be ready to get sniped a lot by these.
And lastly, this game is really short. I played it on hard and managed to beat it in about 7 hours. The ending was... incredibly underwhelming. And I'm not really too excited about going back to it to finish the collect-a-thons and unlocking the rest of the achievements. In the end, I still choose to recommend this game to any Metroidvania fan out there because I'd be lying if I said I didn't enjoy my time with it. This game could've been something much bigger, probably the next best thing since "Dust: An Elysian Tail", but it falls just short of that.

If you're coming to Magic Duels looking for the best way to play Magic online, then look elsewhere. This is a buggy, featureless client wrapped around yet another booster selling scheme. The game is barely supported, so pumping any money into this game is a risk. The card pool is not a standard format, and is constantly meddled with by the devs, so you won't be getting a real MTG experience.
On the positive side, the single-player campaigns have some charm and this is a decent (and free) way for newbies to learn the basics before getting into the physical game or the MTG Online client.
The gameplay experience is adequate, but often frustrating. Only six phases of play are implemented: Start (upkeep/untap/draw), first main, attack, block, [uninteractive damage], second main, and end phase. For most games this is fine, but experienced players may find it too simplistic.
After each opponent play you'll be given a two-second timer which you'll need to pause to respond. If you miss the window, you're screwed, so you'd better be on your toes. The game automatically skips turns where you have no plays. Taking control out of the player's hands yet giving you so little time to react to your opponent creates a dynamic that's a lot like driving in stop-and-go traffic: It'll lull you to sleep, then force a sudden reaction. It's a poor dynamic to have in a game supposedly targeted at newbies.
From a general UI sense, the game is lacking. It tries to replicate a physical experience, but mostly forefeits the potential advantages of a digital medium. On a PC-size monitor, played cards are too small to read, enchantments are stacked underneath the cards, the graveyard is a vertical stack, and far too much room is taken up by the deck, lands, and just empty space in general. Simple aspects like choosing which cards to draw from a group, tapping mana, or distributing spell damage are confusingly implemented. The interface will cause you to screw up occasionally, which is a major sin for a strategy game.
The game insists on hiding cards from view. Each card on the battlefield is a muddy blur, with stats slightly zoomed, and superimoposed icons for keywords. Yet you'll be repeatedly zooming in anyway, since you'll need to read the card texts. Your cards overlap in your hand even with plenty of room to show them all. Irrelevant features are constantly shoved into your face, such as watching a player's health counter tick down one by one, yet it doesn't bother showing you played cards for long enough to read them without zooming.
The single-player campaigns are a good way for newbies to learn the rules and gain some experience playing different types of decks. There are currently five "Origins" campaigns with five bosses each, which explore the lore behind a few of the Planeswalkers. There are also four "expansion" campaigns (5-6 bosses each) which showcase some of the lore behind the new sets. So, around 45 bosses total.
You're given a premade deck for each game. As you progress through a campaign, the difficulty ramps and your deck grows more mechanically complex. Whenever you encounter a new mechanic, a dialog will prompt you to play a short 1-2 turn tutorial explaining how it works. These can be distracting; they're optional but they'll keep pestering you after dismissing them. You can access the tutorials from the main menu, and I suggest getting them all out of the way at once so they won't interrupt your games.
But progressing through these campaigns is not optional, because they unlock the pvp and reward the base sets for each color and expansion. If you're an experienced player, you may find grinding the campaigns to be tedious. It took me around 10 hours to complete all the single-player content.
The deckbuilding screen is shockingly featureless. The card browser is a confusing mess to navigate, made even worse without any way to search for cards. You can filter by type, mana cost, color, rarity (why?), and set for some reason (no cards are restricted, so it doesn't matter). That's it! When you're building a deck you can only see five cards on screen at once, including duplicates. It won't even stack duplicate cards. And even scrolling through the cards you can see is nonintuitive. It's a nightmare, and a huge obstacle to playing.
To add to the confusion, the game needles you into using the automatic deckbuilder, which lets you select a broad archetype, but severely limits customization. It's basically an auto-fill for colors, and you won't be building any serious decks with it. I doubt it'll teach anyone much about deckbuilding either.
When it comes to building your card collection, Magic Duels uses a system inspired by Hearthstone. You'll earn gold from winning duels against opponents or the computer, and by completing daily quests. Gold is spent on booster packs, each containing six cards. In an attempt to promote the physical product, you have to choose from which set to buy boosters, even though a new player is unlikely to know which to pick (start with Innistrad). A win is 30 gold, and 150 gold buys a booster; daily quests range from 40-80 gold each. If you play a lot you'll likely earn 2-3 packs a day. At this rate it would take months to build a full collection.
Wizards wants you to spend real money on packs to speed up the process. This is not a good idea. You can't trade or re-sell cards in Duels. There's also no way to obtain a specific card you need without buying packs until you open it. And the devs may remove cards from the game at their own discretion if they think they're too imbalanced. There's simply no reason to invest real money in cards; you won't be facing many quality players or decks in this game because there's a high investment floor and a low skill ceiling.
Magic Duels is for newbies only. This is not real MTG; it's an introduction. After you've gotten the hang of things, go elsewhere. MTG Online (official, paid) and Cockatrice (unofficial, free) are better, more robust clients, and the interface upgrades in Duels are so wrongheaded that it's often a worse experience. The game is poorly supported, the community of players is very small, and it's hard to see it as anything but a cheap foray into the P2W mobile market by Wizards of the Coast.

Instead of hoping that the same people who call you a noob in trade chat or tell you how much they love to have sexual intercourse with your mother on XBL will finally accept you for knocking this game, I would suggest actually tasking the time out of your busy life of being a pathetic neckbeard and look at video games as art instead of crack cocaine for once. Lucius Demake, as its name indicates, is a demake of the original Lucius game.
It is made to look as if it is actually from the late 80s, complete with 2D pixel graphics and 16 colors. The story in Lucius Demake is the same as it was in the original game.
Lucius is a game with strong links to "The Omen". The player takes the role of Lucius, the son of the devil, who has to clear the mansion of it’s residents. To do this he must orcastrate “accidents” without anyone suspecting him of any foul play.
It takes 3-4 hours to finish the game completely.
For those who liked the original game and for fans of "The Omen" a must have.

Quick Review:
This game has a nice feel of a short story being told where you control the characters in it. The story (for me) was very dark and I haven't experienced a positive ending yet. I would suggest getting it if you can find it on sale for under $3.00.
How I got the game:
I bought a bundle from another site with this game included.
Full review:
The idea behind this game is that something is coming called the Yawhg. It destroyed the town before and you have 6 weeks to prepare for when it returns. This is a choose your own adventure type story that can be played very quickly. You are shown a map where you choose an area to go to then you are given another choice of what to do while you are in that area. You repeat this process using 2 characters for 6 turns. At the end of those turns the Yawhg appears.
What I liked:
I enjoyed the images and graphics used in the story telling, it really gave the feeling of reading a story from an old book. There are 4 different characters and you got to play as 2 of them for one game. The options for what you can have the characters do are limited but they gave some interesting outcomes. I also liked the music playing in the background, it kept me interested in the game and added to the feel of a story.
What I didn't like:
The outcomes from the choices I made were pretty much the same when I had different characters play the same sections. The game is very short. I was able to play it through twice in about 20 minutes. I didn't receive good endings and maybe it prevented me from extending the game play but that is what I experienced. There is a lot of build up for the Yawhg story line but the game doesn't deliver when it comes to the actual action of dealing with it.
Final Thoughts:
I like the game and would suggest getting it if you could find it under $3.00. For me there wasn't enough to spend $9.99 on. The lack of content deterred me from wanting to play it again and see if things could be different using another character in other areas or making various choices with the same characters. I felt that even if I did try the reward wouldn't be worth the effort.
Other Notes:
Let me know what you thought of the review I wrote. I will be writing and re-writing reviews on games I have already played and games I have yet to play. I'm interested to hear if what I've written is helpful or if there are things that people would like to see. I'm also interested in corrections if I have made a mistake about the details of gameplay.
Thank you for reading.

The Yawhg is a choose-your-own-adventure visual novel with RPG aspects from Damian Sommer and Emily Carroll. Lets’ get rocking.
The Good
The art is nice. It has a classic, storybook feel to it and the color palette is pleasingly subdued.
The music is also well done. It crops up every now and then and is, by no means, omnipresent when it doesn’t need to be.
The game has multiple endings for each of the four characters that can be played. This is a nice touch, but, it’s not enough in the end.
The Bad
Normally, pricing issues would land in the “Meh” category, but I really don’t think that this game should be priced at $9.99. Not for what it is.
I know there are multiple endings for the characters, but the story is always going to be the same for each play through and you’ll eventually start repeating the same side stories that get you to the end game.
The Meh
At the end of the day, there just isn’t much (if any) replay value to this one.
Verdict: Nay
If you could get it for next to nothing or, better still, for free, it might be worth your time to pick The Yawhg up and put in a playthrough. Apart from that though, I’d take your money and your time elsewhere.

This game explores, rather deeply in the context of the genre, the depths of the psyche, human empathy, human depravity and the fact that sometimes we don't control what happens to us.
It also features excessively graphic descriptions and depictions  of gore, almost, but not quite taking it into the realm of the ridculous, eyeballs and limbs flying every which way, bathtubs full of blood, eating the neighbours for dinner - you get the picture.
Which brings me to my point: This is a game about dualities. Susan remembers something terrible from the past  - and it may well resonate with you, you may actually relate to this character not only in their strength, but also in their moment of weakness. The characters in the way they are drawn are paper dolls - but in your mind their memories become real. memory. We get a sense of this person, Susan, - enough so that we stay with her when the game yanks us back and forth between the ordinairy and the incredoulous, between the trashy and the artistic, between the expected and new grounds.
If you enjoy serious adventure games and have gazed into the abyss at one point or another - do yourself a favour and give this one a try.

Hammerwatch is a fun 2-D top down rougelike game for PC. It is good, but not perfect. Unlike some rougelikes, you have lives, you have no time limit per floor, and the dungeon layouts do not change. The dungeons are large and detailed. You can play a wide variety of characters, each type feels different to play. Players start out weak but can grab and buy power ups to level up as they progress though the game.
The gameplay of the game is good, but not perfect. The controls feel great. The default controls use only the keyboard. At first I was skeptical whether this would work, but after relocating the strife button to numpad 0, I found the keyboard controls to be solid and intuitive. The player can always use a joystick if they wish.
Enemies attack in patterns. This makes gameplay more skill more then leveling. It can be hard to figure out when and what an enemy is about to attack. But, I didn't feel too overwhelmed as long as the screen didn't become too crowded. There were some bits near where I died repeatedly, but that's probably because I was playing the game for the first time. Food in each level allows the player to heal, and there is a decent amount of food to be found.
Different classes play differently. So, a ranger might attack from afar, whereas a paladin might take on enemies head on. A warlock might blow up bunches of enemies, while a priest might lend support from behind the front lines. So, there's a variety of ways to play the game.
Care is taken to avoid hording of keys and skills. Mana regenerates over time, and there is no time limit per floor. The thief's specials used to take gold, but this was fixed in patch 1.3. Keys are reset at the start of each act. You will always need to find the right key to move forward, and there will always be enough keys to open every door.
Players must manage gold and potions. Potions will give the player a limited boost, but they are one time use and you can carry one at a time. Extra lives can be purchased, but gold is limited. Money spent buying powers can't be used to buy lives or consumables later, and money spent buying consumables and lives can't be used to buy power ups later.
A combo system encourages players to take risks. Once a player buys the right upgrades, their character can heal, attack faster and damage all foes around them by chaining hits on multiple enemies. This encourages the player to engage in large groups of enemies rather than avoiding them, especially when they are at low health.
Although there's a lot of good things about the gameplay, there are a lot of flaws in the game too. There is inconsistent damage between enemies. Differences become larger by end game. By the time I reached the last level, I could take hundreds of arrows and be fine, but would die in two or three hits by an enemy paladin or skeletal knight. This makes the health bar a poor indicator of how many more hits I can take. It also allowed me to ignore some enemies.
Traps feel cheap. They deal massive amounts of damage to the player. The spike floors are easy to see, but will kill the player instantly if stepped on. Others like the "tile arrow" traps deal large amounts of damage and are very hard to see and avoid. I have often died from them because I was busy looking at the minimap while walking though a cleared part of the level.
The maps are large, but there is often no indication on where to go next. I found myself roaming cleared areas looking for the exit / the next area to clear. There is also no indication of where other players are. It's common for players to ask "where are you?" in multiplayer. Although the minimap helps, the default levels are larger than the minimap, so it does not solve all the problems.
Multiplayer comes with it's own problems. The biggest one is the shared life pool. In game, all players share lives with each other. Usually, some players will use more lives than others. This encourages some skilled players to look down upon / kick less skilled players. The shared life pool also gives trolls a way to quickly ruin a multiplayer run.
There's the problem of hosting in multiplayer. As of the time of the writing (early patch 1.3) hammerwatch does not have dedicated servers. This means that all multiplayer games are hosted on a player's computer. All players are disconnected when the host player leaves the game. The likelihood of getting disconnected during a multiplayer game is extremely high because the game takes over four hours of continuous gameplay to complete.
The game saves your progress, but it doesn't feel like it does. There are no indications that tell the player it's a good time to rest. The "save disks" that you find along the way feel more like checkpoints than savepoints. I remember the first time I quit the game. I felt like all my progress had been lost. It wasn't though. My saves were right there, waiting for me when I got back.
The artwork is beautiful. Even though the levels are massive and the game is drawn in a "pixelated" style, you can clearly see lots of detail in there. I saw everything from torches, vines, tapestries, books, shields, cobblestone, carpets there are even paintings on walls!
Each act has it's own theme and it's own enemies. Although there are a few enemies that are palette swaps, a lot of time has been put into making each enemy look and attack differently. I  was really drawn to the floating balls of light (even if they burned me when I touched them.)
The sound well done. I think the music is wonderful. It fits the medieval theme of the game perfectly, and. Each song also fits the theme of it's corresponding act. But it's not perfect. Each track has a jarring transition in the middle. Even so, I occasionally listen to it in my spare time.
The sound effects are good. Most of the sound effects are spot on, whether it's the satisfying "boom" of a wizard's fireball, the "clink" of a sword bouncing off of an enemies shield, or the splats of oversized worms as they fry by ball lightning. The sound the player character makes when they get hit is a bit jarring and out of place, but, I suppose that's better than not knowing that you got hit.
Even with all the problems, I enjoyed the game immensely. I didn't care whether I got to the end or not. I found this game to be all about having fun with your friends and killing monsters. I found it also to be about solving puzzles in an "oh no how do I get out of this one" kind of way. At the time of this writing, the game is $10 on steam and $8 (DRM free) from the hammerwatch official website. If you're looking for a rougelike to kill some time, then give it a try.

This is a very unique game with a couple flaws.
TL;DR Version:
Pros:
- Engaging story
- Well written characters whose very character growth is center to the plot
- Unique and fun combat system
- Quests which fit the story of the game
- Gorgeous drawings and an overall unique visual style
Cons:
- Not a good soundtrack
- The world map doesn't fit the style of the rest of the game
- Some minor bugs
- Dear god don't play it with a keyboard
Long Version:
The game has a very unique setup where it has elements of a classic RPG (your characters level up, you buy/find gear to make the characters even more powerful, etc), elements of an arcade fighter game (battles are fought in this style and the wife of the main pair is a summon monster through similar combos), as well as a unique 'skill system' whose closest similarity I can think of is the materia system.
Enzo's skill system consists of 'Aurions' which you find during the story as the main characters learn more about themselves and comune with the spirits of their ancestors. Later on in the story, you learn how to combine them to make even more Aurions with their own abilities! These Aurions level up similar to the characters, growing in strength and 'becoming easier to use'. This system is pretty fun and directly links the characters' skills to what is happening in the story. When you activate an Aurion in a boss battle, the characters even give lines relevant both to the story and the Aurion being activated (Vengance is a particularly fun one to activate for this reason).
As for the summon character, Erine, she levels up with Enzo and gains skills during the story. In addition to this, the more you summon her, the more 'complicit' she and Enzo get, which gives her access to even better abilities. The story puts a huge focus on her and Enzo's relationship to each other and how their travels affects their relationship. She goes through just as much character growth as Enzo even though she doesn't directly benefit from the Aurion system.
In addition to the great story and characters, the visual aspect of this game is awesome. Everything has a wonderful hand-drawn look to it (except for the world map, which luckily you aren't on much). It has a nice style.
The downsides are unfortunately there. This was definitely a game made for a controller. You can play with the keyboard, but it isn't as good a combat system and feels really clunky on anything other than a controller. The world map looks like they were going for something, but didn't quite make it. Additionally, I did notice a few bugs with the mouse, the hitboxes trying to talk to characters, and the occaisonal screen transition which wanted to be hit just right.
Overall a game I would certainly recommend.

EDIT: Having replayed this game since a MAJOR UPDATE, many of the issues I had detailed below have been fixed.
My experiences and criticisms are set out below:
I found myself identifying with many of the challenges faced by another reviewer (Saint Ceo de la Vegas), where in both my playthorughs, I started the game on easy, and in that setting I found the challenges within the "settlement screen" difficult, but achievable. I managed to unite my region, amass (what I thought was) a substantial army, was constructing buildings quickly and in line with technological advances.
However, as soon the game shifted to an Egypt-wide emphasis ("fog of war map"), any progress I had made seemed woefully limited. The challenges to build, explore, unite and fight cities were just too substantial.
I completely shifted all production to military in order to attempt to build an army that could come close to taking on Seth (or at least defend myself against Seth, which I was able to do), but still couldn't come close to having enough soldiers for this. I was able to unite 4 or 5 tribes at this level, build a 3k + strong army, but I never felt in a position to even confront the smallest Seth settlement.
I was totally unable to build several of the special tombs due to lack of exploration at this point (despite having more than enough workers and resources) ... it just came down to timing and exploration, I wasn't fast enough and the game punished me for it, this can be good and bad.
In this case however, I felt that even if I had sped up my style of play and succeeded in building the tombs, I wouldn't have been able to challenge Seth militarily anyway, and this was confirmed in my second playthough.
I want to qualify this review by saying I enjoyed the game and would recommend it.
In reaction to the developer: I do not think a special mode needs to be created to make the game "much easier". I'd suggest within the current easy mode, just reduce scouting times, and reduce the size of a few of the enemy armies (or make building armies faster/easier... for instance instead of +6 soldiers on a site, make it +12, or whatever).
It's fun for an hour or so, but by the time you realize it isn't worth $9 you have probably already played it too long to return it.

These things make this more of a strategy-puzzle game, and if that's not something you enjoy you're going to be in for a nasty surprise when you start up your second playthrough.
Other than that caveat, the only real complaint I have is the inability to turn off the tutorials, but those are unobtrusive enough. Overall, this is a really solid game.

If you're coming to Magic Duels looking for the best way to play Magic online, then look elsewhere. This is a buggy, featureless client wrapped around yet another booster selling scheme. The game is barely supported, so pumping any money into this game is a risk. The card pool is not a standard format, and is constantly meddled with by the devs, so you won't be getting a real MTG experience.
On the positive side, the single-player campaigns have some charm and this is a decent (and free) way for newbies to learn the basics before getting into the physical game or the MTG Online client.
The gameplay experience is adequate, but often frustrating. Only six phases of play are implemented: Start (upkeep/untap/draw), first main, attack, block, [uninteractive damage], second main, and end phase. For most games this is fine, but experienced players may find it too simplistic.
After each opponent play you'll be given a two-second timer which you'll need to pause to respond. If you miss the window, you're screwed, so you'd better be on your toes. The game automatically skips turns where you have no plays. Taking control out of the player's hands yet giving you so little time to react to your opponent creates a dynamic that's a lot like driving in stop-and-go traffic: It'll lull you to sleep, then force a sudden reaction. It's a poor dynamic to have in a game supposedly targeted at newbies.
From a general UI sense, the game is lacking. It tries to replicate a physical experience, but mostly forefeits the potential advantages of a digital medium. On a PC-size monitor, played cards are too small to read, enchantments are stacked underneath the cards, the graveyard is a vertical stack, and far too much room is taken up by the deck, lands, and just empty space in general. Simple aspects like choosing which cards to draw from a group, tapping mana, or distributing spell damage are confusingly implemented. The interface will cause you to screw up occasionally, which is a major sin for a strategy game.
The game insists on hiding cards from view. Each card on the battlefield is a muddy blur, with stats slightly zoomed, and superimoposed icons for keywords. Yet you'll be repeatedly zooming in anyway, since you'll need to read the card texts. Your cards overlap in your hand even with plenty of room to show them all. Irrelevant features are constantly shoved into your face, such as watching a player's health counter tick down one by one, yet it doesn't bother showing you played cards for long enough to read them without zooming.
The single-player campaigns are a good way for newbies to learn the rules and gain some experience playing different types of decks. There are currently five "Origins" campaigns with five bosses each, which explore the lore behind a few of the Planeswalkers. There are also four "expansion" campaigns (5-6 bosses each) which showcase some of the lore behind the new sets. So, around 45 bosses total.
You're given a premade deck for each game. As you progress through a campaign, the difficulty ramps and your deck grows more mechanically complex. Whenever you encounter a new mechanic, a dialog will prompt you to play a short 1-2 turn tutorial explaining how it works. These can be distracting; they're optional but they'll keep pestering you after dismissing them. You can access the tutorials from the main menu, and I suggest getting them all out of the way at once so they won't interrupt your games.
But progressing through these campaigns is not optional, because they unlock the pvp and reward the base sets for each color and expansion. If you're an experienced player, you may find grinding the campaigns to be tedious. It took me around 10 hours to complete all the single-player content.
The deckbuilding screen is shockingly featureless. The card browser is a confusing mess to navigate, made even worse without any way to search for cards. You can filter by type, mana cost, color, rarity (why?), and set for some reason (no cards are restricted, so it doesn't matter). That's it! When you're building a deck you can only see five cards on screen at once, including duplicates. It won't even stack duplicate cards. And even scrolling through the cards you can see is nonintuitive. It's a nightmare, and a huge obstacle to playing.
To add to the confusion, the game needles you into using the automatic deckbuilder, which lets you select a broad archetype, but severely limits customization. It's basically an auto-fill for colors, and you won't be building any serious decks with it. I doubt it'll teach anyone much about deckbuilding either.
When it comes to building your card collection, Magic Duels uses a system inspired by Hearthstone. You'll earn gold from winning duels against opponents or the computer, and by completing daily quests. Gold is spent on booster packs, each containing six cards. In an attempt to promote the physical product, you have to choose from which set to buy boosters, even though a new player is unlikely to know which to pick (start with Innistrad). A win is 30 gold, and 150 gold buys a booster; daily quests range from 40-80 gold each. If you play a lot you'll likely earn 2-3 packs a day. At this rate it would take months to build a full collection.
Wizards wants you to spend real money on packs to speed up the process. This is not a good idea. You can't trade or re-sell cards in Duels. There's also no way to obtain a specific card you need without buying packs until you open it. And the devs may remove cards from the game at their own discretion if they think they're too imbalanced. There's simply no reason to invest real money in cards; you won't be facing many quality players or decks in this game because there's a high investment floor and a low skill ceiling.
Magic Duels is for newbies only. This is not real MTG; it's an introduction. After you've gotten the hang of things, go elsewhere. MTG Online (official, paid) and Cockatrice (unofficial, free) are better, more robust clients, and the interface upgrades in Duels are so wrongheaded that it's often a worse experience. The game is poorly supported, the community of players is very small, and it's hard to see it as anything but a cheap foray into the P2W mobile market by Wizards of the Coast.

As a 22 year old who has suffered depression as long as he can remember (as far back as age 5) I can attest to the accuracy of the main character's emotions in this story. The way the main character overthinks things, beats himself up over large and small mistakes alike, runs through possible scenarios in his head, only causing himself to worry more - I have experienced all of this. Also, too many times do I hear people telling me to "cheer up" or "get over it," but they just don't understand... it's not that easy - I don't want to be depressed, if it were just a mindset, I would have stopped being depressed long ago. Although many situations in this story I have not experienced (I've never had a girlfriend, or seen a therapist) I can still relate to how the main character feels throughout - the narrative is very thorough, and thus is very effective at portraying the situation, making it easy for me to put myself in his shoes. The choices are well varied, and I always found at least one option that I would do in that situation. After completing the game, I came to what seemed to me to be the best ending. Too bad it's just a game.
By the way, it's funny how many bad reviews this game got by people who aren't depressed, saying, "it's not realistic" when they are the target audience, and yet, a depressed person writing a review gave a positive one saying that it is realistic.

Back then, spending money in this game didn't provide much besides character looks like hair changes, skin color changes, eye changes, hair color changes, etc. Now if you want to have the best item in the game you have to fork over tons of money in HOPES of getting the right stats for an item. MapleStory is an enigma. I love it, as I played it a lot off and on throughout my life; and yet, I absolutely hate it.
===Music===
The music in this game is incredible. it's atmospheric, plus there's FOUR GODDAMN HOURS OF MUSIC. If you were to play every BGM track back-to-back, start to finish, there would easily be over four hours of varied tracks, everything from metal to piano to pop, it's all here. (There's a video that contains every track in the inital 2006 release, it's two hours and fourty-two minutes long.) Needless to say, 10/10.
===Gameplay===
This is where it gets rather complicated to recommend. Obviously, it's an MMO, so grind till your groin is reduced to nothing but a carpet burn. However, the cap level is 250. There are very
few people who have reached this level cap. I, personally, have reached 207. That's on and off gaming from the release date (so that doesn't include the time I have here on Steam). Granted, it wouldn't nearly take that long to reach the point I have; not to mention I don't really care about leveling anymore. The thing is, the game gets super complicated past level 150. There's at least 4 different ways to improve your gear: scrolls/spell traces, enhancement (yes that is it's own separate thing), potential and bonus potential. ♥♥♥♥ explaining all that. There's plenty of guides that will make it easy to understand. If you
want to become a pro, just don't. Pick a private server or another game entirely if you want to hit big numbers. In the end, I find the sheer number of classes, skills, locations and monsters staggering, and exploring the various dimensions and continents enjoyable and a relaxing experience. 6/10.
Sidenote: There are microtransactions in this game. There's the Reboot world which allows you to buy the microtransaction items with the in-game currency, which is a good casual world.
===Community===
Don't talk to other people. They're all either ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, scammers, catfishers or beggars. Sometimes you can find someone who is worth talking to, but generally just try and avoid contact with other players. There's party quests, guilds and guild alliances, a buddy list, marriage and a 'global chat' of sorts (microtransaction-based), but a lot of these ideas fall flat. The party quests are arbitrary until the midgame, and even then they're only relevant for a short while. The guild and guild alliance system is cool, but it depends a lot on have an actively playing community. It's difficult to start your own guild, and just as difficult to get into and stay in a guild. I don't even need to mention why the megaphones ('global chat') are utter garbage. Marriage is virtually pointless now aside from character sheet completion, and the buddy list is inherently flawed in its presentation as a way to communicate, as all of your online friends can see what you say regardless of who you're talking to. God forbid you have a chatty friend. Overall, the community and methods of communication are trash. So trash, in fact, that I completely forgot about Maple Chat, which is basically just Maple Omegle, except you can have up to 6 people. The guilds are cool, I suppose. 3/10.
Should you play this game? Probably not. Should you smoke weed? Probably not, but you're either smoking now or high as hell if you made it this far. All I'm trying to say is that you should smoke some weed and play MapleStory.

Lucius Demake is a bizarre 2-D, pixel art remake of an already bizarre series. Heavily influenced by Richard Donner's 1976 horror classic, The Omen, Demake follows the young anti-christ as he wrecks havoc killing everyone who dares enter his mansion of hell. Utilizing clever puzzle solving, the game requires players to fully explore the mansion in search of items necessarry for each successful killing.
The project is an exact replica of the previous original except with digressed graphics, and a fantastic chip-tune soundtrack that perfectly captures the mood. However, despite its similarities, the core gameplay and exploration point of view has been condensed - drastically affecting the difficulty. No longer are players able to search each drawer and cupboard within each room in search of items. Instead, the essential items needed in order to progress are often found in the chapter starting point (bedroom), or casually sitting beside where they will be needed. It greatly shortened the experience, and I was able to complete the game in its entirety in just about 3.5 hours - unlocking every trophy along the way.
Regardless, Lucius Demake is a great, innovative addition to the Lucius series that provides a unique experience for newcomers and those who have completed the previous two iterations as well.

Developers would have to come up with pretty unique ideas to make modern game titles playable on the little system and in my opionion, created some really cool and original games. Lucius Demake is a really interesting project. It's almost a letter for letter remake of the original (and vastly superior) Lucius - except in 2D with pixel art. It's pretty impressive how much of the same original experence can still be accessed with only a fraction of the graphics.
That said, I'm not really positive who this game is for. Ostensibly it's for fans of the series (or again, at least the original) who have already played the original. I certainly enjoyed it. It makes for an interesting run through to compare with the immersive experience of the first game, but with no mystery as you already know the solutions to every puzzle in advance. At the same time, if you haven't played the original, it's hard to reccomend that you play this version first.
I guess I'm not sure who should play this game and in which order, but I am sure it should be played.
At the end of the day this is (for lack of a better phrase) an "extremely faithful" remake of a great game with an interesting angle.

Beyond Earth (BE) is quite an ambitious combo of words in an ambitious franchise. But it is beyond Alpha Centauri (AC) or the CIV V really?
As far I can see, a surprisingly big number of players seem to be disappointed. That made me absolutely curious about this game. I played AC a lot back in time and wanted to find out how BE works.
After winning the first BE campaign, I think it did the homework quite well. AC did it a little better for its time but I don't think it is a reason for hate. Yes BE is CIV V with aliens. Okay but what did you suspect anyway? In the core it is just as CIV V as AC was CIV II. Some things are modified to fit the sci-fi genre, there is more emphasis on barbarians... er... aliens, there is different mechanics and some base rules are altered, you have to use different battle tactics because of the new type of units and so on.
About the rule changes, what it does really well is creating some sci-fi atmosphere. Also it puts the emphasis on exploration instead of development as it has more content on the scenery and less  in the technology tree that feels simplified when I think of CIV V. That's not a good or bad thing, just an alteration of rules. The development of tehcnologies adds a different route and dealing with the environment adds a different taste compared to CIV V.
The area where BE lacks is the opponents AI. Both dimplomacy options and AI reactions feel reduced so if you play CIV games for the realistic AI opponents, it is not your game. The fellow leaders are quite predictable and there are much less ways to deal with situations than in CIV V (or AC, per se). When I played CIV V or AC, I had the feeling that the opposing leaders / fractions are up to something, make unpredicable moves and so on. There was only one predictable leader in AC, some religious redhead called Miriam or what, she kept on attacking mindlessly my fraction whatever decisions I made from game to game. In CIV V the leaders behave more to their personalities. In BE they react sort of similar to each other, they are flat and there are some not so reasonable reactions (e.g. attacking a huge empire of a powerful leader with supreme force (khm...) after a peace treaty expired when only one city and a couple of units remained for them).
So, as for a final verdict:
- Did CIV V offer more? Slightly, I wish BE had better AI.
- Was AC better? The AI and mechanincs were and it had some sense of humour.
- Is BE a bad game? Definitely not.
- Am I disappointed? I wouldn't say. I expected a sci-fi themed game on CIV V engine with some new twists and it is exacty like that.
- Am I♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off? I'm not angry at all. It is just a game.
- Was it fun? In its way, it was.
Although I miss a little more realistic AI and I like it less than CIV V overall (mind that it is one of the most popular CIV games for a reason, right?) - there is no hate from me at all. Give it a try.
I can see why it did not match the expectations of a big portion of players but I still can't understand the hate wave phenomenon. There are much worse games out there with much lower hate rate. In a way, the game was not disappointing - the reviews were as they suggest something much worse than the reality. I do question if a game can be judged by the reviews at all. Now that I'm writing a review...
It is just a game. If your expectations are unrealisticly high and you don't know what you want (everyone knew that it will be a sci-fi themed game on CIV V engine, right?), it is impossible to satisfy them. Maybe it is not the game that goes wrong.

After a few hours of playing, it becomes apparent that the general consensus about Thief is justified--the game does indeed largely fail to meet expectations. The City feels lifeless and navigating the map can be a pain, many mission structures are linear, the AI can be ridiculous, the gameplay can get repetitive, and the story and characters, most of all Garrett, feel rushed.
Admittedly, this wasn't a huge surprise. I was somewhat prepared for it with all the reviews and forum posts I had read. It's also why I bought the game on sale to begin with. And so I stopped playing for a few days and went back to other games, most notably Skyrim. Then this is where it struck me. This game is actually amazingly fun for those that enjoy playing thieves/assassins/stealthy characters in Skyrim. I am one of those people and so decided I would stop comparing Thief to past games in the series and would simply drop all expectations.
I approached the game just like I would if I had rolled a thief or assassin in an Elder Scrolls game. This might be a workaround, and in no way does it forgive the game's faults, but it made them easier to deal with. It made me play through the game much longer than I would have otherwise, and I ended up having a lot more fun this way. There's a lot of content to burn through, and for those looking for a more fleshed out thieving experience than what is available in Skyrim or similar games like Fallout 3 and New Vegas, you will have your money's worth.

I have loved the series since 1998 and hoped for the best for this installment. I wasn't disappointed.
*POSSIBLE SPOILERS*
I played all the way through. Yes, it's nothing like the classics, I kept waiting for SOME mention of Hammerites, Keepers or pagans but other than that, I liked it. There was just enough old elements and hints to keep me playing so I could keep fuelling the nostalgia. (I'm pretty sure I saw some hammers and definitely saw the keyhole iconography of the Keepers many times and there aren't actual moss arrows but there's a "moss arrow" buff you can buy) Also, I was sad at first that they didn't get the original Garrett voice actor but I got over it because at least the new guy tried to sound like him and did a pretty good job. Didn't like the stuff about Erin. I mean, I loved the fact that they maybe made a use for that little girl that picked Garrett's pocket in an older game cutscene but she just ended up being whiny and ungreatful not to mention turning the people of The City into monsters. I also love that Basso was there too, with the mention of his ex-wife with his magpie of the same name. The City is still The City with a Baron, Sheriff and a City Watch and there is mention of Blackbrook and a few of the well-known districts are there. I just found the story lacking with the Erin character.
I hope they continue to make more Thief games since this was a reboot because I hope they'll touch on classic elements more. Lore-wise, I hate the fact that it appears that they threw out the original origin of his eye. Call me old-fashioned but his eye was torn out for a pagan ritual that he later sabotages and a mechanical replacement by the Hammerites. I just found it disconcerting that there were no obvious mention of Hammerites, Keepers and Pagans-The hints of each were fine, I just would have liked to see more.
Besides any shortcomingS, I do recommend this game. Just please play the first three before this one, you'll appreciate the effort made in this one more.

This game is amazing! It is truely a unique. The RTS aspects of the game is very well done and only takes a few minutes to get the hang of it. The shooting feels very natural and has a very nice class system to it. Playing as the commander (Or RTS mode) is VERY fun even though you are not blowing someone's head off. Without the commander the team is hopeless and can't get basic assets. The commander will build Flame, Machinegun, and rocket sentries to defend the command bunker. They are also in charge of creating health and ammo stations as well as providing all the buildings with power. The goal is for ground units to capture resource collectors to assist in building and expanding the base to help dominate the battlefield. As the round goes on you and your team must destroy the enemy team's command bunker and win the game. The game has four classes which are divided into subclasses based on rank and weaponry. There is Exo (Heavy weapons/Explosives), Assault (Snipers, scouts, infantry), Steath (Spies/Assassins), And Support (Chemical Warfare, Engineers, Medics). This is overall a VERY rich game that is WAY worth the five dollars to buy it. The only thing this game needs are players. The community is still active and we need people to create and populate servers. So grab that Exo suit, and your favorite play style and have a blast!

The Cat Lady is a game that feels like a point & click (P&C) callback to some of the past psychological greats: the game is disturbing, with great story, unique and eerie artwork adding to the awesome atmosphere (especially for a P&C adventure game) the voice acting is top-notch especially when you meet the rather unsavory characters.
Now it's time to talk about some of the cons, the game can be buggy; I've encountered two corrupt saves which wouldn't be so bad if there weren't long periods of unskippable dialogue without a save option (setting me back at least an hour each time) and not many slots in which to save.  You also can't turn off the spoken dialogue, for those who would rather have a more classic or comic-book feel to it.
Despite its setbacks, I recommend the game to anyone who loves horror or classic adventure games.
If you are a fan of both, this is most definitely going to be a game you'll love forever.

In This War of Mine you play as a group of everyday civilians, people who use to go about thier daily lives as teachers, firemen, lawyers, and many more. The game will make you feel heroic whether if its taking someone in, rescue your nieghbors or saving a childs mother by giving her pills.  But the games also unforgiving and cruel and thats when the fun starts  when you scavange the outskirts of town till thier picked clean but then whats next?  The war infested inner city?  What will you do to survive?  Would you steal from the old and doom them to a fate worse than death?  Kill the young to survive?  What happens when you kill the man protecting his family and supplies, what will become of them after you return? After destroying thier only hope of survial?  Will they lie lifeless on the ground after roiters came and took what little supplies remained in thier home after you picked it clean over thier protectors corpse?  Will your survivor be able to live with thier choice or will they take comfort with the rough texture of a roped noose?  or will your friends see you as a monster and leave?  Yeah this game is dark and makes you feel guilty as hell and no matter what you do nothings the right thing....Welcome to War

Ok, so, i bumped in this game (I had never heard of before) through an Humble Bundle and i got curious about the colours and the artwork. Only later i realized its backstory of being an rpg developed by a small cameroonian team and that helped me focus on the pros and cons from a certain perspective.
Long story short, i was at first extremely disappointed, the graphics are inspired but technically preety bad in realization, the engine never eploits truly your graphic cards and the music, although originals are a bit repetitive and not always timed. Moreover initially the combat system was a real mess, the dodges and blows were seemingly without any sense.Luckily enough i kept on playing. In an hour the plot opens and you're introduced into a world that has its roots in African culture and mithology, with many parallels to Africa's current situation (without ever mentioning the european influences) but which doesn't disdain to borrow themes and ideas from the genre of Jrpg and rpg in genre. The Plot revolves around self-discovery with every chacter well depicted and capable of give you emotions, one way of another. The realtionship between the twp protagonists, Enzo and Erine, is extremely dinamic and through their jpurney they are in a constant evolution which interplays with their Legacy and ancestors. That said, one thing that stands out are the FRIGGIN BOSS FIGHTS!!! there are a lot, (in ten hours i've faced 12 bosses) each with his own personality, goals, worldview and peculiar powers, which require you to work pout a proper strategy while they're kicking your♥♥♥♥♥around. This does'nt mean this is dark souls, you hardly die due to lot of healings but neither the fights  are all about throwing punches. It's a good balance beacuse it forces the player to think about a strategy, though giving him the time to do that without having to retry the boss fight 4 times only to learn the attack pattern of the boss. This Way the boss fights are extremely diynamics, and in the whole, they are also fairly epic.
Good Job!
P.S., you're a great Team!

My first impression of Hammerwatch wasn’t positive. It was an impulse purchase, spurred on by the ability to set the game to look like it’s being played on an old CRT screen, complete with phosphor scanlines and curved edges. I’m a sucker for that stuff. The little-hero pixel artstyle is also charming enough, but trudging through the pre-built campaign just didn’t gel with me. It took too long to kill the huge hordes of monsters, to find the keys needed to open doors.
Then I tried it multiplayer, and everything fell into place. This is Gauntlet, for a new generation. Working together, covering each other’s backs, or accidentally killing your partners by triggering traps - it’s a blast. Hammerwatch is an incredibly reserved game design. There are four classes, each unique and upgradeable with new attacks you buy from vendors across the maps, but nothing carries over into a new game. It’s a bit one-shot, and might change as the game evolves since it’s still in a bit of a “beta” state.
Multiplayer works local, LAN and online, and loading a savegame for an online campaign in progress requires a bit of finagling. but it does work. Likely too simplistic for most, Hammerwatch is an acquired taste. But with the right friends, it’s a kind of magic straight out of 1985.

One of the best games I've played recently, it has a very good money-to-value ratio.
It reminds me of Pharaoh and Cleopatra, but on an entirely different scale - you start as a small tribe of several hunter-gatherers and gradually you shift to a more advanced society, creating first religions, alphabets, assimilating or killing other tribes - this is a wonderful experience for anyone who likes pre-civiliazation era.
Once your settlement is large enough, you will proceed to create a proto-state and then a true state. This requires a lot of skill and cunning, and diplomacy and very careful resource allocation is a must.
One word of advice - expand north, FAST, or else you're screwed. Ignore your enemies and they will grow in numbers in no time.
Some cons now:
1. The replayability value is lower because there is no randomly generated map - you will start in the same place, with the same resources and the same tribes. Not exactly the best feature.
2. Personally, I'd like to see some more diplomatic options - marriages, alliances, little more detail about how faith is spread etc.
Despite the cons, I can heartily recommend it. It is a very good game, and has a good price too.

The Yawhg is an interesting game. This review will have small spoilers for gameplay stuff, as there isn't much to spoil in the story as it is different every time you play. I won't spoil specific events that can occur, but I will talk about the general flow of the game.
It IS a text heavy game. It consists of reading text, then choosing how you will respond to a certain event, and then reading the effects of that choice before moving onto the next character. After doing this for each character playing, you move forward 1 week
You spend 6 weeks with 2 - 4 characters living their life. You as the player know a monster called "The Yawhg" is coming, but the characters in game don't. Each character does one action for a week, then a transition to next week occurs with a bit of information about why The Yawhg is scary. You repeat this for 6 weeks, then the Yawhg comes and you choose how the characters react to the aftermath, followed by seeing the fate of the town, and your characters. After that the credits play and a new game starts. I won't go into the specific of what can happen, as that is something you will have to discover that for yourself. I recommend you do, as it is a very interesting game.
As of writing this, I've completed 3 playthroughs and feel there is a lot of game left to play. I've gotten a couple of very different endings and very excited to see more of them.  If you get a dark, bad ending the first couple of times, don't worry that is normal (at least for me) just keep trying to make things turn out better.
In conclusion, I'm not going to call this game "good" or "bad" or give it a rating. Because, in my experience they never really matter. I recommend just buying the game, and experiencing it for yourself as it is well worth the price.

I'm only writing this review because this game showed up in the Metroidvania bundle and most reviews claim it as Metroidvania-esque. On that I would humbly disagree. This game is more like a 2D Souls game minus the RPG elements. If that interests you, then you should look into it.
My criticisms:
If you compare this game to the two greats in the genre, Super Metroid and Symphony of the Night, it is quite clear it is not Metroidvania. Some aspects it shares, notably the map style and mechanically interesting boss fights/arenas. But it fails in what I think are some big important aspects of the genre and that is abilities, items/secrets, and map traversal/exploration.
Momodora essentially offers little in the way of true exploration. You don't get a space jump, or a bat form, or a mist form. You only really gain one ability to allow you traverse new areas and it is very apparent where and what they are and it is more of a way of metering your way through the game. Super Metroid and SOTN offer a plethora of skills or weapons that dramatically alter how you will approach or revisit a level. Momodora does little with that.
Items come in the form of equippable trinkets that are either active or passive. These offer small benefits like a heal, more money, or a vacuum for instance. None of these really help you explore the world like say Missiles, Super Missles, Bombs, Gravity suit. None of them also alter the way you play the game like different weapon types ala Alucard.
There really is nothing to explore too. Sure, there are some hidden things, but they are truly unimaginatively hidden due to the previous two issues. There are no interesting abilities that allow you to explore new areas, so no hidden corners containing new Missile Expansions or Silver/Gold Glasses. Additionally there aren't that many items that can't just be purchased, so there are no avenues containing something interesting/equippable like Alucard's weapons or armors or cards.
It takes away the aspects of Metroidvania that I really enjoy, notably progression through interesting itemization and exploration. What is left is a competent 2D platformer with a heavy emphasis on action combat. Its good at that. Its just not a good Metroidvania.

First Review i've written for steam but i feel this game earned it. I personnaly love MTG and in a little over a year it has become my favorite hobby. Now this game is obviously not perfect but there are positives and negatives that i will go over here. First Let's begin with the positive
1. Probably the most attractive option about this game is that it is free to play. You earn coins which buy boosters that contain 3 common, 2 uncommon, and one rare or mythic.
2. The User interface is amazing. Unlike magic online (which also has many positives) the UI is very smooth and easy to use.
3. Solid card selection from the 5 most recent sets (origins-Eldrich moon) and still growing
4. You can have up to 30 custom decks
5. Load times are usually pretty quick
6. It is just fun to play IMO
7. As of 8/29/16 there are currently 15 planeswalker cards and mo0re to come.
8. When you unlock cards you can not unlock the same cards once you have reached the maximum amount of that card. For example, If you unlock all 4 copies of prey upon (a common) you will not unlock another prey upon ever again. Same for if you get an avacyn you will not get another. It is like what overwatches loot boxes should have been.
Negatives
1. It is free to play which means that it does have microtransactions. I know this turns a lot of people off but IMO if you enjoy the base game then spending a little bit shouldn't be a negative. I feel the quality of the product is worth spending some money on it but i will still count this as a negative.
2. Not all cards from the set(S) are in the game. While the majority of the cards are present i was a little disappointed to see that there was no drana from zendikar or demonic pact from origins.
3. Only 4 updates a year
4. Earning coins could be a little quicker
5. Unlike previous games in the series there is no text chat in game. (some might see that as a positive so you don't have to deal with ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s)
6. Lack of game types. Currently you can only play 60 card standard and two headed giant. So do not expect commander or any limited formats.
7. This bothered me a lot at first but i got use to it, In any given deck you can have 4 copies of any common, 3 of any uncommon, 2 of any rare, and only 1 copy of a mythic. This is to keep the game more balanced but if you dont like that then i get it.
Thats about it. I feel that the positives out weight the negatives with this game and you may disagree and thats cool. I hope this gave some people a better idea of this game and what it is like. :)

It's been several weeks since I finished The Cat Lady, and I still find myself thinking about it. This is the type of game that will never leave you. It deals with a lot of dark, sensitive topics (depression and suicide only being the beginning), but it is all very well done and very thought-provoking. I started this game when I was feeling rather down myself, and I got so immersed in  the plights of Susan and others that I completely forgot about what was stressing me out and ended up actually feeling a bit better after each time I played. I felt as if I knew some of these characters personally as I listened to their own struggles and quickly found myself growing attached to a few of them. Parts of the game had me tearing up, other parts had me swearing vengeance, and other times I found myself smiling. It was very hard to put down, and at one point I had to force myself to stop so that I could eat dinner (which I had told myself I was going to do an hour and a half prior when I started feeling hungry). The thick atmosphere had me always wondering what was going to happen next. It was creepy and unsettling, but not so horrifying that I had to walk away, which I found perfect. While there were a few jumpscares, I found myself able to tolerate them, and I absolutely hate jumpscares.
Something else I absolutely love is that the game features multiple endings. There are many choices during the game and can have a big effect on the final outcome, or change a conversation you are having with another character. I have yet to discover the other endings, but I am looking forward to choosing different paths.
The soundtrack to this game is also amazing. Shortly after finishing the game, I went and purchased a physical copy of the lyrical album (there are two soundtracks to the game, one of which comes with the game on Steam, while the other one does not) and I cannot stop listening to it. In fact, it was when Inside started playing in-game during a particularly intense moment at the beginning that I knew I was going to love this game.
In summary, I highly recommend this game to anybody looking for an immersive story and experience. It's an emotional journey that you will not forget and will leave a lasting impression.

Far Cry 4 is the latest in the series of open-world first-person shooters by Ubisoft.  To many, including myself, Far Cry 3 was one hell of an enjoyable gaming experience.  With Far Cry 4, Ubisoft decided to build upon Far Cry 3's open-world mechanics and add some new features for flavor.  In essence, Far Cry 4 feels a lot like Far Cry 3, but more polished.  For example, now random events happen more frequently, giving the player much more to do in between campaign quests.  There are more weapons and more vehicles to ride.  Outposts can be replayed infinitely for higher points and bragging rights on the global leaderboards.  Graphics have also been improved significantly.  Overall I would say Far Cry 4 improves upon most of the core aspects of Far Cry 3, but as many have mentioned Far Cry 4 doesn't break new ground.  Even so, playing Far Cry 4 is still a hugely gratifying and immersive gaming experience that will definitely keep you entertained for a long time.
As for performance, apparently this game has had its share of performance issues/bugs at launch.  I waited a month for the patches to come through, and the current version of the game is very stable on my computer.  Running a first-gen Intel i7 and an AMD R9 290, I can run this game at 1440p at ultra settings with a decent average fps (about 50-60).  Obviously my setup is not top of the line, but even so I can almost run the game at max settings.  The only setting I cannot max out is the anti-aliasing, but I don't really care since 8x or 16x MSAA is overkill anyways.  If you are experiencing fps lag, I recommend lowering the anti-aliasing.  I'm not too sure why people are still complaining about performance, since I believe the game, in its current state, is optimized to run on PC fairly well (as was Far Cry 3).  37 hours into the game, I have yet to encounter a single bug or crash!
To conclude, if you enjoyed Far Cry 3, you definitely owe it to yourself to get this game.  If you have ever played and enjoyed any open-world action game such as Assassin's Creed, the Batman: Arkham series, or Grand Theft Auto, I highly recommend giving this game a try as well.
Final Rating: 8/10  Very good

Maplestory, oh Maplestory, how I have many fond, bittersweet memories with you. I've been a player of Maplestory for several years, actually for about a decade now. If memory serves, I've been playing since the sixth grade. It used to be all I did once I got back home from school, just played for hours with my cousin and younger brother. We always had a blast and I miss those days. Don't misunderstand, my intention is not to be one of those glorified, Pre-Big Bang era player that preaches the golden era of old Maplestory, but I had one of the most memorable memories when I played back in the days. Made so many friends and everything I did was just, plainly put, magical. I spent countless hours just playing the game, grinding and talking to friend, and through this game I've met friends who I still talk to to this day. Nowadays, I don't really play anymore. I quit the game about 2 or 3 years ago., I play roughly once a week for no more than an hour.
To get to my review of the game, I'll break it into categories and give you my full, honest insight.
Not much to say here, grinding is significantly more easier compared to the past days of Maplestory, where getting to just Lv.70 was a challenge. Even reaching Lv.30 could take a week depending on your training regiment. These days, veteran players can reach Lv.200 in a matter of hours. The game is pretty undeniably pay-to-win, but there's sort of a fine 'line' there. What I mean by that is the game definitely highly benefits you if you're willing put forth the money, which grant you power in a much shorter span of time compared to non-paying methods. However, non-paying methods are still effective, just that it takes more time to progress. I myself have a 950k range (buffed) on my Hayato (Lv.205) and I haven't poured any money onto my equipment. When it comes end-game bossing, however, it's a completely different story. Even with my range, I can't defeat most high-end bosses. You'll need a party, with a similar range, or someone with a ridicoulous amount of range who'd just decimate the boss.
I'll keep this short and simple. Perhaps I haven't been doing things right, or maybe I'm just outdated, but the current community isn't really communicative. Most players keep to themselves and the lack of people joining party quests doesn't help the problem. It's pretty hard to make friends, from my experience, these days. I log in and almost never speak a word. There is a much smaller amount of players playing now than compared to back in the days.
Although Maplestory offers an overwhelming amount of classes, most of them just fill similar roles to others, rendering the ones that are not on top of their respective role rather useless.
Probably an arbitary section, but I just couldn't help but not give this a mention. Maplestory's soundtrack is
beautiful, addictive, and memorable! There's just so many of them that I have a huge affinity for! While playing, I can guarantee that you'll find yourself humming, in sync, to the background music.
Maplestory seems to have recurring issues of poorly running. From frequent disconnection, to just constant latency, to long hours of scheduled and unscheduled maintenance and don't forget the infamous extentions within maintenance, you can be sure enough that this'll happen very often while playing. Regardlesss, a low-end computer should be able to run Maplestory fairly well. Even if you have some problems, you could change the quality of skills and background so that it may run more smoothly.
I barely scratched the surface regarding Maplestory's faults, but I digress, you'll soon understand for yourself if you decide to play. Maplestory may have a number of issues, but it is still a niche and fun game. However, I'd only play the game if you're planning to play with friends, other than that I don't really recommend it, the game can get awfully lonely. Granted, if you're solo playing and enjoy the solitude that is endless grinding, then I suppose this game is right for you! Wish I could give the game a neutral recommendation, but I'll reccommend it. The game is still somewhat fun, in my opinion, if you don't look at the bad.

Civilization Beyond Earth has a lot in common with Civilization V in its gameplay, and some might say that it would just be a clone / DLC of Civilization V and nothing more. I strongly disagree, as this game plays entirely different than any Civilization; the technology tree cannot be remotely compared and involves a strategy of appropriately choosing the correct technologies to acquire the needed amount of points in your desired affinity, these choices also profoundly modifying your development to the point where, you guessed it, you start playing differently than Civilization V (because the number 1 mistake is to play it like you would play Civ V, and not only will you not fair well, but you will also obviously have that feeling of deja-vu).
Speaking of affinities, this is where most of my appeal in the game comes from; it genuinely dives into possible future paths for humanity, especially on the themes of transhumanism, extropianism or simply traditional humanism.
What else, soundtracks are not as great as in Civ V but I am a personal fan of some sound effects, espcially the ones for the quests.
