When I first saw the title of this, I laughed and thought it would be something silly and comedic, and since I'm a little bit of a crazy cat lady myself, I looked closer and was very surprised to see how dark it looked.  Out of curiosity, and because there was a great sale, I picked it up....
...and couldn't stop playing for hours.
This is not going to be for everyone for a few reasons:
1. The psychological darkness of the game won't appeal to people looking for upbeat, shiny, unicorns and flowers.  It may resonate more with those of us that have suffered from some of the subject matter (i.e. severe depression).  There are a lot of disturbing events and imagery which I feel is essential to the story but again, if you're more butterflies-and-puppies, you may not love it.
2. The art style is extremely unique and not traditionally "pretty" but I feel it's done well and draws the player into the scene. However, it's untraditional enough that some people might find it off-putting.
3. The protagonist is likewise not the normal, cookie-cutter heroine and it's extremely refreshing in my opinion.  But if you're looking for a game with more eye candy, this isn't it.
4.  The side-scrolling gameplay takes some getting used to in terms of exploration.  If you're used to playing more standard point-and-click adventure and exploration games, it will take even more getting used to.  The mouse is not used at all in the game, just arrow keys.  Nothing but arrow keys.  Even after a second playthrough to nab some achievements I missed the first time, I still bobbled the key selection once in a while.  It wasn't a problem for me, but it might turn some players off.
The game isn't expensive on a normal day, and is even better on sale, so I feel it's worth giving it a chance if you're waffling on whether to get it or not.  Hopefully this mini-overview helps you make a decision!

The Cat Lady a.k.a. The Five People You Meet in Hell
TL;DR -> Well worth the cost (and probaly even a few dollars more)
As someone who has gone through several of the situations that the protagonist goes through, as well as being extremely introverted, let me just say that the story really hits close to home. It is a truly emotional journey that can easily drudge up the past and really force you to connect with Susan on several levels.
Playing the game won't make you depressed, on the contrary, it will almost make you feel epowered in a way.
For those of you who haven't gone through any such events, you should still play this game. The gritty, dark and quite realistic (with the exception of several key factors) story is just a real heart-felt journey that will occasionally cause you to stop and think about the trials in life that several people have to deal with. TL;DR? -> Sometimes you'll feel sad for the characters and sometimes you'll feel downright♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off at others.
As for the game itself? Each aspect seems to compliment eachother. What I mean is for those of you who have seen the GRAPHICS and immediately thought that the designers were just lazy, let me just say that the art would NOT have worked any other way. This particular style of art works extremely well with the story that is being told. It's not lack of ambition or design resources, it's intentional and rightfully so.
The SOUND was something that I struggled with to accept. Some of the voice-acting was very well done, but quite a few of the characters seemed really forced, such as Doctor X. Often times you can hear that it was just a case of standing too close to the microphone while other times the dialogue just didn't really sound convincing. Sometimes I felt this worked to their advantage as it added a more realistic tone, but it was quite situational. Overall, I didn't feel like this really took anything away from the game.
The MUSIC, however, I found to be really enjoyable all the way through.
The CONTROLS? Not much to be said on that point since you only use the arrow-keys and Enter. Very easy to play and drink coffee at the same time with is a wonderful little bonus.
The PUZZLES in the game aren't of the Myst-type calibre, but are enough to keep it from feeling more like a visual novel. Some of them you will just end up solving without even realizing it's a puzzle while others might take you awhile to piece together. I, personally, found none of them to be truly frustrating.
The REPLAY VALUE is there, but unless you didn't save very often or didn't focus on nailing each achievement, you might cap it off with 2 playthroughs.
Overall, I would recommend this game. Well worth the couple bucks.
Sometimes dialogues are too long and boring, but overall it was a good game. Would recommend it.

Steam needs a "meh" recommendation option.  I neither loved nor hated Far Cry 4 but at $50-60 I don't recommend this game.  Far Cry 4 feels very much like a really nice expansion pack for Far Cry 3.  A new setting, new characters, but ultimately the same core mechanics.  That's not a knock, I loved Far Cry 3, but I expect more from a full-price AAA title.  Even Assassin's Creed manages to iterate slightly on its gameplay.  Don't let my hours on record fool you, much of that time is from leaving the game running over night.
This time around I just could not get in to the story.  Where FC3 had a great 'Lost' vibe, FC4 lacks a suffciently compelling story to drive the action forward.  The opening sequence is such a frenetic mess of disjointed scenes that by the time I was in control of the protagonist I had no idea why he cared enough to stick around in Kyrat.  Nothing in the next 10+ hours convinced me that my character had sufficient motivation to do the things he was doing.  Nor were the side characters fleshed out well enough for me to understand or care about their stories.  Pagan Min's lieutenants are introduced briefly and killed just as quickly.  They could have been fodder #2935 for all I knew except they had unique clothes and hair.
Gameplay is identical to FC3.  That's great and all but I wanted some more interesting challenges.  Like FC3 once you unlock a few of the more advanced weapons the game is a cake walk.  The fortress capture events provide the game's only real challenge and even these are only as difficult as you make them.  Sniping is so effective at clearing fortresses and outposts you'll start to wonder why the game bothers with assault rifles or pistols.  If the AI discovers a body or sees a comrade go down to sniper fire they'll usually run in your direction but if you are sniping from an unreachable vantage point then forget about them doing anything intelligent.  Seriously, how do you stride over the growing heaps of dead friends and not think to pull the alarm?
Biggest negative:  As of this writing the mouse controls are dicey at best.  You cannot fully disengage the mouse acceleration and smoothing options implemented for console gamers.  There are tutorials for monkeying about with the configuration files but aiming always feels just a little *off*.  These issues are amplified by graphical lag, I opted to play on lower graphics settings and for the most part I could forget about the aiming.

Far Cry 4 is basically an updated Far Cry 3, which isn't a bad thing since Far Cry 3 was an outstanding game. I'm going to list the pros and the cons of this game.
Pros:
Beautiful Graphics.
Runs Smoothly After The Recent Patches (Has always ran smooth for me, I play on max settings).
A ton of content: The world is huge, a lot bigger than FC3 and had a ton of missions, guns and customization.
Great Characters (In my opinion).
Map editor is great and there are tons of awesome maps out on the browser.
Nice interface.
Cons:
Multiplayer doesn't run very well and not many people play it.
Gets a tad repetitive, especially after most of the same things were in Far Cry 3.
Overall the game is really fun and enjoyable and I think deserves a positive review.
Verdict: 9/10

As the king of the elves calls for his annual challenge, you are on your way to participate in the competition which this year requires you to find the queen, hidden somewhere in the kingdom of the elves. Equipped with nothing more than his lute, Finn the Bard gets ready for a very enjoyable adventure that entertained me more than many of the modern Telltale, Daedalic, etc. games.
'The Order of the Thorne - The King's Challenge' is an old style point and click adventure that reminds a lot of 'Kings Quest' and the old 'LucasArts' games. It’s short, lovely, funny and heart warming. Take a break from the AAA scene and relax for a couple of hours with caring elves, treacherous pixies, introvert fisherman, nasty gnomes, helpful turtles, beautiful ladies and a spider woman with the most sexiest voice ever (please tell me one more time I may not pass...)
Pros:
- good music
- good puzzles
- you can't die
- great humour
- great narrator
- very good voice acting
- visit a graveyard with tombstones for each developer
- most sexy voice of a spider lady in a PC game ever
- easy achievements
Neutral:
- pixel graphics (I won't put them on the cons list because they are still beautiful)
- some might say the game is too short. I think it's OK. It took me six hours to finish the game. But I took my time and enjoyed playing it slowly.
Cons:
none

Im glad I only paid 99c for this game.  I completed this game inside 5 hours.  Very Small.
I was pleased that you're giving tasks to complete from the very beginning.  The character instantly has a sense of
purpose and  you're not having to spend time to find it.  The dialog is short and sweet wich I think is fanastic.  This doesnt
take anything  away from the overall story or from the overall game play.    The UI is very simple which is not a bad thing,
it just shortens the completion time.
Simple, and worth playing.

Fantasic game. I like that it is short and the puzzles are a good balance of not too difficult and not dead simple. Good kickback to the old Sierra days. Only complaint is that the acheivements seems buggy. I completed them all but two didn't register in steam.
Great game is the vein of classic Sierra titles.

This is a great throwback to the old adventure games of the 1990s, this particular game is in the style of the wholesome King's Quest series, making it a good choice for children to play as well. The game has a Loom like gameplay mechanic where you play special songs on your lute to affect the world around you - a peace song would calm down an angry bear, a protection song would create a barrier of protection etc. I wish the devs added more variety to these songs because most of them are variations of making people happy songs. The puzzles aren't difficult at all but that's okay, this is the first game in a series so it makes sense things start off easy. To summarize, this is a fun, charming game that really scratches that nostalgia itch. My only complaint is that it's too short - I finished at 5 hours and a lot of it is just me playing songs for people to see how they react.

Nice game. Kind of remind me of old King's Quest game. Puzzles are not really hard, but that was fun notheless.
I felt the voices were a bit slow and ended up skipping most of them.
7/10

It's one of those 'What the f*** do I have to do?' kind of games, but this is probably what you expect from a game of this style. Wandering aimlessly through the woods of a charming fairy world without anyone giving you hints about where to go or what to do next feels just like the old games it wants to mimick. It lacks the always present fear of dying of the latter, though. I liked the game nevertheless, knowing it would be rather short but fairly priced.
A huge dissapointment from the company that brought us Quest for Infamy. I'm not sure how the quality of absolutely every aspect of this game managed to drop from QfI like a lead balloon. Tragic.

it's a fun blast from the past, similar to games like "quest for glory" from the late 80s, early 90s that many of us grew up on, with a few modern embellishments that were very nicely done. i recommend it if you get it on sale for $4.99 or less as it is a very brief game, 7-10 hours at most with little replay value as the same tasks will have to be done. but the music is fantastick and the voice acting pretty good. the art style verrry niiice! i had a good yet all-too-brief time with it. looking forward to getting the sequel, also on sale if possible.

It's a nice game, the visuals are great (if you like pixelstyle) the music is alright and the voiceacting is quite good. The game mechanics are solid and exept for problems from the steam overlay I couldn't find a single bug. I especially liked the bardsongs (though there could be a slight improvement so that you wouldn't have to "listen" to the song everytime before playing it but just play it and the game recognizes it) as they gave the game a very nice extra much like in Loom for example. I also enjoyed the easter eggs throughout the game. The story-quality overall is hard to tell as this game only serves as an introduction but that part is good so far, but herein lies maybe the games biggest flaw it took me about three hours to finish (had some idling and such) and I got all achievements (I guess you automatically get them all?) so it's pretty short (well it's just 10 bucks so that's alright with me).
Overall I'd say 4/5 and a definitive recommendation.

This game is a great example of how there are no true quality metrics in video game design.  Graphics?  This game is entirely un-animated and the still images consist completely of low-res cartoons.  Gameplay?  You pick options off a menu.  Music?  One guitar.  Story?  You will finish it in less than a half hour.
And yet The Yawhg is probably worth twice its $10 asking price.  In a market saturated with "gameplay advancements," "4K resolution," "roleplaying elements," and hundred-hour lengths, very few game developers stop to ask themselves whether they are using these tools to do something worth doing.  The Yawhg does something worth doing and does not need any of these tools to do it.
To nitpick the game's description, The Yawhg is not a "Choose Your Own Adventure."  Choose Your Own Adventure books very rarely had multiple main characters or stats to track.  The Yawhg is a /Gamebook,/ and while these were great fun in the 80s before we had real branching-path video games, today this is the best possible format for the medium.  The Yawhg is a perfect example of the synergy of right tools and right task, and it is worth the time of anyone who enjoys a good interactive story.  I suppose you might call this a visual novel -- I don't know, really, I feel like genre has become largely irrelevant in describing video games.
The story of The Yawhg is different every time you play it, so I can't comment on its quality universally, but if you find yourself telling a story you don't care for, it will only last for 20 more minutes.  Suck it up and then start a new one.  I still recommend you finish the playthrough, however, because what comes to pass may surprise you.
More like this, please, industry.  More like this.

Excellent casual cooperative role-playing game.
For this game, you can choose from 4 characters (you need at least two) who take turns each week for 6 weeks at 16 different jobs around the city. Each job comes with stat upgrades and varying events that are at their best when they relate to each other: something that happens to one character can have an effect on what happens to another character later. Generally, the outcome of an event depends on whether you made a choice that your current stats will support: physique, finesse, mind, charm, magic, and wealth. Then the Yawgh comes, then there's another round that determines if the group has won or lost the game, and then each character gets their own ending. The writing is really nice, surprising at times, and the music supports it well.
You can easily play this game on the couch with up to 4 players, just pass the controller/keyboard around (or connect more controllers), but of course you can also control all of the characters yourself. We did three quite enjoyable couch play-throughs on another account, and they took about half an hour each.
It is not difficult to win this game. We wanted to play it more than once because one time is clearly not enough to see all the different things that can happen, and to reach all of the endings would take many more. Events start to repeat at some point, noticably so on our third game, but since there are choices and stats involved, many consequences of known events are still unknown.
This is a good game.

This is an easy-going game that anyone can get the hang of instantly. With so many events that can happen at each location, you'll never have the same play through twice. The only downside to this is that I want there to be DLCs to add extra characters and locations so that I can play with a larger group of friends!

As much as I'd like to recommend The Yawhg, I just can't. It's beautiful and it has a great core idea, but it's awfully short and unfulfilling.
The "unique story" is far from unique and it gets repetitive on the second play-through. It is also pretty shallow and the fate of the characters often seems to ignore their background and your efforts (for example,
). And just when you think that you're going to have any real impact on the story, it turns out that the game is over and you can only start from the beginning, hoping to come along a line of text that you haven't yet seen.
Furthermore, the characters don't meet each other and not all of their actions result in changes to the whole town that can be experienced by the rest of the protagonists. I played the game alone and I really can't imagine it being more fun with more people, because you just don't interact with them in any way. You can have some laughs about the choices each of you makes, but there's no actual co-op play - you do what you want with your character and you hope that his or her skills will be useful in the end.
Finally, I don't see any improvements and/or fixes coming to The Yawhg. There are no game options whatsoever, so you can't change the resolution, or sound, or anything; alt-tabbing and window mode workarounds bug the game. Besides the local co-op, there is no option to play with someone else, because, according to the developer, "online multiplayer would be silly and underwhelming". There was a word of a "MASSIVE free expansion", but nothing has been heard about it since 2014. The game could've at least had some achievements to keep me interested for a bit longer, but it seems like it was too "silly" to include such things. The final nail in the coffin is the ridiculously high price for a game that's completed in 10 minutes and only pretends to offer a high replay value.

First time I played Depression Quest (about a year ago now), I wasn't doing too well mentally. I didn't want to admit anything was wrong to the people around me and felt shameful about many parts of myself. At some point, I came across the game, made by a few indie developers I hadn't heard of before, and decided to give it a shot.
Of all of the games I've played, this one has had the biggest impact on my life. It managed to show me that, just maybe, what I was experiencing in my head wasn't "normal", but neither did I need to feel ashamed about it. I've since sought out professional help and I'm dealing with my mental issues much better.
This game may or may not be for you. It is not a fun game - don't expect to come out all smiles. Some even say it's not a game (not me, although I can understand their point based on their definition of the word). If you're easily triggered by stories or discussions about depression, I recommend avoiding playing it if you're trying to stay in a positive mood.
However, if you're looking for an understanding of what depression is like, to help you understand what someone else might be going through... or even yourself, this game offers a perspective. It is not the be all or end all of descriptions of what it is like - for sure, some parts of the game's perspective differ from my own experiences with depression - but if you're looking for a starting place to help you develop that understanding, this game is worth a try.

What a little gem of a game... "This War of Mine" is a 2D survival simulator, that depicts the lives of a small group of civilians in the ruins of a city, torn apart by war. You will start the game with your characters taking shelter in a decrepit building, and will, right from the start, have to address security issues, fight hunger, cold and psycologic depression. Your characters will need to scavenge around the city for food and useful materials, during the night. During the day, they will need to use these materials to improve their shelter, patch up holes in the walls, build some basic furniture, cook food, burn wood for warmth etc...
Survival will be a brutal business, and you will be faced with harsh moral dilemmas. A helpless child turns up at your door, in a cold winter morning, asking medicine for his sick mother? You take pitty of the child, give him the last of your medicine... BUT... remember that character of yours, who caught a nasty flu a few days ago (because you had no more fuel for heating...)? Now his chances of surviving the winter have become very slim. His sickness quickly becomes debilitating, and he is forced to stay in bed. The other 2 characters have to do everything they can to keep him alive. They pass many sleepless nights, scavenging around, desperate for food and medicine. Very soon, they become depressed and, one morning, one of them simply disappears. He has had enough, could not take it anymore, and  decided to abandon the shelter. Now you are left with just two characters, one of them severely depresssed, and the other one sick, forced to bed. Very soon, the depressed guy commits suicide. The lone survivor also meets a miserable death a few days later, sick, hungry and depressed. Game over.
This is just one of the possible scenarios, a grim and sad one. There are many others. If you are efficient, if you pay attention to each character's strenghts and needs, and if you make the right decisions, there wiil be hope. The game offers you the possibility to play with a variety of characters, in a variety of settings, with different starting conditions. So, a fair number of different playthroughs is possible.
Combine all these decent gameplay features with some beautiful 2D art and some haunting, atmospheric music and you get yourself a trully unique experience, unlike anything else you have played until this day. This title will really make you realise what a privilige it is to enjoy freedom in real life, have food on your table everyday, have free time and money to enjoy your hobbies (like gaming for example). But it will also teach you that there is always  hope, even in the most desperate situations. And that people need not only food and shelter to survive, but also solidarity, kind words and support from other human beings.
Tldr: "This War of Mine" has been one of the most memorable experiences in my (long) gaming life, and I recommend it without reservations.

Hey Guys,
Since the game ask me for a review every time I play a ranked versus match here it is:
I play Magic the Gathering since the first Zendikar and I really like the paper Game.
Especially the draft mode is very skill based and does not require you to spend a lot of money...
BUT, this PC game as well as all of it's previous versions is poorly implemented.
The Random Number Generator or whatever shuffels your deck is totally borked.
You get 1:1000 results far too often and with consistency.
The round timer is static and does not evolve with the number of rounds or the board state.
It feels painfully long in the beginning and can be short once the Game reaches a certain state.
The game also robs you of options you would normally have,
like ending your turn once the game thinks you can't play anything (which is sometimes just wrong).
The ranking system is terrible. You get matched with an opponent that should have about the same level as you do.
It still happens very often that you get matched with an opponent that is 20 levels below or above you.
This could be compensated for by implementing an ELO system, but the game just gives you a point for a win and takes once for a loss no matter the opponent.
Finding an opponent sometimes takes so painfully long.
So if you like the paper game it does not mean you will like this game.
The good things in this game are:
- Daily rewards are pretty high for a F2P game
- The solo part gives you an acceptable start into versus matchmaking by rewarding you with cards and currency
- If you don't feel up to the task to play against other players you can do some quest vs the AI
(less than before but still enough)
I think I can still recommend the game, but you should know what to expect.
You can't compare it to the quality of Hearthstone or other big budget titles even though it has the better and more complex basis with paper Magic the Gathering...

was so good for its time that everyone understood - no matter what next
would be, it will be constantly compared with predecessor. To be successful, it is vital for it not to look bad in comparison.
Designers bore that in mind. Almost every aspect of game has evolved.
has been balanced, and now you cannot grab things instantly and without moving. Light gem mechanic was simplified, now containing only three distinct states (at first I was quite dissatisfied with this, though, as I saw later, it did not harm gameplay complexity). Imbalanced wall-flattening was removed, replaced by fixed location hiding places - empty closets. Focus feature introduction made gameplay more smooth, it is almost impossible to get stuck now (and, because Focus resource is quite limited, it was achieved without significant complexity loss). Ghost-Opportunist-Predator rankings is great and encourages rich non-linear gameplay. Combat is more dynamic and now, with proper player skill, Garrett poses real threat in one-on-one combat.
is just great. Models, textures, sounds - everything is beyond expectations. I do not value these things much, so cannot tell deep detail, but even I can see work well done.
Still, as you can see, I do not recommend this game. In evaluating
I, like many others, compare it to
. But from my point of view,
loses the match with a huge score gap. This is because the things I liked in
the most were the
, the
and
who acted in it.
In
, there is only one lively character for the whole game. It could be fine with a thieving game if it was protagonist. But no, it is a fence, Basso. To add insult to injury, Basso does practically nothing in whole storyline. Beside some quest-giving in beginning of game, his only appearance is in chapter four, where Garret has to rescue him from prison (a princess in tower could be there instead of Basso with no impact on the narrative). With no bright characters there is no bright story.
Atmosphere is ruined. Introducing collectible sets is the most dubious thing, it turns Garret from cold-blooded and cold-minded thief into some short-sighted kleptomaniac, who stashes valuables worth thousands of coins in dirty destroyed clock tower for some unknown reasons.
Remember brilliant mission in Shalebridge Cradle? Compare atmosphere in Cradle and in Moira Asylum. Compare mission narratives. Double facepalm is not enough to describe a feeling when you see a crude fake copied from masterpiece. This mission just should not have been added to the story. It looks worthless for those who played
and loved it.
All strong ideologies in the City are dead and this is explicitly shown to us: Keeper Library and Hammer Cathedral are abandoned and there is no trace of their inhabitants. Designers burned with desire to destroy the City as player remembers it, and this desire provoked blunders. Abandoned buildings look like they were abandoned for centuries, not for decades, with no rational explanation for that scope of destruction. The City is dead and agonizing, with no purpose to exist, which impacts on playing experience in form of question 'Why should I care and try to save it?' In urge to destroy, nothing was proposed in return. Designers performed just like Orion's revolutionaries - they kill all guards, set city on fire and then... nothing. It just stays burning forever, until you finally close
to never run it again.
Greatest forces you encounter are just some power-hungry feudal lords. Remember how exciting was first mission in
, in Rutherford Castle, reading about all of those intrigues they were plotting against each other? And how worthless they all started to look when Keepers, Hammers and Pagans stepped on the stage? On day four or five you would not even remember that there are some 'Great Families' and that they mean anything in the City.
Nothing like that anymore. You just stick to all those nobles' dirty underwear. No big ideas. Only realpolitik, only hardcore.
Having read all above, you should understand why the story is primitive and predictable (and quite secondary too - revolution line looks like another crude fake copied from masterpiece - this time
).
is another unfortunate example of a game that was created with huge budget and effort of specialists, but without aim to be a piece of art. It is good for killing time, but there is nothing truly beautiful in it. Just business.
Do not have any illusions - it will not 'unfold in the end' like

If you enjoyed Civ V you might enjoy this one too.
It's fairly similar as a game (some would argue it plays more like a mod than its own thing, though I disagree) but the setting is moved into space colonization in the style of the old Alpha Centauri. The base game has the same pitfalls as the base Civ V game with odd diplomacy that the rising tide expansion irons out relatively smoothly.
The plot is relatively simple but has an evocative wealth of imagination and speculative science that carries into the tech trees. A "great mistake" occured roughly 300 years prior to the game's launch point which ruined much of Earth's climate and habitability along with setting scientific progress back a bit as nations and political blocs realigned in a new dark age.
Emerging from this mess into roughly modern technology as we know it, mankind must send out colony ships to habitable worlds to seed the universe and guarantee mankind's survival as Earth seems to be on its last legs. A great number of ships are sent out amongst the stars with roughly 100,000 colonists each along with whatever else they may need to allow mankind a foothold on a new homeworld.
The great nations and superpowers of this dying Earth represent different gameplay aspects. As an example, the Khavitan Protectorate who roughly make up india, pakistan and iran are good at expansion and cultural growth while the unified south american state of Brasilia act and feel more like Verhoven's starship troopers, built to fight.
Speaking of starship troopers, you aren't alone on your new homeworld. The local flora may well be semi-sentient mushrooms and for some odd reason there will be strange buglike aliens on every planet, be they desert, jungle, ice or fungal. As is own aspect of the world's ecosystem, these aliens (or natives since you're technically the alien invader) will respond to the way they're treated. Exploring peacefully and staying out of their way might make them beyond friendly while a kill on sight policy will eventually turn the bugs hostile to everyone on the planet, not just you. In a particularly swarmy campaign, this sort of thing might doom you or your enemy outright.
Aside from the aliens, each strange new world has a number of ancient ruins and artifacts to discover with your resident scout/explorer unit. These may yield scientific insight, resources and treasures that you can combine into unique buildings. This also applies to any odd crashed colony ship that might have arrived before you did, yielding survivors and ancient human relics like the mysterious espresso maker allegedly used in daily religious observances in the past. How you combine alien antimatter mirrors with coffee beans into a communications device to upgrade your city potential is a mystery your scientists keep to themselves...
These ruins and the like also play a part in a quest system wherein you can pursue minor side stories on the side of your campaign by dedicating resources toward exploring certain ruins, building the right labs to analyze the findings and so forth, culminating in a special reward like bonus tech points, affinity upgrades (more on it later) or other goodies. In the expansion, this is taken a step further with each basic map type having a great wonder such as an ancient alien city wherein the player(s) must rush to pursue its secrets by seeking out other sites on the map. When this grand quest is complete, the winning faction recieves a permanent bonus for the duration of the game.
Onto the subject of technology; you can further develop your civ along three different "affinities" which essentially express various forms of futuristic thinking and transhumanism. These in turn affect the strengths of your upgraded units, the nature of unique buildings in your cities and to some extent the appearance of your faction's leader. In a brief rundown; the Supremacy affinity is all about robotics and cybernetics and geared toward upgrading mankind to withstand any threat. The Harmony affinity is more about acclimating to the new homeworld, helping humankind adapt and become one with the planet by eco friendly tech, bioengineering, genetic manipulation and domesticating the local bugs. Purity affinity rejects all that, asserting that humankind is perfect in its base form, must not be subjected to mutations nor robotic replacement and ought to reshape the world to suit them by terraforming.
Affinities understandably split civilizations apart since Purity would consider Harmony civs nonhuman and so forth, affecting the diplomatic meta and this grows even further in the expansion with mixed affinities that allow for a blend of upgrades but also a wild divergence in appearances. A Purity/Supremacist army will have human units directing drones while a Harmony/Supremacist force will have extreme biomechanical things barely recognisable as humans. These things give a wealth of units, tactical considerations and long game plans since each affinity rank also grants minor upgrades like immunity to the deadly spore clouds of the planet or free upkeep for roads.
If you want to win, which you should at least consider at some point, there are several ways to do so as per Civ standard. Three of these are tied to the affinities themselves which I will list here:
Purity's endgame is to build a portal back to Earth and evacuate what's left of humanity and resettle them on this new world. This necessitates a certain degree of control over the local area, dedicating an army to wiping out local wildlife and any bothersome human neighbours.
Supremacy will at some point consider their ascension beyond flesh into code and silica to be a sort or perfection and will want to share it with the unenlightened. Going full Borg on the hapless remaining humans, you build a portal to Earth and dedicate an army to feed into the portal as they "liberate" the earth they left behind.
Harmony with its focus on the world here and now will pursue the knowledge that the planet is in fact a living thing with a dormant consciousness and work toward awakening it so that all may share in its glory. This basically demands growing a giant artificial brain the size of a city and jolting it, cheesing off local bugs, demanding an army to defend it until done.
There's also an economic victory of sorts in which you piece together fragments of an alien signal left behind by the so called progenitors in the various ruins on the planet. With everything in place, you construct a beacon and feed it energy (which is money in this game) until done and join a greater galactic community of sentient beings. This is essentially also a tribute to Carl Sagan's Contact.
In addition, the expansion slaps on a new depth of diplomatic features and a new currency called diplomatic capital which you use to upgrade your base faction traits as well as various economic, industrial, cultural and military bonuses that your opponents may or may not approve of. If saved up, this sort of capital can also be used to buy new units and buildings in a pinch. As a not so insignificant aside, the expansion also adds seaborne cities that can move, allowing you to relocate where resources are needed and almost every hex on the map, land or sea becomes useful for something.
The soundtrack is very nice with pleasant ambience, evocative etheral choirs and cyberpunky tunes that bring home the general image of the game's setting as a new hope and new dawn for mankind.
In summary; it's a good game for what it is. It doesn't innovate too much compared to Civ V and may well fall short because of it but there's some genuine dedication toward exploring the setting with interesting depths to gameplay mechanics and lore (if you're into the science behind it) that makes for an enjoyable experience. Personally, I'd buy this just for the soundtrack but I urge whoever's interested to pick up the base game + expansion when possible on sale as you will get more than your money's worth.

Hammerwatch is a hack 'n' slash dungeon crawler that starts off pretty strong for the first couple floors. The combat is satisfying and has a nice feel to it, while the levels are sprawling and labyrinthian with lots of secrets scattered about. I'm a fan of the detailed pixel art style and the soundtrack is fun and fits the game nicely. The keyboard controls felt way too clunky, but using a 360 pad instead made for a much smoother experience.
The big problem with the game is that after those first couple floors, I started to realize how tedious and repetitive everything was becoming. The basic structure boils down to going from room to room, running past enemies to aggro them and bunch them together, killing off these groups of enemies, then going to the next room and doing it all over again. New enemies are introduced along the way but they're essentially re-skinned versions of old ones. Room layouts also vary and there are the occasional traps that make planning your attacks more interesting, but other than that, there's so little difference between an encounter on the third floor and one on the tenth. The floors themselves are huge in size, which I like, but this can be a double-edged sword since they start to drag on after a while. There is some joy in taking down dozens/hundreds of enemies at once and racking up a huge combo, but that joy is almost entirely gone after doing it hundreds of times repeatedly.
I also wasn't a fan of the fact that in order to reach the legitimate ending, you'll need to collect 12 wooden planks along the way. There's never any suggestion that these planks were anything other than optional, so I never sought them out. And since you can't go back to previous floors after completing boss fights, once you miss them, they're gone. It felt like a cheap tactic and left me somewhat disappointed.
Hammerwatch has a few things going for it and some really nice ideas. Unfortunately, the monotony of fighting large hordes over and over in the same manner overshadows a lot of them. Instead of being a fun experience, it turns into a grind and stays that way until the end.

Where do I begin ... I randomly bought this game because it was very cheap (sale) and because the theme looked interesting to me. I normally never play games like this, but I can say I was positively surprised.
This game isn't for everyone, its subjects are dark: depression, suicide, murder, cancer ... It's for people who want to enjoy a good story about these kind of things. Even if you've never been in contact with them, the game is very good at explaining how a depressed person goes through life. The game can be quite confronting towards people who've suffered from any of the topics above, but it's still an interesting experience.
STORY: really good. At chapter 1 I was interested, but I wasn't blown away or anything. At the end of chapter 2 I was completely hooked though. I thought this game was going to give me a nice, regular story about depression, but I was wrong. It throws things at you you wouldn't expect. Well the game is tagged "horror", so I guess I should've expected the story would become even darker & sicker than it already was ... Quite linear story, but you can make some choices that change the plot a little bit.
GAMEPLAY: Oddly satisfying. You play through each of the 7 chapters and have to explore your environment to gather items and to find out more about the characters. This game works with a kind of puzzle system: find X, so you can get to Y, so you can finally do Z. Quite obvious puzzles, but here and there you might have to think. Also, there's a good balance between watching dialogues (that you can alter; really fun) and getting to play yourself.
ART: I honestly love the art of this game. The game often presents itself in a white/black-ish style, which I guess is quite logical regarding the subjects of this game. Now and then, there's also some colour to be found which emphasizes certain items/events in the game. There are some areas that could've been made better, but the most important areas in the game look really good, so no problem.
SOUNDTRACK: Just absolutely fantastic. Really makes the game a much better experience. The music changes from pretty calm, to eerie, to sometimes even agressive ... all depending on the situation you find yourself in. Also, pretty cool  (and eerie!) sounds/noises are used, like cracking stairs and doors, screaming women, the typical jumpscare sounds you'll fall victim to everytime (or maybe the total opposite).
ATMOSPHERE: By far the most amazing thing about this game. Nothing much to say about it, you really just have to play it yourself to feel it.
So yeah, really good game. Love it a lot, despite not expecting it would be this good. Again, not for everyone, but if you want to give this game a fair chance and open yourself up to it, you'll find yourself dragged into this game and just want to keep playing. At the end credits, you'll just find yourself staring at the screen, asking yourself what the ♥♥♥♥ you have been playing (and most of all; why you enjoyed it so much).
P.S: some people have unanswered questions after playing the game. Apperently playing "downfall" would answer some of these questions (though I can't confirm as I have not played it myself).

What a little gem of a game... "This War of Mine" is a 2D survival simulator, that depicts the lives of a small group of civilians in the ruins of a city, torn apart by war. You will start the game with your characters taking shelter in a decrepit building, and will, right from the start, have to address security issues, fight hunger, cold and psycologic depression. Your characters will need to scavenge around the city for food and useful materials, during the night. During the day, they will need to use these materials to improve their shelter, patch up holes in the walls, build some basic furniture, cook food, burn wood for warmth etc...
Survival will be a brutal business, and you will be faced with harsh moral dilemmas. A helpless child turns up at your door, in a cold winter morning, asking medicine for his sick mother? You take pitty of the child, give him the last of your medicine... BUT... remember that character of yours, who caught a nasty flu a few days ago (because you had no more fuel for heating...)? Now his chances of surviving the winter have become very slim. His sickness quickly becomes debilitating, and he is forced to stay in bed. The other 2 characters have to do everything they can to keep him alive. They pass many sleepless nights, scavenging around, desperate for food and medicine. Very soon, they become depressed and, one morning, one of them simply disappears. He has had enough, could not take it anymore, and  decided to abandon the shelter. Now you are left with just two characters, one of them severely depresssed, and the other one sick, forced to bed. Very soon, the depressed guy commits suicide. The lone survivor also meets a miserable death a few days later, sick, hungry and depressed. Game over.
This is just one of the possible scenarios, a grim and sad one. There are many others. If you are efficient, if you pay attention to each character's strenghts and needs, and if you make the right decisions, there wiil be hope. The game offers you the possibility to play with a variety of characters, in a variety of settings, with different starting conditions. So, a fair number of different playthroughs is possible.
Combine all these decent gameplay features with some beautiful 2D art and some haunting, atmospheric music and you get yourself a trully unique experience, unlike anything else you have played until this day. This title will really make you realise what a privilige it is to enjoy freedom in real life, have food on your table everyday, have free time and money to enjoy your hobbies (like gaming for example). But it will also teach you that there is always  hope, even in the most desperate situations. And that people need not only food and shelter to survive, but also solidarity, kind words and support from other human beings.
Tldr: "This War of Mine" has been one of the most memorable experiences in my (long) gaming life, and I recommend it without reservations.

Considering the fact that I suck at stealth games, you should probably take what I say below with a grain of salt.
Pros: Visuals and gameplay. When playing the game, I found myself really enjoying the movements and the design of almost everything. The graphics are beautiful (and I have never been so fascinated by the hand movements of a character in my entire life until I played this game....). As for the gameplay: again, it's a stealth game so confrontation with enemies are not recommended or encouraged and, while the option is available, the tools and abilites you're provided within the game support this. One of the better reviews for this game points out the limited range of weapons/tools you're given to use, and makes a good point that that makes it difficult to kill someone when you're discovered via beating them to death with a blackjack (I honestly laughed out loud when I read that section of the review). And adding to that (or would this be pointing against?), you have to remember that you're a thief not an assassin, the limited range of weapons you have support stealth and distraction. Plus you have a number of actions to do when caught: attempt to run and hide (with varying results) or beat the crap out of the guard with the risk of catching the attention of others (if there are any). Also, the only way you'd possibly kill someone in this game is if you've missed the takedown option while you were beating them within an inch of their life, you're shooting arrows at them, or setting nearby things on fire (I don't know if piling their unconscious bodies on top of each other count, but the loud cracking sounds they make when you do makes me wonder...)
Cons: Storyline and characters development and narration are okay. Could it be better? Probably (but you probably know something's wrong when you're more heartbroken about Jenivere the bird than that one girl you're trying to save). While traveling the city, you're still liable to be lost and confused even while using the map, because it's that useless unless you're tracking an objective or you remember the general places of things (but then that's what online guides are for I guess). I've edited this from my original review - it had been a borderline thumbs-down and on completion of my last game, I realised I couldn't stand by my original verdict as the logic I'd used to say no was that I couldn't recommend it in good conscience, due to the number of issues it has... which is false. I can, and I do.
HOWEVER - I wouldn't consider this title to be worth it without the Rising Tide pack. The base game is still pretty good but is lacking in multiple areas and not really worth the money - worse than Civ V prior to Gods and Kings.
.
If you're like me and always felt the Civ formula doesn't really make sense in a historical context but really enjoy sci-fi, then this should scratch that itch. It's very much the black sheep of the Civ franchise - people complain about *everything* in this title, and tend to ignore how many things it does well. The Affinity system in particular - giving you the option of charting humanity's future in the stars along 3 distinct paths (essentially change humanity into mutants, cyborgs or XCOM) and the expansion-added sub-affinities (which sit between these) allows you to do some crazy things, with everything from War of the Worlds-esque robots, anime-style battlemechs, hovering battleships and goddamn Kaiju from Pacific Rim at your disposal. The tech web looks impenetrable to begin with, but actually gives you far more customisation for your sciences. The only aspect I felt was originally lacking altogether was diplomacy, which the Rising Tide expansion fixes admirably (and throws in submarines, gunboats and floating cities to boot).
Graphically, it uses the Civ V engine to great effect and brings the typical Firaxis gloss - interesting cutscenes, excellent art and epic music. There's still a few bugs here and there even this long after release but I haven't seen anything game breaking during any of my runs.
Much of what triggered my previous negative review is still valid - the game feels like it staggers between too easy and too hard, and it's often a matter of luck when things work out. However, I think we'd be kidding ourselves to pretend these kind of epic 4X games always get this right... and this one gets more stuff right then wrong, with a lot of panache to boot. Honestly, it's my fave title of the series.

I don't think a game has ever made me feel so conflicted on its value.
I'm not sure I can justify spending money on this game. Even $1 seems like a high asking price. The game has beautiful art, relaxing music, and the writing is amusing or even heartwarming at times. The way the game maintains continuity over a single playthrough is nothing new for video games, but in a "board game" it might lend it a small air of novelty.
But, frankly, there's almost no gameplay. It's pretty much a very short, interactive, multiplayer visual novel. A match will last around 8-10 minutes per player. There are 6 turns, and they amount to picking one of eight locations, then making two binary choices at each of these locations to somewhat randomly gain or lose stat points. These points will affect how successful you are at succeeding the second binary choice each turn, depending on what, precisely, the choice is. With a very small number of art assets and almost no gameplay, the game survives entirely on its writing. At a maximum of 40 minutes per game and low variety per playthrough, you are unfortunately likely to get more value out of riffing on a movie with friends than The Yawhg.
I really want to recommend this game, but its brevity and shallowness just keep me from being able to justify saying anyone should spend money on it. The experience was enjoyable, but there's just not enough there.

is a series of comic cutscenes unfolding the story, interwoven with parts of an actual gameplay. Frederic Chopin (1810-1849, a great Polish composer and pianist) suddenly appears in the modern times to fight duels with musicians of different genres.
It is a rhythm game - notes dropping to the seven-key piano-like keyboard prompt a player to press a corresponding key - that's all. What does not seem specially interesting in the writing, proves a great challenge and a rewarding and fun experience, due to the quality of audio presentation and elegant simplicity of the game.
The story is nothing to write home about - it is a mere excuse for another musical clash.
The game is a comic story sparkling with the music inlaids. Graphical layout is polished and competent; yet it never is anything more than just a introduction for musical fight and you will rather skip it after watching it once. Fortunately skipping with
key is easy.
The core of the game are compositions of Chopin, reworked for the game. The main theme of the great works is still there, but a beat line and a stylization towards a particular music genre, makes the whole fresh and enjoyable. The music is fantastic and the tunes stay in the head for long after the games has finished. And there is always room for improvement as there are 4 difficulty levels.

, if you find yourself even remotely interested in metroidvania-type games.
Colors, backgrounds, character sprites, animations and music: everything flawlessly blends into a stunningly atmospheric and coherent 2D game world. Seriously, Momodora knows its aesthetics. I absolutely loved this aspect of the game!
You won't find a ton of useless items, spells or use one of many gazillion button input combos. Nope. You've got your basic melee 3-hit combo, a chargeable bow, 3 active and 2 passive items. Combat works and feels just right!
Movement is also tight and responsive: running, jumping, rolling and dashing through the world is a real pleasure!

Weirdly enough it gets a lot easier towards the end since you find tons of HP upgrades and more powerful items. Looking back I'd recommend starting out on Hard.

The Order of the Thorne: The King's challenge is a fun traditional adventure game. With it's beautiful art, a freely explorable world and a charming fairy tale setting, it evokes the spirit of the King's Quest games. The game is a lot more playable than those classics though. There are no deaths or dead-ends, and the puzzles are all fair and logical. The music puzzles are a nice touch and not too difficult.
I love exploration in adventure games, and this game really delivers in this regard, with many interesting places to visit and characters to talk to. Almost the whole map is accessible from the beginning, giving you a very non-linear feeling. It quickly gets more linear as the player gets a clearer picture of what he must do and in which order the puzzles have to be solved. Still it never feels forced.
The story is also very reminiscent of King's Quest, and that is probably the only real weakness, because it is as simple and straightforward as it possibly gets. The intro explains the quest, then you go out, explore, chat and solve puzzles in order to fulfil your quest. Dialogues and and a few books give you an insight into the backstory, but as far as the main quest goes, there's not much else. The story does get a lot more interesting later, but this is also when the game ends. Though with this exposition, I have high hopes for the sequels.
In short, this is a beautiful and calm introduction to the series that leaves you wanting for more. It's well worth the price, and if the planned sequels deliver a little more in terms of story and character depth, the whole series could become a masterpiece.

This is really a delightful game in the tradition of classic adventure games.  If you're familiar with the King's Quest series you'll even notice some direct allusions and homages.
The graphics imitate that classic style and the music, voice acting and dialogue are all very good (lots of Scots voice actors).  I did turn off the narrator though, I couldn't handle someone slowly reading the description whenever I clicked on anything.
In terms of weak points, the game is on the short side and the puzzles are pretty easy (I finished the game in 3.5 hours). Speaking of puzzles (most of which are inventory based), the designers did a good job of giving clues and letting you know when you were on the right track but hadn't quite gotten it right.
One more inventive aspect of the game is that, playing as Finn the bard, you have a lute and can play a number of songs (you learn more as the game progresses--this part is a lot like Loom).  Playing the right song in the right situation is often necessry to progress.  But going back and experimenting, I noticed that trying out songs in different places can spark interesting interactions I missed the first time around and even help you perform one or two additional good deeds.  So there are a few secrets to uncover that lend the game a little replay value.

In almost every way that matters, this game is a thoroughly charming, and extremely well executed point and click adventure game  that could easily play ball with the old school Sierra/Lucas Arts franchises.
The art is clearly inspired by the era, and is masterfully done.  My limited review here wouldn't do it justice, but it really was very well done.
The play style functions intuitively for the novice and will be very familiar to fans of the genre. (Save save save!).
The story was fun.  It was certainly characteristic of the genre, perhaps even a little canned, but I  truly didn't mind.  I would have preferred it it to be a bit longer though.
Lastly, and perhaps most importantly, it is clear that the design team thoroughly tested the game, which I found to be completely free of any bug that would crash the game.  The team took the testing a step further and made sure that there were no logical dead-ends either.  I'm sure there's an official name for it, but basically where you advance to a point in the plot without obtaining something, and then can't proceed without reverting back to an earlier save/start. (KQ5 and the cat chasing the mouse still makes me grind my teeth.)
I am thrilled that the point-and-click adventure game market seems to be picking back up after what seems like an eternity.  I really thought I'd seen the last of this sort of game until just a few years ago.  If you're a fan, there's a whole community of sites out there devoted to this type of game. Just like any other genre it is not without its fluff or repetition.
This game isn't fluff, and I enjoyed it beginning to end.  If you're a fan of the genre you will like this game.

This game is great. I'll start by telling what I don't like about it first. After playing Dark Souls some of the animations in this game, especially the jumping, looks a bit arcade-y and unrealistic. Apparently they used mocap for this game too according to credits. Not sure what went wrong there. Another thing I don't like is that the progression at start is difficult. You suck at everything eventhough you were also the hero of the first game and being stripped off all your abilities doesn't make any sense. Leveling in this game works like this: You kill things, you level up but you can also buy skills with gold that you can use after leveling up. But in order to get gold faster you need to level up Cunning for example which also needs gold. So, at start progression is kinda slow and everything kicks your♥♥♥♥♥ Thankfully, most of the time you can rely on your companions who can draw aggro while you beat on enemies. Companions cannot die. NPCs pathfinding isn't great. They can get lost, so you need to keep an eye on them when they are following you. Saving and reloading doesn't work. You need to retrace your steps to find them. If you fast travel or force the game to reload an area by jumping in deep water for example, your companion(s) will reappear.
The music in this game is outstanding. I love it. It's really fitting too. Totally makes you feel like a pirate in a tropical land filled with natives. The graphics are nice. I installed a mod called AntiWarp. It gets rid off a weird visual glitch where foliage expands as you get close to them. It's kinda funny but immersion breaking. The lighting is really pretty. Lots of godrays. Caves are dark and they feel atmospheric as the whole game do. Enemies are varied. For combat you have several choices. Melee (swords), ranged (guns, rifles, shotguns etc. or spears, throwing knives etc.) and voodoo. I haven't used any voodoo in my play time but as far as I could understand it lets you debuff your enemies or buff yourself. There is also stuff like possessing enemies or make them do what you want. There are intimidate/silver tongue/pickpocket skills that you can use during conversations. The story is also fine.
I found voice acting to be really good in English version. I can't say anything about other languages. There is lots to talk about with NPCs and it's usually funny. The level design is really good. If you enjoy exploring every nook and cranny in RPGs, this is your kind of game. You can use your map in every area once you get a map of the area to fast travel to key points on islands once you discover them. There is booty everywhere. Literally. There are secret treasure maps with which you can track down riches and dig them up. I find this mechanic really fun. It reminds me of the Fable: The Lost Chapters. There is no real sailing. You get cutscenes travelling between islands. Don't expect Assassin's Creed Black Flag levels of sailing here. To be honest I'm glad. I found travelling like that tedious in that game. NPCs feel alive. They usually have things to say when you do something or something happens to their friend etc. For example
The amount of detail that they got into while designing quests, NPC dialogues is really something.
Guns are busted in this game. Really overpowered. I leveled them up to 4 but they still were totally viable in the last boss battle. Yes, there are some boss battles in the game. Swordfighting becomes fun when you learn to parry and riposte. Combat takes some getting used to. Btw, aiming with controller sucks. I had to use keyboard and mouse during a couple of boss battles because you need the mouse precision. You flick the analog stick just a little but the aim flies off to lord knows where. Other than that controller works nicely for this game. Before I give my thumbs up, I suggest you save often. Seriously. Because you might want to reload a quest after failing it or doing something out of the intended order and ♥♥♥♥ing up your game is possible.
I realized I didn't even talk about your crew and the DLC. In short your crew is awesome. You get them throughout the game. You can use them as companions and the DLC is worth it. There might still be some things I intended to talk about but I forgot. This game is chock full of content.

Great version of magic.  Plays true to the mechanics, "the stack" and control of what lands to tap etc... Fully customizable decks.
My background: I come from the early days of magic were we all cursed the "Balance"  and the land destruction decks and designed decks  to excel on 2-3 lands
Playing totally free to play, slow to gain cards but not frustratingly slow. Large enough card pool so you feel their is always something to try or to shoot for.  Can play the AI for high win rate and decent coin or go at humans for bigger payoff and a peek at what a bigger card pool might allow you to do.  Both fun.  First rate tutorial with a coin payoff too.
Not all the cards from the paper version are in the sets but this might be bacause of the special rules.  The special rules are that deck may have 4 copies of any given  common, 3 of uncommons, 2 of rares and 1 of legendaries and mythics (planes walkers)  This adds more diversity to decks and more splash cards which I think gives decks more flavor.  Magic min maxers may not like it but within the format you can still min max considering these rules.  Overall I think the rarety restrictions are good.  They for some diversity and the card set is big enough that there are usualy two or 3 cards with similar enough characteristics to compensate.
General Magic changes for old schoolers:
Despite some minor changes to the stack rules the game plays like the game we know from the prestack (and early stack) days of magic.  Its much more creature focused and the efficiancy of creatures power for the cost is increased. For example 2 mana (one color one colorless) can get you a 2/2 with a special ability now.  3 mana creatures have some awesome effects by old days standards.
Generally speaking there seems to be more "bombs" in the game now.   Cards that force you to deal with them or suffer a quick death.  Kind of like the early days with Erhnams and Juzams plopping down on you early game... but the whole format has that power level of creature so in that sense its balanced.
Planeswalkers are a somewhat annoying version of this (at least when you first see them)  since they essentially provide you a life buffer (kind of)/ immediate effect and are immune to most removal.  They tend to dominate when in play and take a way form the classic feel of Magic but ultimatly are better balanced once you gain enough cards in your set to deal with them..and have them on your side!
The lack of color protection and color hosers is very disappionting.  So simplistic burn decks can do well with no CoP red or Karma to punish the "noobs" playing mono red or black lol.  That said control is still alive just looks a little different.  Black is a more viable control color now with its less restricted creature removal.
Maddness is the only new mechanic I dont really like, just has no real flavor and makes self discard effects more abusable.  Delirium too is kind of unflavorful.  They seem to be high on using the graveyard as a resource for all colors; thats really blacks domain and  maybe spashes in the other colors, but its just too much for my tastes.
Also considering the power level of the creatures in the format its surprising that counterspells are still "punished" to cost more that 2U... but most have some other effect (such as castible via maddness or something like that)  as a partial compensation.
There is a new "color" called colorless (different than the traditional colorless meaning any color) its seems entirly unnecessary to me but seems to part of some Pacific Rim movie inspired "monsters attacking" theme that emerged at some point.
There are a lot more counters and cards dependant on different conditions now.  I cant imagine playing the paper game having to count xyz card types from the graveyard and keep track of tons of tokens and +1/+1 counters all the time.  The original game was easily palyable with just the cards, life total was the only real extra you needed to track (barring a few rare exceptions)   Luckly the computer format does all the calculating for you and keeps it fun.
All in all a great game.  For those from back in the early days of Magic I say its the same great game just expect to see A LOT more utility out of your creatures than you may have been used to in the past.

My graphics card had decided to die on me and as I was waiting for my new one to come in the mail I decided to get my gaming fix from a little game called "The Cat Lady".  I like cats, and I joke about becoming a cat lady one day.  It was supposed to be strange and dark which i'm never opposed to, and the graphics were at the level I needed them to be so I figured why not?  What started out as a half-joke became one of the best gaming experiences i've ever had.
If you are used to high end graphics you might initially be put off by the visuals of the game, but trust me when I say you will get over that very quickly.  I, in fact, became fond of the dark 2D visuals.  The voice acting was of a quality that is difficult to find in even blockbuster games; very believable and genuine.  I was honestly impressed with the way they were able to make these characters come to life and provide authenticity to the story.
The soundtrack was immersive and lulled you into the events appropriately.  It was never jarring or detracted from the experience, but in fact enhanced it (i'm one of those gamers who is sensitive to soundtracks, the music chosen for a game is very important to me to fully realize the experience so this is a big plus).
The gameplay involved the expected puzzle solving sequences and other tasks (like performing investigative jobs, eliminating subjects and completing day-to-day activities), but it also involved a lot of decision making, often relating to some very powerful subject matter.  Life, death, depression, abuse, suicide, and more.  I found myself completely wrapped up with the impactful dialogue and accompanying visuals, this was truly the highlight of the game.  Although it was satisfying to take out the "parasites" in this game, I was much more concerned with the welfare and communications of the main protagonists, and very curious about the introduced supporting characters.
You will care about Susan and Mitzi.  You will actually want these 2D images to survive, to get stronger, to get better.  You will wonder who Joe Davis is and what his story and motivations are.  You will want to adopt a cat.  Most importantly, you will be given some powerful insight into the nature of depression and how isolating it can be.  It truly is a very unique experience.  Highly recommended, even to the most hardened headshot-junkie gamer.

Some people say that this FPS (with a tactical RTS element for one player per side) has no story. So I've added my own story and it's true, storyline makes a huge difference. Since I added a story, this game has become much more fun. If you find you need a storyline for this game, feel free to use mine. Here is the story: The red side hates the blue side, because the blue side wins at everything. This war has no end in sight, because red will never give up until they win, but blue refuses to lose. With each loss, red gets a little better and the next battle is a little closer... Will red ever win?
This story has added hours of replay value to my game.
Gameplay:
Each side has four classes, each with 2 or more weapon loadouts
-Stealth: hides so he can shank, sabotage or snipe you. Huh, all "S" for stealth.
-Exo/Heavy/Demo: a tank with legs, he fire missiles or rivers of bullets.
-Vanilla: He's great at running, so he can get to the combat and die faster.
-The Handyman: Part doctor, part mechanic, he can probably resurrect your dog too. Also has the BBQ mode, where he wields a flamethrower.
Commanders:
Each side has a commander and this is what sets this apart from other games of this type. The commander manages all the RTS elements. He must build spawn points, power stations, resupply points, artillery and of course, turrets. Lots and lots of turrets. Heavies will kill them, stealth will slip past and handymen fix yours while vanilla runs around and gets eaten. To counter this, the commander can build a special station that allows them three godlike powers. The smiting power, where enemies within a small circle all die, a circle of life power, where your minions heal within a small circle and the "I'll help you out" power, where enemies are poisoned within a small circle. They don't die, they're just weaker for your minions to kill.
Overall, great game. I'd buy it for $15.

As a fair warning, others are saying this game is too much like Civ V to justify getting both. I did not get Civ V, so I don't feel like I was cheated.
The premise in SMC:BE is interesting, being in space in the near future, and it offers a different aesthetic from traditional Civ. It also does not advance through historical ages the way that the traditional series does, which can be a good or a bad thing: good because it's a new play-style; bad because that's what kept other Civ games interesting. In place of historical ages, the society that you play advances towards three different futuristic "affinities": either superhuman, robotic, or alien-hybrid (or a mix of all three).
Diplomacy is somewhat lacking, but let's face it: there's yet to be a 4x game with perfect diplomacy AI (leave comments if you know the best ones out there!). All in all, this game is fun to play, there are multiple different play styles (different maps), and various victory modes for return-play. Definitely worth checking out if you didn't get Civ V.

The issue I have with this game is not necessarily the length of gameplay - short playthroughs can be fine in theory.
The Yawhg throws you in with little to no introduction, with no context and then asks you to make more or less binary choices. I don't think I'm equipped to choose as a person living in this world would. It's not roleplaying, because I don't know which role I'm playing. Consequences to these choices are often bizarre and do not create what I'd call a coherent consistent world that's reacting to my actions - simple hunting trip may leave you a crazed mass murderer, while pushing a nobleman does nothing but reward you.
It's possible these play out differently based on your stats, but the game is simply too short to learn any kind of consistent expectation pattern.
In the end, it's all just random and it doesn't matter what you pick, you just do. I didn't feel needed, like the game could just go on for the few minutes and show me the results just the same.
I couldn't care less about the people of the town, if they rebuild after the storm or anything else - there's no time and no plot that would make me attached to anything.
The visuals are nice, the music is pleasant. The controls and UI are TERRIBLE! (no options and I can't use the mouse?! What.)
I don't even feel like spending another five minutes on another playthrough, it's just...not worth it. (which is awful, considering how much time I waste in general.)

The Yawhg's main draw is the art and stories of Emily Carroll.  I liked her comics and so bought the game, but was honestly disappointed.  The 'game' is nothing more than a collection of Carroll's stories told in a branching narrative fashion.  The game functions by having you choose what each character is doing each week but results are unpredictable and seem arbitrary.  Each game of The Yawhg is very short, not allowing for any sense of attachment to develop with the characters you're controlling.  Ultimately, you're just clicking around to see what pops out next.   While I love the artwork and scenarios that occured, I can't help but feel this really should have just been a series of webcomics rather than a video game.  Overall it left me wanting.

First, I'd like to give a bit of background on this genre for credibility's sake. I've played:
Suffice it to say I have an idea of how these sorts of games are meant to be played, and what may or may not work in them.
Onto the review thus far!
That's the short of it so far, but for a more detailed review continue reading!
Visually, I'm loving the art style! It very much reminds me of Dawngate's or a slightly higher poly, more detailed League. The animations aren't all perfect but for the most part they fit their purpose and the theme of the character. The UI is clear, simple, and out of the way of the action - the ability icons even lower themselves to show that they are on cooldown, which is nice so you don't have to look at the time remaining, you sort of just see it in your peripheral.
Telegraphing indicators are easy to see for impact and effect zones, and most animations of the Champs themselves clearly present what action they are doing or will do after a delay. These are extremely important details in a game with so many skills being thrown out constantly where you want to allow players to react. Effects' names are also presented above the health bar just in-case, for whatever reason, you can't tell what someone is inflicted with or protected by, but it's usually not required. The visual effects of each CC stand out unto their own and are easy to recognize at a glance. In other words: you most likely will not confuse Petrify for a Stun or Snare.
Mechanically, I love that they did away with mana or any other sort of boring resource gating on your most basic abilities. The charge resource they do have is earned by dealing damage and landing other abilities rather than freely generated, making it feel both more rewarding and fair when someone gets to use their ult (think Overwatch in this regard). It's also used for the R which is usually some sort of high-impact utility spell, and EX abilities which are alternate versions of either LMB, RMB, Q, or E. (Champs have 2 EX abilities). So it's not a one-off mechanic, which is great!
I have also enjoyed every character I've played thus far, for a few reasons. First off I love that each character has so many abilities, and that each kit has it's own unique form of self-synergy. At the same time there is a sort of uniformity in how the kits are put to their keys, which makes picking up a new character fairly easy at the most basic level of performance. For the most part your LMB is going to be the equivalent of an Auto Attack in other MOBA (though signifcantly more unique in most cases), your RMB is usually a line shot, and Space is almost always a mobility button. The Q, E, R, and F abilities probably have the most freedom in what they do, but even so I've never felt lost looking at a kit so far.
Customization of a character has been extremely enjoyable for me. Coming from League's Mastery trees, Runes, and now it's new Rune System It was nice to get a hold of loadout system where my choices actually have very character-specific changes rather than universally applicable generic stats and effects. It reminds me of the talent tree effects in Heroes of the Storm, and now Dota 2. However, the difference is that these effects are chosen statically before a game rather than dynamically during, and you choose 5 from a varying sized list per character. A cool example of what these effects can do would be one for Thorn where you can pick an augmentation for his pull, where after it's completed you can then recast to spin-move on enemies for more damage, and/or you can pick the utility option to root them after the pull as well. There are admittedly a few stat-stick options where you just get a % increase on X or a +25 on Y sort of deal, but that can all change.
Finally, my absolute favorite thing about this game is simply that it is basically the amazing teamfights of other MOBAS minus the filler crap of farming, tower defense, and phases. It is pure adrenaline, action packed, in-your-♥♥♥♥ing-face fun in about a third of the time of the alternatives. The only thing I might add is different objectives other than Orbs to contest based on the map.
