NOTE: This is a very big "IF" recommendation.
This game is made by a greedy company that only cares about getting money. Wether the developpers of the game care or not, they are probably forced into decisions that realllly encourage paying.
That is, if you actually plan on playing the game efficiently.
This game is simple, unless you're going into high level end game raids with people, that is the only time I can think where this game gets complexe and requires actual planning.
Until then, most of the game is litteraly just pressing a single OP power button and watching a screen full of enemies dying with massive numbers showing up on screen?
So WHY would I recommend this game?
Because somehow, MapleStory makes that sensless room clearing one shotting grinding for days entertaining to watch.
Its not complex, its not complicated, pick the weapon with the highest stats, apply all your buff/debuffs, then just spam away with that one attack that fills the whole screen with pretty explosions and lights and make you feel somehow like you're REALLY powerful, way over the top, and just sit back and enjoy the fireworks.
That's really all you do, and when you reach the job advancements, you suddenly get even cooler looking and prettier powers to enjoy.
And now they have a 5th job advancements with even BIGGER and PRETTIER attacks to use.
Their are so many choices, all the classes, all the different job advancements, just choose what looks the coolest to you, find the nearest NPC that tells you where to go to kill 100 enemies or collect 100 items of one type, go there, and just watch and have fun seeing massive numbers pop up.
But if none of that sounds fun, if you're looking for a well polished, super complex RPG, you wont like this game for the first 100 levels or more.
I've heard that the end game raids can be tough and require a planned out raid party, no idea if its true, I never got that far. But the time it takes to reach that level isn't as bad as it looks since this game loves its level up events where you get like 3 levels per level up, slicing the time it takes to 1/3 of the ammount. Either way, it still takes a bit though.
And in the end, the game still isn't as complex as some other MMORPG, I'm not an expert but I've heard better from other MMORPG games, so look elsewhere for super in depth and interesting MMORPG games.
But if you're looking for some time to kill, to just sit back and watch things die as you watch some stream or youtube video or you're just waiting for something to be done, this game does a surprisingly good job, for free. All the in game purchases are usually for people who want to level faster or who want to get end game stuff quicker or reaaaallly max out their characters but, if you're just trying to kill time, this game does an amazing job at entertaining you for a few hours before you move on with your life.
I'll never take this game seriously, but if I'm ever bored and got nothing to do, this game is always one of my go to picks for killing time and simply having a casual fun time with the game.
Once again, no idea exactly how complex this game gets at the higher levels, I'm sure it does get "better" later on as any hardcore maplestory player might say. But until you get to that point, it all depends on how much you enjoy watching hundred of enemies fall to that massive screen filling energy blast you just used.

With labyrinth-esque dungeons, deadly traps, and hordes of enemies all skinned with a stylized 16-bit retro flair, Hammerwatch presents near endless hack-and-slash rogue-like action for up to four players to enjoy together. Reminiscent of old classics such as Gauntlet, players are thrown into the bowels of Castle Hammerwatch as one of six playable classes, and must proceed through four Acts of increasing difficulty as they struggle to ascend to the top of the castle and find what treasure awaits them; fighting off seemingly endless enemies and four blood-thirsty bosses as they do.
Each class in the game has its own unique traits and abilities along with upgrade paths available for purchase from hidden merchants throughout the various dungeons. Of these classes, the Thief is the one I frequent the most. With high mobility and a wide attack range from his dual wielded daggers, the thief is all about getting in and out dangerous situations while cutting down swathes of enemies with his blisteringly high attack speed. As for skills, the Thief starts out with Fan of Knives, which upon activation throws multiple knives in an arc in front of him, damaging and piercing through multiple enemies. His two other unlockable skills are Grappling Hook and Smoke Bombs, the first of which can be used to hook any nearby wall and then quickly pull you towards it, stunning foes in the process; while the latter acts as a large area of effect (AoE) stun. A unique feature that only applies to the Thief however is that while all his skills cost significantly less mana than the other classes, they also have a secondary cost of gold, which partially balanced by his passive ability to steal gold off the corpses of slain enemies. In addition to the Thief, the other five playable classes available at this moment are the Paladin, squaring off behind his towering shield, the Ranger, which focuses on ranged attacks with his bow and wave clearing bombs, the fireball casting Wizard, the treacherous Warlock, wielding a poisoned dagger and blood magic, and lastly the Priest, who you guessed it, has a knack for healing teammates.
A feature that really adds to the depth and replayability of Hammerwatch is it’s accessibility to being modded. This means custom campaigns, custom game types, new enemies, and hell, I’ve even seen prototypes for brand new playable classes on the forums. When the game first came out, it was all about downloading custom files and then manually adding them to the correct file folder the game’s directory for the mod to be installed correctly, but recently this all changed when the game finally got full Steam Workshop support, nearly a year after its initial release. This gives a huge new audience access to the piles of custom campaigns already out there, as well as inspire new modders to create even more content for that larger audience. In addition to its accessibility to installing and using mods, Hammerwatch also comes packaged with its own custom Level Editor/Development Program. With this tool you can do anything from drag and drop existing resources onto your workspace and make your own custom dungeons to even going as far as scripting and uploading your own custom resources. While the level editor program has a ton to it and can be rather intimidating to get into and start working in it, there are multiple Youtube video tutorials on the subject which will walk you through at least the basics.
Although at its core, Hammerwatch is a retro hack-n-slash dungeon crawler, the base difficulty and default settings give a very rouge-like feel to the game as well. The players have a set amount of lives shared among them and once you run out, your progress is lost; and on top of that, even on normal difficulty, the game can be incredibly dangerous and difficult, with most traps and some enemies being able to kill you in just a single hit. And even though I happen to find enjoyment in getting dismembered time after time and then drowning in my own pity and incompetence at the game, others who have issues with the initial difficulty of the game can give themselves handicaps such as having infinite lives in the game settings to get rid of these rouge-like elements.
With more than 25 hours logged in on it already and more to come once I gather my old group together to tackle some of the new Workshop content, I can say it’s been more than worth the low price point, and even more so if bought on Steam Sale. So if you’re into any game with high difficulty, looking for a game with some great nostalgic vibes, or just an enjoyable easy to get into Co-op game to play with some friends on your day off, then I highly recommend looking at Hammerwatch.

Have you played Nethack? How about Crawl, or SLASH'em? Have you made fun of them behind their backs, and then smiled politely when you saw them walk by on the street?
This will be the Roguelike for you. It contains tons of classic elements -- the randomly designed levels, the urge to kill you approximately constantly, and difficult layouts -- and then lampoons as much as it can along the way. You'll get monsters yelling at you, incredibly useless-seeming items, abilities that may or may not help you at any point, and a hearty congratulations upon your eventual death.
Luckily, for those of you not as adept with the concept of 'Permadeath' (think hardcore mode in ol' Diablo 2 -- die, and your character is gone permanently) the game does offer a mode on each difficulty level that removes the permadeath in lieu of saving when you need it. But, then again, I'm a purist.
For the genre faithful, this game offers plenty of challenge. For the new, it can be a fun, if wildly difficult, romp.

I want to point out that over the years I’ve gotten to know Steven Alexander and pretty much everyone at Infamous Quests pretty well and they’re always willing to listen and talk to their fans, going so far as to take any feedback to heart and improve upon each game that they release. And this one is no different. So far they’ve delivered on the promise of a fun retro style adventure game set in a beautiful pixelated world with well crafted puzzles and an engaging storyline. While still a bit on the short side, especially for those used to playing games of this type, The King’s Challenge is a polished game and perfectly sets the stage for the next installment.

Solid little game!
As a fan of old school point-and-click adventure games I was very excited for this release, and I have to say I did have a lot of fun with this game.
The basic plot is that you are taking part in the King's Challenge and must locate the Queen who has hidden somewhere in the Kingdom.
The controls are quite simple; only left and right click (use and examine). No text commands, but there is the lute interface which works well and is the "unique selling point" of the game, as it were. While the puzzles are easier than I've become accustomed to for this genre, they are not trivial by any means.
The art and music are beautiful and the characters and environment are really well done. Considering everything is hand-drawn pixel art, the kingdom and forest are pretty extensive. The voice acting was a really nice addition and I also appreciated having the option to skip ahead if you've read faster than them.
The game has a lot of unique touches and personality to it. While the adventure is fairly short and contained only to one setting, there is plenty of detail within which still gives the player a rich experience.
There is humour in it too; I liked the running gag where you kept bumping into the two women trying to befriend the gnome who wasn't having any of it. Really amusing.
My main gripe with the game is how "bare bones" it still felt with regards to the amount of interaction available other than that which was needed to continue the plot. This could just be that I'm used to having text commands available though, and they did the best they could with the two click system. There are also a couple of bugs (at the time of writing this) such as some conversation trees still being available when you'd already progressed past that part of the game. This was a little jarring although nothing game-breaking.
On the other hand the forest and swamp are large enough that you have a lot of area to just walk around, explore and try things out. Did I mention it's really beautiful?
Overall this was a very enjoyable game with lots of personality and a nice story, despite being quite short and small-world.
It was extremely good value for the price paid (£6.99) and I will probably get the next episodes when they come out. Would recommend to fans of the genre.

(NOTE: spoilers contained within)
First of all, I want to thank Steve for giving us the opportunity to stream an early version of OotT for our Extra Life charity event (which you can see here:
remember, early version, not all of the voices were in, and some things have been moved around in the final version).
Second, I'm the narrator and did a bit of playtesting on the game as well. Just want to put that out there so no one cries foul on me posting a review (I even bought a copy of the game, as I do for most games I record for).
That being said, I think what I like most about IQ's games is that they look one way on the surface, but you start to see the depth behind the characters/story/concepts when you have some time to think about it later on.
For example, some people complained that QFI treated women poorly, based upon some of the scantily clad female characters featured in the game. But once you actually interacted with them, it became clear that the game was mocking the archetype of the scantily clad female warrior and the games that had used it in the past. Voleris, the head of the Tyr's Arrows clad in a metal bikini, sounded entirely fed up with her lot in life. She rebuffed all of Roehm's advances, not in a "playing hard to get" manner, but in a way that suggested that she knew just how dumb it was that she was in the employ of a man that made her dress this way. She was sick of being an archetype.
Flash forward to OotT and a few things pop to mind about the way I've seen people react, and since you know I liked the game already, I'll instead say a few things about some concerns I've seen raised...
First of all, some folks have complained that the game is "too happy". Yes, the game is overall filled with characters who are content with their lot in life, but the first thing you see when you gain control of Finn are two pillars inscribed with the names of everyone who died in the last great war.
In fact, when you talk to the king, he'll tell you that the primary reason for holding the challenge is because he knows that, even in peace time, it's important to give potential champions something to strive for, to keep them vigilant. This is a peace that was obviously paid for in blood. Later in the game, you'll visit a graveyard that also reflects just how true this is (and how backing one of IQ's kickstarters is a very dangerous undertaking, heh).
So yes, the general tone of this game is one of peace and happiness, just like how the first Harry Potter had an overall light-hearted tone to it but things only got darker from there. We had to see Uir at peace to know just how much we have to lose (and the end of the game sets up some dark clouds on the horizon...).
Second, I've seen some complain that Finn (the protagonist) is "too sweet".
Right in the beginning of the game, we learn two important things about Finn: his father was a heroic bard of the Order of the Thorne who died in its service, and Finn seeks to do his father proud by following in his footsteps and becoming an amazing bard himself.
We immediately know that Finn has taken some lumps from life already, but despite this, he's still a kind, compassionate artist who wants to make life better for others (and his wish reflects this most of all). However, we see a bit of cynicism poke through from time to time, like when he talks to the snobbish jerk of a priest, Abdon, and says something to the effect of "A bard's job is to make life better for people, but I'm sure that's something YOU wouldn't understand", or when Finn was sure that Skelton was going to kill him for trying to take his treasure, even while Snowy and Red (who are by far the MOST naive characters in the game) thought there was still good in Skelton. Finn certainly knew better.
Finn is the person who has "lost his innocence", so to speak: he knows the world isn't all sunshine and rainbows, but he's not letting that drag him down to its level and turn him into an angry cynic (and I also have to add that Matt Curtis absolutely NAILED Finn's voice. Sometimes a voice just clicks with a character and that was definitely the case, here).
So that's my take on the game and some of the concerns: some things that may seem simple on their face are in actuality a great deal more complex underneath, and I hope Finn's story arc (which clearly isn't finished) involves him accomplishing the goals he set out to achieve in TKC (and no, I don't know where his story goes from here).

I was one of the kickstarter backers for this game, having played Quest for Infamy and enjoying that.  I'm not sure I would purchase Order of the Thorne again, but it is a nice little game for what it is.
First off, what this game is NOT:
People have been comparing this to both King's Quest and Quest for Glory.  I will agree with the first and disagree with the second.  The game is definitely similar to some of the later KQ games, but its lack of RPG elements, combat, etc, make it a marked difference from QFG.
The impression I got from the game's pitch also isn't quite on target.  The game was initially billed as follows -
"Our first game is about an intrepid bard who embarks on the King's Challenge to save his Queen!  Action, adventure and a touch of fairy tale magic take you away on this quest.  The King's Challenge also features fun and interesting puzzle mechanics, including the use of Finn's Lute - and a magical, music based GUI that controls spells to aid you on your quest!"
The impression I took away from their description was an adventure game possibly similar to the old Loom title crossed with a somewhat dangerous King's Quest like environment.  However, you're not actually 'saving' the Queen - you're just taking part in a contest where the Queen is playing hide and go seek and the first to find her wins.  The lute system, while somewhat interesting, was also very underplayed.  For the most part, you had to use each song exactly once, and there weren't really any puzzles designed around clever use of the lute.  It was pretty obvious when and how you'd have to use it.
NOW, all that being said.
The game is quite enjoyable, if simple.  It does hearken back to the King's Quest series with more of a simple/kiddy feel to it.  Not the sort of thing I'd normally play nowadays, and not much in the way of replay value, but it was a fun, nostalgic game to play through.
On top of that, it entranced my 3 year old son.  He loved watching as I played.  If he were a year or three older, I'd have turned him loose on this game to play himself with zero hesitation.
Summary:
Do not get this game if you are looking for:
1) Action or RPG elements such as you'd find in QFG
2) Challenging puzzles
3) A sophisticated plot and/or moral ambiguity in the story
DO get this game if you are looking for:
1) A nostalgic trip reminiscent of the KQ series
2) A simple, charming fairy-tale story
3) Rather delightful music and respectable art.
4) Something engaging to play with your children or let them play
5) A game where you don't have to worry about dying or doing something "wrong" and getting stuck.  There's always a path forward.

This is the first installment of the in-development Order of the Thorne anthology series by Quest for Infamy developer Infamous Quests. The game takes place in the Faerie Realm where the King has proposed a challenge: If anyone can find his Queen, who has hidden somewhere in their kingdom, he will grant them one wish. And so Finn the Bard takes up the challenge out of a selfless wish to help every musician far and wide.
The King's Challenge is a traditional adventure game which reminded me quite a bit of the early King's Quest games and Loom. Take my comparison to King's Quest with a pinch of salt though, as I only played a bit of the original first game at a friend's house many years ago, and the AGD Interactive remakes of the first two games are to this day the only games of the franchise I have ever completed. The reason why I also compare this game to Loom is that you get to play songs on a lute, which will sometimes have effects that are required to solve puzzles, like putting people in a certain mood.
Choosing a song on the lute will display a sequence of notes that you will then have to repeat in the correct order for the song to be played. If that sounds tedious or difficult though, you can switch between hard and and easy mode at any point in the game. The easy mode will just play the song at the press of a button, freeing up your hands to do something else in the meantime.
Most puzzles in the game are of the conventional variety though, and even though none of them are particularly hard to figure out, I found them enjoyable and they all fit well in with the theme and setting of the game. This game uses a two-button control scheme, with left-click for interaction and right-click to examine things. There are no dialogue puzzles, but you have to talk to a rich cast of characters to acquire information that you need to get through the game.
One thing I greatly appreciated about this game is that there are a lot of scenes stretching out from the huge tree housing the Royal Court, which gave me a sense of exploring a vast kingdom. But even though there is a big area to cover in search of the Queen, the scenes are connected in such a way that it never takes you long to get back to the massive tree in the middle. I also never found myself "pixel hunting" in any of the scenes, since objects of interest either stand out in their placement or are signposted through dialogue or cutscenes.
The story is well written and concise, with several nods to fairy tales and classic adventure games. There wasn't anything in the writing that really stood out to me, but I appreciate a game that delivers its story efficiently and with respect for the player's time, and this game certainly does that. There are few things I find more annoying in a game than clicking on a hot-spot for the second or third time and be forced through the same long-winded speech again, so I value it all the more when a game gives you just enough information on repeat delivery of dialogue to nudge you along in the plot and puzzle solving.
Like Infamous Quest's previous game, this one also uses the now open-source
. This means that the Linux version also has many of the limitations and issues of other games using the engine, and I've been unable to Alt+Tab out of the game or switch virtual desktops. Features like the Steam overlay and screen capture do not work, and achievements only occasionally unlock at the moment. You can launch a graphical settings panel that I don't think I've seen in any previous AGS games on Linux, which saves you the trouble of having to manually edit the acsetup.cfg file if you want to put the game in windowed mode or change graphics filters.
Overall, I greatly enjoyed The King's Challenge, and I wished I could have continued playing when it was over after three hours of play. The ending and post-credits scene allude to things to come in the next installment, Fortress of Fire, which I can now almost not wait to experience.

Star Ruler 2 is an exceptional game that puts together multiple revolutionary systems into a very unique 4X/RTS experience. Perhaps the biggest flaw with Star Ruler 2 is that its systems are so different and out of the norm that most players have a hard time grasping its mechanics.
For starters, Star Ruler 2 does away with basic money hoarding system that 95% of other 4X games do. Instead, Star Ruler 2's economy system is modeled after real life economies. Your income is based on a budget cycle representing the total purchasing power of your economy, similar to GDP. Any income you do not spend gets converted into welfare programs that boosts one of your other resources. This system forces players to consider what structures and units they wish to field and serves a softcap on players, preventing someone from running away in units or resources.
Diplomacy in Star Ruler 2 is enjoyable. Let that sink in for a moment. The diplomacy mechanic in a 4X game is enjoyable. Star Ruler 2's diplomacy is conducted by a card system, in which player spends influence points to purchase cards, which allow for certain diplomatic actions, such as the annexation of a planet of system. After playing the card, all players vote on the action in a sort of intergalactic congress. Thus, diplomacy becomes an important element in which all parties have a vested interest, creating interesting alliances and allowing for a player to be a diplomatic power.
The last major system in Star Ruler 2 is the ship design. Ships in Star Ruler 2 are constructed via a hex system. Damage is directional, and players are tasked with implementing various technologies and weapons on to their ships. This hex system allows for incredible customization in a player's military, lending way to personalized doctrines that players develop. For instance, one player may focus on building powerful capital ships while other player focuses on smaller ships with troop pods for capturing planet. Combined with the different FTL types, ship design becomes an integral part of the gameplay, with player designs dictating how wars are fought.
There are many little quirks and interesting design choices in Star Ruler 2. Because of this, the game has a very steep learning curve, as players may have to "unlearn" habits from other games. Yet, it is exactly because of all these unique systems that makes me rank Star Ruler 2 at the top of my list of 4X games.

Update: The newest nVidia Driver (384.94) has corrected the issue (at least it seems to have on my system. I have built, viewed, and used a ring world in a test game now without problem.)
I am changing the review to positive (as it no longer needs to be an attention grabber and I truly enjoy the Fork out of this game. ;)
========== Original Review Included Below for History and Refernece should anyone else need it, or wish to test that the newest driver works for them ==========
WARNING! WARNING!
If you use an nVidia graphics card that uses the Fermi chip, this game may become unplayable at the time you create a Ring World.
I've contacted the developer about the issue but have received no reply (in all fairness, this is an older game, so he may no longer be maintaining it.) I've contacted nVidia, and they are aware of the problem, and have basically told me it's not a big enough issue for them. So if you get a game crash when you build (or view) a Ring World, and you have an nVidia graphics card, call (408) 486-2300 and ask for Josh, then tell him you have the problem with Star Ruler 2 and your nVidia graphics card.
Arguably, not being able to build a Ring World can be seen as a somewhat minor issue. Especially if you don't play longer games that get to that point before being completed. However, this will also crash your game if you give your AI opponents an Privilege at creation, and they get the start with a ring world random starting advantage. Meaning you can't do that either. Also, it becomes very difficult to impossible to create enough labor in large/high diffficulty games/invassions to play to the end game/as far as possible. So for me, it feels like the game just kind of stops at the point where ringworlds become necessary.
Because of this issue, and because I haven't heard back from the developer of even an acknowledgement of this issue, I am giving this game a negative review to grab the attention of potential buyers who may not be aware of the potential game-ending bug. Which is sad, because it's a really wonderful game otherwise (especially with the Wake of the Heralds DLC) and I've racked up countless hours of enjoyment before this issue crippled my ability to play it. I fully realize this may be entirely beyond the developer's ability to correct, and I certainly hold no ill-will against him. But I cannot in good conscious not warn potential buyers of the potential problem with the game either. In fact, it is my hope that at some point the develoepr, or nVidia, will correct the issue and I'll be able to update this review. However, both the develoepr and nVidia have had this problem for nearly a month now and neitehr has shown any tangible progress towards fixing the issue and as a result, I feel it necessary to provide a heads-up to future potentiial buyers of the issue.
I have not been able to test the game extensively on a wide variety of video ccards, and many video cards may play the game without this issue. If you're unsure if this issue will impact your video card/system try creating a game with several AI opponents and give them all Privileges (when starting a game, click on the difficult for each opponent and check the box marked "Privilege") then start the game. If it doesn't crash immediately, then you most likely are ok. To double check, hit F2 and switch to each of the other empires (or enter observer mode) until find a race that started with a ringworld (it's random, not every race will receive a ring world as its Privelage). If you can see a ringworld, and zoom in/out on it, and even click it to view its planetary contents, then most likely your system does not have this bug, and you will be safe. If it crashes to your desktop immediately after the ring shows up in front of your camera, then you have the bug and may want to consider geting a refund before the 2hr/2week valve cut-off.

Risen two picks up right where Risen 1 left off and offers quite an enjoyable journey over roughly a dozen different islands. The gameworld, contrary to usual Piranha Bytes design is compartmentalized that way, which is the one main flaw in my personal opinion about Risen 2: The gameworld, while diverse and not small, all things considered, feels remarkably less epic than in prior installments. I'm also not a particular fan of the graphical art design for Risen 2, both Risen 1 and 3 did a way better job in that regard, but it gets things done.
Personally I would have wished for more armor variants, as there are none except coats and more weapon diversity, but Risen 2, although it has its share of combat, is more a bonafide roleplaying game with stories to tell and people to meet than to bash hundreds of monster heads in.

War never changes but who is telling the story does with This War of Mine, a unique game that focus on the hardships a civilian population has to go through during a conflict.
The concept of war is not new to gaming from titles that have taken player to a generation’s finest moment to the war in Afghanistan and through the eyes of Tom Clancy. However in every single one of those games the focus has been the combat and the story was always told from the perspective of the soldier. This War of Mine is a break from the typical war bravado and instead focus on the hardship of the innocent who are trapped in the crossfire.
This War of Mine instead focuses on the struggles and hardships that civilians have to overcome when trying to survive the brutality of war. Inspired by the horrors that civilians had to endure during the Siege of Sarajevo, players are responsible of managing a makeshift shelter populated by a group of civilians. Players must manage their survivors by having them strengthen the shelter while venturing out to look for supplies.
Compared to other games that focus on the struggle for survival, this presents both a strategic and emotional challenge for the player. The choices made will not only affect the shelters well being but also the characters morality while playing with one’s emotions after having made some difficult choices.

This might have been such a good game.  As a long-time fan of the Thief franchise, I really, really wanted to like it. Unfortunately, the longer I played, the more the game's faults started to irk me, up to the point that I couldn't in good conscience recommend it unless the price goes down dramatically.
Initially, my opinion was quite favourable. The game certainly looks pretty. Light effects and dynamic shadows are very realistic, and the first-person camera works better here than in almost any other game I can think of. Garrett's hands are just gorgeous and there's a strong sense of being physically present in the world. I didn't even mind the much-maligned context specific movement. Some of the missions were quite enjoyable. The story might be utterly forgettable and both the protagonist & the City have been given an unnecessary makeover (what's with the eyeshadow, Garrett?) but nevermind, it's a reboot and I can live with change... as long as the stealth gameplay itself offers the thrilling and robust experience I remember from previous Thief games.
Unfortunately, this is where the game falters. Previous reviews have pointed out the outrageous flaws in Thief's audio design so I won't go there except to say that yes, it really *is* bad. NPC awareness seems to fluctuate wildly: guards often won't react to loud noises like breaking glass and knocking stuff over, but on other times they seem to magically detect the player even when crouching well clear and in dark shadow. The game's light gem is really inconsistent and visually it's difficult to see the dark spots the designers have meant for you to hide in, as opposed to darkish-looking places that are only there for show and offer no cover whatsoever.
I played the game on Master difficulty, and about half-way through I started hoping I didn't - not because the game was too hard (it really wasn't), but because it made moving around the City hub an exercise in tedium. The City is a hopeless, frustrating mess of constricted pathways that at first promises freedom of exploration but quickly reveals itself to be just a claustrophobic maze with only few ways to pass through. There are certain choke points in the City that you end up crossing dozens of times as you track side quests and missions, and slowly sneaking around the same set of guards for the umpteenth time quickly grows old. By mid-game, I really wanted to play on an easier difficulty so I could just snipe the city guards full of arrows, or simply run past them. These choke points are made even more maddening by a terrible audio glitch that replays snippets of NPC dialogue over and over in an endless loop for as long as you stay in that area. An example:

Should you resort to blackjacking the guards to shut them up, well... bad news,  every time you go through a loading screen the guards are reset and back in action. And there's a lot of loading screens, even entering one-room random apartments often results in one.
So, moving around the City is time-consuming and frustrating, and the maps are no help at all. They're confusing, badly executed and glitchy: at one point, the minimap went crazy and reversed north, south, Garrett's direction and the location of the quest markers completely. The most frustrating thing, however, is the lack of freedom in missions and the City hub. Instead of free-form exploration and clever tactics that made the first two Thief games (and the third, to a lesser degree) so exhilaratingly immersive, the game wants you to follow pretty narrow pre-designed paths. What's worse, sometimes in missions you open a door or a window, and without warning the game will transition you to a new area... with no way back. No matter that you still had half a manor to explore and loot to grab - the designers think that the plot has moved on and so should you!
Adding insult to injury, there are several scripted points when you are detected and need to flee, following an exact path decided by the designers. Trying to be creative by attempting to climb a wrong wall or taking a wrong turn results in a quick scripted death. There are weird platform jumper sections and puzzles that are so insulting to the player's intelligence that it begs the question why they were included in the first place. Most times there simply is no way to get the puzzle wrong: you just need to press the buttons the game tells you to press, in the order that the game tells you.
Thief is not an absolute disaster of a game. I certainly enjoyed some of it. It's just an unpolished, awkward mess that tries to include every trick the designers learned from recent games like Assassin's Creed and Dishonored, while getting wrong the core experience of original Thief classics.

This game was a few ups and downs for me. It started off pretty great. I was really enjoying the idea of being a master thief. Sneaking around and being able to find my way into different places on the map. As the game went on though you learn that you obtained special powers; that if you "focus really hard" things become clearer.

This is were I had my first down. I was expecting this to just become a cop-out over the rest of the game. Giving you god-like abilities (a la Dishonored) in a situation where you seem to be just a normal guy we some practiced thieving abilities (unlike Dishonored which made the powers an integral mechanic of the game). For most of the game these powers, to my delight, did not make you god-like. You are fragile enough (without "massive upgrades") that if you don't at least attempt to stay hidden and sneak around, you WILL be punished. You certainly aren't a damage drinker like you would be in a Call of Duty game. This made for a fun play through with some good challenges in many areas. I must say though that if you're looking for the "choose your own path" approach this is where this game seems to falter again.
There are clearly places in the game at which you are funneled into a specific path. Usually at these choke points if you were playing a Ghost playthrough you are going to have a stupidly difficult time trying to pass it, when a Predator, or an Opportunist, will pass it in a matter of seconds. It feels like it's an artificial difficulty spike. If each play-style is apparently weighted the same then don't make areas that are stupidly difficult for just one of them. This of course is just my opinion. Maybe I missed something in the surroundings that could have made it easier, and so my opinions may be unfounded.
The last up and down came towards the end of the game. I was enjoying how the story was developing and how the levels were becoming longer, demanding a more thought out approach to each level. This all came to a head, though, when you reach the last story mission. Here you end up put in multiple situations in which the game is effectively linear. You have to reach ONE door, or ONE opening, to proceed (if there were more openings I must be blind because I spent forever on that last mission searching places). In a game that sold itself as you being able to choose how you get places this was a kick in the teeth. The last mission, the one where everything is supposed to come together, validate your experience, you're forced into a cookie-cutter, one-size-fits-all experience. It felt like everything I had done for the rest of the game didn't really matter. I lost any choice that I could have and that spoiled the times when I did have choice. It wasn't just the lack of choice that really spoiled the end for me, though.
The ending of the game is one of the most abrupt and least fulfilling that I've ever encountered. There are no answers to anything you may be wondering throughout the game, it just ends. Well, not before they give you a plot convienience that allows them to market you another game in the future. It seems like they just gave up and sold the game, without spending time to wrap it up. Maybe its just me but it sucked.
All in all I'd say buy the game, if its on sale. I paid $15 for it and my 23 hours of play time was worth that. I plan on finishing out some of the extra side content and that will probably round out the value of the game for me.

The Cat Lady gets an easy TWO thumb recommendation from me. It has it's minor flaws and I would not say it's for everybody but it's most definately still great.
The music is ordinary and the interface is below average at best. The art is mediocre and the animations are just plain laughable. However, rising out of this morass are a story and central character so good that you start to see this game as a glittering diamond from a dull bit of coal.
Susan Ashworth struggles with depression, isolation and is recovering from a suicide attempt.  While in a limbo/bardo state of consciousness, she meets a harbinger-of-woe type figure that warns her of coming tribulations. She returns to life to face these obstacles with a very unique power; she cannot die. The game then unfolds as she meets these adversities as she struggles with ongoing depression and the dark events that somehow plague her. Susan also eventually befriends another character, Mitzi. Mitzi has her own crosses to bear and their two destinies dramatically entwine as they share a part of each others burden.
You may think that being unable to die would make a central character seem omnipotent and render a game unchallenging but this is NOT the case. It's true that the puzzles in this game aren't particularly taxing but it's unlikely you'll play the game perfectly the first time and Susan will still suffer. Oh, she'll suffer. Likewise, you may think that a game which deals with such topics as murder, isolation, bitterness, loss, domestic disputes, sadism, addiction etc would be a downer. Again, it's NOT. This game deftly walks such a fine line.
Much of this game entails a lot of storytelling, flashbacks and lots and lots of dialogue. This, coupled with Susan's occasional forays into deathless states, results in some very non-linear story and gameplay. This is why I would warn some players off this game. Some gamers just want constant action and thrills and spills. They should avoid this one as they'll find it slow and uninteresting (it's their loss).
Ultimately, this is a game that examines some of the darkest aspects of humanity yet leaves us feeling optimistic. It tackles difficult subjects such as depression and it's ramifications hopefully and realistically. It's refreshing to play a character that's so flawed and heavily burdened. It's also rewarding to play such a character who's capable of learning and positive growth; friendship can overcome isolation and hope can trump despair. It's no wonder that so many people (those who suffer depression/isolation and those who don't) have responded to this game so positively. I am full of admiration for its creator and regard this game as something of a groundbreaking achievement.

The Cat Lady is a psychological horror/adventure game where the player takes up the mantle of Susan Ashworth-- a forty-year-old manic depressive who commits suicide only to find herself returned to life (and with immortality to boot) so that she can enact the wishes of an apparitional old woman dubbed the Queen of Maggots. Susan is tasked with finding five 'parasites' (murderers) and killing them; only THEN will she be granted death. Through the course of the game, the player learns about Susan's dark history, and is introduced to a cast of deliciously flawed and fleshed-out characters. It's a somewhat inconsistent game, but it's also one of the most memorable horror titles I've ever played-- matched only by Silent Hill 2.
+ The artwork is beautiful; dark, gritty, and wholly original. You'll often find yourself pausing and taking in everything the game has to offer. It's all very visceral and surreal.
+ The music is fitting and helps maintain a consistent tone throughout the game. Most of the soundtrack is dark and ambient, but there are a few vocalized tracks by indie musicians that are well suited to their particular cutscenes.
+ The story is engaging and refreshingly honest about adult themes.
+ The voice acting is stellar.
+ The puzzles aren't arbitrary, and they're neither too hard nor too easy to solve.
+ The protagonists are well written and tragic, and you'll be invested in their stories.
+ The controls are simple and suit the game well.
+ No two chapters have the same gameplay.
+ The endings are all appealing in one way or another, and there's high replay value.
- The writing can be juvenile at times (particularly in Chapter 5, when Susan is taking a bath, and Chapter 2, where there's some cringeworthy dialogue about depression).
- The gore approaches splatterhouse levels on some occasions, and it comes off as arbitrary.
- Everything after Chapter 4 seems a bit rushed.
- Chapter 5 feels like it was shoehorned into the game, and would be a complete throwaway if not for the section dealing with the genesis of Susan's depression.
- The voiceover recording is a bit shoddy. Mic pops and static are pervasive.

I really like Magic Duels, on a whole I think it's better than Magic 2014 and Magic 2015.
Hoever, there are two downsides:
The first downside is the lack of a chat feature. I understand why this probably is; there was a big problem with extremely rude haters in Magic 2015, for instance, where there was a chat feature, so I understand why the devs omitted it for Magic Duels. Still I feel that the lack of one in Magic Duels massively depersonalizes things in what is supposed to be a game for ladies and gentlemen.
The second downside is that the timers are way too quick. There often isn't enough time to read the cards your opponent played and to find out what exactly is going on, much less to plan a counterplay before *zzzzzzziiipp*, the timer is over, or you didn't even get a chance to stop play in the first place because the yellow circle timer for that is even more notoriously fast than the blue line timer that shows up once the play is stopped.
On the whole, great game, I especially love the cutscenes which really detail the story of the Planeswalkers in a way not seen before. They really fill in gaps in the Magic story.

Honesty time. We don't have a lot of games about depression, and we need them. And this game, despite the furor surrounding it, is a decent shot at describing depression. It's purpose is to help relate to depression, and for people who recognise the feelings to examine them.
If you came to this expecting "gameplay" or "graphics" or any other number of things which a lot of the downvotes complain about it not having, then you really should read what things are before trying them out. There's no point going to a McDonalds and then complaining that they won't sell you shoes. Depression Quest isn't trying to give you gameplay. It's trying to describe what depression is like, and so is more akin to a visual novel. While playing the game, the positive options in the story are often unavoidably closed off to you to simulate what depression does to the mind ... knowing that something would be good for you, but simply being unable to do it.
Whether it succeeds at describing depression is going to resonate differently with a lot of different people. Depression isn't one catch-all term which describes everybody's experiences with depression. This is a different kind of experience to, say, Actual Sunlight (another excellent game about depression and suicide). But the experiences described within ARE real and recognisable, and it does a decent if limited job of describing what many people can't seem to relate without massive melodramatic overtones.
There you have it. An actual review of Depression Quest, free of all the crap and hate and similar derailment. Deal with it, internet.

I wanted to check out this game and see if it stood up on its own merit, barring all the controversy around its developer. It doesn't. I've played some games similar to this style, such as the infinitely better Digital: A love story, and this one is kind of♥♥♥♥♥♥ Overall, the visual style is pretty plain. Each screen is essentially block text of black font on white backgrounds with 3 polaroids at the top showing some pictures that look like something jacked from shutterstock. The game introduces you to the depressive protagonist, a shut-in with a deadend day job and a sympathetic girlfriend, and presents you with choices on how to deal with different problems in their daily life. This could be anything from fights with said girlfriend to adopting pets. While this could potentially be interesting, the writing is pedantic and completely artless. Normally, prose is probably the last thing you would give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about in a game, or you would at least be willing to look past it. Unfortunately, this is what boils down to an interactive adventure novel, meaning looking past the garbage writing would require you to find meaning or at least enjoyment in the menu layouts. The message is delivered in a very heavy handed and completely unengaging way. Each choice event is usually 3-5 options. Of those, 1 or 2 are red and crossed out options that those of a more balanced brain chemistry would most likely choose. Obviously, the player is supposed to see these options and feel frustrated, much like how a person with depression would feel, given their inability to help themselves or make the "right" choice. Where a more talented developer would have used visual cues/environment/well-written script to make the player feel depressed, they instead decided to use a very simplisitic crutch. The truth is, I really do like these kinds of games. D:LS, Slouching Towards Bedlam, Cypher, etc. Unfortunately, this game is just really not good. To be honest, its pretty boring and nothing deserving of a download. I normally wouldn't even bother to write a review, but I felt that it was good to have some posts from people who are relatively impartial. I could care less about the politics of the developer and all the other controversy surrounding this game. I just wanted to say that Depression Quest, when judged solely on its own merit, is not worth your time.

Quick Summary: a quick mainly text game that is best played locally with 2-4 players. I reccomend it to anyone if the price range is maybe $4-6 or if it ever adds more content.
So the Yawhg is a fantasy/fairy tale game where 2-4 players play as one of 4 color themed characters. In each round of the game every player takes a turn before control passes to the next player. In each player's turn there is a particular order or structure to the turn. First the player picks a place to go and picks from one of two pre-set actions for that location. For example the player can go to the "alchemy tower" and "brew potion" or "clean lab".  (They are limited by only being able to choose where no one else has gone yet on that turn.) The game then rewards you a stat bonus for your action (usually +2 to one stat and +1 to another) and then generates a particular scenario based on that selection. You are given a choice during that scenario and the game will tell you how your choice went. The outcome of this choice is frequently dependent on your stats. For example, brewing potions give you +2 magic and +1 mind. After that the game says that the other wizards are thowing a cantrip party (cantrips are low-level easily-cast spells). After hearing what some other people do you can decide to do a "simple trick" or "complex trick". If you don't have high enough of a magic stat and choose "complex trick", you end up hurting and embarrassing yourself in the process which then causes a -2 in charm. However successfully completing the complex trick may have given you rank among your peers in the form of +2 charm. Additionally, these scenarios are interlinked and frequently someone may do something in thier turn that causes another scenario to occur in another players turn. This is seen in the demon baby excerpts from the gameplay demo above. After several round of this "the yawhg" arrives. Without going into too much detail, your stats and one final choice determine the outcome of the town in this trying time. The town's fate is delegated to one of 3 options, the best of which is easily obtainable. Then the game gives each player a personal ending which is dependent on the town's ending, the player's stats, thier last choice, how they spent their time, and what scenarios happened to them. For example if you get the good town ending and spent a lot of time doctoring there are at least two specific doctor endings. But if you also happened to encounter a supernatural creature at some point, then you may get an ending where you try to wrap up loose end involving that encounter.
In the end, the number of outcomes and scenarios are limited and if you enjoyed the game you are left wishing there was more content to the game. (I particularly want an update or DLC). However, even after 7.5 hours on record playing this game, a new event occurred last time and a new ending. And we have yet to explore any of the towns subpar endings. This is a great game to buy on sale and then whip out to play with family or friends. It has easy intuitive menu and allows for any combination of controllers or keyboards. Players can assign both of thier characters to the same device and then pass the controller between them.

In the vast sea of choose-your-own-adventure games out there, why are so few multiplayer? Why do so many forego gorgeous illustrations and lovingly hand-lettered title cards for plain black-on-white text? Why do so few have the brief playtime that makes for a perfect party game? Why do none of them have you cast the deciding vote in an election for a rat president?
The Yawhg succeeds on all of these fronts. It's also solidly, but not perfectly replayable (as you'll run into many events again on repeat plays). I only wish that there were more cooperative CYOAs like it. Developers, take note.

SO much about this game to love. High marks for content but, moreover, using interface and usability to supplement immersion.
The features are many and the interface is very intuitive; meaning I don't find myself getting lost or caught in mouse-click Hell. The subtle differences in how you use the various features (economy, diplomacy/card, building/grids) makes each aspect of the game a unique mini-game in some cases.
Other examples include:
- ability to "build" support fleets which automatically move to reinforce active fleets
- Budgeting cycle which applies any unused budget to a "welfare" bonus
- Diplomatic decisions which incorporate voting and civilian "pressure" modifiers
Nuanced features like this provide a simple yet highly effective means of adding depth, which I feel is often times hard to do in 4X games where it can quickly feel like you're simply micro-managing balance sheets and stat margins.
Graphics are reminiscent of Homeworld/Sins of a Solar Empire, though not as basic as titles like Distant Worlds where often times models are little more than blobs of pixels. Considering the mentions of "death by Dysentery" in the begining tutorial, I can assume the developers were playing the same games as I was growing up and no doubt found themselves pulling all-nighters through both Homeworld and SOS.
Furthermore, the cross-platform nature of the development gives me high hopes for a vibrant community.
Overall, the game instills a "by gamers for gamers" experience.

Going back and rewriting my review because my opinion has changed somewhat.  I had a large number of issues with this game and I still do but most of the my problems are different.
Every 4x game that I have come across has used several 'gimicks' to address some very complex issues.  In this game you have a population level that is associated with your planet level that requires you to accumulate certain numbers of tier based resources to increase.  Personally I do not believe in the arbitrary notion of a population limit or cap.  This is a gimick that almost all city/empire ect management games all use.  Instead they should be using a system of growth and decay.  In this game we see a glimse of it in how empire energy is handled.  Add in various environmental factors that and make them either both dynamic or one of the two could be static.  This sort of system woould make it so each environment would have a natural population limitation based on the point where growth equals decay.  But that point would always be in flux based on various different factors such as:  events, technologies, internal and external pressures, trade, governement, religion, resources, density and many more.  The population cap seriously inhibits the flexibility of the system and makes a requirement for a methodology to increase that cap.  I find that Star Ruler 2 has one of the worst of the arbitrary methods that I have seen in a game.
I like the idea of pressure that this game offers.  One thing that needs to be changed is how pressure is handled.  Currently pressure is a one planet at a time thing for the most part.  All it does is cause small buildings to be built 'by the planet's population'.  These buildings are basically generator's for the six empire resources and labor.  I would like to have the pressure system more associated with modifiers instead of just static bonuses.
_____________________
One thing that Star Ruler 2 does very well is having some very easy to use mod tools built right into the game.  It is rather limited mostly to effects that are already in the game which makes the creation of new features through moding rather difficult.
On another note this game does have a rather steep learning curve.  All of the games that allow you to custom design your units, in this case your space ship all add a level of complexity to the games that changes your learning curve drasticly.  What happens if you spend an hour or two designing a ship that theoretically should be better than an opposing ship by the numbers, but because you made some bad placement descisions your ship tends to die easily without much impact because either the mix of equipment is bad or your placement just did not work well.  Of course some of the enjoyment of this type of game is all about the designing of the ships.
In this game we also have a very limited selection of availible subsystem modules.  There is also a gloat of useless subsystems in the research tree.
Overall I recommend this game less as a great game and more as something that has a lot of great concepts and some interesting gameplay for many people, yet is still very far from what I would call a quality 4x game.

This is one of those games that takes on 'King's Quest' or 'Quest for Glory' mostly in style, than in gameplay.
There's only 2 buttons (interact and look) making it more of a point and click adventure.
This is done very well though. The premise of the game is interesting, the plot is rather engaging, but really slow in its buildup. The atmosphere is nice, the music is decent and the quirk of the game is playing a lute.
I personally thought it'd be more like Quest of Infamy and got rather disapointed at first. It's completely different from this game in nearly every aspect. There's no dry humour or well thought out slapstick humour... It's really more of an innocent point and click adventure, with some quirky moments.
The story is about a bard that wants to do good in the world, while being on a quest to find the queen for a contest. It's simple enough at first, then the story slowly starts to unravel. Like in most point and clicks, there are small objectives to be done to achieve your goal. Aside from one instance, the items you need to progress are, in a way, obtainable through these side quest so it's pretty hard to get off the beaten track.
However, for this one instance... It wasn't obvious. The item I needed was nearly 1 pixel, surrounded by a whole mass of pixels. Even with the walkthrough, I had trouble finding it. It also didn't help that the narrator said 'you don't need anything from here' while there clearly was something I needed from that section.
The game is short though, which is pretty much of a let down. As per standard, it's going to be episodic and who knows when the next chapter will arrive.
Despite that, I... Would recommend this game if people are into point and clicks that aren't too hard, but not too easy. I wouldn't recommend it for people that'd get a kick out of complicated games, or people that hate shorter games. I would also like to advice people that love the old King's Quest or Quest for Glory series... This is nothing like it.
The asthetic is the same, but beyond that, it's a point and click adventure.

Having played the alpha and beta versions of the game, I've been looking forward to reviewing the game now that it is finally out. As per my reviews of games I have backed, I was in on the Kickstarter for the game so if that is too biased for you, you might be happier elsewhere!
The King's Challenge is a good old fashioned adventure game where you wander over a nice large map, meeting folks, collecting a rather odd assortment of goods, and then helping others help you in your goal. You play as Finn the Bard, the son of a well known bard. You aspire to be like your father and you enter the King's Challenge to help inspire you to create a great ballad. Unlike many games, you don't have a sword, dagger or even bad breath to take on your challengers; you have a lute. You learn to play songs on the lute that help you progress through the game. A nice nod to Loom but many of the Sierra adventures get nice little nods as well. Finn is a fun character, young, ambitious and willing to learn, he survives by his wits, not his brawn.
Like their title, Quest for Infamy, The King's Challenge offers a variety of places to visit, multiple characters to interact with, lovely backgrounds and sprite work, and fine music and dialogue. Unlike QFI, the King's Challenge is a G rated game and is a game that the younger set can enjoy too.
I would describe the puzzles as "medium" in difficulty; there are plenty of clues and the more you chat with others in the game, the easier the puzzles become. The objectives are clear and quite logical and help often comes from where you would expect it to come.
The game also sets up the universe for future titles. You meet several characters who knew your father and thus you learn about the Order of the Thorne and yourself as the game goes on. The game comes to a nice conclusion but clearly sets the stage for further chapters. I, for one, am looking forward to the further adventures.

Order of the Thorne: The King’s Challenge is the first episode in a series. It follows a Bard named Finn who wants to create the ultimate adventurer ballad. He sees the opportunity to create this song by taking part in The King’s Challenge to find the missing Queen of the realm.

The dialogue in Order of the Thorne is very much in the classic style of games like King’s Quest. Everyone is polite, honorable, and happy go lucky in the way that only fantasy characters can be. Needless to say, the game takes its world very seriously during dialogue but is not without its comedy as well. It does get a bit long-winded in places but it remains nostalgic of the genre.
That being said it doesn’t have a deep conversation system and most characters are fairly one dimensional. There will be a few places where you’ll just want to skip through the dialogue to get back to the adventure.
The voiceover in-game is for lack of better words is “standard” for the genre. No one particularly stands out as believable denizens of this fantasy world. It definitely gets the job done with the eclectic cast of characters. There are far too many pleasant townies, but it does help showcase the more interesting characters like Esmerelda the Spider-Lady and Skelton the Dwarf.

I make more comparisons to King’s Quest as this game immediately begins with a contest to find the King’s wife. It’s as straight-forward as it sounds and it propels the player to stumble through Crann Naoimh and get into all sorts of shenanigans. Mainly, it’s everything you’d expect from a King’s Quest title and that seems to be the point.

Your standard point and click gameplay for an adventure title. Nothing really stands out as an advancement, beyond the Simon says style guitar playing. Finn will discover a person or object that requires an item he has discovered while wandering the land. He can combine items and use them to solve problems or complete quests only to collect more items and repeat. Fortunately, this game has a clear goal when it comes to puzzles and doesn’t allow us to wander around confused about all these items in our pants.

Nothing really stands out in the music department other than the fact that it can get a bit loud despite being on the lowest setting.

I feel like I’m making a lot of mentions of King’s Quest, but that’s exactly the nostalgic look that this title is trying to hit. Sierra would be proud to see that their visual style have been properly replicated. While it’s not exactly the most detailed of titles, it does paint a unique world filled with  slick character portraits, beautiful backgrounds, and old-school pixel animation..

Combining all the things I’ve played in this game, It’s very obvious that this title is targeting the earliest fans of the genre.. It really makes no advances to the adventure formula, and generally doesn’t take much from modern adventure titles. This is a great game for those people that saw the newest King’s Quest and harrumph’d at the lack of 2D pixels. Order of the Thorne: The King’s Challenge is definitely worth a look for adventure seekers. I’d personally catch it on sale myself, but if you’re looking for a true old-school adventure title… dive right in.

War never changes but who is telling the story does with This War of Mine, a unique game that focus on the hardships a civilian population has to go through during a conflict.
The concept of war is not new to gaming from titles that have taken player to a generation’s finest moment to the war in Afghanistan and through the eyes of Tom Clancy. However in every single one of those games the focus has been the combat and the story was always told from the perspective of the soldier. This War of Mine is a break from the typical war bravado and instead focus on the hardship of the innocent who are trapped in the crossfire.
This War of Mine instead focuses on the struggles and hardships that civilians have to overcome when trying to survive the brutality of war. Inspired by the horrors that civilians had to endure during the Siege of Sarajevo, players are responsible of managing a makeshift shelter populated by a group of civilians. Players must manage their survivors by having them strengthen the shelter while venturing out to look for supplies.
Compared to other games that focus on the struggle for survival, this presents both a strategic and emotional challenge for the player. The choices made will not only affect the shelters well being but also the characters morality while playing with one’s emotions after having made some difficult choices.

Simply put, I can play Chopin on a real piano, and maybe even on a guitar, but I can't play this game on a PC keyboard.
Even remapping the keys to fit fingers better, it's hard to feel the music and play by hearing as you would. On 1 hand it's too easy to press the wrong keys on the PC keyboard. On 2 hands the fact that there are 7 keys makes it awkward to split the keys between 2 hands (3 on left, 4 on right or the other way around). Feels very unnatural. Frustrating.
On a device without touchscreen the only options are keyboard and mouse, and it isn't a game really meant to be played on a PC keyboard or mouse. Unfortunately, there's also no option to play it on a gamepad (even though I suspect it'd still feel awkward to have 7 keys on 2 hands).
I still want to play this, as the game is graphically and musically good, but I can't recommend you buy it, unless you have some kind of piano keyboard connected to it - that can be mapped to letters such as A, S, D, F. I'm now looking for a piano-shaped PC keyboard, maybe as a DIY project... Until then, I think Frederic will have to rest in peace again.

2) Themes: This game touches on all kinds of dark, twisted, and disturbing themes, from being turned into art, psychological torture, mutilation, poisoning, dying of cancer, and the main theme of suicide, this game has it all. Everything necessary to make you go "oh my gawd..." and remain speechless throughout.
3) Replayability: There is a good amount of replayability in this game, as the longer you play into it, the more invested you absolutely will become. Decisions you make towards the end shape the entire ending in ways that will make you cry. I mean that, whole heartedly. You will cry. Even you, Mountain Man with the big biceps eating a woodchuck. Tears will fall.
4) Graphics: The graphics are amazing. The... well, everything visual is just visually striking and brilliant.
Do I recommend it?
I've never recommended another game more in my entire life.
Really.
Buy it.
You don't have to wait for a Steam sale.
You won't regret it.

As a huge fan of adventure games like the original LucasArts games, this is excellent.
As a huge fan of games that excel in horror, atmosphere, story and characters, this game goes above and beyond.
It reminds me of the first few Silent Hill games in that it uses its horror to build the atmosphere that it wants. Its emotional and tragic story hits very close to home, and its characters deep and relateable.
The gameplay itself looks awful. But when you actually play it, its inspirations become clear. Gameplay elements and even whole set pieces and characters are an homage to Maniac Mansion, IMO one of the greatest games ever made. The character's voice actors went to the school of Silent Hill 2 where they seem force, stilted and unnerved on purpose.
The story itself is about a middle aged woman, alone and surrounded by cats, who kills herself and is forced into immortality by a mysterious force. Living forever being the last thing she would ever want, she is told that she can die again once she kills "parasitic" people who during the course of the game will come for her and others. The topic and execution of suicide is a constant theme in the game. But unlike a lot of media these days, it's never done wrong once. The characters are real, depressed people who just want it to be over. Whatever it is.
During one sequence, the player must guide the main character through avoiding a breakdown. This is pretty much impossible on the first go, for obvious and intentiona reasons. A game that uses the subject of mental illness and suicide without being brash about it is incredibly rare, but it's here.
It's disturbing, saddening and most of all... Actually scary for a horror game.
The story isn't just about depression and suicide either. It's about forgiveness, moving on from the past and friendship. All of which it does better than most games have ever tried.
It looks low budget, janky and rough around the edges. Because it is. Give it a try, it will surprise you.

- you can loot citizens flats where is nobody inside houses and all civilians in streets one can count on fingers of both hands

I have put a decent amount of time into the game, but I have by no means learned all that there is to know about it.  These are my major observations thus far:
PROS:
- ALIENS! These replacements for barbarians make the game far more interesting, since they start off (mostly) neutral and come in all shapes, sizes, and strengths. Your choices may affect their behavior toward you.
- New tech web is really sexy, lets you branch out in whatever manner you see fit.
- As the game progresses, you can choose from the three Affinities (Harmony, Purity, and Supremacy) to shape your victory path and unit appearances/types.
- Spying is also more interesting. I STOLE SOMEONE'S CITY WITH A SPY!!
- You can find resource pods scattered around the map, like ruins but better. Also, excavating discoveries with your explorers can bring you interesting and helpful loot.
MEH:
- The leaders themselves. I get that this is supposed to be different from the historical civ games (read: "Beyond Earth"), but the new leaders lack the interesting quirks and backgrounds that made the previous leaders so enjoyable. Diplomacy is interesting but can still give you a headache.
- The graphics are okay, but nothing really unique compared to civ 5. Different textures, same feel.
- Stuff generally takes a lot longer to research and produce. Gives you time to enjoy each "phase" of the game, but often gets a bit boring.
- Miasma on many tiles adds a new layer of difficulty, but becomes largely obsolete late-game.
- Satellites are neat but aren't as useful as they could have been.
CONS:
- AI is still very dumb. It seems a bit better in Rising Tide, but:
- RISING TIDE IS TOO GODDAMN EXPENSIVE CONSIDERING HOW LITTLE IT ADDS. The aquatic cities are cool though.
- Cities start off as little outposts that you form, but they can take a long time to become cities and in the meantime you can't do much with them.
- Resources sometimes spawn VERY far apart, meaning that you won't often be able to have a close-knit empire.
The game really isn't as bad as a lot of people like to say, but I think it's safe to say that much of the enthusiasm was killed off by the lack of progress with AI and, more recently, the release of Civ 6.  The DLC, Rising Tide, makes the game more enjoyable, but I personally don't think it's worth $30 more on top of the original game's price.  Despite its shortcomings, Beyond Earth is a reasonably good game, though I would recommend either getting it (and the DLC) while it's on sale or bullying someone else into buying it for you.

I'm thirty-two, at the time of this review. That means I have fond memories of playing the original Gauntlet in arcades with strange old men while I was using a little stool to be able to reach the controls and see what I was doing. I also have the experience of pumping literally hundreds of dollars in quarters (one machine had me tracked at over 400 credits, and I played on about four machines between the two newer releases) into the later 3D Gauntlet arcade machines, and I'm pretty damn excited for the new Gauntlet (that looks like an old Gauntlet) that is set to come out in a couple weeks.
Hammerwatch is a love letter to Gauntlet, and it's a great one.
The graphics are simple, yet effective, and show care and attention to detail. There are various enemies of each type, and they aren't just simple pallet swaps, instead each being slightly different visually to help you easily assess the situation and pick your targets.
The game has a fair number of classes, and each one plays differently enough to make it worth your time to try them all. For instance, the Wizard starts off a close ranged powerhouse, with high risk bringing high reward. The developers even added a Priest class recently, which is more work than a lot of devs would put into an already released game.
Something the older Gauntlet games lacked that Hammerwatch brings to the table are shop keepers. You can spend the tons of loot you find to tweak your character to your liking, choosing to upgrade certain attributes and make various attacks more powerful, or increase their range. There's enough of a shortage of coin that you can't simply max out everything as you go, and will have to make some choices and calculations along the way
The co-op is great, and really fun, and since the last couple patches, the networking has been improved to remove the need for port forwarding nonsense. Again, the developers put in extra work to fix things for the community rather than just forget about their product and count your money in silence.
There are hidden areas behind false or breakable walls, with some secret levels directly referencing the levels found in the original Gauntlet.
My one real complaint with the game is that the levels aren't randomly or procedurally generated.
This has been offset a bit by the release of the editor, and integration with Steamworks. While I haven't yet spent time with the editor myself (I plan to, soon), content is being created by the community.
If you enjoy Gauntlet, this is really a no brainer for the price. Even a four-pack is only thirty dollars, and the game is much more fun when played with friends. If you're not sure, or haven't played Gauntlet, you can easily google to find a flash version of the original game and see if it is your cup of tea.

I honestly don't know how to feel about this interactive fiction. I mean, I don't hate it, but I can't honstly recommend it to anyone. There are some positives, though. It uses the wiki engine exceptionally well, and it even comes with controller support. Sadly, the writing and general feeling of Depression Quest just brings the entire experience down.
I get it, the protagonist is supposed to be depressed. As someone who's legitimately dealt with depression, it isn't a hard concept for me to grasp. The thing is, I don't get
he's depressed. He seems to be surrounded by people who legitimately care and love him, has a supposedly well paying job, and (at least in what i've seen) doesn't have the very real threat of getting thrown out of his housing situation. Even just a small amount of context would have made him a more compelling character. Without it, it just feels like "Wah, my upper/middle-class lifestyle is so hard" has made him depressed.
Beyond that, This IF visually limits your choices, without giving you any real reason as to why. Even the illusion of a choice would have made this a much more enjoyable experience. Instead, it just comes off as "If you're depressed, you won't be looking for a way out", something which I personally found offensive.
I probably would have liked Depression quest if it game me any real kind of context, and if the author would've given me the illusion of choice. It's really hard to care about a piece of Interactive fiction if you're never given a real reason to care.

You're are given multiple choices to progress, with the option someone without depression could do crossed out, such as:
You're feeling heavy from the stress of how far behind you are on your work, the thought of doing it makes your breathing short and heart heavy. Normally, you would just bunker down and do the work but, for someone suffering from Depression it just isnt an option so you have to make do with what little options are left.

This 'game' isnt for everyone and it is not for fun.
It is here to give others that do not suffer from depression, an insight into what it is really like and to give true understand of how hard it can truly be.
